->**Front Cover**<-

The volume is bound in a brown **calfskin** <term>calfskin</term><note>A high-quality, smooth leather made from the hide of young cattle, commonly used for prestigious bindings.</note>. The leather is heavily worn and pitted, showing a mottled texture from centuries of age. The gold-leaf decoration is rubbed away in several places due to handling.

### The Heraldic Device

At the center of the cover is a gold-stamped (<term>gilt</term>) coat of arms. The design features two oval shields placed side-by-side under a single large royal crown.

*   **The Left Shield:** This shield bears the heraldic symbols of **Castile and León** <note>The historic kingdoms of Spain, represented by a castle and a lion.</note>.
*   **The Right Shield:** This shield shows horizontal bars and a **patriarchal cross** <note>A cross with two horizontal bars; a symbol frequently used in Central European heraldry.</note> standing atop a triple mount, identifying it as the arms of the **Kingdom of Hungary**.

The shields are framed within an oval wreath of laurel foliage, joined at the base by a decorative floral element. The combination of these arms suggests the book belonged to a member of the **Habsburg** dynasty <note>The Habsburgs ruled over a vast collection of territories including Spain, Hungary, and the Holy Roman Empire.</note>.

### The Spine

Along the left edge, the spine is constructed with raised bands. A small, partially legible red leather label remains, bearing the title:

->**ACTS...**<-

<meta>This page continues the discussion of magical practices and the scholarly reputation of Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa, transitioning from specific divinatory methods to a critique of his sources.</meta>

Georgius Pictorius <note>A 16th-century physician and writer on the occult</note> in his *Epitome on the Species of Magic*, chapter 21:

**Coscinomancy** <term>Coscinomancy: divination using a sieve and shears</term> is that which, at the urging of a demon, teaches how to rouse a divination through a sieve to discover who might be the author of a deed, or who has lost something by theft, or who has dealt a wound, or any such thing. For they suspend a sieve by a pair of shears between the middle fingers of two bystanders, and then, having spoken six words which are understood neither by themselves nor by others, which are:
> DIES MIES IESCHET BENEDOE FET, DOUVINA, ENITEMAYS. <note>These are "words of power" or *voces magicae*; they are traditionally nonsensical formulas intended to compel spiritual forces.</note>

They drive the demon into this [the sieve] so that when the guilty party is named (for it is necessary to name all who are suspected), it immediately spins around, or rather moves slantwise toward the shears, as Erasmus proves in his *Adages* <note>original: "Adagij"</note> under the entry: *To divine by a sieve*.

Christoph Binder, Abbot of Adelberg <note>A Lutheran theologian, 1519–1596</note>:
You will <unclear>perceive</unclear> that this magic of Cornelius [Agrippa] is nothing other than a patchwork quilt of his <gloss>reading</gloss> study, if you read through the books of two most noble men of character: Johannes Reuchlin’s *Cabala* and his three books *On the Miracle-Working Word*; likewise the *Apology* of Johannes Pico, Count of Concordia, and his books *Against the Astrologers*. The names of these authors are unworthily published along with others by this stitcher-together <gloss>through harmony</gloss> <note>The writer suggests Agrippa plagiarized or "stitched together" his work from these famous scholars without proper credit</note>; with what praise and glory that is done, you shall judge for yourself. He wishes to seem excessively ingenious even in the nighttime labors of others. It is a most kind thing and full of ingenuity to confess through whom you have made progress, not as many of those whom I have touched upon have done. — Pliny in the *Preface to Vespasian*.

H. Khunrath <note>Heinrich Khunrath, a famous alchemist and physician</note> in <unclear>paterspichalt</unclear> degree VII, in his writings on page 99, says: H. C. Agrippa, in his genuine written works, was a good man and a philosophical Evangelist, because his words display a Theosophical mind, not a Necromantic one.

--- Page 9 ---
<meta>This page serves as the author's preface to the reader, establishing the philosophical and defensive tone for the work on Occult Philosophy.</meta>

# TO THE READER.
<note>original: "AD LECTOREM"</note>
## A ij
<note>This is a signature mark used by early printers to keep the pages in the correct order during binding.</note>

<image-desc>A large decorative historiated initial 'N' depicting a scholar or philosopher seated in a study, pointing to a book on a desk, with several other books visible on the floor and a window in the background.</image-desc>

I DO NOT DOUBT that the title of our book concerning *Occult Philosophy*, or *Magic*, will by its rarity entice many to read it. Among these, some of a weak mind and crooked opinion, and many who are malicious and ungrateful toward our genius, will approach. These men, in their rash ignorance, taking the name of "magic" in the worst sense, will—scarcely having seen the title—shout that we teach forbidden arts, sow the seeds of heresy, are a stumbling block to pious ears, a scandal to noble minds, and that I, being a magician, am a sorcerer <note>original: "maleficum," specifically one who performs harmful magic</note>, superstitious, and demonic. 

To these men, if I should respond that among learned men the word "magician" does not signify a sorcerer, nor one who is superstitious or demonic, but rather a wise man, a priest, and a prophet. The Sibyls <note>Ancient prophetesses of the Greek and Roman world</note> were magicians, and therefore prophesied most clearly concerning Christ. Furthermore, the Magi <note>The "Wise Men" from the East</note>, through the wonderful secrets of the world, recognized Christ the author of the world as being born, and were the very first of all to come and adore him. Thus, the name of magic itself is accepted by philosophers, praised by theologians, and not even unwelcome to the Gospel itself. 

I believe those censors of such stubborn arrogance would sooner forbid themselves the Sibyls, the holy Magi, and even the Gospel itself before they would receive the name of magic into their favor. They are so concerned for their own consciences that neither Apollo, nor all the Muses, nor an angel from heaven could rescue me from their curse. To these people, I now give this advice: let them not read our writings, nor understand them, nor remember them; for they are harmful, they are poisonous. The gate of Acheron <note>A river in the underworld; here meaning the entrance to Hell</note> is in this book; it speaks stones—let them beware lest it knock out their brains. 

But you, who come to read with an unbiased mind, if you apply as much prudent discretion as bees do when gathering honey, then read in safety. For I think you will receive no small amount of utility and a great deal of pleasure. If you find anything that does not please you, set it aside and do not use it; for I do not approve those things for you, but merely relate them. Do not, however, reject the rest on that account; for it happens to those inspecting the volumes of physicians that they read of poisons at the same time as antidotes and medicines. 

I confess, moreover, that magic itself teaches many superfluous things and curious wonders intended for ostentation; leave these aside as vain, yet do not remain ignorant of their causes. But those things which can be done for the utility of men—to avert evil events, to destroy sorcery, to cure diseases, to drive away phantoms, and to preserve the soundness of life, honor, and fortune, without offense to God or injury to religion—who would not judge those things to be as useful as they are necessary? But because I have warned you that I have written many things by relating them rather than by affirming them (for it seemed necessary to do so so that we might omit fewer things), we have furthermore followed many of the opinions of the Platonists and other Gentile <note>Non-Christian or Pagan</note> philosophers where they suggested an argument for our method of writing. Therefore, if I have erred anywhere, or if anything has been said too freely...

<summary>In this preface, the author defends the study of "Magic" by distinguishing it from sorcery and aligning it with ancient wisdom and Christian history. He warns hostile readers to stay away while encouraging the fair-minded to extract useful knowledge like bees gathering honey.</summary>
<keywords>Occult Philosophy, Magic, Magi, Sibyls, Platonism, defense of magic, intellectual history</keywords>

--- Page 10 ---
<meta>This page serves as the author's preface or "Apology" to the reader, explaining the origins of the work and its relationship to his later, more skeptical writings.</meta>

<sig>A</sig>

Forgive my youth, for I composed this work when I was less than a young man, so that I might excuse myself and say: "When I was a child, I spoke as a child, I understood as a child; but when I became a man, I put away childish things" <note>original: "dum eram paruulus... euacuaui quæ erāt paruuli" — a reference to 1 Corinthians 13:11</note>. Indeed, in my book *On the Vanity and Uncertainty of the Sciences* <note>original: "de Vanitate ac incertitudine Scientiarum" — Agrippa's later work where he famously attacked all human knowledge, including the magic he defends here</note>, I retracted much of this book. But here you might perhaps rebuke me again, saying: "Behold, you wrote this as a youth and retracted it as an old man; why then have you published it?" I confess that I began to write these books when I was very young, yet with the hope of eventually sending them out more corrected and enriched; for that reason, I first offered them for correction to Johannes Trithemius <note>A famous Benedictine abbot and polymath (1462–1516) who was a mentor to Agrippa in the study of "secret things" or the occult</note>, Abbot of Würzburg and formerly of Sponheim, a man most industrious in secret matters.

It happened afterwards, however, that the work was intercepted before I had put the finishing touches to it. Because the copies were corrupted, it was circulated in a mutilated and unpolished state, flying through the hands of many in Italy, France, and Germany. Already, some—I know not whether through impatience or impudence—wished to expose this unformed work to the printing press. Struck by this one danger, I decided to publish it myself, thinking there would be less peril if these books went forth from my own hand a little more refined, rather than being made public by the hands of others as mangled and disordered fragments. Furthermore, I deemed it no sin if I did not allow this specimen of my youth to perish. 

We have, however, added several chapters and inserted many things which it seemed negligent to omit—which the curious reader will easily be able to detect from the inequality of the prose style itself. For we did not wish to
-> renew the entire work or (as they say) re-weave the entire web, <-
-> but only to correct it a little and <-
-> pour in some brilliance. <-
-> Therefore, I ask you again now, <-
-> honest reader, not to judge <-
-> these books by the current <-
-> time of their publication, but <-
-> to grant pardon to a curious <-
-> youth, if by chance you <-
-> find anything in them <-
-> other than what <-
-> might please <-
-> you. <-

<summary>Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa addresses the reader, explaining that he wrote this work on magic in his youth and is only publishing it now to prevent unauthorized, corrupted versions from being printed.</summary>

<meta>Continuity: The previous page concluded the author's "Apology" to the reader, where Agrippa explained that although he had once retracted his interest in magic in a later book, he is now publishing a corrected version of his early work on "Occult Philosophy" to prevent poor-quality, unauthorized versions from circulating. This page begins the formal dedication of the work to his patron, Hermann von Wied.</meta>

# TO THE MOST REVEREND FATHER IN CHRIST,
## and Most Illustrious Prince, Hermann, of the Counts of Wied, by the grace of God Archbishop of the Holy Church of Cologne, Prince-Elector of the Holy Roman Empire, and Arch-Chancellor throughout Italy, Duke of Westphalia and Angria, etc. Legate born of the Most Holy Roman Church, and Vicar General in matters pontifical, from Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa of Nettesheim.

->Sends Greeting<-

<image-desc>Decorative historiated woodcut initial 'E' depicting a seated man, possibly a scholar or figure of authority, in an outdoor setting with foliage in the background, contained within a square frame with cross-hatched shading.</image-desc>
SUCH IS the celebrity of your illustrious fame, most reverend and illustrious Prince, such the greatness of your virtues and the splendor of your learning, your frequent exercise in the finest literature, your grave speech joined with solid prudence, your elegant readiness in speaking, your knowledge of many things, your constant religion, and your most praiseworthy character—qualities with which you are endowed far beyond the common habit of others. I am silent regarding the ancient images of your eminent nobility <note>original: "nobilitatis imagines" — a reference to the Roman custom of displaying wax masks of ancestors to prove noble lineage</note>, the treasures of wealth both old and new, the breadth of your domain, and the miters <note>The ceremonial headdress of a bishop, representing his high ecclesiastical office</note> of your sacred dignities, the excellence of which you surpass even with the decent form and strength of your body. 

Yet, though all these things are great, I consider you far greater than all of them because of those heroic and super-illustrious virtues of yours. By these, you have surely brought it about that the more learned and the more devoted to virtue a person is, the more they desire to find a place in your goodwill. For this reason, I too decided that I must seek that honor of yours, but in the manner of the Parthians—that is to say, not without a gift <note>original: "Parthorum more... non ſine munere" — the Parthians were famously known for the custom of never visiting a ruler or superior without offering a present</note>. Indeed, we see this custom of greeting a Prince has been derived from the centuries of the ancients into our own times, and observed even until now. 

And when I saw other men, who are excellently learned, adorning you with the beautiful and great gifts of their teachings, I did not want to be the only one who, like a deserter of your service and veneration, would dare to approach your Greatness with empty hands. While I was thinking and looking around in my library for what gift I might bestow upon so distinguished a Prince, behold, among my hidden things, there suddenly offered themselves the books *On Occult Philosophy, or On Magic*. I had begun to write these as a very young man, and for many years now, as if I had forgotten them, I had left them set aside. Soon, out of veneration for your Greatness, I hastened to complete them, as if to fulfill a vow. 

Truly, I persuaded myself that I could give you nothing more pleasing than a new work on an ancient and most abstruse doctrine—a work, I say, of my curious youth, but containing the doctrine of antiquity, which I dare say no one until now has attempted to restore. Nevertheless, these works of ours are not dedicated to you because they are worthy, but so that they might open a path for me to your goodwill. I ask, therefore, if it is not improper, that they might have some excuse before you. I offer all my prayers to you, that if these studies of my youth come into public notice under the auspices of your Greatness, and with envy put to flight by the right of eternity, they...

<sig>A iii</sig>

He explains that he has finally completed this work from his youth specifically to honor the Archbishop's patronage.</summary>

<meta>Continuity: This page completes the dedication to Archbishop Hermann von Wied. Agrippa explains that while the work was drafted in his youth, he has revised and expanded it in his maturity. This is followed by a "Table of Retractions," where Agrippa cross-references this book with his later work, "On the Vanity and Uncertainty of Arts and Sciences," in which he had previously criticized his own interest in magic.</meta>

...labors <note>The Latin text begins mid-word with "lorum," likely the end of "laborum" (labors) or "studiorum" (studies) from the preceding page.</note> might remain in our memory for the benefit of a good conscience, since many things in them appeared to me, even now in my older age, to be both very useful and necessary to be known. You have, therefore, a work not only of my youth, but also of my present age; for I have corrected many errors of the youthful work, inserted much in several places, and expanded it with many chapters—changes which can be easily detected by the inequality of the prose style itself. Thus, you will know that I will be devoted to your service for my entire life.

->Farewell, most happy Prince of happy Cologne.<-
->From Mechelen.<-
->The year 1531.<-
->In the month of January.<-

How Mages gather virtues from the triple world <note>Agrippa divides the universe into three levels: the Elemental (natural), Celestial (mathematical/astrological), and Intellectual (angelic/divine). This first book deals with the Elemental world.</note> will be shown in these three books. Chapter 1. folio 1
What Magic is, what its parts are, and what kind of person a professor of Magic ought to be. Ch. 2. the same
On the four elements, their qualities, and their mixtures with one another. Ch. 3. 2
On the threefold reasoning of the elements to be considered. Ch. 4. the same
On the wonderful natures of fire and earth. Ch. 5. 3
On the admirable natures of water, air, and the winds. Ch. 6. 4
On the types of compound things, how they relate to the elements, and what the elements themselves have in common with the soul, senses, and character. Ch. 7. 6
How the elements are in the heavens, in the stars, in demons <note>original: "dæmonibus" — in this context, these are often neutral "spirits" or mediating entities rather than purely evil beings</note>, in angels, and finally in God himself. Ch. 8. 6
On the virtues of natural things depending most closely on the elements. Ch. 9. 7
On the occult virtues of things. <note>Occult virtues are "hidden" powers that cannot be explained by simple physical qualities like heat or cold—for example, a magnet attracting iron.</note> Ch. 10. 8
How occult virtues are infused into the species of things from the Ideas, through the reasoning of the World Soul and the rays of the stars; and which things abound most in this virtue. Ch. 11. 8
How different virtues flow into different individuals, even of the same species. Ch. 12. 9
From where the occult virtues of things proceed. 13. the same
On the Spirit of the World—what it is, and that it is the bond of occult virtues. Ch. 14. 10
How we ought to investigate and test the virtues of things through the path taken from similarity. Ch. 15. 11
How the operations of different virtues are transferred from one thing to another and are mutually communicated to one another. Ch. 16. 12
How the virtues of things are to be investigated and tested through strife and friendship. <note>The concept that certain things in nature naturally repel (strife) or attract (friendship) each other.</note> Ch. 17. the same

## HENRY CORNELIUS AGRIPPA

¶ It shall be shown in these three books how Mages collect virtues from the triple world. Chapter I.

<margin>The triple world.</margin>
SINCE THE WORLD IS TRIPLE—Elemental, Celestial, and Intellectual—and every inferior world is governed by its superior and receives the influence of its powers, so that the Archetype <note>The "Archetype" refers to the divine original pattern or the mind of God from which all creation is modeled.</note> and Supreme Creator himself, through angels, heavens, stars, elements, animals, plants, metals, and stones, pours the virtues of his omnipotence into us, for whose service he founded and created all these things: Mages do not think it unreasonable that we can ascend by these same steps, through each individual world, to that same Archetypal world, the creator of all things and the 
<margin>The First Cause.</margin>
First Cause, from whom all things are and from whom all things proceed. They believe we can not only enjoy these virtues which pre-exist in the more noble things, but also attract other new ones from above. Hence, they hunt for the powers of the elemental world through various mixtures of natural things via medicine and natural philosophy; next, they connect celestial virtues to those things by the rays and influences of the celestial world, according to the rules of astrologers and the disciplines of mathematicians; furthermore, they corroborate and confirm all these things by the powers of various intelligences <note>In this context, "intelligences" refers to spiritual or angelic beings that govern the celestial spheres.</note> through the sacred ceremonies of religions. I shall now attempt to hand down the order and process of all these things in these three books: of which the first contains Natural Magic, the second Celestial, and the third Ceremonial. But I do not know if I—a man of lesser genius and learning—am fully worthy of pardon for having so freely undertaken such a difficult, arduous, and intricate business in my very youth. For this reason, regarding whatever has been said by me here or will be said hereafter, I wish for no one to agree more than I myself do, except insofar as these things have not been rejected by the Catholic Church and the assembly of the faithful.

# ON OCCULT PHILOSOPHY

<margin>The triple division of philosophy: Physics and its contents.</margin>
...mysteries, encompasses the deepest contemplation of the most secret things: their nature, power, quality, substance, and virtue, as well as a knowledge of the whole of nature. It instructs us in how things differ from one another and how they agree, producing its wonderful effects by uniting the virtues of things through their mutual application, and by "marrying" <note>Agrippa uses the metaphor of marriage (maritans) to describe the magical act of linking earthly materials to their corresponding heavenly powers.</note> the lower things to the gifts and virtues of the higher. This is the most perfect and supreme science, this higher and holier philosophy—in short, the absolute perfection of all noble philosophy. For since all systematic philosophy is divided into Physics, Mathematics, and Theology: Physics <note>In this context, "Physics" refers to Natural Philosophy, the study of the physical world and its laws.</note> teaches the nature of those things which are in the world, investigating and searching out their causes, effects, times, places, modes, events, entireties, and parts.

<margin>Theology, and what is contained within it.</margin>
Theology, however, teaches what God is, what the mind is, what intelligence is, what an angel is, and finally what a demon <note>In this context, "demon" (daimon) refers to a spirit or intermediary being, not necessarily a malevolent one.</note> is; it teaches of the soul, of religion, of sacred institutions, rites, temples, observations, and sacred mysteries. It also instructs on faith, miracles, the power of words and figures, secret operations, and the mysteries of seals. As Apuleius says, it teaches us to "rightly know and master the laws of ceremonies, the divine law of sacred things, and the rights of religions." But now I will collect myself. Magic itself embraces, unites, and activates these three most powerful faculties; therefore, it was rightly held by the ancients as the highest and holiest science. This science is found illustrated by the weightiest authors and most famous writers, among whom Zamolxis and Zoroaster shone so brightly that they were believed by many to be the inventors of this science. <margin>Followers of Theology.</margin> Following in their footsteps were Abaris the Hyperborean, Charmondas, Damigeron, Eudoxus, and Hermippus. Other more famous high priests stood forth, such as Trismegistus <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary "Thrice-Great" Egyptian sage to whom many occult texts were attributed.</note>, Mercury, Porphyry, Iamblichus, Plotinus, Proclus, Dardanus, Orpheus the Thracian, Gog the Greek, Germa the Babylonian, and Apollonius of Tyana. Osthanes also wrote excellently on this art; his books, unearthed from a tomb, Democritus of Abdera illustrated with his commentaries. <margin>Pliny, Natural History, book 32, chapter 1.</margin> Furthermore, Pythagoras, Empedocles, Democritus, Plato, and many of the most noble philosophers sailed away to learn this art; having returned, they preached it with the utmost holiness and held it among their secrets. Indeed, we know for certain that Pythagoras and Plato, in order to learn it, approached the priests of Memphis and traveled through almost all of Syria, Egypt, Judea, and the schools of the Chaldeans, so that the holiest monuments of Magic might not be hidden from them and they might be imbued with divine things. Therefore, whoever now desires to study this faculty, if they are not learned in <margin>Physics and its contents.</margin> Physics (in which the qualities of things are declared, and in which the hidden properties of every being are revealed), and if they are not a practitioner of Mathematics (and in the aspects and figures of the stars, upon which the sublime virtue and property of every thing depends), and if they are not learned in <margin>What Theology is.</margin> Theology (where the immaterial substances are revealed, which dispense and administer all things), they will not be able to understand the rationality of Magic. For no work stands perfected by Magic itself, nor is there any truly magical work, that does not embrace these three faculties.

# ON OCCULT PHILOSOPHY.

<margin>Transmutation of the elements.</margin>
of bodily things: fire, earth, water, and air. Out of these, all the elements in these lower regions are composed; this happens not merely by piling them together, but through their transformation and union. Likewise, when things perish, they are resolved back into these elements. None of the elements we perceive with our senses are pure; they are mixed to a greater or lesser degree and can be transformed into one another. For example, earth that is moistened and dissolved becomes water; water that is thickened and condensed becomes earth. When evaporated by heat, water passes into air, and when air is intensely heated, it passes into fire. When fire is extinguished, it returns to air, and when cooled after being scorched, it becomes earth, or stone, or sulfur—as is clearly seen in the case of lightning.

<margin>The immutability of the earth according to Plato.</margin>
Plato, however, believes that the earth is entirely unchangeable, while the other elements are transformed both into earth and into one another. Thus, he argues that the earth is divided by the subtler elements—not transformed, but dissolved or mixed into the substances that dissolve it—and then returns to its original state. Furthermore, each of the elements has two specific qualities: it retains the first quality as its own and shares the second as a middle ground with the next element in the sequence.

<margin>
Nature of Fire
Nature of Earth
Nature of Water
Nature of Air
</margin>
For fire is hot and dry; earth is dry and cold; water is cold and moist; and air is moist and hot. In this way, because of these two contrary qualities, the elements are opposites: fire is the opposite of water, and earth is the opposite of air. There is another way in which the elements are opposed: some are heavy, like earth and water, while others are light, like air and fire. For this reason, the Stoics <note>A school of ancient Greek philosophy that taught that the universe is a rational, organized whole; they categorized elements by their "activity" or "passivity."</note> called the former "passive" and the latter "active."

<margin>
Quality of Fire
Quality of Earth
Quality of Air
Quality of Water
</margin>
Furthermore, Plato distinguishes them in another way, assigning three qualities to each: to fire, he gives sharpness, thinness, and motion; to earth, bluntness, density, and rest. According to these qualities, fire and earth are opposites. The other elements borrow their qualities from these, so that air receives two qualities of fire (thinness and motion) and one of earth (bluntness). Conversely, water receives two qualities of earth (darkness <note>The Latin here uses *obscuritatem* (darkness/obscurity), likely referring to its density and lack of transparency compared to air/fire.</note> and density) and one of fire (motion). But fire is twice as thin as air, three times more mobile, and four times sharper. Air is twice as sharp as water, three times thinner, and four times more mobile. Likewise, water is twice as sharp as earth, three times thinner, and four times more mobile. Just as fire relates to air, so air relates to water, and water to earth; and conversely, as earth is to water, so water is to air, and air to fire. This is the root and foundation of all bodies, natures, powers, and wonderful works. Whoever knows these qualities of the elements and their mixtures will easily perform marvelous and stupendous works and will be perfected in Natural Magic <note>term: "Natural Magic" (original: *Magia naturalis*). This refers to the practice of using the inherent physical and "occult" (hidden) properties of natural substances—like the heat of fire or the density of earth—to produce effects, without involving spirits or demons.</note>.

...twelvefold: and by proceeding through the sevenfold into the tenfold, let a progress be made toward the supreme unity, upon which all power and wondrous operation depend.

<margin>Elements of the first order.</margin> In the first order, then, the elements are pure; they are neither composed nor changed, nor do they undergo mixing, but they are incorruptible. It is not *from* them, but *through* them that the powers of all natural things are brought into effect. No one can explain their virtues, because they can do all things in all things. He who is ignorant of these can reach no operation of wondrous effects.

<margin>Elements of the second order.</margin> The elements of the second order are composed, manifold, varied, and impure; yet they are reducible by art to pure simplicity. Once they have returned to their simplicity, their virtue gives completion to all hidden operations and the operations of nature. These are the foundation of all natural Magic <note>Natural Magic refers to the study and use of the inherent physical and sympathetic properties of the material world, distinct from ceremonial or demonic magic.</note>.

<margin>Elements of the third order.</margin> The elements of the third order are not elements in and of themselves at first, but are thrice-composed <note>original: "decomposita," referring to complex mixtures far removed from the primary state</note>, varied, manifold, and changeable among one another. They are the infallible medium, and therefore are called the "middle nature" or the "soul of the middle nature." There are very few who understand their deep mysteries. Within them, through certain numbers, degrees, and orders, is the completion of every effect in any thing—be it natural, celestial, or super-celestial. They are wondrous and full of mysteries, which can operate in both natural and divine Magic. For through them descend the bindings and loosings <note>Techniques used to restrain or release spiritual or physical forces; original: "ligationes etiam solutiones."</note> and transmutations of all things, the knowledge and prediction of the future, even the driving out of evil demons and the conciliation of good spirits. Therefore, without these three kinds of elements and the knowledge of them, let no one trust that he can work anything in the hidden sciences of Magic and nature. However, whoever knows how to reduce these into those—the impure into the pure, the manifold into the simple—and knows how to discern their nature, virtue, and power in number, degrees, and order, without dividing the substance: such a person will easily obtain the knowledge and perfect operation of all natural and celestial secrets.

...[compre]hended, needing nothing else, secretly growing from itself, and manifesting its own greatness to the materials it receives; active, powerful, and invisibly present to all things at once, it does not allow itself to be ignored. Fire is an immense and rogue portion of the nature of things (as Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, the Roman author of Natural History, who wrote extensively on the properties of the physical world.</note> says), and it is doubtful whether it consumes more or brings forth more. Fire itself is one, and it penetrates almost everything, as the Pythagoreans <note>Followers of Pythagoras who believed that fire was a central, animating force in the universe.</note> say. But in heaven it is expanded and illuminating; in hell it is constricted, dark, and tormenting; and in the middle region <note>The terrestrial world where humans dwell, situated between the heavens and the underworld.</note> it partakes of both. Thus fire is one in itself, but manifold in the receiver, and distributed into different types in different things, as Cleanthes <note>A Stoic philosopher who viewed the universe as a living being animated by fire.</note> testifies in the works of Cicero. Thus there is this external fire which we use; there is fire in stones <margin>Fire of stones</margin>, which is struck out by the blow of steel; there is fire in the earth <margin>Fire is in the earth, in water, and in air.</margin>, which smokes when dug up; there is fire in the waters, which warms springs and wells; there is fire in the air, which we often see grow hot; and every animal and all living and growing things are nourished by heat; indeed, everything that lives does so because of the fire enclosed within it. <margin>Celestial fire. Therefore, the celestial and bright fire puts to flight dark demons; and even this wood-fire of ours does the same <margin>Book 2, Chapter 32.</margin>, insofar as it holds the image and vehicle **of that superior light.** Indeed, it reflects Him who says, **"I am the light of the world,"** <margin>True fire.</margin> <note>original: "Ego sum lux mundi"</note> who is the true fire, the **"Father of lights,"** <note>original: "pater luminum"</note> from whom every good gift comes. He sends out the splendor of his fire, communicating it first to the sun and other celestial bodies, and through these as intermediate instruments, he flows into this fire of ours. Just as the demons of darkness are stronger in the darkness itself, so the good demons <margin>Who are good demons.</margin>—who are angels of light—receive an increase of strength from light; not only from divine, solar, and celestial light, but even from the fire that is among us. For this reason, the first and most wise founders of religions and ceremonies decreed that prayers, psalm-singing, and all sacred rites should only be performed with lights burning. <margin>Why lights in sacred rites.</margin> Hence that symbol of Pythagoras: "Do not speak of God without a light." # BOOK ONE.

[Being fertilized] by the other elements and the heavens, the Earth is generative of all things from itself. She is the receiver of all fecundities and, like the first parent, is the producer of all sprouts, the center, the foundation, and the mother of all. Take from her whatever is secret, washed, purified, and refined; if you leave it for a time in the open air, it will soon be fertilized and pregnant with celestial powers. From itself, it will produce plants, worms, and living creatures; it will produce small stones and the bright sparks of metals. In the Earth are the greatest secrets, especially when it has been purified by the craft of fire and reduced to its proper simplicity by washing. <margin>Adamic Earth</margin> This is the first material of our creation <note>Often called "Adamic Earth," referring to the red clay or pure earth from which the first human was said to be formed.</note> and the truest medicine for our restoration and preservation.

### ¶ On the wonderful natures of water, air, and winds. Chap. VI.

The remaining two elements, namely water and air, are of no less power; nor does nature cease to perform miracles within them. For there is such a great necessity for water that without it no animal can live: no herb, nor any plant whatsoever, can sprout without the moistening of water. In water resides the seed-like virtue of all things; <margin>The seed of all animals.</margin> first of all for animals, whose seed is clearly watery. Furthermore, although the seeds of shrubs and herbs are earthy, they must nevertheless be dissolved by water if they are to be fertile, whether that happens by the moisture absorbed from the earth, or by dew, or rain, or by water added with intention. Indeed, only Earth and Water are described by Moses <note>A reference to the Book of Genesis in the Bible, where the creation of life from the waters and the dust of the ground is detailed.</note> as producing a living soul. However, he attributes a double production to water: specifically, those things swimming in the waters and those flying in the air above the earth. That the production of terrestrial things is also partly due to water is testified by the same Scripture, saying that after creation, the bushes and plants had not sprouted because God had not rained upon the earth. So great is the power of this element that even spiritual regeneration cannot occur without water, as Christ himself testified to Nicodemus <note>Referring to the Gospel of John 3:5: "Except a man be born of water and of the Spirit, he cannot enter into the kingdom of God."</note>. <margin>The power of rain.</margin> Its power is also greatest in religion, in atonement and purification, and its necessity is no less than that of fire. Its benefits are infinite and its use manifold, and all things consist of its power, as it possesses the strength to generate, nourish, and increase. Hence, Thales of Miletus <note>An early Greek philosopher (c. 624–548 BCE) who taught that water was the fundamental substance of the universe.</note> and Hesiod <note>An ancient Greek poet who wrote the *Theogony*, describing the origins of the gods and the world.</note> established water as the beginning of all things, and said it was the oldest and most powerful of the elements, since it rules over all the others. For, as Pliny says, waters devour the lands; they kill flames; they climb to the heights and, by the covering of clouds, they claim the sky for themselves; and these same waters, falling, become the cause of all things growing from the earth. Countless are the miracles of water described by Pliny, Solinus, and many historians; and Ovid <note>The Roman poet Ovid, whose poem *Metamorphoses* describes many such transformations and natural wonders.</note> mentions the miraculous virtue of waters in these verses:

That can change not only bodies but also minds.
Who has not heard of the obscene waves of Salmacis? <note>According to myth, the waters of Salmacis in Caria made men effeminate or merged them with the nymph of the spring.</note>
And the Ethiopian lakes? If any man drinks of them, 
He either goes mad or falls into a strange, heavy sleep.
Whoever quenches his thirst at the Clitorian fountain 
Flees from wine, and, being now abstinent, rejoices in pure water.
Conversely, the Lyncestian river flows with an opposite effect: 
Whoever draws too much into his throat 
Staggers no differently than if he had drunk pure wine.
There is a lake in Arcadia which the ancients called Pheneus, 
Suspect for its ambiguous waters; fear them at night, 
For they are harmful if drunk at night, but are drunk without harm by day.

<margin>The nature of the Sabbath River.</margin>
Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus, a first-century Roman-Jewish historian.</note> reports, moreover, the marvelous nature of a certain river between Arcea and Raphanea, cities of Syria: which, while it flows with a full bed through the entire Sabbath, soon fails as if the springs were blocked, providing a dry crossing for six whole days; then on the seventh day, by unknown causes of nature, it returns to its former abundance of water. For this reason, the inhabitants called it the "Sabbathian," because of the <margin>A day sacred to the Jews.</margin> seventh day, which is sacred to the Jews. The Gospel also testifies to us concerning the "Probatica" pool <note>The Pool of Bethesda or the Sheep Pool in Jerusalem.</note>, into which—after the water was stirred by an angel—whoever first descended was freed from whatever sickness he suffered. The same power and force is read to have belonged to the fountain of the Ionid Nymphs, which stood in the territory of Elis near the village of Heraclea by the river Cytheron: into which whoever descended with a diseased body would come out healthy and whole, with every physical defect driven away. Pausanias <note>A second-century Greek traveler and geographer.</note> relates that on Mount Lycaeus in Arcadia there is a fountain called Hagno <note>transcribed in OCR as "Agriae".</note>, <margin>Wonders of the fountain of Hagno.</margin> to which, whenever the dryness of the region threatened the destruction of crops, the priest of Lycaean Jupiter would go. After sacrificing victims and venerating the sacred waters with holy prayers, holding an oak branch in his hand, he would lower it to the surface of the sacred fountain. Then, the waters being stirred, a vapor would rise from there into the air and thicken into clouds; as the mists gathered, the whole sky was covered with clouds, which shortly after dissolved into rain and healthfully irrigated the entire region. Truly, concerning the miracles of waters, besides many other authors, Rufus of Ephesus <note>A famous physician of the 1st/2nd century AD.</note> wrote wonderful things, found in no other author that I know. It remains now to speak of the Air.

<margin>What Air is.</margin>
Air is the vital spirit <note>original: "spiritus vitalis".</note>, permeating all beings, providing life and consistency to all, binding, moving, and filling all things. Hence the doctors of the Hebrews <note>Likely referring to Kabbalistic traditions where Air is seen as the mediating "Spirit" between the elements.</note> do not count it among the elements, but as a medium and glue...

# BOOK ONE.

...continuous, joining diverse things together at once; and they possess it like a resounding spirit of the world-instrument. For it [the Air] most closely receives within itself the influx of all celestial things and communicates them to the other elements as well as to individual mixed things. No less also does it receive and retain within itself the forms <note>original: "species" — in this context, "species" refers to the outward forms or mental images of things that emanate from them.</note> of all things, whether natural or artificial, and of any speeches whatsoever, like a kind of divine mirror. Carrying these forms with it and entering the bodies of men and animals through the pores, impressing them both in sleep and in waking, it provides the matter for various wondrous dreams, presages, and omens. Hence they say it also happens that one passing a place where a man has been killed, or where a fresh corpse is hidden, is moved by fear and dread: because the air in that place is full of the horrible forms of the homicide; when it is inhaled, it affects and disturbs the human spirit with similar forms, from which fear happens to follow. For everything <margin>The causes of dreams.</margin> impressing itself suddenly causes nature to be stunned. Hence many philosophers have judged the air to be the cause of dreams and of many other impressions on the soul, through the carrying of "idols" <note>original: "idolorum" — here meaning mental images or "simulacra" that things cast off into the air, not religious icons.</note>, or likenesses, or forms, which are shed from things and words and multiplied in the air itself, until they reach the senses, and finally the imagination and the soul of the receiver—namely, that soul which, free from cares and unimpeded, waits to meet such forms and is shaped by them. For these forms of things, although by their own nature they are carried to the senses of men and animals, can nevertheless acquire some impression from heaven while they are in the air, by which, combined with the aptitude and disposition of the receiver, they are carried more to the senses of one person than another. And from this it is naturally possible, and far from all superstition, with no other spirit mediating, for one man to be able to communicate the concept of his mind to another man at any distance, however long or unknown, and in his dwelling, in a very short time; and if the time in which this happens cannot be precisely measured, yet it is absolutely necessary that it happens within twenty-four hours. I know how to do this, and have done it quite often. The Abbot Trithemius <note>Johannes Trithemius (1462–1516), a German abbot and polymath famous for his writings on cryptography and hidden communication.</note> also knew and formerly did the same. Plotinus <note>A major Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 204–270 AD) who wrote on the soul and perception.</note> proves and teaches how certain "idols"—not only spiritual but also natural—flow out from things (for instance, through a certain influx of bodies from bodies) and grow strong in the air itself, and then offer and show themselves to us through light, motion, sight, and even other senses, and sometimes work wonders in us. And we see how, when the south wind blows, the air thickens into thin clouds, in which—as if in a mirror—far distant images of castles, mountains, horses, and men, and other things are reflected, which soon vanish as the clouds depart. And in the *Meteorology*, Aristotle <note>The famous Greek philosopher; his *Meteorologica* deals with earth sciences and atmospheric phenomena.</note> reveals that the rainbow is conceived in a cloud of air through a certain similarity to a mirror. And Albertus <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a medieval scholar who wrote extensively on the natural sciences.</note> says that the effigies of bodies can easily be shaped by the power of nature in moist air, in the same way that the images of things exist in the things themselves. # ON OCCULT PHILOSOPHY.

...reaching the senses. This has been known to happen from a weakness of sight, such that the nearby air became like a mirror for the viewer, and the visual ray was reflected back upon itself because it could not penetrate further. Thus, wherever the person went, they believed their own image <note>original: "idolum suum" — a reflected form or phantom image</note> was walking before them face-to-face. Similarly, through the craft of certain mirrors, images that we choose can be projected into the air, even from a distance, outside of the mirrors themselves. When unlearned men see these, they think they are seeing demons or the shades of souls, when in fact they are nothing but certain likenesses related to the objects themselves and entirely devoid of life. It is also well known that if someone is in a dark place devoid of all light—except for where a sunbeam might enter through a very small hole—and a white paper or a flat mirror is placed in its path, everything that is happening outside in the sunlight will be seen upon it. There is also another even more marvelous trick <note>original: "prestigium" — often used for a feat of illusion or magic</note> where, by painting images or writing letters with a certain skill, one faces them toward the rays of the full moon on a clear night. Their likenesses, being multiplied in the air and carried upward, are reflected back together with the moon's rays; another person, who is aware of the matter, can then see, read, and recognize the message at a great distance upon the very disk or circle of the moon.

<margin>Letters legible by night.</margin>
This is a most useful craft for sending secret messages to besieged towns and cities; it was practiced long ago by Pythagoras, and today it is still known to some, including myself. All these things, and many more even greater, are founded in the very nature of the air, and find their explanations in mathematics and optics. And just as these likenesses are reflected to the sight, so too are they sometimes reflected to the hearing, as is clearly seen in an echo. But there are even more hidden crafts by which one can hear and understand what another is saying or whispering in secret, even across a vast distance.

<margin>Where do winds come from?</margin>
Winds also come from the element of air; for they are nothing other than air in motion and stirred up. There are four principal winds blowing from the four quarters of the heavens: namely Notus from the south, Boreas from the north, Zephyrus from the west, and from the east, Apeliotes or Eurus. Pontanus <note>Giovanni Gioviano Pontano (1426–1503), an Italian humanist and poet.</note> encompassed these in two short verses, saying:

> -> From high Olympus Boreas blows, and Notus from the low. <-
> -> Zephyrus settles in the west, while Eurus comes from the east. <-

<margin>The principal winds. Notus.</margin>
Notus is the southern wind; it is cloudy, moist, hot, and sickly, and Jerome <note>St. Jerome, the Church Father, known for his Latin translation of the Bible.</note> calls it the "cup-bearer of rains." Ovid describes it thus:

> Notus flies out on soaking wings,
> His terrible face veiled in pitch-black gloom;
> His beard is heavy with rain-clouds, water flows from his white hair,
> Mists sit upon his brow, and his feathers and chest drip with dew.

<margin>Boreas.</margin>
Boreas, however, is the opposite of Notus; it is the northern wind, violent and loud. It clears the air by scattering the clouds and binds the water with frost. Ovid introduces it speaking of itself in this way:

> -> Force is fit for me; with it I drive away the dismal clouds, <-

### Concerning the kinds of compound things, how they relate to the elements, and what the elements themselves have in common with the soul, the senses, and character. Chapter VII.

After the four simple elements, there follow closely the four kinds of perfect compound things derived from them, which are stones, metals, plants, and animals. And although in the generation of each one all elements come together in the composition, nevertheless each follows and imitates one principal element.

<margin>The nature of stones.</margin>
For all stones are of the Earth; in nature they are heavy and descend, and are so hardened by dryness that they cannot be melted.

<margin>The nature of metals.</margin>
Metals, however, are of Water and are liquefiable; and what the physicists confess, the alchemists <note>original: "alchimici"</note> prove by experience, that they are generated from viscous water or from watery quicksilver <note>original: "argentoviuo" — mercury</note>.

<margin>The nature of plants.</margin>
Plants agree with the Air in such a way that they do not sprout or grow together except under the open sky. So it is for all animals:
*A fiery vigor is in them and a heavenly origin.* <note>A famous line from Virgil’s Aeneid describing the life-force.</note>

<margin>The nature of animals.</margin>
Fire is so kindred to them that once it is extinguished, all life soon fails. Again, each of these kinds is distinct within itself through the grades of the elements.

<margin>The difference of stones.</margin>
For among stones, those are called primarily earthy which are opaque and heavier; those are watery which are transparent and which are hardened from water, such as crystal, beryl, and pearls in shells. There are also airy ones, which float on water and are spongy, such as the "sponge-stone" <note>original: "lapis spongię" — likely a calcareous deposit</note>, pumice, and tufa. # CONCERNING OCCULT PHILOSOPHY.

<margin>The difference of metals.</margin>
...and into it they are eventually resolved, or from it they are born: such as the thunderstone, the pyrite stone, and asbestos. Similarly among metals, lead and silver are earthy; mercury <note>original: "argentum vivum," literally "living silver."</note> is watery; copper and tin are airy; while gold and iron are fiery. In plants also, the roots imitate the earth because of their density; the leaves resemble water because of their sap; the flowers represent air because of their delicacy; and the seeds represent fire because of their generative spirit. Furthermore, some are called hot, others cold, some moist, others dry, borrowing the names of the elements from their own qualities. Among animals, some are more earthy than others and inhabit the bowels of the earth, such as worms, earthworms, moles, and many reptiles. Others are watery, such as fish. Others are airy, which cannot live outside the air. There are also <margin>The habitation of the Salamander. 8. f.</margin> fiery ones inhabiting fire, such as salamanders and certain crickets called fire-fliers <note>original: "pyraustas," a mythical insect thought to live in fire.</note>, and those which glow with a certain fiery heat, such as doves, ostriches, lions, and those which <term>the Wise Man</term> <note>Likely referring to Solomon or a specific classical authority.</note> calls beasts breathing fiery vapor. <margin>The agreement of animals with the elements.</margin> Furthermore, in animals, the bones represent earth, the flesh represents air, the vital spirit represents fire, and the humors <note>The four "fluids" believed to control health and temperament.</note> represent water. These are also divided among the elements: for red choler <note>Yellow bile.</note> yields to fire, blood to air, phlegm <note>original: "pituita."</note> to water, and black bile to earth. <margin>The harmony of the senses with the elements.</margin> Finally, in the soul itself—as Augustine testifies—the intellect represents fire, reason represents air, imagination represents water, and sense represents earth. And these senses are also distributed among the elements: for sight is fiery, since it perceives nothing without fire and light; hearing is airy, for sound is produced by the striking of air; smell and taste are referred to water, without whose moisture there is neither flavor nor odor; finally, touch is entirely earthy, taking to itself the coarser bodies. Even the acts and operations of man are governed by the elements: for slow and solid movement is marked by earth; fear, sluggishness, and slack work are marked by water; cheerfulness and friendly manners by air; and sharp, angry impulse by fire. <margin>The elements are the first of all things.</margin> Thus the elements are the first of all things, and all things are from them and according to them, and they themselves diffuse their powers in all things and through all things.

### ¶ How the elements are in the heavens, in the stars, in demons, in angels, and finally in God himself. Chapter VIII.

<margin>The corporeal world.</margin>
It is the unanimous opinion of all the Platonists that, just as in the <term>archetypal world</term> <note>The divine blueprint or original model of the universe.</note> all things are in all things, so also in this corporeal world, all things are in all things, though in different ways, according to the nature of those receiving them. Thus <margin>Elements are in all things.</margin> the elements are not only in these lower regions, but also in the heavens, in the stars, in demons, in angels, and finally in the Maker and Archetype of all things. But in these lower regions, the elements are certain coarse forms, immersed in matter, and material elements; in the heavens, however, <margin>Celestial elements.</margin> the elements exist through their natures and powers: that is, in a celestial and far more excellent way than beneath the moon. For the solidity of the celestial earth is there without the coarseness of water; and the agility of the air is far from...

There are also among the signs of the Zodiac some that are fiery, some earthy, some airy, and some watery. These elements rule in the heavens by distributing those four <term>triplicities</term> <note>Groups of three zodiac signs that share the same element.</note> to them, granting each element a beginning, a middle, and an end. Thus, Aries has the beginning of fire, Leo its progress and increase, and Sagittarius its end; Taurus has the beginning of earth, Virgo its progress, and Capricorn its extreme; Gemini has the beginning of air, Libra its process, and Aquarius its termination; Cancer possesses the beginning of water, Scorpio its middle, and Pisces its end. From the mixtures of these planets and signs together with the elements, all bodies are composed. Now, even the <term>daemons</term> <note>In this historical context, "daemons" refers to spirits or mediating beings, not necessarily evil "demons."</note> are distinguished from one another by this same logic: so that some are called fiery, others terrestrial, others airy, and others watery.

### ¶ On the virtues of natural things which depend most closely upon the elements. <span style="float: right;">Chapter IX.</span>

<margin>
Various natural virtues of things.
Qualities of things.
</margin>
The natural virtues of things are, in some cases, elemental—such as heating, cooling, moistening, and drying. These are called the "primary operations" or "primary qualities," and they act according to their nature; for these qualities alone are able to entirely transform a whole substance, which no other qualities can do. However, other virtues reside in things because of the elements that compose them, even beyond these primary qualities. These include virtues that are ripening, digesting, dissolving, softening, <note>original: "mellificatiue," likely a printer's error for "mollificatiue" (softening).</note> hardening, styptic <note>A substance that stops bleeding by contracting tissue.</note>, cleansing, corrosive, burning, opening, evaporating, strengthening, soothing, binding, obstructing, expelling, retaining, attracting, repelling, numbing, enlarging, lubricating, and many others. For an elemental quality in a mixture has much to do that it cannot accomplish on its own. These operations are called "secondary qualities," because they follow the nature and proportion of the mixture of the primary virtues, just as they are discussed at length in the books of physicians. For example, "ripening" is the operation of natural heat according to a certain measure in the substance of the matter; "hardening" is the operation of cold, as is "freezing," and so on with similar effects. Furthermore, these operations sometimes act upon a specific part of the body—such as those that provoke urine, or milk, or menstruation—and these are called "tertiary qualities," which follow the secondary just as the secondary follow the primary. It is according to these primary, secondary, and tertiary qualities that many illnesses are both caused and cured.

<margin>
Many admirable artificial things.
<insert>Of a free art</insert>
Fire burning in water.
<insert>fire burning in water</insert>
<insert>Fire which is extinguished by oil.</insert>
<insert>inextinguishable fire.</insert>
</margin>
Many things are also made artificially that men greatly admire; such as "Greek Fire," <note>A famous incendiary weapon used by the Byzantine Empire that could burn on water.</note> which is a fire that burns in water. Aristotle teaches several compositions for this in his treatise on this singular subject. In a similar way, a fire is made that is extinguished by oil, but is ignited by cold water when it is sprinkled upon it; or a fire that is ignited by rain, or wind, or the sun. There is also a fire made called "burning water," <note>original: "aqua ardens." A term often used for distilled alcohol or "spirit of wine," which appears like water but is highly flammable.</note> the preparation of which is very well known, which consumes nothing but itself. Inextinguishable fires are made, as well as incombustible oils and perpetual lamps which can be extinguished neither by wind, nor water, nor by any other means. This would seem entirely incredible, were it not for that most famous lamp that once shone in the temple of Venus, in which the stone <term>asbestos</term> <note>Agrippa refers to the ancient belief that asbestos was a stone that, once lit, could never be put out.</note> burned; for once it is truly ignited, it is never extinguished.

<margin>

Nature of the asbestos stone.
Preparations against fire.
</margin>
Furthermore, preparations are made for wood or other combustible things so that they cannot be harmed by fire. Compositions are made which, when rubbed on the hands, allow us to carry glowing iron, or put our hand into molten metal, or even walk through fire with the whole body without any harm, and other things of this sort.

<margin>
Nature of asbestos linen.
</margin>
There is also a type of linen that Pliny calls "asbestos"—the Greeks call it ασβεστov <note>English: asbestos; literally "unquenchable."</note>—which is not consumed by fire. Of this, Anaxilaus says that a tree wrapped in it can be cut down with "deaf" blows—that is, blows that cannot be heard.

BOOK ONE. VIII

### ¶ On the Occult Virtues of Things, Chapter X.

<margin>ii</margin>Furthermore, there are other virtues within things which do not belong to any element—such as driving away poison, expelling carbuncles <note>Inflammatory skin boils or sores, often associated with the plague.</note>, attracting iron, or other such effects. This virtue is a consequence of the species and the form of this or that thing. Because of this, even a tiny amount of a substance can have a very great effect in action, a power which is not granted to a mere elemental quality. For these virtues, because they are highly "formal" <note>In philosophy, "formal" refers to the "substantial form" or essence of a thing, rather than its material components.</note>, can achieve a great deal with very little matter; conversely, an elemental virtue, because it is material, requires a great deal of matter to act with great force. <margin>Why they are called occult properties.</margin> These are called "occult properties" because their causes are hidden, so much so that the human intellect cannot fully investigate them. For this reason, philosophers have discovered the greatest part of them through long experience, rather than through the use of reason. Just as food is digested in the stomach by heat, which we recognize, <margin>The transformation of food in the stomach.</margin> it is also transformed by a certain occult virtue which we do not understand. Indeed, it is not transformed by heat alone, for if that were the case, food would be transformed better in a fireplace near a flame than in the stomach. Thus, there are certain other virtues innate to things beyond the elemental qualities we recognize; these are created together by nature. We admire and are often stunned by these virtues because they are unknown to us, or because they are seen only rarely or never at all. For example, one reads in Ovid concerning the Phoenix, that unique bird that renews itself:

> There is one bird that restores and reseeds itself;
> The Assyrians call it the Phoenix.
<note>original: "Vna est quę reparat, sese ipsa reseminat ales, Assyrii phœnica vocant." — Ovid, Metamorphoses, XV, 392-3.</note>

->And elsewhere:<-

> Egypt gathers to witness the miracle of such a sight,
> And the cheering crowd greets the rare bird.
<note>original: "Conuenit Aegyptus tanti ad miracula visus, Et raram volucrem turba salutat ouans." — Ovid, Amores, II, 6.</note>

Matreas once stirred great admiration for himself among both the Greeks and Romans. <margin>The beast of Matreas.</margin> He claimed that he was raising a wild beast that would devour itself. <note>Matreas of Pitane was a writer of parodies; this "beast" is likely a metaphorical or satirical reference to greed or a specific riddle.</note> Even today, many people still anxiously search for what Matreas's beast might be. Who would not marvel at the fish found fossilized in the earth, of which Aristotle, Theophrastus, and the historian Polybius have written? Or at the "singing stones" mentioned by Pausanias? All of these are the works of occult virtues. <margin>The ostrich digests iron. Seneca, Natural Questions, Book 4, f. 2.</margin> Likewise, the ostrich bird cooks and digests cold, hard iron as nourishment for its body; it is even said that its stomach is not harmed by glowing hot iron. <margin>The power of the echeneis. 7. xiii. fac. 2.</margin> So too, that little fish, the echeneis <note>The Remora or "suckerfish." Ancient naturalists believed it could stop a ship in full sail simply by attaching itself to the hull.</note>, so restrains the force of the winds and tames the fury of the sea that, no matter how much the storms command and rage, and even with infinite sails stretched by the wind, it checks the ships by its touch alone and forces them to stand still so that they cannot be moved in any way. <margin>The nature of the Salamander and the Pyrausta.</margin> In the same way, the salamander and the little creatures called pyraustae <note>A mythical insect said to live in the fire of smithies.</note> live in fire; and although they sometimes appear to burn, they are not harmed. It is similar with a certain bitumen <note>A naturally occurring petroleum or tar-like substance.</note> with which the weapons of the Amazons were said to be coated, which could be dissolved by neither iron nor fire. It is also fabled that Alexander the Great coated the Caspian Gates <note>Legendary bronze gates supposedly built by Alexander in the Caucasus to keep out the "unclean" northern tribes.</note> with this material, which were forged from bronze. <margin>The bitumen with which Noah's ark was coated.</margin> One also reads that Noah’s Ark was glued together with similar bitumen, and it has remained [intact] for so many thousands of years upon the mountains.

...of Armenia still remaining. There are many other such wonders, scarcely believable, which are nonetheless known through experience itself: such as what antiquity records about Satyrs, which are animals half-human and half-brute in form, yet capable of speech and reason. The holy **Jerome** <margin>In the life of Paul the first Hermit</margin> himself reports that one of these once spoke to the blessed Anthony the hermit, condemning pagan error in the worship of animals and begging him to pray to the common God on its behalf; he further affirms that one was once brought alive into public and shortly thereafter sent to the emperor Constantine.

### ¶ How occult virtues are infused into the species of things from Ideas, through the seminal reasons of the World Soul and the rays of the stars; and which things abound most in this virtue. Chapter XI.

The Platonists hold that all lower things are modeled <note>original: "ideata," meaning formed according to an archetype.</note> after superior Ideas. They define an "Idea" as a form existing above bodies, souls, and minds—one, simple, pure, immutable, indivisible, incorporeal, and eternal; and they maintain that the nature of all Ideas is the same. They place Ideas first in the "Good" itself—that is, in God—by way of cause. There, they are distinct from one another only by certain relative reasons <note>In this context, "reasons" refers to the logical distinctions or blueprints for different types of created things.</note>, lest everything in the world be one and the same without any variety; yet they agree in essence, lest God be a "multiple" or divided substance. 

They place them second in the Intelligible <note>The realm of pure intellect.</note> itself—that is, in the Soul of the World—properly as forms; here, they are distinct from one another as absolute forms. Thus, while in God all Ideas are a single form, in the Soul of the World they are many. They are then placed in the subsequent minds <note>Individual angelic or celestial intelligences.</note>, whether joined to a body or separate from a body, through a kind of participation, becoming more and more distinct by degrees. They place them in Nature as certain "seeds," the lowest of the forms infused by the Ideas; and finally in matter, they place them as shadows. 

Added to this is that there are as many seminal reasons <note>Lat. "rationes seminales" — generative principles that act like spiritual seeds.</note> of things in the Soul of the World as there are Ideas in the Divine Mind. By these reasons, the Soul of the World built for itself figures in the heavens beyond the stars and impressed properties upon all of them. From these stars, figures, and properties, therefore, all the virtues and properties of lower species depend, such that every species has a celestial figure corresponding to it. From this figure proceeds a marvelous power in its operation, a specific "dowry" received from its own Idea through the seminal reasons of the Soul of the World. For Ideas are not only the causes of a species' existence, but also the causes of every virtue inherent in that species. This is what many philosophers mean when they say that by certain virtues—those having a certain and stable reason, not fortuitous or accidental, but effective, powerful, and unfailing, doing nothing in vain or without effect—the virtues existing in the nature of things are moved. These virtues are indeed the operations of the Ideas; which were not...

except by accident, namely from the impurity and inequality of matter; for in this way, things even of the same species are found to be more or less powerful, according to the purity or confusion of the matter. Indeed, all celestial influences can be hindered by the confusion and inability of matter. Whence it was a proverb among the Platonists themselves that celestial virtues are infused according to the "merit" of the matter <note>The "merit of matter" refers to the idea that physical substance must be properly prepared or "pure" to successfully receive and hold spiritual or celestial power.</note>. Of this, **Virgil** also makes mention where he sings:

> A fiery vigor and a heavenly origin belong to
> those seeds, so far as harmful bodies do not retard them. <note>original: "Igneus est ollis uigor, & cœlestis origo / Seminibus quantum non noxia corpora tardant." From the Aeneid, Book VI.</note>

Therefore, those things in which the Idea is less immersed in matter—that is, those which receive a greater likeness to the "separated things" <note>The "separated things" are the pure, incorporeal Ideas or spiritual essences that exist apart from physical bodies.</note>—possess virtues that are more powerful in their operation, similar to the operation of the separated Idea itself. We know, therefore, that the position and figure of the celestial bodies are the cause of every noble virtue found in the lower species.

### How different virtues are infused into diverse individuals, even of the same species.
->Chapter XII.<-

The singular gifts of individuals are also present in many things, and are just as wonderful as those found in whole species; these also arise from the celestial figure and the position of the stars. For every individual, when it begins to exist under a specific <term>horoscope</term> <gloss>the configuration of the heavens at the moment of birth or beginning</gloss> and celestial constellation, contracts at its birth a certain marvelous virtue for acting and for being acted upon. This is a wonder beyond even that which it possesses from its species, arising both through the influx of the celestial bodies and through the "obedience" of generable matter to the **World Soul** <note>The *Anima Mundi*, or World Soul, was a central concept in Neoplatonism, viewed as an animating spirit that connects the divine intellect to the physical universe.</note>. This obedience is much like the obedience of our own bodies to our souls. For we feel within ourselves that whatever form we conceive in our minds, our body is moved toward it—whether with delight, or horror, or by fleeing. In the same way, the celestial souls frequently conceive diverse things, and then matter is moved through obedience to those conceptions. Thus, many prodigies appear in nature from the "imagination" of the superior movements. In this way, not only natural things, but sometimes even artificial things <note>Agrippa suggests that man-made objects, like talismans or tools, can "catch" these celestial virtues if the person making them is focused and the timing is right.</note> receive diverse virtues, especially if the soul of the worker is intently striving toward that same end. Whence **Avicenna** says: whatever happens here must first exist in the movements and conceptions of the stars and the spheres. Thus, various effects, inclinations, and characters are produced in things, not only from the various dispositions of matter (as many believe), but from a varying influx and a diverse form—not indeed a diversity of the species, but one that is particular and proper to the individual. And the degrees of these are distributed in various ways by the first cause of all, **God**, who remaining the same distributes to each as He wills; yet in this, the second causes—the angelic and celestial—cooperate, disposing the corporeal matter and other things committed to them. Therefore, all virtues are infused by **God** through the World Soul, though by the particular power of the presiding images and <term>intelligences</term> <gloss>the angelic spirits believed to guide the planets</gloss>, and the concurrence of rays.

### Whence the Occult Virtues of Things Proceed. Chapter XIII.

<margin>10. f. 2.</margin> It is known to all that a certain power exists within the magnet by which it attracts iron; and that the diamond, by its mere presence, takes away this power <note>A common medieval and Renaissance belief was that diamonds could "neutralize" a magnet's pull.</note> from the magnet. In the same way, <term>amber</term> <note>original: "electrum"</note> and the <term>balagius</term> <note>A type of pale red ruby or spinel, also known as a Balas ruby.</note> stone, when rubbed and warmed, draw straws to themselves. The <term>asbestos</term> stone, once set on fire, is never—or only with great difficulty—extinguished. The <term>carbuncle</term> <note>A term used for any red gemstone that glows, such as a ruby or garnet.</note> shines in the darkness. The <term>aetites</term> <note>Also called the "eagle-stone"; it was believed to be found in eagles' nests and had two parts, one "pregnant" with the other.</note> strengthens the fetus of women and plants when placed above them, but draws it forth when placed below. <term>Jasper</term> stops the flow of blood. The <term>echineis</term> <note>The remora or "suckerfish," which was legendary for its ability to stop large ships by clinging to their hulls.</note> brings a ship to a standstill. <term>Rhubarb</term> drives out bile. The liver of a **Chameleon**, if taken from the top of a roof, is said to stir up rain and thunder. The **Heliotrope** stone <note>Likely the "bloodstone," not the plant of the same name.</note> dazzles the sight and renders the wearer invisible. The **lyncurius** stone <note>Legendary stone supposedly formed from the solidified urine of a lynx.</note> removes illusions from the eyes. The **lipparis** stone, when its smoke is used, calls forth all manner of beasts. The **Synochitides** stone brings out the shades of the underworld. The **anachitides** causes images of the gods to appear. The **Ennectis**, when placed under those who are dreaming, provides oracular visions. There is an **Ethiopian herb** by which they say ponds are dried up and all closed things are opened. We also read of the herb **latace**, which is given by the Persian kings to their ambassadors so that, wherever they might go, they should abound in a plenty of all things. There is also the **Spartan** or **Scythian herb**, which, if tasted or even held in the mouth, they say allows the Scythians to endure twelve days of hunger and thirst. **Apuleius** <note>A 2nd-century Roman philosopher and author of "The Golden Ass," often associated with magic.</note> even says that he was taught by a divine power that there are many kinds of herbs and stones by which men can even grant themselves perpetual life; but he claims it is not lawful for men to know this science, for since they study evil so greedily even while living such short lives—and dare every kind of crime—if they were granted a great length of time, they would not even spare the gods themselves.

Truly, none of those who have published vast volumes on the properties of things have revealed from whence these virtues come: not **Hermes**, not **Bochus**, not **Aaron**, not **Orpheus**, not **Theophrastus**, not **Thebith**, not **Zenothemis**, not **Zoroaster**, not **Euax**, not **Dioscorides**, not **Isaac the Jew**, not **Zacharias the Babylonian**, not **Albertus**, nor **Arnoldus** <note>This list includes a mix of legendary figures (Orpheus, Zoroaster), ancient scientists (Theophrastus, Dioscorides), and medieval scholars (Albertus Magnus, Arnold of Villanova).</note>. And yet all of these have confessed—as **Zacharias** writes to **Mithridates**—that a great power and even human fate itself reside within the virtues of stones and herbs. Therefore, a deeper investigation is required to find where these things come from. **Alexander the Peripatetic** <note>Alexander of Aphrodisias, a famous commentator on Aristotle.</note>, not departing from his own senses and qualities, thinks these proceed from the elements and their qualities. This might perhaps be thought true, were it not that those qualities are of the same species, while the operations of stones are many and agree neither in species nor in genus. Therefore, the **Academics**, along with their leader **Plato**, attribute these virtues to the "Ideas," the formative patterns of things. **Avicenna**, however, traces such operations back to the "Intelligences," **Hermes** to the stars, and **Albertus** to the specific forms of things. And although these authors seem to oppose one another, none of them—if rightly understood—departs from the truth, since all their words tend toward the same effect...
