# BOOK THE FIRST.

...agree in their effects. For God, who is the beginning and end of all virtues, provides the seal of <term>Ideas</term> <note>In Platonic philosophy, Ideas are the eternal, perfect patterns of all things existing in the Divine Mind.</note> to his ministers, the <term>Intelligences</term> <note>Original: "intelligentiis." In this context, these are angelic or spiritual beings that govern the celestial spheres.</note>. These Intelligences, acting as faithful executors, stamp every thing committed to them with an "ideal" virtue through the heavens and the stars, which act as their instruments. Meanwhile, matter is prepared to receive those forms which reside in the Divine Majesty and are brought down through the stars, as **Plato** says in the *Timaeus*. These forms are distributed by the "Giver of Forms" through the ministry of the Intelligences, whom He has appointed as rulers and guardians over His works. To these Intelligences is granted the power over the things committed to their care, so that every virtue found in stones, herbs, metals, and all other things, originates from these presiding spirits.

Therefore, form and virtue proceed first from the **Ideas**, then from the presiding and ruling **Intelligences**, then from the aspects of the heavens which dispose the influence, and finally from the balanced temperaments of the **elements** that correspond to the celestial influxes by which the elements themselves are organized.

These operations, therefore, exist in these lower things through "expressed forms"; in the heavens, they exist through "disposing virtues"; in the Intelligences, through "mediating reasons"; and in the <term>Archetype</term> <note>The "Archetype" refers to the original model or God Himself, the source of all patterns.</note>, through "Ideas and exemplary forms." All of these must coincide in the execution of the effect and virtue of any given thing. Thus, there is a virtue and a wonderful operation in every single herb and stone, but a greater one in a star; and beyond that, each thing acquires much from the presiding Intelligences. Most of all, however, virtues come from the **Supreme Cause**, to whom all things correspond in mutual and consummate agreement, sounding together in a harmonic concert—much like hymns—always praising that Great Architect. This is just as the holy youths in the <term>Chaldean furnace</term> <note>A reference to the biblical story of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego in the book of Daniel, who were thrown into a furnace but remained unharmed while singing praises.</note> invited all things to sing:

> Bless the Lord, all things that grow in the earth; and all things that move in the waters, all birds of the heaven, beasts and cattle, together with the children of men. <note>original: "Benedicite dominum vniuersa germinantia in terra..."</note>

There is, therefore, no cause for the necessity of effects other than the connection of all things with the **First Cause**, and their correspondence to those Divine Exemplars and Eternal Ideas. From these, every thing has its specific and particular place in the Archetype, from which it lives and draws its origin. Every virtue of herbs, stones, metals, animals, words, and speeches, and of all things that exist, is implanted by God. Although God operates through the Intelligences and the heavens upon these lower things, He occasionally performs acts immediately by Himself, setting aside these intermediaries or suspending their ministry. Such works are then called **miracles**. For while the secondary causes—which **Plato** and others call "ministers"—act by necessity according to the command and order of the First Cause, God may, at His pleasure, release or suspend them so that they cease to follow the necessity of that order. These are the greatest miracles of God. Such was the case with the fire in the Chaldean furnace...

### Of the spirit of the world, what it is, and that it is the bond of occult virtues. Chapter 14.

<margin>d</margin>
**Democritus**, **Orpheus**, and many of the **Pythagoreans**, having most diligently searched into the powers of celestial things and the natures of the lower world, said that all things are full of gods. Nor was this without reason, for nothing is of such excellent power that, if deprived of divine help, it would be content with its own nature. They called the <term>divine virtues</term> <note>Original: "virtutes divinas." In this context, "virtues" are not moral traits, but inherent spiritual powers or "essences" infused into matter.</note> diffused through all things "gods." **Zoroaster** called these "divine lures," **Synesius** "symbolic attractions," and others called them "lives" or even "souls." They said that the virtues of things depend on these, because it belongs only to the soul to be extended from one matter into other things upon which it acts—just as a man extends his intellect to things that can be understood, and his imagination to things that can be imagined. This is what they meant when they spoke, saying that the soul of one being goes out and enters into another, fascinating it and hindering its operations; 
<margin>
The magnet attracts iron. The diamond hinders it.
</margin>
just as the diamond <note>Original: "adamas." It was a common medieval belief that a diamond could negate the magnetic pull of a lodestone (magnet).</note> prevents the magnet from attracting iron. But since the soul is the "first mover" and is, as they say, movable by and through itself—while the body or matter is ineffective when moved by itself and falls far short of the soul—they say there is a need for a more excellent medium. This medium must be something that is almost not a body but almost a soul, or almost not a soul but almost a body, by which the soul may be connected to the body. They imagine such a medium to be the **Spirit of the World**, which we call the <term>Fifth Essence</term> <note>Original: "essentia quinta," or Quintessence. This was considered a pure, celestial substance distinct from the four earthly elements of earth, water, air, and fire.</note>, because it does not consist of the four elements but is a certain fifth thing subsisting above or besides them. Such a spirit is therefore necessarily required as a medium so that celestial souls may dwell in a denser body and bestow wonderful gifts. Thus, this spirit is in the body of the world just as our spirit is in the human body. For as the powers of our soul are applied to our limbs through the spirit, so the virtue of the **World Soul** is dilated through all things by the fifth essence. Nothing is found in the whole world that lacks a spark of its virtue. Yet <gloss>namely, the spirit</gloss> is poured more and most abundantly into those things which have drawn in the most of this kind of spirit. It is drawn in through the rays of the stars, insofar as things make themselves conformable to them. Through this spirit, every occult property is propagated into herbs, stones, metals, and living creatures—by the sun, the moon, the planets, and by the stars higher than the planets. Moreover, this spirit can be of benefit to us...

# BOOK ONE.

...even more so, if one knows how to separate that spirit from other elements, or at least how to use those things which most abound with this spirit. Indeed, those things in which that spirit is less submerged in the body and less constrained by matter act more powerfully and perfectly, and they generate their own likeness more readily; for all generative and <term>seminary virtue</term> <note>The power of "seeds" or "essences" to reproduce their own form in nature.</note> is within it. For this reason, alchemists strive to separate that <margin><unclear>The error of Alchemists regarding what they suffer [...] to the impure</unclear></margin> spirit from gold and silver. Once it is properly segregated and extracted, if they then apply it to any matter of the same kind—that is, to any of the metals—they may instantly produce gold or silver. And we know how to do that, and have sometimes seen it; but we could not manufacture more gold than the weight of that gold from which we extracted the spirit. For since that spirit is an extended and not an intensified <term>form</term> <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "form" is the internal principle that gives a thing its specific identity and properties.</note>, it cannot transform an imperfect body into a perfect one beyond its own measure. However, I do not deny that this might be accomplished by another skillful method.

### How we must investigate and test the virtues of things through the path taken from similarity. Chapter XV.

It is clear, therefore, that the <term>occult properties</term> <note>Hidden powers that cannot be explained by the four physical qualities of hot, cold, moist, or dry.</note> in things are not derived from their elemental nature, but are infused from the heavens. These are hidden from our senses and are barely known even to reason; they proceed from the life and spirit of the world through the very rays of the stars. We can investigate these in no other way than through experience and conjecture. Therefore, O seeker, you who desire to labor in this study, you must consider that every thing moves and converts toward its own like, and inclines toward itself according to its full power—both in its property (that is, its occult virtue) and in its quality (its elemental virtue). Sometimes this happens even in the substance itself, as we see in salt: for whatever stands for a long time with salt becomes salt. For every agent, when it begins to act, does not move toward something inferior to itself, but rather, as far as possible, toward its own equal and like. We see this clearly in sentient animals, where the <term>nutritive virtue</term> <note>The biological faculty responsible for growth and sustenance.</note> does not transform food into grass or plants, but converts it into sensible flesh. Therefore, in those things where there is an excess of any quality or property—such as heat, cold, boldness, fear, sadness, anger, love, hatred, or any other passion or virtue—whether it be in them by nature or sometimes by art or chance (such as <term>boldness</term> <note>Original: "audacia." In Renaissance thought, even social traits like the "boldness" of a prostitute were seen as transferable qualities that could be used in magical preparations.</note> in a prostitute), these things greatly move and provoke toward such a quality, passion, or virtue. Thus, fire moves toward fire, water moves toward water, and the bold moves toward boldness. It is well known among physicians that a brain helps the brain, and a lung helps the lung. Thus they say that the right eye of a frog, hung from the neck in a cloth of its natural <margin>A remedy for bloodshot eyes.</margin> color, heals <term>bloodshot eyes</term> <note>Original: "lippitudo," an inflammation or watering of the eyes.</note> in the right eye, and the left eye of the frog heals the left. A similar remedy is also reported concerning the eyes of a crab.

...they say: thus the feet of a tortoise are beneficial to those suffering from <term>gout</term> <note>original: "podagra"; a painful form of arthritis often affecting the feet.</note>, when they are tied on so that foot is joined to foot, hand to hand, right to right, and left to left. In this same way, they say that every sterile animal leads to sterility; and from such an animal, the testicles, the matrix, or the urine are most effective. Thus they claim a woman will not conceive if she takes every month some urine from a mule, or something infused in it. Therefore, if we wish to work toward some specific property or virtue, let us seek out animals or other things in which such a property exists most excellently, and from these let us take for ourselves that part in which such a property or virtue is most vigorous. 

For example, if we should ever wish to promote love, let us seek some animal that loves most intensely, such as the dove, the turtle-dove, the sparrow, the swallow, or the <term>wagtail</term> <note>original: "motacilla"; a small bird associated in folklore with restlessness and aphrodisiacs.</note>. From these, let us take the members or parts in which the <term>Venereous appetite</term> <note>Desires or physical functions associated with Venus, the goddess of love.</note> is most vigorous: which are the heart, the testicles, the matrix, the <term>phallus</term> <note>original: "priapus."</note>, the sperm, or the menses. And let this be done at that time when these animals are most seized by and intent upon such a passion; for then they strongly provoke and bring about love. 

In a similar way, to increase boldness, let us seek the lion or the rooster, and from these let us take the heart, the eyes, or the forehead. And so it is to be understood what <term>Psellus the Platonist</term> <note>Michael Psellos (c. 1017–1078), a Byzantine philosopher and politician who wrote extensively on demons and ancient Greek thought.</note> says: that dogs, crows, and roosters contribute to wakefulness; as do the nightingale, the bat, and the owl—and from these, especially the head, heart, and eyes. Therefore they say that if someone carries the heart of a crow or a bat upon themselves, they will not sleep until it is removed. The dried head of a bat tied to the right arm of a person who is awake does the same; for if it is placed upon a sleeper, it is said they will not be awakened until it is removed. 

In the same way, the frog and the owl bring about talkativeness, and from these especially the tongue and the heart. Thus, the tongue of a water-frog placed under the head makes one speak in their sleep; and the heart of an owl placed upon the left breast of a sleeping woman is said to make her reveal all her secrets. The heart of a <term>screech-owl</term> <note>original: "noctua."</note> is said to do the same, as is the <term>suet</term> <note>original: "sepum"; animal fat.</note> of a hare placed upon the chest of a sleeper. 

In the same manner, all long-lived animals contribute to a long life; and whichever ones have in themselves a power of renewal contribute to the renewal of our bodies and the restoration of youth, which physicians have many times shown themselves to know—as is manifest regarding the <term>viper</term> and serpents. And it is known that stags renew their old age by eating serpents. In the same way, the phoenix is renewed by the pyre which it builds for itself; and a similar power is in the pelican, whose right foot, if placed under warm dung, is said to regenerate a pelican from it after three months. ### ¶ How the operations of various virtues are transfused from one thing into another, and are mutually communicated. Chapter XVI.

You ought to know that the power of natural things is so great that they not only affect all things near them with their own **virtue** <note>In this context, "virtue" refers to the inherent power or magical property of an object.</note>, but beyond this, they infuse a similar power into them. Through this, these things may also affect others with this same virtue, just as we see in the **lodestone** <note>original: "magnete"; a naturally magnetized piece of the mineral magnetite.</note>. This stone not only attracts iron rings but also infuses its power into the rings themselves, so that they are able to do the same thing—a phenomenon that **Augustine** and **Albertus** <note>Referring to St. Augustine and Albertus Magnus, a 13th-century philosopher and alchemist.</note> report having seen. In this way, it is said that a public harlot, in whom there is bold and banished impudence, affects all things near her with this same property, which then return it to others. Therefore, they say that if someone puts on the garment or shirt of a harlot, or keeps with them a mirror in which she has looked at herself daily, that person will be rendered bold, fearless, impudent, and lustful. In a similar way, they say that a cloth that has been at a funeral conceives from this a certain property of sadness and **Saturnine** <note>Associated with the planet Saturn, which in astrology governs melancholy, gloom, and death.</note> nature; likewise, the noose of a hanged man is said to have certain marvelous properties.

It is a similar thing that **Pliny** <note>Pliny the Elder, author of "Natural History."</note> relates: if someone places earth beneath a green lizard that has been blinded, and includes iron or gold rings with it in a glass vessel, when it appears that the lizard has recovered its sight, 
<margin>A remedy for blear-eyedness.</margin>
the rings, having been taken out through the glass, are effective against **blear-eyedness** <note>original: "lippitudo"; a chronic inflammation of the eyelids or eyes.</note>. He says the same holds true for weasels and rings: when their eyes have been gouged out with a point, it is certain that their sight returns. In a similar way, rings are placed for a certain time in the nest of sparrows or swallows, which we afterwards use to procure love or goodwill.

### ¶ How the virtues of things are to be investigated and explained through strife and friendship. Chapter XVII.

It remains now to see how all things have among themselves friendship and enmity. Every thing has something to be feared—a horrible, inimical, and destructive enemy—and conversely, something exulting, gladdening, and comforting. Thus in the elements, fire is opposed to water, and air to earth, yet they otherwise agree among themselves. Furthermore, among the celestial bodies, the friends of **Saturn** are **Mercury**, **Jupiter**, the **Sun**, and the **Moon**; his enemies are **Mars** and **Venus**. All the planets are friends to **Jupiter** except **Mars**. Likewise, all hold **Mars** in hatred except **Venus**. ### ON OCCULT PHILOSOPHY.

Venus and Saturn are enemies, as are the Sun, Moon, and Mars <note>In traditional astrology, certain planets are considered "inimical" to one another based on their qualities (hot/cold, wet/dry).</note>. To the Moon, however, the friends are Jupiter, Venus, and Saturn, while its enemies are Mars and Mercury. There is another enmity among the stars when they possess opposite **houses** <note>original: "domus"; the zodiac signs where a planet's power is most at home</note>: such as Saturn against the "luminaries" (the Sun and Moon), Jupiter against Mercury, and Mars against Venus. Even stronger is the enmity between those whose **exaltations** <note>original: "exaltationes"; specific degrees of the zodiac where a planet's influence is most heightened</note> are opposite: such as Saturn and the Sun, Jupiter and Mars, or Venus and Mercury. 

On the other hand, the strongest friendship exists between those who agree in nature, quality, substance, and power—such as Mars with the Sun, Venus with the Moon, or Jupiter with Venus. Friendship also exists between those where the exaltation of one is in the house of the other: such as Saturn with Venus, Jupiter with the Moon, Mars with Saturn, the Sun with Mars, Venus with Jupiter, and the Moon with Venus. Just as these friendships and enmities exist among the higher celestial bodies, so too are the inclinations of all things subjected to them here in the lower world. Therefore, these states of friendship and enmity are nothing other than the inclinations of things toward one another: desiring a certain thing if it is absent, moving toward it if not hindered, and resting once it is obtained; or conversely, fleeing from what is contrary, dreading its approach, and never finding rest within it. Led by this opinion, **Heraclitus** <note>A pre-Socratic Greek philosopher (c. 535 – c. 475 BC) known for his doctrine that change is central to the universe and that "strife" and "harmony" drive all creation.</note> declared that all things are brought into being through strife and friendship.

<margin>The nature of the Emerald. The power of Jasper.</margin>
Indeed, these inclinations of friendship appear in plants and minerals, much like the attraction the **lodestone** has for iron. The **emerald** <note>original: "smaragdus"</note> attracts wealth and favor; **jasper** aids in childbirth; and **agate** promotes eloquence. In a similar way, **naphtha** <note>A flammable oil or petroleum derivative.</note> draws fire to itself and leaps toward it from wherever it is seen. Similarly, the root of the **proxis** <note>A legendary herb mentioned by ancient naturalists, possibly referring to a type of "fire-stone" or plant with similar properties.</note> herb attracts fire from a distance, just like naphtha. A similar inclination exists between the male and female **palm tree**: when the branch of one touches the branch of the other, they wrap themselves in a mutual embrace, and the female bears no fruit without the male; even a solitary almond tree is less fertile. Vines love the elm and the **maple** <note>original: "oppium"; often referring to the field maple used as a support for vines.</note>, and the olive tree and myrtle mutually delight in each other, as do the olive and the fig. 

Among animals, friendship exists between the blackbird and the thrush, the crow and the heron, and between peacocks and doves, or turtledoves and parrots. Whence **Sappho** <note>The famous Greek lyric poet from the island of Lesbos.</note> writes to Phaon:

> And white doves are often joined with various ones,
> And the black turtledove is loved by the green bird. <note>original: "Et variis albę iunguntur sepe columbę, / Et niger à viridi turtur amatur aue."</note>

<margin>The friendship of animals with other things.</margin>
Furthermore, the pilot-fish <note>original: "musculus"; here referring to a small fish said to guide whales.</note> and the whale are friends. Nor is friendship found only between animals themselves, but also with other things, such as metals, stones, and plants. Thus the **cat** <note>original: "feles siue catus"</note> rejoices in the herb **catnip** <note>original: "nepeta"</note>; it is said that by rubbing against it, cats may conceive and supply the lack of a male. In **Cappadocia** <note>A region in ancient Asia Minor (modern Turkey).</note>, mares expose themselves to the blowing wind and are said to conceive from its breath and inhalation. Similarly, frogs, toads, serpents, and all manner of venomous reptiles delight in the plant called **laughing parsley** <note>original: "apium risus"; likely *Ranunculus sceleratus*, the Cursed Buttercup, which causes a "sardonic grin" or facial spasms in those who eat it.</note>, of which doctors say: if anyone eats it, they die laughing.

### ¶ How the virtues of things are to be investigated and tested, which are present in them either from their whole species, or are joined to a thing as a gift belonging to a particular individual. Chapter XIX.

<margin>Virtues exist in things in two ways.</margin> 
Furthermore, you must consider that the virtues <note>In this context, "virtues" refers to the innate powers, qualities, or occult properties of a thing.</note> of things are present in some according to their species: such as boldness and courage in the lion and the rooster; fearfulness in the hare and the lamb; rapacity or greed in the wolf; treachery and deceit in the fox; flattery in the dog; avarice in the raven and the crow; pride in the horse; anger in the tiger and the wild boar; sadness and melancholy in the cat; lust in the sparrow, and so on with similar examples. Indeed, the greatest part of natural virtues follows the species. 

However, certain virtues are present in things according to the individual. For example, there are certain men who so vehemently abhor the sight of a cat that they cannot look upon one without a most heavy horror; this horror is certainly not present in them according to the human species, as is manifest. And Avicenna <note>A famous Persian polymath and physician (c. 980–1037 AD)</note> tells that in his own time there lived a man from whom all venomous creatures would flee; any that happened to bite him would die, while he himself remained entirely unharmed. Albertus <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280 AD), a Dominican friar and philosopher known for his writings on natural science</note> also reports that in the city of Cologne <note>original: "Agrippina Colonia"</note> he saw a girl who hunted spiders for food, and by eating that kind of food she was remarkably well-nourished and delighted. Likewise, there is boldness in a prostitute and fearfulness in a thief. In this way, philosophers say that a certain individual who has never suffered from a sickness can grant health to all; thus they say that the bone of a dead man who never had a fever, if hung over a patient, frees them from a quartan fever <note>A fever (often associated with malaria) where the paroxysm occurs every fourth day.</note>. There are also many singular virtues in individuals infused by the celestial bodies, as we have shown above.

<meta>This page continues Agrippa’s exploration of "Natural Magic," specifically how specific objects in nature—animals, plants, and minerals—possess hidden powers. While the previous page focused on the "antipathies" or natural enmities between different species (like the donkey and the bird, or the elephant and the ram), this page shifts to how these magical virtues are distributed within the physical body of a thing—whether they reside in the whole object or only in specific parts like the eyes or the heart.</meta>

# OF OCCULT PHILOSOPHY.

### ¶ That natural virtues are present in some things through their whole substance, but in others only in certain of their particles or members, Chapter XX.

<margin>Faculty of virtue.</margin>
<note>The large initial 'V' is accompanied by a small 'r' in the left margin, indicating the word should be 'Rursus'.</note>Furthermore, you must consider that the virtues of things are present in some through the whole—that is, according to their entire substance or all of their parts. For example, that little fish, the echeneis <note>original: "echeneis"; the remora or suckerfish, famously believed in antiquity to be able to stop a ship mid-voyage by clinging to its hull</note>, which is said to stop a ship by its touch alone, does not do this through any one specific part, but through its entire substance. Likewise, the hyena possesses a quality through its entire substance such that dogs become struck dumb by the contact of its shadow. So too, celandine <note>original: "chelidonia"; a plant in the poppy family traditionally used to treat eye ailments</note> benefits the sight not through any one part, but through all its parts: no less in the root than in the leaves and seed; and so it is with similar things. On the other hand, certain virtues are present in things according to specific parts—for instance, only in the tongue, or the eyes, or some other limbs or parts. Thus, in the eyes of the basilisk and the catablepa <note>original: "catablepae"; a legendary Ethiopian beast said to have a head so heavy it always looks down, killing anyone who meets its gaze</note>, there is a most violent power of killing men as soon as it sees them. A similar power exists in the eyes of the hyena: whatever animal it gazes upon remains fixed to the spot, stunned, and unable to move itself. A similar power is in the eyes of certain wolves; if they see a person first, that person is stunned and becomes so hoarse that if they wish to cry out, they find they have no use of their voice. Virgil mentions this where he sings:

-> The voice also flees Moeris <-

> Now it flees him; the wolves saw Moeris first. <note>original: "Vox quoque Moerim / Iam fugit ipsa, lupi Moerim videre priores"; from Virgil's Eclogues, 9.53-54</note>

<margin>Why sorcerers primarily use the eyes and not other parts. Whom dogs flee.</margin>
So too there were certain women in Scythia, and among the Illyrians and Triballi, who were said to kill whenever they looked upon someone in anger. Similarly, we read that the Telchines were a people of Rhodes who changed all things for the worse with their gaze, for which reason they were submerged by Jupiter. Therefore, sorcerers of this kind use the eyes of such animals in eye-salves to perform similar effects through fascination <note>In this context, "fascination" refers to the "Evil Eye" or the ability to cast a spell through sight</note>. In a similar way, ants flee from the heart of a hoopoe bird, but not from its head, foot, or eyes. So also, the gall of a spotted lizard rubbed in water is said to gather weasels together, but not its tail or head. The gall of goats, shut in a bronze vessel and buried in the earth, gathers frogs; and a goat’s liver is contrary to all butterflies and moths. Dogs flee from one who carries the heart of a dog; and foxes will not touch poultry if they have eaten a fox's liver. Thus, many things have diverse virtues dispersed differently through their various parts, just as they are infused from the heavens according to the diversity of what can receive them—much like how in the human body, the bones receive nothing but life, whereas the eyes receive sight, and the ears receive hearing. And there is in the human body a certain very small bone, which the Hebrews call <term>Luz</term> <note>Luz: In Jewish folklore, an indestructible bone (often identified as the coccyx or a bone in the skull) from which the body will be reconstructed at the resurrection</note>, about the size of a peeled chickpea, which is subject to no corruption; it is not even conquered by fire, but is always preserved unharmed. From this bone (as they say), just as a plant grows from a seed, our animal body will sprout again in the resurrection of the dead. These virtues are not explained by reason, but by experience.

<summary>This chapter explains that magical or natural powers may reside in an entire creature or plant, or be concentrated in specific organs, such as the eyes of a basilisk or the "Luz" bone in humans. Agrippa emphasizes that these properties are discovered through observation and tradition rather than logic.</summary>

# BOOK ONE.

### ¶ Concerning the virtues of things which are in them only while living, and those which remain in them even after death. Chapter XXI.

<margin>
A remedy for quartan fever.
Excellent for memory and divination.
</margin>
Furthermore, it is necessary to know that certain properties exist in things only during life, while others remain even after death. Thus the remora <note>original: "echeneis"; a small fish believed to be able to stop ships</note> halts ships, and the basilisk <note>original: "regulus"</note> and the catablepa <note>a legendary Ethiopian beast</note> kill with their gaze while they are alive; yet after death, they perform no such thing. Similarly, it is handed down that in cases of colic <note>original: "torminibus"; severe abdominal pain</note>, if a live duck is placed against the belly, the disease passes into the duck and the duck dies. Archytas <note>A Greek philosopher and mathematician</note> says something similar: if a heart is taken, recently extracted from an animal and still warm and living, and is hung over a patient suffering from quartan fever <note>a fever that recurs every four days, often associated with malaria</note>, it drives the fever away. Likewise, if anyone swallows the heart of a hoopoe, a swallow, a weasel, or a mole while it is still alive and palpitating, it grants them memory, recollection, understanding, and the power of divination.

<margin>Things to be collected from animals while they remain alive.</margin>
From this arises a general precept: that whatever things are to be collected from animals—whether stones, limbs, or excrements such as hair, dung, or claws—these ought to be taken from the animals while they are still living, and even, if possible, while they remain alive afterward. Hence they instruct that when you collect the tongue of a frog, you should return the frog alive to the water. If you collect the tooth or the eye of a wolf, they must be taken without killing the wolf, and so it is with similar things.

<margin>
A remedy for ophthalmia.
For toothaches.
To suppress the barking of dogs.
</margin>
Thus Democritus <note>The Ancient Greek "laughing philosopher," frequently cited in magical texts for his natural observations</note> relates that if someone extracts the tongue of a living sea-frog <note>likely the anglerfish or monkfish</note> without any other part of the body adhering to it, and after letting the frog back into the sea, places that tongue over the heart-palpitations of a sleeping woman, she will answer truthfully to whatever she is asked. In a similar way, they promise that the eyes of frogs, bound to a patient before sunrise—provided the frogs are returned to the water blind—will drive away tertian fevers. They also report that these same eyes, bound in a deer skin along with the flesh of a nightingale <note>original: "liscinie," likely a variation of "lusciniae"</note>, will cause wakefulness and put sleep to flight. Similarly, the spine of a stingray <note>original: "pastinacae radius"</note> bound to the navel is said to make childbirth easy, provided it was taken while the fish was alive and the fish was then returned to the sea. They also say that the right eye of a serpent, if bound on, is beneficial against eye-fluxes <note>original: "epiphoras"; watery or inflamed eyes</note>, if the serpent is let go alive. And there is a certain fish, or rather a very large serpent called the *myrus* <note>a type of sea eel</note>, whose eye, if plucked out and bound to the forehead of a patient, is said to cure ophthalmia; the eye is said to regrow in the fish, but the fish will lose its sight if it is not released alive. Likewise, the teeth of all serpents, when taken from them while living and hung over a patient, are said to cure quartan fever. Similarly, if a tooth is taken from a living mole and the mole is released, it cures toothaches; and dogs will not bark at those who carry the tail of a weasel that has been set free. Democritus also tells that the tongue of a chameleon, if snatched while it is living, is powerful for the outcome of legal trials, and is also helpful to women in labor when kept near the house; however, one must take care not to bring it inside the house, for that would be most dangerous.

<margin>Those things which retain their powers after death.</margin>
There are still other properties that remain after death. Regarding these, the Platonists <note>Followers of Plato's philosophy, who believed in a hierarchy of Form and Matter</note> say that in things where the "Idea" <note>the divine spark or formal essence</note> is less submerged in the "Matter," those things retain their powers even after they have died and passed away.

### ¶ How lower things are subject to celestial bodies, and how the human body, and even human occupations and manners, are distributed among the stars and signs. Cap. XXII.

It is manifest that all lower things are subject to higher ones, and in a certain way (as Proclus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who argued for the interconnectedness of all levels of reality</note> says) they exist within each other: namely, the highest things in the lowest, and the lowest in the highest. Thus in heaven there are earthly things, but in a celestial manner and cause; and on earth there are celestial things, but in a terrestrial manner, namely, according to their effect. So we say there are certain "solar" beings here, and certain "lunar" ones, in which the sun and moon cause something of their virtue. From this, such things receive many operations and properties similar to the operations of the stars and signs to which they are subject: thus we know solar things are related to the heart and the head, because of Leo being the house of the Sun, and Aries the Sun's exaltation. Likewise, Martial <note>related to the planet Mars</note> things contribute to the head and the testicles, because of Aries and Scorpio. 
<margin>A remedy for drunkenness.</margin>
Hence, for those intoxicated with wine, whose senses falter and whose head aches, placing the testicles in cold water, or washing them with vinegar, is an immediate remedy. But concerning these things, it is necessary to know how the human body is distributed among the planets and signs. 
<margin>The parts of the human body and which planets they are subject to.</margin>
Know therefore, according to the tradition of the Arabs, that the Sun presides over the brain, the heart, the thigh, the marrow, the right eye, and the spirit of life. But Mercury presides over the tongue and the mouth, and the other instruments or organs of the senses, both internal and external; furthermore, over the hands, feet, shins, nerves, and the power of imagination <note>original: "virtuti phantasticę"</note>. Saturn presides over the spleen, the milt, the stomach, the bladder, the womb, and the right ear, and the receptive power itself. Jupiter presides over the liver and the more fleshy part of the stomach, as well as the belly and the navel: 
<margin>Why the image of a navel was in the temple of Jupiter Ammon.</margin>
whence antiquity hands down that an image of a navel was placed in the temple of Jupiter Ammon <note>The famous oracle in the Libyan desert where Alexander the Great was declared a god; the deity was often symbolized by an "omphalos" or navel-stone</note>. There are besides those who attribute to him also the ribs, the chest, the intestines, the blood, the arms, the right hand, the left ear, and the natural power; but to the blood and the bla... <note>catchword "ves" refers to "vesicam" or bladder</note>

From this, a remedy applied to one benefits the other; just as when the feet are warmed, the pain in the belly ceases.

Therefore, mindful of this order, you should know that things which are subject to any of the planets have a certain unique aspect or inclination toward the members attributed to that same planet, and especially to its own houses and exaltations <note>Astrological positions where a planet's influence is considered most powerful.</note>; for the other dignities, such as triplicities, terms, and faces, have little influence in this matter. Furthermore, things belonging to Saturn contribute to sadness and melancholy. Things of Jupiter to joy and dignity. Things of Mars to boldness, strife, and anger. Things of the Sun to glory, victory, and courage. Things of Venus to love, lust, and desire. Things of Mercury to eloquence. Things of the Moon to the common life of the people.

### ¶ How it is to be known which natural things are subject to which stars, and which things are solar. Chapter XXIII.

Which thing is subject to which star or sign is very difficult to know; however, they are recognized through the imitation of the rays, the motion, or the shape of the higher [celestial] bodies; some also by colors and odors, and some by the effects of their operations which harmonize with certain stars. BOOK ONE.

<margin>
The Pyrophilus.
</margin>
...[The eagle-stone] possesses power from the Sun against poisons and pestilential vapors; it makes the wearer safe and pleasing, contributes to wealth and intellect, and strengthens the heart: held in the mouth, it greatly cheers the spirit. Likewise, the **Pyrophilus** <note>literally "fire-lover"</note> is a reddish mixed stone; Aesculapius, as Albertus Magnus <note>a famous 13th-century philosopher and scientist</note> testifies, mentions this stone in one of his letters to Octavius Augustus, saying that a certain poison is of such extreme coldness that it preserves the heart of a slain man from burning; thus, if it is placed in fire for some time, it is turned into a stone: and this is that which is called the Pyrophilus because of the fire. It has a wonderful power against poisons, and it makes the wearer glorious and formidable to their adversaries. But above all, there is a solar stone which Apollonius <note>Apollonius of Tyana, a 1st-century philosopher</note> is said to have found, named the **Pantaura** <note>meaning "all-breeze" or "all-gold"</note>, which attracts other stones to itself just as a magnet attracts iron; it is most effective against all poisons, and is called the *Pantherus* by others because it resembles the spotted animal, the panther: for this reason it is also called *Pantochras* because it contains all colors. Aaron <note>likely referring to a traditional lapidary author</note> calls it the *Evanthus*. Furthermore, solar stones include the topaz, chrysoprase, ruby, and the balas ruby <note>original: "balagius"</note>. Likewise, solar substances include orpiment <note>a yellow arsenic mineral</note> and anything of golden color and great brilliance.

Among plants and trees, solar things are those which turn toward the sun, such as the **heliotrope**, and those which fold their leaves as the Sun recedes and unfold them gradually when it rises: such as the **lotus**, which some testify to be a solar shrub by the shape of its fruit and leaves. So too are the Peony, celandine, citron tree, ginger, gentian, dittany, and also vervain, which is excellent for prophecy and purification, and for putting evil spirits <note>original: "cacodaemones"</note> to flight. The Laurel is also sacred to Phoebus <note>a name for the sun god Apollo</note>, as are the cedar, the palm, the ash, the ivy, and the vine: and whatever things repel poisons and lightning, and being evergreen do not fear the cold of winter. Likewise, solar plants include mint, mastic, zedoary, saffron, balsam, amber, musk, yellow honey, aloe wood, cloves, cinnamon, aromatic calamus, pepper, frankincense, marjoram, and rosemary <note>original: "Libanotis"</note>: which Orpheus calls the "incense of the sun."

Among animals, solar ones are the magnanimous, courageous, and those eager for victory and glory: such as the **lion**, king of beasts; the crocodile, the lynx, the ram, the goat, and the bull, king of the herds, which was consecrated to the sun by the Egyptians at Heliopolis, and whom they call Mnevis <note>original: "veritẽ", likely a corruption of Mneuin/Mnevis</note>; and the Apis bull in Memphis, and in Hermonthis a bull named Phatis <note>original: "Patim"</note>. The wolf is also sacred to Apollo and Latona.

<margin>
Why the Egyptians depicted the Dog-headed Baboon on water-clocks.
</margin>
Furthermore, the **cynocephalus** <note>a dog-headed baboon</note> is solar, which barks twelve times a day, once every hour, and at the time of the equinox urinates twelve times every hour; it does the same at night, which is why the Egyptians used to carve it on their water-clocks <note>original: "hydrologiis"</note>. Also solar among birds are the **phoenix**, the unique bird, and the **eagle**, queen of birds. Likewise the vulture, and the swan: and those birds which applaud the rising sun with certain hymns as if calling to it, such as the cock and the crow; the hawk also, because in Egyptian theology it is a symbol of spirit and light, is numbered among solar things by Porphyry <note>a 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher</note>. ### Which things are subject to the Moon, Chapter 24.

<margin>1</margin> Among the elements, those that are **Lunar** are the earth and then water—both of the sea and of rivers—and all moist things: the juices of trees and animals, especially white ones, such as egg whites, fats, sweats, phlegm <note>original: "pituite"</note>, and the superfluities of bodies. Among flavors, the salty and the tasteless. Among metals, silver. Among stones, its own is the **crystal**, the silver marcasite, and all white and green stones. Likewise, the **selenites** stone <note>the moonstone</note>, which is a translucent white with a honey-like glow, imitating the lunar movement and containing within itself the figure of the moon, reflecting its shape as it increases or decreases day by day. Likewise, pearls, which are generated from droplets of water in shells; similarly, crystal and beryl.

<margin>Lunar trees and plants.</margin> Among plants and trees, the lunar ones are the **selenotropion** <note>literally "moon-turner"</note>, which turns toward the moon just as the heliotrope turns toward the sun; and the **palm tree**, which sends out a new branch at every rising of the moon. Also the **hyssop**, a species of rosemary <note>original: "roris marini"</note>, which is the smallest of trees and the largest of plants, participating in the nature of both. The **chaste tree** <note>original: "agnus castus"</note> is also lunar, as is the olive. Similarly, the herb **chinostares**, which grows and shrinks with the moon—not only in its moisture and power, but in its physical substance and the number of its leaves. This is a quality that individual plants share in some way, except for **Martial onions** <note>onions associated with the planet Mars</note>, which alone have the contrary power of increasing or decreasing their strength against the moon's phases. In the same way, among birds, the bird of Saturnian origin <note>likely referring to the owl or a similar nocturnal bird</note> is most hostile to both the moon and the sun at once.

<margin>Lunar animals.</margin> Lunar animals are those that enjoy human company and those that excel in the various natural impulses of love and hate, such as **dogs** of every kind. The **chameleon** is also lunar, for it always takes on a color similar to the object before it, just as the moon varies its nature according to the zodiac sign in which it is found. Likewise, lunar creatures include sows, does, goats, and any animals that observe and imitate lunar movement, such as the **baboon** <note>original: "cynocephalus" or "dog-head"</note> and the **panther**. Indeed, it is said that the panther has a spot on its shoulder like the moon, growing into circles and curving its horns in the same fashion. **Cats** are lunar, for their eyes become larger or smaller according to the phases of the moon. Other such things include menstrual blood, with which mages perform many wonders and monstrous acts.

## ¶ Which things are subject to Jupiter. Chapter XXVI.

Jovial things among the elements are the air; among the humors, blood and the spirit of life; also everything that pertains to the increase, nourishment, and growth of life. Among flavors, those that are sweet and pleasant. Among metals, tin, silver, and gold, because of their balanced temperament. Among stones, the hyacinth <note>zircon or sapphire</note>, beryl, sapphire, tutty <note>zinc oxide</note>, emerald, green jasper, and colors that are perpetually green or airy. Among plants and trees: the houseleek <note>original: "barba Iovis," or Jupiter's beard</note>, basil, bugloss, mace, spikenard, mint, mastic, elecampane <note>original: "inola"</note>, violet, darnel, henbane, and the poplar. Also those known as "fortunate trees," such as the oak, the winter oak, the holm oak, the beech, the hazel, the poplar, the service tree, the white fig, the pear, the apple, the vine, the plum, the ash, the cornel cherry, as well as the olive and its oil. Furthermore, corn, barley, wheat, raisins, licorice, sugar <note>original: "zaccarum"</note>, and all things whose sweetness is manifest and subtle, yet sharing something of a dry and sharp flavor, such as almonds, pine nuts, hazelnuts, and pistachios; also the roots of the peony, myrobalans <note>a medicinal plum-like fruit</note>, rhubarb, and manna. Orpheus also attributes the resin storax <note>original: "styracem"</note> to him. Among animals, those are Jovial which display a certain dignity and wisdom, and those that are gentle, easily disciplined, and of good character, such as the stag, the bull, and the elephant; and all tame animals, such as the sheep and the lamb. Among birds, those of a temperate complexion, such as hens and egg yolks. Also the partridge, pheasant, swallow, and pelican. Likewise the hoopoe <note>original: "cucupha"</note> and the stork, which are most pious birds and symbols of gratitude.
<margin>The eagle, the emblem of emperors, is a symbol of justice.</margin>
The eagle is also consecrated to him, being the Imperial emblem and a symbol of justice tempered with mercy. Among fish, the dolphin, the anchovy, and the sheatfish <note>original: "silurus"</note>, because of their devotion.

## ¶ Which things relate to Mars. Chapter XXVII.

Martial things among the elements are Fire; likewise all things that are burnt and sharp. Among the humors, it is yellow bile <note>original: "cholera"</note>. Among flavors, those that are bitter, pungent, stinging the tongue, and those said to be "tear-inducing." Among metals, iron and red brass <note>or copper</note>; and all things fiery, red, and sulfurous. Among stones: the diamond <note>original: "adamas"</note>, the magnet <note>lodestone</note>, bloodstone <note>original: "lapis sanguinaris"</note>, jasper, variegated stones, and amethyst. Among plants and trees: hellebore, garlic, euphorbium, cardamoms <note>original: "cartabana"</note>, ammoniacum, radish, spurge laurel, monkshood <note>original: "napellus"</note>, scammony, and all poisonous things resulting from an excess of heat. Also those armed with stinging thorns or those which burn, prick, or blister the skin upon contact, such as the thistle, the nettle, and spearwort <note>original: "flammula"</note>. Also those which, when eaten, force out tears, such as the onion, the shallot, the leek, mustard, and castoreum <note>a medicinal secretion from beavers</note>. Finally, all thorny trees, and the cornel cherry, which is sacred to Mars.

### ¶ That the whole sublunary world, and those things which are in it, are distributed to the planets. Cap. XXX.

<margin>
To Mercury and the starry heaven, while the whole mass is to Saturn. But in the middle
</margin>
Furthermore, whatever is found in the whole world is affected according to the domains of the planets and receives its power: thus in fire, they vitalize light; heat belongs to the Sun, and to Mars on the earth; the varied surface belongs to the Moon; and in the elements where they rule, the airy moisture is subject to Jupiter, the watery indeed to the Moon, while the mixed nature obeys Mercury and Venus. By a similar reasoning, the active causes follow the Sun, but the matter follows the Moon; the fertility of active causes follows Jupiter, the fertility of matter follows Venus; a swift dispatch toward the effect follows Mars and Mercury: the former because of vehemence, the latter because of dexterity and multiform power; however, the permanent continuation of all things is dedicated to Saturn. But also in the number of vegetables, everything bearing fruit is from Jupiter, and everything bearing flowers is from Venus, and every seed and bark is from Mercury, but every root is from Saturn, and all wood from Mars, and the leaves from the Moon. Hence all things that bear fruit and do not bloom belong to Saturn and Jupiter; but those which bloom and produce seeds, but not fruit, belong to Venus and Mercury; those indeed which are produced spontaneously without seed are from the Moon and Saturn. All beauty is from Venus, and strength from Mars: and each one of the planets rules and disposes that which is assimilated to it. Similarly in stones, weight, gluey consistency, and astringency are from Saturn; benefit and temperament from Jupiter; hardness from Mars; life from the Sun; grace and beauty from Venus; occult virtue from Mercury; common benefit from the Moon.

### ¶ On the seals and characters of natural things. Ch. XXXIII.

All stars have their own proper natures, properties, and conditions, whose seals and characters they produce through their rays even in these inferior things—in the elements, in stones, in plants, in animals, and in their members. Hence, every single thing receives a special seal or character impressed upon it from the harmonic disposition of its particular irradiating star. This mark is a signifier of that star or harmony, containing within itself a special virtue that differs from others in genus, species, or number, depending on the underlying matter. Thus, every thing has its own character impressed upon it by its star for some peculiar

<margin>
Every thing has its own character.
</margin>

effect, especially by that star which holds the primary dominion over it. These characters contain and retain the proper natures, virtues, and roots of their stars, and they produce similar operations in other things upon which they reflect. They provoke and assist the influences of their stars, whether of the planets, the fixed stars, or even the celestial images and signs—provided, of course, they are fashioned in the proper material, at the proper time, and with the proper ceremonies. Considering this, the ancient sages (who labored greatly to investigate the hidden conditions of things) noted the images, figures, seals, and characters of the stars, which nature itself depicted in these inferior things through the stars' rays: some in stones, some in plants (in the joints and nodes of twigs), and others in various members of animals. For the laurel, the lotus, and the heliotrope—which are solar plants—show the characters of the **Sun** in their roots and cut nodes. <margin>Signs and seals of celestial influences are found within human nature.</margin>
Since human wisdom can perceive only a few things, we shall now leave aside those signs that can be investigated in plants, stones, and other things, as well as in the limbs of many animals. Indeed, these marks are all the more effective the less they are removed from celestial nature. However, just as the number of stars is known to God alone, so too are their effects and signs upon these lower things; for this reason, no human intellect can ascend to a full knowledge of them. From this, very few things have become known, which the ancient Philosophers and Chiromancers <term>Chiromancers: practitioners of palmistry, the art of reading the lines and marks of the hand to determine character or destiny</term> attained partly through reason and partly through experience; many things still lie hidden, locked away in the treasuries of nature. These signs remain always the same and consistent with themselves across all nations and languages. Later Chiromancers, both ancient and more recent, discovered many other signs beyond these; whoever wishes to know them should seek out their volumes. It is sufficient here to have shown from where the characters of nature derive their origin and in what things they are to be sought.

## How by natural things and their virtues, we are able to allure and attract the influences and virtues of the celestial bodies. Chapter XXXIIII.

<margin>n</margin>Now, if you wish to receive the virtue of a star or from any part of the world, by applying those things which belong to this star, you undergo its proper influence—just as wood, prepared with sulfur, pitch, and oil, is ready to catch fire. Nevertheless, when you properly apply many things to a certain species or individual, which are scattered but conform to the same Idea <note>In the Platonic sense, an "Idea" is the perfect, spiritual archetype of a thing that exists in the divine mind.</note> and star among themselves, a singular gift is soon infused from that Idea into the matter so opportunely prepared, through the mediation of the World Soul <term>World Soul: *Anima Mundi*, the spiritual essence thought by Neoplatonists to permeate the universe and connect the physical and spiritual realms</term>. I say "opportunely prepared," namely under a harmony similar to the harmony that had originally infused a certain virtue into that matter.

For although things possess some virtues of the kind we have spoken of, yet those virtues are so hidden that a result completed by them is rarely seen. But just as the crushing of a mustard seed excites its hidden sharp heat; and as the heat of fire brings into view letters written with onion juice or milk, which were previously hidden; and as letters inscribed on stone with the fat of a goat—entirely invisible—come forth and stand out as if sculpted when the stone is submerged in vinegar; and just as the touch of a broom or a strawberry tree <note>Original: *arbuti*. Reference to ancient folklore regarding plants that stir dormant states or "madness."</note> rouses a dormant fury; so too does celestial harmony itself bring forth, excite, strengthen, and make manifest the virtue hidden in matter. It brings it, so to speak, from potentiality into action when things are properly exposed to it under a celestial opportunity. 

For example: if you wish to attract virtue from the Sun, seek those things which are solar—among vegetables, plants, metals, stones, and animals. These are to be applied, these are to be taken, especially those which are higher in the solar order, for these contribute more. In this way, you will draw a singular gift from the Sun through the rays of the Sun received at the right time, and through the Spirit of the World <term>Spirit of the World: *spiritus mundi*, a subtle substance that acts as the "glue" between the material world and the World Soul</term>.

### ¶ Of the mixtures of natural things with one another, and their utility. Chapter XXXV.

<margin>A twofold power in mixture.</margin>
We have discovered that in lower nature <note>The physical world here on Earth, as opposed to the higher, celestial realms.</note>, the various gifts and talents of the celestial bodies are not all found gathered within a single object. Instead, they are dispersed among many different species around us. For example, there are many "solar" things <note>Items believed to be under the astrological influence of the Sun.</note>, yet no single one of them contains every one of the Sun’s virtues; rather, each one possesses different properties from the Sun. Therefore, it is sometimes necessary in our magical operations to create mixtures. If a hundred or a thousand virtues of the Sun are scattered through as many plants, animals, and similar things, we can "melt" these down together and reduce them into a single form. In this new form, we will see all those mentioned virtues united and contained. There is, moreover, a twofold power in such a mixture. One is that which was already implanted in the individual parts, which is celestial. The other is acquired through a certain and skillful mixing of many things blended together according to specific proportions, which harmonize with the heavens under a specific constellation <note>A specific arrangement of stars and planets chosen for its favorable influence.</note>. This power descends through a certain similarity and relationship of the things to one another and to the higher powers, especially when the "receiver" (the mixture) is properly adjusted to its "actor" (the celestial influence). Thus, from a specific composition of herbs, vapors, and similar things—prepared both physically and astronomically—there results a certain common form, endowed with the gifts of many stars. We see this in the honey of bees, which is collected from the juices of countless flowers and reduced into one form, containing the virtue of all of them through the almost divine and wonderful craftsmanship of these flies <note>original: "muscarum"; Agrippa uses the term "flies" generally to describe bees.</note>.

<margin>Artificial honey.</margin>
It is no less wonderful what Eudoxus of Cnidus <note>A Greek astronomer and student of Plato.</note> relates concerning artificial honey, which a certain race of giants in Libya knew how to produce from flowers. It was so excellent that it seemed to differ very little from the honey of bees. Furthermore, every mixture composed of many parts is most perfect when it is so bonded together that it becomes one, consistent throughout, and not easily separated. We sometimes see stones and diverse bodies joined and united by a certain natural force so that they appear entirely as one. Examples include two trees joined by grafting, or oysters fused with stones by a hidden power of nature. Animals have even been seen turned into stone <note>Likely a reference to fossils, which were often viewed as magical transformations.</note>, so united with the substance of the stone that they appeared to form a single, uniform body. Thus ebony, among the types of trees, is sometimes wood and sometimes stone. Therefore, when someone crafts a mixture from many materials under celestial influences, the variety of celestial actions on one hand, and the gathered natural powers on the other, produce wonderful results through ointments, eye-salves, fumigations <note>The practice of burning incense or herbs to produce magical smoke.</note>, and the like. These are described in the books of Chiramis, Archytas, Democritus, and Hermes—specifically the one titled *Alchorat*—and many others.

### ¶ On the union of mixed things, and the introduction of a more noble form and of sensitive life. Chapter XXXVI.

It must be understood that the more noble a thing’s **form** is, the more ready and inclined that thing is to receive, and the more powerful it is to act <note>original: "nobilior forma". In Renaissance philosophy, "form" refers to the internal essence or soul of a thing that gives it its specific properties.</note>. Thus, the miraculous wonders of things are rendered beyond comprehension when materials are mixed and prepared at the right times to be brought to life. Life is drawn into them from the stars, along with a **sensitive soul**, as if it were a more noble form <note>original: "animamq; sensibilem". A "sensitive" or "sensible" soul is the level of soul that grants animals the ability to feel and move, as opposed to the "vegetative" soul of plants.</note>. Indeed, there is such great power in these prepared materials—which we see obtain life only when a perfect mixture of qualities has finally broken the previous **contrariety** <note>The conflict between opposing qualities like hot and cold or wet and dry.</note>. They achieve perfection in life to the degree that their **complexion** <note>The specific balance of qualities or "humors" within a body.</note> is further removed from this opposition. Heaven, being the all-powerful cause from the beginning of any generated thing, bestows celestial influences and wonderful gifts along with life itself, once the material has reached perfect **concoction** and **digestion** <note>original: "concoctione materie & digestione". These are alchemical terms for the "cooking" or natural ripening of matter until it is ready for a new form.</note>. This occurs because within life and the sensitive soul, there is a capacity to conceive more noble and sublime virtues. Furthermore, celestial virtue sometimes lies dormant, like sulfur kept far from a flame; but in living bodies, it often blazes forth like ignited sulfur, filling everything nearby with its vapor. In this way, certain wonderful works are produced, such as those read about in the book of **Nemith**, which is also titled *The Laws of Pluto* <note>An obscure magical or alchemical text often cited in the Middle Ages and Renaissance.</note>. For generations of this kind are **monstrous** because they are not produced according to the standard laws of nature.

<margin>The various procreation of different animals.</margin> 
Indeed, we know that mosquitoes are generated from worms, wasps from horses, bees from calves and oxen, and scorpions from a buried crab with its legs removed. From a roasted duck ground into powder and thrown into water, frogs are generated. If, however, the duck is cooked in a pastry, cut into pieces, and left in a damp, underground place, toads are generated. From the herb **basil** <note>original: "basilicone"</note> crushed between two stones, scorpions are generated. 

<margin>Serpents from the hair of women.</margin> 
And from the hair of a menstruating woman placed under dung, serpents are made. A hair from a horse’s tail thrown into water conceives life and turns into a harmful worm. There is even a craft by which, in an egg being sat upon by a hen, a form similar to a human is generated. I have seen this and know how to compose it; magicians claim it is effective with wonderful virtues, and they call this the **true mandrake** <note>Agrippa is describing a "homunculus," an artificially created miniature human-like being, which he distinguishes from the natural mandrake plant.</note>. 

It is necessary, therefore, to know which materials—whether natural, started by art, or perfected, and whether gathered from many sources—can receive specific celestial influences. For the **congruity** of natural things to celestial things is enough for us to draw influence from them. Since nothing prevents the heavens from diffusing their light to the lower things, they permit no matter to be devoid of their virtue. 

<margin>The binding of matter to the Soul of the World.</margin> 
Therefore, however much matter is perfect and pure, it is not unsuited for celestial influence. Such is the **binding** <note>original: "colligantia"</note> and continuity of matter to the **Soul of the World** <note>original: "animã mundi". The vital spirit that Renaissance philosophers believed connected the entire universe into a single living organism.</note>, which daily flows over natural things.

### ¶ How we draw down certain celestial and vital gifts from above through specific natural and artificial preparations. Chapter XXXVII.

<margin>d</margin>
<margin>The origin of magic.</margin>
The Academic philosophers <note>Followers of Plato's Academy.</note> say, and **Hermes Trismegistus** <note>The legendary Egyptian-Greek figure credited with the foundational texts of Hermeticism and alchemy.</note>, **Iarchas the Brahmin** <note>A legendary Indian sage and sorcerer mentioned in ancient accounts of the life of Apollonius of Tyana.</note>, and the **Kabbalists** <note>original: "Mecubales." Referring to practitioners of Jewish Kabbalah, a mystical tradition of interpreting the divine structure of the universe.</note> of the Hebrews all confess, that all things beneath the sphere of the moon in this lower world are subject to generation and corruption. These same things also exist in the celestial world, but in a "celestial" manner; likewise, they exist in the intellectual world, but in a much more perfect and superior form; and finally, they exist in their most perfect state in the **Archetype** <note>original: "archetypo." In this philosophy, the Archetype is the divine mind or God, containing the original "blueprints" for all creation.</note>. In this ordered series, every lower thing corresponds to its superior, and through that to the highest, according to its kind. From the heavens, things receive that celestial power which is called the **fifth essence** <note>original: "quintam essentiam." Also known as the "quintessence" or "ether," the pure, celestial element that makes up the stars.</note>, the **spirit of the world** <note>original: "spiritum mundi." A vitalizing "glue" that connects the physical body of the world to its soul.</note>, or the "middle nature." From the intellectual world, they receive a spiritual and living vigor that transcends all mere physical qualities. Finally, from the Archetype—through these intermediate layers—they receive the original power of all perfection. Thus, every single thing can be traced back from these lower realms to the stars, from the stars to their presiding **Intelligences** <note>Spiritual beings, like angels, believed to govern the movements and powers of specific planets and stars.</note>, and from there to the Archetype itself. From this hierarchy, all magic and all occult philosophy flows. For every day, something natural is drawn out through art, and every day something divine is drawn out through nature. Observing this, the Egyptians called nature "the Great One"—that is, the magical power itself, found in the attraction of like by like and compatible things by compatible things. The Greeks called this kind of attraction, based on the mutual agreement of things with one another (the higher with the lower), **sympathy** <note>original: "συμπαθίαν" (sympathian).</note>. In this way, water agrees with earth in its coldness; air with water in its moisture; air with fire in its heat; and fire agrees with the heavens in its substance. Fire does not mix with water except through the medium of air, nor does air mix with earth except through water. In the same way, the **soul** is not joined to the **body** except through the **spirit** <note>In Renaissance psychology, the "spirit" is a thin, vaporous substance that acts as a bridge between the physical body and the immaterial soul.</note>, and the **intellect** is not joined to the spirit except through the soul. Thus we see that when nature has shaped the human body in the womb, by that very preparation it immediately draws the spirit from the universe. This spirit acts as the **fuel** <note>original: "fomes." Literally "tinder" or "kindling."</note> in the spirit and body for attaining the intelligence and mind granted by God. It is just as dryness in wood prepares it to be penetrated by oil; the oil soaked into the wood is the food for fire; and the fire itself is the vehicle for light. By these examples, we see how we can receive certain celestial gifts from above through specific natural and artificial preparations.
<margin>The agreement of things.</margin>
For stones and metals agree with herbs, and herbs with animals, and animals with the heavens, and the heavens with the Intelligences, and the Intelligences with divine properties and attributes, and ultimately with God himself, in whose likeness and image all things were created.

<margin>The wondrous binding of nature</margin>
The first image of God is the world; the image of the world is man; of man, animal; of animal, the **zoophyte** <note>original: "zoophitum." In early modern science, this referred to organisms like sponges or corals that appeared to be halfway between plants and animals.</note>; of that, the plant; of the plant, metals; and the stones of these reflect their likenesses and forms. Furthermore, in spiritual matters, the plant agrees with the beast in its power of growth, the beast with man in its senses, man with the spirit in intellect, and the spirit with God in immortality. They are joined in this way: divinity to the mind, the mind to the intellect, the intellect to intention, intention to imagination, imagination to sensation, sensation to the senses, and these finally to physical things. For such is the binding and continuity of nature that every superior power flows down through each lower thing in a long, continuous series, spreading its rays to the very last; conversely, lower things reach the highest through each of their superiors. For lower things are so connected to the superior in turn that an **influx** <note>original: "influxus." A flow of celestial or divine influence descending from the stars or higher realms into the physical world.</note> from their head—the first cause—proceeds like a stretched string down to the lowest parts. If one end is touched, the whole suddenly vibrates, and the touch resonates to the other end. When one lower thing is moved, the superior thing to which it corresponds is also moved, like strings on a well-tuned lute.

### ¶ How we may receive not only celestial and vital gifts, but even certain intellectual and divine ones from above. Chapter XXXVIII.

<margin>The mage attracts hidden things through visible ones.</margin>
<margin>Artificial divination.</margin>
The Magi teach that through lower things that conform to the superior, celestial gifts can be drawn down under the right influences of the heavens. Thus, through these celestial gifts, celestial spirits—acting as the attendants of the stars—can be reconciled and introduced to us. Therefore, when certain materials that possess the natural power of divinity (that is, those which are naturally in harmony with the higher realms) are properly gathered and combined—partly through physical means and partly through astronomical timing—gifts can be received from above. These include not only celestial or vital gifts, but even intellectual, spiritual, and divine ones. This is confirmed by **Iamblichus, Proclus, and Synesius** <note>Important Neoplatonist philosophers who wrote on theurgy and the spiritual properties of nature.</note>, along with the entire school of Platonists. **Hermes Trismegistus** <note>The legendary sage of the Hermetic tradition.</note> also writes that a statue properly constructed from specific things that correspond to a particular spirit is immediately animated by that spirit. **Augustine** <note>St. Augustine of Hippo, who discusses (and critiques) this Hermetic idea of "making gods" in his book *The City of God*.</note> also mentions this in the eighth book of *The City of God*. Such is the harmony of the world that even super-celestial things are drawn by the celestial, and supernatural things are drawn and harmonized by the natural. This is because a single "maker-power" and a shared participation in "Forms" is diffused through all things. Just as this maker-power produces visible things from hidden principles, so the mage takes visible things to attract the hidden: pure things, through the rays of the stars, through **suffumigations** <note>original: "suffumigationes." The ritual burning of incense or herbs.</note>, through lights, through sounds, and through natural objects harmonious with the heavens. Within these objects, beyond their physical qualities, there also exist incorporeal and divine principles, senses, numbers, and measures. Thus we read that the ancients were often accustomed to receive something divine and wondrous through certain natural things; for example, the stone found in the pupil of the **hyena's** eye, if held under the tongue, was said to grant the power of foretelling the future...

is said to stand still. The same is said of the **moonstone** <note>original: "selenites." A stone believed to wax and wane with the moon.</note> to have the same effect. Likewise, they say that with the **anchitis** stone, images of the gods are summoned, and with the **synochitis**, the shades of the underworld, once summoned, are held fast. The herb **aglaophotis** <note>original: "aglaoptis," also called "marmoritides." A legendary herb used for warding off demons or summoning gods.</note>—which they also call *marmoritides* because it grows in the marble of Arabia on the Persian side—produces similar effects, as Pliny tells us. He notes that the Magi use it when they wish to summon gods. There is also an herb called **theangelis**, which the Magi drink to gain the power of divination. Furthermore, there are even certain herbs by which the dead are recalled to life.

<margin>Tillo restored to life by an herb.</margin>
For this reason, the historian Xanthus tells a story of an herb called **bali**, with which a young dragon that had been killed was restored to life by its parent; and by that same herb, a certain man named **Tillo**, whom a dragon had killed, was also resuscitated. Juba likewise reports that in Arabia, a man was brought back to life with a certain herb. Truly, whether such things can actually happen by the power of herbs, or by any other natural thing acting upon a human being, we shall discuss in the following sections.

<margin>Animals can be restored to life; man not so.</margin>
However, that this can happen in other living creatures is certain and manifest. For instance, flies that have been drowned, if placed in warm ashes, come back to life. Bees that have drowned recover their life similarly in the juice of **catnip** <note>original: "nepete."</note>. Eels that have died from a lack of water, if their bodies are still intact and they are placed under manure in vinegar, with the addition of vulture's blood, will all recover their life after a few days. If someone cuts a **remora** <note>original: "Echeneim." A suckerfish legendary in antiquity for its power to stop ships; here, Agrippa cites a myth that its severed parts can reunite.</note> into pieces and throws them into the sea, they say the parts soon come together and return to life. We also know that the **pelican** recalls its dead young to life with its own blood.

### Chapter XXXIX. That we can attract worldly powers and the daemons who serve them through certain materials of the world.

<margin>Evil daemons are attracted by evil arts.</margin>
No one is ignorant of the fact that evil **daemons** <note>original: "demones." In this context, Agrippa refers to intermediary spirits that can be either good or malevolent, though here he specifies the "evil" ones.</note> can be attracted by evil and profane arts, just as Psellus relates the Gnostic magicians were accustomed to do. Among them, cursed and abominable outrages were performed, such as those once seen in the rites of **Priapus** <note>A minor Greek fertility god, often depicted with permanent arousal; his rites were famously lewd.</note> and in the service of the idol called **Panor**, to whom sacrifices were made with the private parts uncovered. Not dissimilar to these is the story—if it be truth and not fable—of the detestable heresy of the **Knights Templar**. Similar accounts are established regarding malevolent women <note>meaning witches</note>, whose elderly delusions are often found to wander into such shames. By these and similar things, evil spirits are attracted and enter into conspiracies, just as the malignant spirit said to John regarding the magician **Cynops**: "All the power of Satan dwells there, and he enters into a conspiracy with all the principalities, and we ourselves are with him. Cynops obeys us, and we in turn obey him."

<margin>Good angels are won over by good works.</margin>
On the other hand, no one is ignorant that by good works, pure minds, mystical prayers, devoted supplications, and similar things, the **supercelestial angels** are won over to us. Therefore, let no one doubt that in a similar way, through certain materials of the world, **worldly deities** <note>original: "mundana numina." These are the spiritual powers associated with the planets and the natural elements of the physical universe.</note> can also be attracted, or at least the daemons who are the ministers or followers of these powers. As **Hermes** <note>original: "Mercurius," referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of Hermeticism.</note> says, these are aerial daemons, not supercelestial, much less those that are more sublime...
