### Regarding bindings, of what kind they are, and in what ways they are usually performed. Chapter 40.

*We have spoken of the virtues and the wonderful efficacy of natural things.*

<margin>Multiple types of binding.</margin>
**d** It remains now to consider a matter of great wonder, and that is the **binding** <note>original: "ligatio." In magic, this refers to a spell that restricts, compels, or fixes a person or object into a certain state.</note> of men into love or into hatred, into sickness and health, and the like. Also the binding of thieves and robbers, so that they cannot steal in a certain place; the binding of merchants, so that they are unable to buy or sell in a certain place; the binding of an army, so that it cannot cross a certain boundary; the binding of ships, so that by no force of the winds—even with infinite sails spread to the wind—they are able to leave the harbor. Also the binding of a mill, so that it cannot be turned by any force; the binding of a cistern or a well, so that water cannot be drawn from it; the binding of a field, so that crops cannot be produced in it; the binding of a certain place, so that nothing can be built in it; the binding of fire, so that it cannot be lit in a certain place, and so that some combustible material does not burn even when placed in the strongest fire. Also the binding of lightning and storms, so that they cannot do harm. Also the binding of dogs, so that they cannot bark; the binding of birds and wild beasts, so that they cannot fly or flee; and things similar to these, which are scarcely believable, yet have often been known through experience. 

Now, bindings of this kind are performed through **sorceries** <note>original: "veneficia." In this context, it refers to magical preparations, often involving herbs or animal parts.</note>, through eye-washes <note>original: "collyria," used here for magical ointments or vision-altering substances</note>, ointments, drinks or love potions <note>original: "philtra"</note>, through tying and hanging items [as amulets], through rings, through fascinations <note>original: "fascinationes," the power to influence others via the gaze or "evil eye"</note>, through strong imaginations and ecstasies of the mind, through images and characters <note>original: "characteres," referring to specific magical signs or sigils</note>, through incantations and imprecations, through lights, through sounds, through numbers, through words and names, invocations, sacrifices, adjurations, exorcisms, consecrations, devotions, and through various superstitions and observations, and things similar to these.

By the touch [of menstrual fluid], things are harmed forever: crops become sterile when touched, grafts wither, the sprouts of gardens are scorched, and the fruit of trees falls away. The brightness of mirrors is dulled by its very sight, the edge of steel in barbers' knives is blunted, and the luster of ivory is tarnished. Even iron is immediately corrupted by rust. Bronze, when touched, takes on a heavy, foul-smelling poison and verdigris. Dogs that taste it are driven into madness, and their bite is infected with an incurable poison. Hives of bees die off, and the bees flee when the hives are touched. Linen turns black when boiled in its presence. Mares, if they are pregnant, suffer a miscarriage if they touch it; it also causes abortion in pregnant women if applied to them. Donkeys do not conceive for as many years as the grains of barley they have eaten which were touched by it. If the ash of menstrual cloths is sprinkled on laundry, it changes the color of purple garments and strips the color from flowers.

<margin>A remedy for Fever.</margin>
They say that tertian and quartan fevers <note>Tertian and quartan fevers are historical terms for malaria-like fevers that recurred every three or four days.</note> are driven away by menstrual fluid kept in the wool of a black ram and enclosed in a silver bracelet. Furthermore, it is said to be most effective for these fevers to smear the soles of the patient's feet with it; it is much more effective if the woman herself does it, even if the patient is unaware.

<margin>A remedy for the Falling Sickness.</margin>
In this way, even the attacks of the "comitial disease" <term>comitialis morbus (Falling Sickness): A historical term for epilepsy, so named because it was considered an ill omen if someone had a seizure during the 'comitia' (public assemblies) of ancient Rome.</term> are healed. Moreover, it is agreed among all that if water or drink is feared because of the bite of a mad dog, a small piece of a cloth dipped in menstrual fluid, if placed under the cup, immediately dispels that fear.

<margin>A remedy for Hydrophobia.</margin>
Furthermore, they report that if women uncover themselves during their monthly period and walk around a cornfield, caterpillars, worms, beetles, and all harmful things fall off. However, care must be taken that they do not do this at sunrise, for then the seeds will wither. Similarly, it is said to drive away hail and whirlwinds, and to be useful against lightning; Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder (23–79 AD), a Roman naturalist whose *Natural History* is the source for many of these folk beliefs.</note> himself recounts many of these things. You should know that the "poison" is greater if it occurs during a waning moon, but its power is greatest if it happens during a "silent moon" <note>original: "silente luna". This refers to the New Moon, when the moon's light is not visible.</note>. If it occurs during an eclipse of the moon or sun, it becomes incurable. It is of the greatest and most potent vigor when that purging occurs in the first years of puberty, during the first instance of virginity; at that time, everything it touches is affected by it. Indeed, if the doorposts of a house are touched by it, every evil spell <note>original: "maleficium"</note> in that house is rendered powerless. Furthermore, they say that the threads of a garment touched by it cannot even be overcome by fire, and if they are thrown into a blaze, the fire does not spread further. It is also said that if the root of a peony is given to a patient along with castoreum <note>A pungent secretion from beavers used in historical medicine.</note> and the ash of menstrual cloths, the falling sickness is cured. Furthermore, if you burn or roast a stag’s stomach and add the fumes from menstrual cloths, it is said that ballistae <note>A type of ancient missile weapon or crossbow used here in the context of hunting.</note> would be of no use for hunting. Even the hair of a menstruating woman, if placed under dung, is said to generate serpents; and if they are burned, the smell of them drives serpents away. So great is the force of this magical substance <note>original: "veneficii"</note> that it is a poison even to poisonous things.

There is also "hippomanes," a small piece of flesh not at all unknown among magical preparations. It is the size of a dried fig, black in color, and appears on the forehead of a newborn foal. If the mother does not devour it immediately, she will have a heart utterly turned away from her offspring and will not nourish it. Because of this, they say its power is greatest for inciting love, when it is turned into a powder with...

Its flower, he says, is like saffron, with a Corycian color <note>Mount Corycus was famous for its high-quality saffron.</note>, a double stalk, a cubit in height, and a root under the earth like freshly cut flesh that emits a black sap like pitch. <margin>The magical workings of the Hyena.</margin>
The **Hyena** also infects many things with its magical workings. For, as Pliny records, if doorposts are touched with its blood, the arts of deception <note>original: "prestigiarum," referring to illusions or magical tricks.</note> are said to be hindered, and the gods cannot be summoned or spoken to, no matter how one tries. Likewise, the ash of its left knucklebone boiled with the blood of a weasel makes those anointed with it hated by everyone. The same happens with a boiled eye. Again, the very end of its intestine is used against the injustices of leaders and powers, and it is powerful for the success of petitions and the outcomes of trials and lawsuits, if one carries even a little bit of it. Also, if a piece of its den is tied to the left arm and one looks at a woman, it is an aphrodisiac so immediate that she follows at once. But the skin from its forehead resists fascinations <note>The "evil eye" or malevolent enchantments.</note>.

<margin>The magical workings of the Basilisk and its blood. A remedy for enchantment. A remedy for diseases.</margin>
They say the blood of a **Basilisk** <note>A legendary serpent-king said to kill with its gaze.</note>, which they also call the **Blood of Saturn**, has such great power in magic that it grants the one carrying it success in petitions to authorities and prayers to the gods, as well as remedies for diseases and the granting of favors. They also say that a **tick**, if plucked from the left ear of a dog that is nothing but black in color, possesses great power in divining life. For if a sick person responds to the one who brings it—while the questioner stands at the feet and asks about the illness—there is certain hope for life; but they will die if they do not respond. They also say a stone bitten by a rabid dog has the power of discord if placed in a drink. And one will not be barked at by a dog if a dog’s tongue is placed in a shoe under the big toe, especially if it is joined with the herb of the same name, namely **cynoglossum** <note>Greek for "dog's tongue," a common name for the plant *Cynoglossum officinale*.</note>.

<margin>The power of a dog’s heart.</margin>
Likewise, a membrane is made from the afterbirth of a dog [that has power]; moreover, dogs flee from one who carries a dog's heart.

And Pliny relates that there are frogs known by the name of **bramble-toads** <note>original: "rubetarum"</note>, which live only among brambles and are full of sorcery <note>original: "veneficios"</note>, and that marvelous things are done with them. For he says that if a small bone from the left side is cast into cold water, it immediately begins to boil; that the attacks of dogs are restrained by it; and that love is stirred and quarrels provoked if it is added to a drink. If tied to the body, it stimulates lust. Conversely, with the small bone from the right side, boiling water is cooled and will not boil again unless the bone is removed. He notes that quartan fevers <note>A fever that recurs every third day, often associated with malaria.</note> are cured by this bone when tied in a piece of fresh snakeskin, as are other fevers, and it also inhibits love and lust. Pliny further reports that the spleen and the heart of these same frogs act as effective remedies against the very poisons made from them. It is also said that **iron** with which a man has been killed possesses a marvelous power among magical workings. For they say that if horse-bits and spurs are made from it, any horse—even the most ferocious—is very easily ruled and overcome by them. And if horseshoes were made from such iron, they say the horse becomes the swiftest and never grows weary from any labor. Furthermore, they maintain that certain characters and names ought to be inscribed upon them. They also say that if someone dips a sword with which people are beheaded into wine, whoever drinks from it will be freed from a quartan fever. They even say that a potion prepared from a **bear's brain**, and drunk from the skull of the same, induces a "bear-madness" <note>original: "ursinam rabiem"</note> such that the man who drinks it believes himself transformed into a bear, judging everything he sees under the appearance of a bear; he persists in that madness until the power of the potion is dissolved, though no other harm is perceived in his physical temperament.

### On fumigations: their logic and power. Chapter XLIII.

Certain **fumigations** <note>The practice of burning substances to produce smoke for ritual or medicinal purposes.</note> also, when adapted to the stars, have great power, insofar as they vehemently affect the air and the spirit so as to opportunely seize celestial gifts under the rays of the stars. For our own spirit <note>In this context, "spirit" refers to the "pneuma," a subtle substance that bridges the gap between the physical body and the soul.</note> is greatly transformed by vapors of this kind, since both are a type of vapor and similar to one another. The air, being easily affected by these vapors with the qualities of things both lower and celestial, and penetrating the heart <note>original: "praecordia"</note> continually and suddenly, wonderfully reduces us to similar qualities. For this reason, those about to prophesy are accustomed to use fumigations to affect the imagination; these, being in harmony with certain divine powers, prepare us to receive divine inspiration.

<margin>Fumigation leading to prophecy.</margin>
Thus they say that a fumigation made from flax seed, psyllium seed <note>The seeds of the fleawort plant.</note>, and the roots of violet and wild celery <note>original: "appii"</note> makes one see future things and contributes to prophecy. No one should wonder at how much fumigations can do in the air who hears, with Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 234–305 AD) who wrote on the nature of spirits and demons.</note>, that by certain vapors exhaling from their proper fumigations, aerial spirits <note>original: "aëreos dēmones"</note> are immediately attracted and enter in, and that thunder and lightning are induced, and similar things. Just as it is well known that the liver of a **chameleon** burned upon the highest roof-tiles incites rain and lightning; similarly, if its head and throat are burned with oak wood, they cause the crashes of rain and thunder. Fumigations are also made under opportune...

Thus, whenever we direct a work toward the Sun, we fumigate with solar substances; if toward the Moon, with lunar ones, and they did the same for the others. ### ¶ The composition of certain fumigations adapted to the planets. Chapter 44.

<s></s> **S**o we compose for the **Sun** a fumigation made from saffron, ambergris, musk, aloes-wood, balsam-wood, and from the fruits of the laurel, with cloves, myrrh, and frankincense. All of these, crushed and mixed in a certain proportion—namely, that which yields a sweeter scent—are incorporated with the brain of an eagle or the blood of a white rooster, in the form of pills or troches <note>original: "trociscorum"; small medicinal cakes or lozenges.</note>.

Indeed, we compose a **Lunar** fumigation from the dried head of a frog, the eyes of a bull, and the seed of white poppy, with frankincense and camphor, which shall be incorporated with menstrual blood or the blood of a goose.

For **Saturn**, one takes the seed of black poppy, henbane seed, mandrake root, loadstone <note>original: "lapis magnes"; a naturally magnetic mineral.</note>, and myrrh; and they are prepared with the brain of a cat or the blood of a bat.

For **Jupiter**, one takes ash-tree seed, aloes-wood, storax <note>A fragrant resin.</note>, gum benzoin <note>original: "benzac"</note>, lapis lazuli, and the tips of peacock feathers; and they incorporate these with the blood of a stork, or a swallow, or the brain of a stag.

For **Mars**, we take euphorbium, bdellium, gum ammoniac <note>original: "armeniacum"</note>, the roots of both types of hellebore, loadstone, and a little sulfur; and they are all incorporated with the brain of a stag, human blood, and the blood of a black cat.

For **Venus**, we compose a fumigation from musk, ambergris, aloes-wood, red roses, and red coral; and they are prepared with the brains of sparrows and the blood of doves.

For **Mercury**, a fumigation is made from mastic, frankincense, cloves, and the herb cinquefoil <note>original: "pentaphyllo"; literally "five-leafed" herb.</note>, as well as agate stone; and they incorporate all of these with the brain of a fox or a weasel with magpie <note>original: "pice"; likely a misspelling or variant of *picae*.</note> blood.

Furthermore, the fumigations of **Saturn** include all fragrant roots, such as costus and frankincense-herbs. The fumigations of **Jupiter** are all fragrant fruits, such as nutmeg and cloves. Of **Mars**, all fragrant woods: sandalwood, cypress, balsam, and aloes-wood. Of the **Sun**, all gums: frankincense, mastic, benzoin, storax, laudanum, as well as ambergris and musk. Of **Venus**, the flowers: roses, violets, saffron, and the like. Of **Mercury**, all the barks of woods and fruits, such as cinnamon, cassia, mace, citron peels, and laurel berries, and also any fragrant seeds. The **Moon** has for its fumigation the leaves of all vegetables, such as the Indian leaf <note>original: "folium Indum"; malabathrum, a fragrant leaf used in ancient perfumes.</note>, and the leaves of myrtle and laurel. ### ¶ Of eye-salves, ointments, love-potions, and their virtues. Chapter 45.

<term>Collyria</term> <note>Eye-salves or medicinal lotions for the eyes.</note> and ointments, by combining the powers of natural and celestial things to act upon our spirit, are able to multiply, transmute, transfigure, and transform it in various ways. Indeed, they can even induce a transposition of the powers inherent within the spirit, so that it can now act not only upon its own body, but also upon those nearby. Through visual rays, through <term>fascinations</term> <note>The "evil eye" or the power to bewitch others through a look.</note>, and through contact, it can affect others with a similar quality. Because our spirit is a subtle, pure, bright, airy, and oily vapor of the blood, it is effective to prepare eye-salves from similar vapors that harmonize more closely in substance with our spirit; for through this similarity, they more strongly entice, attract, and transform the spirit. 

Certain ointments and other preparations possess similar virtues. Hence, through contact, diseases, enchantments, or love are sometimes induced by anointing certain things, hands, or garments. Similarly, through kisses, love is induced by holding certain things in the mouth, as we read in Virgil that Venus prayed to Cupid:

> That when most happy Dido receives you into her lap
> Amidst the royal tables and the Lyæan liquor <note>Wine; Lyæus is a title for Bacchus, the god of wine.</note>,
> And she gives you her embraces and plants sweet kisses,
> You may breathe into her a hidden fire, and deceive her with your poison.

<margin>Sight is purer than hearing.</margin>
Moreover, because sight is purer and perceives more clearly than the other senses—imprinting the marks of things upon us more sharply and deeply—it is more compatible than the others with the <term>phantastic spirit</term> <note>The "spiritus phantasticus" is the part of the spirit responsible for imagination and dreams.</note>. This is evident in dreams, where visions offer themselves to us more often than sounds or other sensations. Therefore, when eye-salves transform the visual spirits, that spirit easily affects the imagination. Once the imagination is affected by various images and forms, it transmits them through that same spirit to the external sense of sight. In this case, a sensation of such images and forms is caused in the eye, just as if it were moved by external objects, so that a person thinks they see terrifying images, demons, and similar things. In this way, eye-salves are made which cause us to see...

Through bindings, suspensions, wrappings, placements, and contacts, the accidents of the body and soul are changed into sickness or health, into boldness or fear, into sadness or joy, and the like. They render the wearers graceful or terrifying, accepted or rejected, honored and beloved, or hateful and abominable. Indeed, it is believed that such passions are infused through the aforementioned methods in no different a way than is manifest in the grafting of trees, where the vital power <note>original: "virtus vitalis"; the life-force believed to animate all living things.</note> is transferred from the trunk into a shoot grafted into it, even with a different binding, provided that the contact allows them to cling to one another. So it is with the female palm tree: when it approaches the male,

its branches lean toward the male and are bent. Seeing this, the gardeners tie ropes from the male to the female; she then returns to an upright position, as if she had already attained the power of the male through the continuation of the rope. Furthermore, if anyone should touch a sea hare <note>A type of large sea slug, considered highly toxic or magical in ancient texts.</note>, either with a hand or a stick while it is in a state of decay, he suffers a failing of the mind. Similarly, they say that if a starfish is fixed to a door with fox’s blood and a copper nail,

evil medicines <note>original: "mala medicamenta"; often referring to poisons or hostile spells.</note> cannot cause harm. Now, by these examples we see how, by certain bindings or suspensions of things, and by a certain simple contact, or through the continuation of some thread, we can receive certain powers from them. However, it is necessary to know the specific law and manner of binding and suspending congruent to this art; 

<margin>Bindings and wrappings: how they ought to be done.</margin>

namely, that they be done under a certain and harmonious constellation, and that the said bindings and suspensions be made with metallic or silk threads, or from hair, nerves, or the bristles of certain animals. Wrappings, indeed, should be made in the leaves of herbs, or the skins of animals, or certain cloths and similar things, so long as the things agree with one another. For example, if you wish to procure for yourself the Solar power of some thing, you should suspend it from your neck—wrapped in a laurel leaf, or a lion’s skin, with a gold thread or yellow silk—while the Sun is reigning in the figure of the heavens. In this way, you can become the possessor of that thing's Solar power. But if you desire the power of some Saturnine thing, you should wrap it in a similar way—while Saturn is ruling—in the skin of an ass or a funeral cloth (especially if you are working toward sadness) and suspend it with a black thread. One should judge the other planets in a similar fashion.

The method of constructing rings of this kind is as follows: specifically, when a particular star rises fortunately and is favorably aspected by the Moon, or joined to it, we must take the stone and herb subject to this star, and fashion a ring from a metal conforming to this star, and set the stone in it with the herb or root placed beneath it. Finally, do not omit the inscriptions of images, names, and characters, nor the fumigations <note>The ritual practice of burning specific incense or herbs to consecrate or "charge" the object with celestial power.</note>; but we shall discuss these elsewhere, where images and characters are to be treated. Thus we read in Philostratus that Iarchas, the prince of the Indian sages, gave seven rings made according to this rule and marked with the powers and names of the seven planets to Apollonius <note>Apollonius of Tyana, a famous 1st-century Greek Neopythagorean philosopher often credited with supernatural powers.</note>. These he wore one for each day, distinguishing them according to the names of the days; by their benefit, he lived over one hundred and thirty years, furthermore always retaining the radiance of youth. In a similar way, it is read in Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus, the Jewish-Roman historian.</note> that Moses, the legislator and prince of the Hebrews, having been steeped in the magic of Egypt, crafted rings of love and of forgetfulness. There were also, according to the account of Aristotle, the rings of Battus among the Cyrenians, which served as a token of gratitude and honor. We read furthermore that a certain philosopher named Eudamus crafted rings against the bites of serpents, enchantments, and demons. Josephus relates the same concerning Solomon.

<margin>The ring of the King of the Lydians.</margin>
Moreover, we read in Plato that Gyges, the King of the Lydians, possessed a ring of wonderful and unusual power. When he turned its seal toward his palm, he became invisible to everyone while seeing all things himself; relying on the opportunity of this ring, he committed adultery with the queen, killed the king his master, and slew whoever he thought stood in his way, and in these crimes no one could see him. Finally, by the benefit of that ring, he became King of Lydia.

### On the powers of places, and which places correspond to each of the stars. Chapter XLVIII.

There are also wonderful powers in places, either resulting from the things located there, or from the influences of the stars, or arriving in some other way. For as Pliny reports concerning the cuckoo, in whatever place one first hears that bird, if the right foot is traced and that footprint is dug up, fleas will not grow wherever it is scattered. So they say that dust collected from the track of snakes, if bees are sprinkled with it, causes them to return to the hive. Similarly, dust in which a mule has rolled, when sprinkled on the body, tempers the fires of love. The very quarters of the world also pertain to this.

### ¶ On light and colors, on torches and lamps, and which colors are distributed to which stars, houses, and elements. Chapter XLIX

Light is also a highly formal quality, a simple act of intelligence, and an image: first diffused from the divine mind into all things. But in God the Father himself, who is the Father of Lights, there is the first true light; then in His Son, it is an illuminating splendor and overflowing; in the Holy Spirit, it is a burning brilliance, surpassing even the understanding—as Dionysius <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian theologian and philosopher whose works on celestial hierarchies were highly influential in the Middle Ages and Renaissance.</note> says—of the Seraphim <note>The highest rank of angels, associated with light and fire.</note>. Thus, in the angels, it is a diffused, shining intelligence and an overflowing joy beyond the limits of all reason, yet received in different degrees according to the nature of the receiving intelligence. Next, it descends into the celestial bodies, where it becomes an abundance of life and an effective propagation, as well as a visible splendor. In fire, it is a certain natural vigor implanted by the heavens. Finally, in humans, it is a lucid discourse of reason and a knowledge of divine things, entirely rational; yet even this is manifold, either by the disposition of the body, as the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle’s philosophy, who emphasized physical observation and logic.</note> hold, or, more truly, according to the pleasure of the Bestowing Cause, who divides to each as He wills. From there, it passes to the imagination <note>original: "phantasiam"</note>, though still above the senses; but finally, it becomes imaginable only to the senses, especially to that of the eyes. In the eye, it becomes visible clarity and is extended through alternating transparent bodies, in which color and reflecting beauty are formed; but in opaque bodies, it becomes a certain beneficial and generative power, penetrating even to the center, where—its rays being gathered into a narrow space—it becomes a dark heat, agonizing and boiling. Thus, all things feel the vigor of light according to their capacity, which connects all things to itself with life-giving heat; then, permeating all beings, it carries their qualities and powers through everything. Therefore, the Magi <note>Practitioners of "natural magic," which sought to use the hidden properties of the natural world.</note> forbid that the shadow of any sick person be cast upon another, or that the urine of any sick person be exposed to the sun or moon: because the penetrating rays of light, carrying harmful qualities with them from the diseased body, suddenly transfer them into what is opposite, and affect it badly with that same quality. This is the reason why those who cast spells <note>original: "fascinantes," referring to the practice of fascination or the "evil eye."</note> take care to cover the victim with their own shadow; likewise, the hyena, by the touch of its shadow, makes dogs go silent. Artificial lights are also made through lamps, torches, candles, and the like, from certain substances and liquids chosen opportunely according to the standard of the stars and composed among themselves for their harmony. When these <margin>The miraculous effect of lights.</margin> are lit and shine alone, they are accustomed to produce some wonderful and celestial effects that men often marvel at, just as Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, a Roman naturalist.</note> relates from Anaxilaus <note>A physician and Pythagorean philosopher.</note> that the discharge from a mare in heat <note>original: "virus a coitu"</note>, when lit in lamps, represents a monstrous vision of horses' heads... fictitious <note>original: "fictus," the catchword for the next page's beginning: "fictas."</note>.

->¶ On certain observations that produce marvelous virtues.<-

<margin>The effects of nail parings.</margin>
They also teach that certain acts and observations possess a specific natural power, so they believe that some diseases can sometimes be taken away or brought on in this manner. Thus they say that quartan fevers <note>A fever that returns every four days, historically associated with malaria.</note> are driven away if the nail parings of the sick person are tied to the neck of a live eel in a linen cloth, and the eel is then released back into the water. Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder (23–79 AD), a Roman naturalist whose "Natural History" is a primary source for these ancient folk remedies.</note> relates that certain nail parings from the feet and hands of the sick are mixed together to create a remedy—as they say—for quartan, tertian, or daily fevers; and if these are fixed to another person's door before sunrise, it will serve as a remedy for these diseases. In a similar way, if all the nail parings are thrown at an anthill, and the first ant begins to drag one away, they command that ant to be caught and tied around the neck, and so the disease is dispersed. They also say that something of a disease is removed by using wood struck by lightning, thrown behind one's back. For quartan fevers, they tie a fragment of a nail from a cross <note>Specifically, a nail used in a crucifixion.</note> wrapped in wool around the neck, or a rope from a cross; once the person is cured, they hide the object in a hole where the sun cannot reach it. Likewise, they affirm that scrofula <note>A swelling of the lymph nodes in the neck.</note> and parotid tumors <note>Swelling of the glands near the ear, such as in mumps.</note> are healed if the throat is touched by the hand of someone who was snatched away by an untimely death. They also say that difficult births are immediately resolved when someone throws a stone or a missile over the bed in which the pregnant woman lies, provided it is an object that has killed three animals in single strikes—specifically a man, a boar, and a bear. They also say that a military spear pulled from a man's body has the same effect if it has not touched the ground; likewise, arrows drawn from a body, if they have not touched the ground, are said to be an aphrodisiac when placed under those who are sleeping. They also say that the "comitial disease" <note>Epilepsy; so called because its occurrence was considered an ill omen that could dissolve the *comitia*, or public assemblies, of ancient Rome.</note> is healed by eating the meat of a wild beast killed with the same iron that killed a man. They say that eye defects do not occur, nor do eyes become bleary, for those who, when they wash their feet with water, touch their eyes three times with that same water. Some heal groin ailments by pulling a thread from a loom and tying it with nine or seven knots, naming a certain widow at each knot. Likewise, the spleen of a beast is stretched over those suffering in the spleen, while the one who heals says he is making a remedy for the spleen; after this, they command the spleen to be enclosed in the wall of the bedroom or in the roof and sealed with a ring, while a charm is chanted three times nine times. The same defect is cured by the urine of a green lizard, suspended in a pot before the bedroom door of the one being healed, so that the sick person touches it with their hand when going out and returning. Also, they say that the libido of the one who does it is restrained if a lizard is killed in his own urine...

### Chapter 52. Concerning the face, gesture, bodily habit, and figure; and which stars they correspond to, whence physiognomy, metoposcopy, and chiromancy—the arts of divination—derive their foundations.

<margin>How much the face and gesture affect the imagination.</margin>
Indeed, the face and gesture, the motions and positions of the body, and the figures we adopt, lead us toward receiving celestial gifts and expose us to the higher powers, producing certain effects in us. This is no different than in the case of hellebore <note>A plant used in ancient medicine, often associated with purging or treating madness.</note>; when someone is gathering this herb, whether they pull the leaf upward or downward, this very motion causes the plant to draw the humors <note>The bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) believed to determine health and temperament.</note> of the person who takes it either upward or downward. No one is ignorant of how much the face and gesture affect the sight, imagination, and the animal spirit <note>original: "spiritum animalem"; a historical term for the subtle substance that carries sensory information and motor commands through the nerves.</note>. Thus, when people come together for procreation, the faces they either make or imagine at that time usually leave an impression on the children to be born. In the same way, the merciful and joyful face of a prince in a city gladdens the people, while a fierce or sad one suddenly terrifies them. Similarly, the gesture and figure of a mourning person easily move one to pity, and the figure of a lovely person easily excites love. You should know, moreover, that these kinds of gestures and figures—as the harmonies of the body—expose the person to celestial influences no differently than scents and medicines expose the spirit, or internal passions expose the soul. For just as medicines and passions of the soul coalesce with certain celestial arrangements, so also gestures and movements of the body gain efficacy through specific celestial influxes.

<margin>Which gestures relate to certain planets.</margin>
Now, there are gestures that relate to Saturn, which are sad and mournful, such as lamentations or striking the head. Likewise, religious gestures like kneeling with the gaze fixed downward, as if pleading; striking the chest and similar expressions belonging to an austere and Saturnine man, such as the Satirist <note>The Roman poet Persius (Satire 3, lines 79-81).</note> describes:

> With head bowed low, and fixing his eyes on the ground,
> When he gnaws on murmurs within himself and a mad silence,
> And words are weighed out from an outstretched lip.

Those that relate to Jupiter, however, are cheerful and honorable faces, and gestures of honor: the joining of hands, as if applauding or praising; likewise, kneeling with the head raised upward, as if worshiping. To Mars relate sharp, fierce, cruel, angry, and grim gestures and similar expressions. To the Sun <note>original: "Solares"</note> relate courageous and honorable faces, and similar expressions; also walks and kneeling on a single knee, as if honoring a king. To Venus belong dances, embraces, laughter, and faces that are lovely and joyful. Mercurial [gestures]...

<margin>The art of Physiognomy.</margin>
Finally, from these figures and gestures, the arts of divination—**physiognomy** <note>The study of determining temperament and character from outward physical appearance.</note> and **metoposcopy** <note>A form of divination predicting a person's character or fate based on the lines and marks of the forehead.</note>—depend, as does **chiromancy** <note>Palmistry; the interpretation of the lines and features of the hands.</note> itself. These arts predict future events, not as the direct causes of those events, but as signs produced by the same underlying cause. And although these types of divination may seem to prophesy through lower and weaker signs, their judgments are not to be despised or condemned when they are predicted not from superstition, but from the **harmonic correspondence** of all parts of the body. Whoever, therefore, by nature, study, action, motion, gesture, countenance, the passions of the mind, and the opportunity of time, better imitates the celestial things, is like those higher beings and can receive more abundant gifts from them.

# ¶ On the divination of auspices and auguries. Chapter LIII.

There are certain other types of divination depending on natural causes, which consist in their own art and experience in various matters: by which physicians, farmers, shepherds, and sailors each foretell from probable signs: of which Aristotle handed down many in the book *On Times*. <margin>The Romans did nothing without taking auspices.</margin> Among these types of divination, auspices and auguries hold the primary place: which were once in such high esteem among the Romans that they performed nothing pertaining to public or private business without auspices <note>original: "inauspicate"; meaning without the ritual observation of birds or signs</note>; indeed, Cicero in his book *On Divination* copiously declares that the Etruscan people <note>The Etruscans were an ancient Italian civilization famous for their complex religious rituals and "disciplina," or the art of interpreting omens.</note> most excelled in this skill. <margin>Species of auspices.</margin> There are indeed many species of auspices: for some are called **pedestrian**, which are clearly taken from quadrupeds; some **auguries**, which are from birds; some **celestial**, which are from thunder and lightning; some **fallen**, as when something falls in a temple or elsewhere; some **sacred**, which were taken from sacrifices. Of these, some were called **expiations** and **gloomy auspices**, as when a sacrificial victim fled from the altar, or when struck gave a lowing sound, or fell on a different part of the body than is proper. To these is added **Exauguration**, namely when the wand <note>The *lituus*, a curved staff used by Roman augurs to mark out a ritual space in the sky.</note> falls from the hand of the one taking the augury, with which it was the custom to contemplate and take the auspice. <margin>Twelve types of auguries.</margin> Michael Scot <note>A 13th-century mathematician and scholar who served as the court astrologer to Holy Roman Emperor Frederick II.</note> recites twelve types of auguries, namely six from the right, whose names he says are *fernona*, *feruetus*, *confert*, *emonenthem*, *sonnasarnoua*, *sonnasaruetus*, and six others from the left: whose names are *confernoua*, *conferuetus*, *viaram*, *herenam*, *scassarnoua*, *scassaruetus*. Then, explaining those names, he says: *Fernoua* is an augury when you leave your house for the purpose of doing something, and while going you see a man or a bird, either walking or flying, so that it places itself before you on your left side; this is a sign of good meaning for your business. *Feruetus* is an augury when you leave the house for the purpose of doing something, and while going you first find or see a bird or a man pausing before you on your left side; this is a bad sign for your business. *Viaram* is an augury when a man or a bird, in its journey or flight, passes before you, coming from your right side and tending toward the left, and vanishes; this is a good sign for your business. *Confernoua* is an augury when you first find a man or a bird, going or flying, and it pauses before you on the right, in your sight; this is a good sign for your business. *Conferuetus* is an augury when you first find or see a man or a bird, reclining on your right in your sight; it is a bad sign for your business. *Scimafarnoua* <note>This name appears as 'sonnasarnoua' in the initial list above; such spelling variations are common in early modern transcriptions of medieval terms.</note> is an augury when a man or a bird follows behind your back and passes you, but before it reaches you, or you it, it pauses somewhere in your sight on your right; it is a good sign. *Scimafaruetus* is au

From this also comes the saying that whatever word unexpectedly comes to the mouth or mind of one rising in the morning is said to hold some presage and augury.

### ¶ On certain diverse living creatures, and other things, and what significance they have in auguries. Chapter LIIII.

<margin>The beginnings of auspices.</margin>
The very first auspices must be taken at the beginning of any work. **P** For instance, if you feel your garment has been gnawed by mice <note>original: "foricibus"; likely a scribal error for "soricibus" (mice), as mice gnawing clothes was a classic Roman ill omen.</note> at the start of a task, stop what you have begun. If, when going out, you stumble on the threshold or trip your foot on the road, turn back from your journey. If any bad omen occurs to you at the beginning of your business, delay what you have started, <margin>The beginning of business.</margin> lest your entire purpose be frustrated or come to a useless end; instead, wait until you can seize a favorable hour for your affairs under a better omen. We see that many animals are deceptive and prophetic through a certain power implanted in them by nature. Does not the rooster most skillfully indicate the hours with his song, <margin>The rooster puts the lion to flight.</margin> and with open wings put the lion to flight? Many birds do so by their song and chatter; flies predict rain with their sharp biting; and dolphins run ahead of storms with frequent leaps <margin>Augury of dolphins.</margin> above the waters. It would be a long task to recount all the presages which the Phrygians, Cilicians, Arabs, Umbrians, Tuscans, and other peoples who followed auguries learned from birds and animals. These things have been proven by them through many experiments and examples. For in all things are hidden oracles of the future; however, the ominal birds will foretell all the greatest things to you. These are the ones which the poets report were transformed from humans into birds. Therefore, listen diligently to what the crow <note>original: "cornix"; can refer to a crow or a raven.</note> says, and carefully attend to everything: its position while sitting, whether it flies to the right or the left, whether it is talkative, noisy, or silent, whether it precedes or follows, whether it waits for the arrival of one passing by or flees, and where it departs. Horapollo <note>original: "Orus Apollo"; the legendary author of the *Hieroglyphica*, a work that attempted to explain Egyptian symbols.</note> says in his *Hieroglyphics*: A pair of crows signifies marriage, since this animal <margin>The birth of the crow.</margin> lays two eggs, from which it is necessary that a male and a female are born...

<margin>Augury of ravens.</margin>
You should observe ravens with no less diligence, for it is said that they are preferred for greater matters and take precedence over the crow. Epictetus <note>Epictetus (c. 50–135 AD) was a Stoic philosopher who taught that while we cannot control external events, we can control our reactions to them. Here, Agrippa cites him as a serious authority on the prophetic nature of animal behavior.</note>, the Stoic philosopher and a grave author, felt that if a raven croaked toward someone, it portended adversity either to the body, fortune, honor, a wife, or children. 

<margin>Augury of swans.</margin>
Next, you shall consider the swans, who foreknow the secrets of the waters; for their cheerfulness foretells happy outcomes not only for sailors but for any others traveling abroad, unless they are overcome by the arrival of a stronger bird, 

<margin>Augury of the eagle.</margin>
such as the eagle. By the most powerful majesty of its empire, the eagle voids the reliability of all other birds if it speaks against them. Indeed, it flies higher than all birds and perceives more deeply, and it is never excluded from the secret of Jupiter <note>In Roman mythology, the eagle was the sacred messenger and animal of Jupiter, the king of the gods.</note> himself. It portends height and victory, but through blood, because it drinks blood rather than water. When the Locrians were fighting against the Crotonians, an eagle flying over brought victory to Hiero. To Alexander <note>Hiero I was a tyrant of Syracuse, while Alexander refers to Alexander the Great.</note>, as he was going out to the first battle of the war, an eagle suddenly landing on his shield announced that he would be king. 

<margin>The birth of Alexander the Great</margin>
At the birth of Alexander of Macedon, two eagles sitting upon the house all day portended the omen of a double empire over Asia and Europe. The same happened to Lucius Tarquinius Priscus, the son of Demaratus the Corinthian, who was a fugitive from home due to sedition; as he traveled through Etruria toward Rome, an eagle took away his cap and, flying high, placed it back upon his head, portending the kingdom of the Romans for him. 

<margin>Augury of vultures.</margin>
Now, truly, vultures signify difficulty, hardness, and greed, which was proven by experience at the origin of the city’s founding <note>This refers to the legendary contest between Romulus and Remus, where the sighting of vultures determined who had the gods' favor to found Rome.</note>. They also show the locations of future slaughter, anticipating them by seven days; and because they look toward that part where the lower side will be, as if gaping for a greater number of those to be killed, ancient kings used to send out scouts to report which way the vultures were looking. 

<margin>Auguries to be taken from greater birds.</margin>
The Phoenix, however, promises the success of singular happiness; when it was seen, "New Rome" <note>Constantinople, often called the "New Rome" by later Roman and Byzantine authors.</note> was founded under better auspices. The Pelican, because it puts itself in danger for the sake of its children, signifies a man who will undergo peril out of the devotion of his friendship. 

<margin>Augury of the stork.</margin>
The "Painted Bird" <note>The Latin *Picta auis* likely refers to the woodpecker (Picus) or a bird associated with the city of Poitiers (Pictavia).</note> gave its name to the city of Poitou, and its color and voice prefigured the gentleness of that people. The Heron <note>original: "Ardea"</note> is an omen of arduous <note>The author is making a pun on the Latin *Ardea* (Heron) and *Ardua* (lofty or difficult things).</note> matters. The stork, 

<margin>Augury of cranes.</margin>
being a bird of concord, creates harmony. Cranes <note>original: "Grues"</note>, named from the ancient verb *gruere* (as if to say "to agree" or *congruere*), always bring what is useful and cause one to beware the snares of enemies. 

<margin>The nature of the Hippopotamus.</margin>
The Hoopoe <note>original: "Cucupha"</note> indicates gratitude, for it alone returns the favor to its parents when they are worn out by old age. Conversely, the Hippopotamus, a parricide, announces ingratitude for favors and injustice. The Oryx-bird <note>original: "Origis auis." # BOOK ONE. 36

<margin>Auguries taken from smaller birds.</margin>
The talkative magpie <note>original: "pica"</note> announces guests; the hen-harrier <note>original: "albanellus"</note> flying past indicates the joy of hospitality if it carries itself from the left to the right, but if the opposite, it indicates the contrary. The screech-owl <note>original: "strix"</note> is always an unlucky bird, as is the little owl <note>original: "noctua"</note>; because it attacks chicks unexpectedly at night, just as death comes unexpectedly, it is therefore said to foretell death. Sometimes, however, because it is not blinded by the shadows of night, it signifies a man's diligence, which was proven when one perched upon Hiero’s spear <note>Hiero II, King of Syracuse (c. 308–215 BC).</note>. Dido, while she was joined with <margin>Omen of owls.</margin> Aeneas, felt the horned owl <note>original: "bubonem"</note> to be unlucky, as the poet <note>The Roman poet Virgil in the Aeneid.</note> sang:

> And the lone owl from the roof-tops with its deathly song
> Often seemed to complain and draw out long voices into a wail. <margin>And elsewhere:</margin>
> The sluggish owl, a dire omen to mortals.

The same bird sang on the Capitol when Roman affairs were failing at Numantia, and when Fregellae was destroyed because of a conspiracy made against the Romans. Almadel <note>Likely a reference to the "Ars Almadel," a medieval grimoire attributed to Solomon, or an Arabic authority on divination.</note> says that when horned owls and night-ravens <note>original: "nycticoraces"</note> divert to unusual regions and dwellings, it is a judgment that the people of those same regions and houses are about to die; this is because those birds are delighted by corpses and sense them beforehand, and men who are about to die are already corpses in potentiality. But Naso <note>The Roman poet Ovid (Publius Ovidius Naso).</note> also sings of the hawk as a harbinger of strife: <margin>Augury of the hawk.</margin>

> We hate the hawk, because it always lives in arms.

<margin>The death of Laelius foretold by augury.</margin>
Laelius, a legate of Pompey in Spain, was killed among the foragers; that fate is said to have been foretold to him by a hawk flying over his head. And Almadel says that birds of the same species fighting among themselves signify a change in the kingdom; but if they wage war against each other being of different species, and if those meet that are not usually seen, they portend a new fortune for that region. Even tiny birds, by their arrival or departure, portend that a family will be increased or diminished; the more serene their flight, the more praiseworthy it is. From this, Melampus the augur <note>A legendary healer and seer in Greek mythology who understood the language of birds.</note> conjectured the slaughter of the Greeks from the flight of small birds, when he said: "You see how almost no bird drives our course." Swallows <note>original: "hirundines"</note>, because they prepare <margin>Augury of swallows.</margin> hiding places for their chicks when they are dying, portend an ample patrimony or a legacy from the dead. A bat <note>original: "vespertilio"</note> meeting one who is fleeing signifies escape; for although it <margin>Omen of the bat.</margin> has no feathers, it nevertheless flies out. A sparrow <note>original: "passer"</note>, however, is a bad omen for one who is fleeing, for while fleeing the hawk itself, it runs to the owl, where <margin>Augury of the sparrow.</margin> it is equally endangered; yet in matters of love it is of good auspice, since, being stirred by lust, it mates seven times in an hour. Bees are good omens for kings, <margin>Omen of bees.</margin> for they show an obedient people; but flies signify <margin>Omen of flies.</margin> persistence and impudence, because although they are often driven away, they nevertheless return immediately. <margin>Auguries of domestic birds.</margin> Even domestic birds are not without auguries, for roosters by their song promote hope and the start of a journey. Indeed, when <margin>The birth of Tiberius announced by augury.</margin> Tiberius was to be born, his pregnant mother Livia took an egg from under a hen and cherished it in her bosom until a rooster with a remarkable crest was hatched; from this, the augurs interpreted that the boy to be born would be a ruler.

# OF OCCULT PHILOSOPHY.

<margin>Auguries taken from all animals:</margin>
Cicero writes in *The Thebaid* <note>While the *Thebaid* is an epic by Statius, Cicero discusses this rooster omen in his own work *De Divinatione*. Agrippa may be citing a commentary or misattributing the title.</note> that roosters <note>original: "gallos gallinaceos"</note> crowing all night in Boeotia foretold victory for the inhabitants against the Spartans. The augurs interpreted this because that bird remains silent when defeated but crows if it is the victor. <margin>Presage of horses.</margin> By a similar reasoning, omens of all events are gathered from animals and beasts. For meeting a weasel <note>original: "mustela"</note> is ominous; meeting a hare is to be feared by a traveler, unless he succeeds in capturing it. The mule is also ill-favored because it is sterile. The pig, however, is considered destructive, for such is its nature; therefore, it signifies destructive men. The horse pertains to the nature of quarrels and battle. This is why in Virgil’s writings, Anchises exclaims at the sight of white horses:

> Thou bringest war, O hospitable land;
> For war are horses armed; these herds threaten war.

However, when they are met joined to a chariot, because they pull with a harmonious yoke, <margin>Omen of the donkey.</margin> they signify that peace is to be hoped for. The donkey is generally useless, yet it profited Marius <note>Gaius Marius (c. 157–86 BC), a Roman general and statesman.</note>. When he had been declared an enemy of his country, he saw a donkey refuse the fodder offered to it and hasten toward water. Thinking that by this augury a path to safety was shown to him, he begged the crowd of friends helping him to provide this one kind of aid: to lead him to the sea. Having obtained this, he was placed upon a small boat and escaped the threats of the victor Sulla. Nevertheless, whenever a little donkey appears in an augury, it always signifies labor, patience, and obstacles. <margin>Presage of the wolf.</margin> But meeting a wolf is a good sign, the efficacy of which was seen in the case of Hiero of Sicily <note>Hiero II, King of Syracuse.</note>; a wolf snatched his writing tablet in the schoolroom, which confirmed the future success of his reign. However, a wolf takes away the voice of anyone it sees before they see it <note>A common ancient folklore belief mentioned by Pliny the Elder and Virgil.</note>. During the consulship of P. Africanus and C. Fulvius, a wolf at Minturnae mauled a sentry at the time the Roman army in Sicily was being defeated by runaway slaves. Furthermore, the wolf signifies treacherous and bad-faith men, as is well known in the progeny of Romulus: for the "faith" <note>original: "fides"</note> which they once sucked from their mother the wolf and kept for each other from the beginning, flowed down to their descendants as if by a law of nature. <margin>Omen of the lion.</margin> To meet a lion—since this animal is the strongest among all others, striking terror into everyone—is good. But for a woman to meet a lioness is bad because it hinders conception, for it is said a lioness does not give birth a second time. <margin>Meeting sheep and goats.</margin> Meeting sheep and goats is a good sign. It is also read in the *Etruscan Book of Portents* <note>original: "Ostentario Tuscorum," a lost Roman collection of Etruscan divination rules.</note> that if one of these animals is found clothed in an unusual color, it portends for the ruler an abundance of all things along with happiness. Hence Virgil sings to Pollio:

> But in the meadows the ram himself shall change his fleece,
> Now with sweetly blushing purple, now with saffron-yellow.

<margin>Presage of oxen.</margin> It is also good to meet oxen threshing, but better still to meet them plowing; for although they break the path and block the way, they compensate for this delay with the <margin>Omen of the dog confirmed by the event of Tobias.</margin> grace of hospitality. The dog became a sign on a journey because Cyrus <note>Cyrus the Great. According to legend, he was abandoned as an infant and nursed by a female dog (or a woman named Spako, meaning "bitch").</note>, when exposed in the woods, was nursed by a dog for his future kingship; and the angel who was the companion of Tobias did not scorn the dog as a comrade. The beaver <note>original: "castor"</note>, because it bites off its own testicles and leaves them behind for hunters <note>A popular medieval myth used to symbolize self-sacrifice to escape sin or danger.</note>, is a bad omen, signifying harm to a man by his own hand.

<margin>
Omens of small animals.
</margin>
...portends that loss will be brought. Indeed, even among small animals, **mice** signify loss; when they gnawed the gold in the Capitol, on that very day both consuls were intercepted by Hannibal’s ambushes near Tarentum. The **locust**—so named because it "makes one stand in place" <note>original: "loco stare faciens"</note> or because it "burns up places" <note>original: "loca exurens"</note>—hinders one's vows and is an omen of evil. In contrast, **cicadas** <note>likely meaning crickets or grasshoppers in this context</note> promote a journey and announce a favorable outcome of affairs. <margin>The omen of cicadas.</margin>
<margin>The augury of spiders.</margin>
A **spider** drawing a thread from above is said to announce the hope of coming money. Similarly, **ants**—because they know how to provide for themselves and prepare safe hiding places—portend security and wealth; a multitude of them signifies an army. Hence, when ants devoured a tame dragon belonging to Tiberius Caesar, the response from the seers was that he should beware the tumult of the multitude. If a **snake** should cross your path, beware of a slandering enemy; for this animal possesses strength in no other member but its mouth. A snake crawling into the palace <margin>The auspices of snakes.</margin> prophesied his own fall to Tarquin <note>Tarquinius Superbus, the last king of Rome.</note>. Two snakes were found in the bed of Sempronius Gracchus; he was told by a soothsayer <term>haruspice</term> <note>A priest in ancient Rome who practiced divination by inspecting entrails or interpreting unusual phenomena.</note> that if he let the male or the female go, either he or his wife must shortly die. Preferring his wife’s life to his own, he killed the male and let the female go, and he departed from life a few days later. <margin>The augury of Gracchus.</margin> In the same way, the **viper** signifies wicked women and criminal sons, and the **eel** signifies a man hostile to everyone, for it lives apart from other fish and is never found joined with them. Among all auspices and omens, however, none is more effective, none more powerful, and none that exposes the truth more clearly than a **human being**. <margin>The most effective auspice is from a human.</margin> Therefore, if you meet one, you must diligently note and inquire into their condition, age, sex, profession, location, gesture, motion, company, complexion, clothing, name, words, and speech. For since so many lights of presage exist in other animals, there is no doubt that many more effective and clearer ones are infused into the human soul. Cicero <note>original: "Tullius"</note> himself bears witness to this, saying that by nature a certain power of augury exists in human souls regarding their own eternity, allowing them to recognize all series of events and causes. In the foundations <margin>A presage of the city of Rome.</margin> of the city of Rome, a human head with an intact face was found; it foretold the greatness of the empire and gave its name to the Capitoline Hill <note>from "caput," meaning head.</note>. The soldiers of Brutus, about to battle against Octavian and Mark Antony, encountered an Ethiopian at the gate of the camp; although they slaughtered him on the spot as an omen of an adverse matter, the battle was nevertheless fought unsuccessfully, and both leaders, Brutus and Cassius, perished. Even the meeting of **monks** is commonly held to be ominous, <margin>The presage of monks.</margin> especially if it occurs in the morning; for that class of men lives largely off the dead, like vultures off carrion.

<meta>This page continues the discussion on animal omens, moving from external signs to the internal "sense of nature" that allows animals and some humans to perceive hidden truths or future events. ### ON OCCULT PHILOSOPHY.

...certain lights of divination descend upon four-footed beasts, birds, and other living creatures, through which they are able to presage human events for us. This is a sentiment that even **Virgil** <note>Publius Vergilius Maro, the Roman poet; this quote is from his *Georgics*, Book 1, lines 415–416.</note> seems to perceive when he sings:

> *I do not believe, for my part, that they possess a divine spirit*
> *Or a greater foresight of things granted by fate.*
> <note>original: "Haud equidem credo, quia sit diuinius illis / Ingenium, aut rerum fato prudentia maior." Virgil argues here that animal behavior is due to physical changes in the atmosphere, whereas the author uses this to introduce a more mystical "sense of nature."</note>

<margin>The sublimity of the sense of nature.</margin>
This kind of **sense of nature**, as **William of Paris** <note>Guillaume d'Auvergne (c. 1180–1249), Bishop of Paris and a prominent philosopher who wrote on the "universe of creatures."</note> says, is itself more sublime than any human apprehension; it is very close to and powerfully similar to prophecy. From this sense, a certain wonderful splendor of divination is naturally endowed in some animals. This appears clearly in certain **dogs**, who—by this kind of sense—recognize, find, track down, and seize thieves and hidden men who were entirely unknown both to themselves and to other people, rushing at them with their jaws and teeth.

<margin>The sense of dogs.</margin>
By a similar sense, **vultures** foresee future slaughters from battles and gather in the places where they will occur, as if they foresee their future food.

<margin>The sense of vultures.</margin>
By the same sense, **partridges** recognize their own mother whom they have never seen; they will leave a partridge that steals the mother’s eggs and hatches them <note>This refers to a common medieval belief that partridges were "stealers" of eggs and that the chicks would instinctively return to their true mother upon hearing her call.</note>.

<margin>The sense of partridges.</margin>
By this same sense, certain harmful and terrifying things are felt even while the human soul is entirely unaware of them. This is why terror and horror often invade men who are neither feeling nor thinking anything about such matters. Thus, a thief hiding in a house—even when no one knows or suspects he is there—strikes horror, fear, and a restlessness of heart into the inhabitants of that house. Perhaps this does not happen to everyone, because this kind of "splendor" is not in all men, but in a few. Likewise, a prostitute hidden in a very large house is sometimes sensed by someone who is entirely unaware she is there. It is handed down in histories that a certain **Heraiscus the Egyptian** <note>A 5th-century Neoplatonist philosopher said to possess the ability to distinguish between "sacred" and "profane" souls.</note>, a man of divine nature, could recognize unchaste women by their eyes alone, or even by hearing their voice from a distance; he was immediately affected by a significant headache because of it. William of Paris also reports that in his own time, a certain woman sensed the arrival of the man she loved from two miles away by this kind of sense as he approached the place where she lived.

<margin>The adultery of the stork.</margin>
He also reports that in his time a certain **stork** was convicted of adultery through the male’s sense of smell. After the male gathered a multitude of storks and exposed the crime of the female, she was judged guilty by that entire assembly—as if by a universal verdict—and was plucked of her feathers and torn apart. He also recounts a story of a certain **horse** who, having unknowingly mated with its own mother, later discovered it; he then bit off his own genitals with his teeth as if avenging the incest upon himself. **Aristotle**, **Varro**, and **Pliny** <note>Standard classical authorities on natural history: Aristotle the Greek philosopher, Marcus Terentius Varro the Roman polymath, and Pliny the Elder.</note> recount similar things about horses. Pliny himself tells of a similar deed by a certain **asp** <note>A venomous snake.</note> in Egypt. Having been fed daily at a man’s table, she gave birth to young, one of whom killed the host’s son. She—

### BOOK ONE.

...returned. Now, by these examples, we see how certain lights of presage can descend upon living creatures, such as signs of things established in their gestures, movements, voices, flight, gait, food, and color. For according to the doctrine of the **Platonists** <note>Followers of Plato who believed in a "World Soul" and the interconnectedness of all things.</note>, there is an innate power in inferior things through which they largely correspond with superior things. From this, the silent agreements of animals seem to harmonize with the divine bodies <note>The "divine bodies" refer to the planets and stars.</note>, and their physical forms and behaviors are affected by these powers, after whose names they are categorized. 

Therefore, it is necessary to consider which animals are **Saturnine** <note>Influenced by Saturn, associated with solitude, darkness, and decay.</note>, which refer to **Jupiter**, which to **Mars**, and so on for each, and to elicit presages according to their properties. Thus, those which refer to Saturn and Mars are all called "dire" and "funereal" birds, such as owls, screech-owls, and the others we listed above. The **horned owl** <term>bubo</term> also, being a Saturnine bird—solitary and nocturnal—is said to be an omen of the most unpromising kind, of which the Poet <note>Agrippa refers here to the Roman poet Ovid, specifically *Metamorphoses* 5.549–550.</note> says:

> And the sluggish owl becomes a foul messenger of coming grief,
> A dire omen to mortals.
> <note>original: "Foedaque fit volucris venturi nuntia luctus / Ignavus bubo, dirum mortalibus omen."</note>

The **Swan**, however, is a delightful bird, associated with **Venus** and even sacred to **Apollo** <note>Agrippa uses "Phoebus," another name for Apollo, the god of prophecy and music.</note>. It is said to be an omen of the happiest sort, especially in the auspices of sailors, because it is not submerged by water; hence **Ovid** sings:

> The Swan is always the most joyful bird in auspices.
> <note>original: "Cycnus in auspiciis semper laetissimus ales."</note>

<margin>Oscine birds</margin>
There are, moreover, **oscine birds** <note>From the Latin *oscines*, birds that provide omens through their song or speech rather than their flight.</note> which provide an auspice by their mouth and song: such as the raven, the woodpecker, and the crow. Hence **Virgil** <note>From Virgil's *Eclogues* 9.15.</note> writes:

> Often the crow from the hollow oak predicted the sinister.
> <note>original: "Saepe sinistra cava praedixit ab ilice cornix." In Roman augury, "sinistra" (left) could be interpreted as favorable or unfavorable depending on the context.</note>

<margin>
What must be considered in the flight of birds. 
The augury of Cranes.
</margin>
Truly, the birds that portend the future by their flight are those such as buzzards, ospreys <note>original: "sanqualae," a rare term for a type of eagle or bird of prey sacred to the god Sancus.</note>, eagles, vultures, cranes, swans, and the like. In their flight, one considers whether they fly slowly or hurriedly, whether they fly to the right or to the left, and how many fly together at once. In this way, when **cranes** fly hurriedly, they signify a storm; when they fly silently, they signify fair weather. Likewise, when two birds fly together and are of a funereal kind, they are said to portend evil, because two is the "number of confusion" <note>In Pythagorean numerology, the number two (the dyad) represents division and falling away from the unity of the divine.</note>. 

In a similar way, you shall investigate the reasoning for other creatures by applying the logic of numbers here. Furthermore, observing **similarity** <note>The Hermetic principle that "like affects like."</note> in these conjectures is a masterly skill, just as **Venus** herself, in disguise, teaches her son **Aeneas** in these verses by Virgil:

> Unless my vain parents taught me augury in vain,
> Behold twice-six swans rejoicing in a flock,
> Whom the bird of Jove <note>The eagle.</note>, gliding from the ethereal region,
> Was disturbing in the open sky; now in a long line they seem
> Either to take the land, or already look down upon the land taken.
> As they, returning, play with whirring wings,
> And have circled the pole in a group and given a song,
> Not otherwise do your ships and the youth of your people
> Either hold the port, or enter the mouth with full sail.
> <note>original: "Ni frustra augurium vani docuere parentes / Aspice bis senos laetantes agmine cycnos..." From Virgil's *Aeneid*, Book 1, lines 392–400. Venus uses the behavior of swans to reassure Aeneas that his lost ships are safe.</note>

### ON OCCULT PHILOSOPHY.

<margin>The wonderful teaching of Apollonius of Tyana.</margin>
A most wonderful kind of augury <note>The practice of interpreting omens from the behavior of animals.</note> is that of those who hear and understand the languages of animals, as was the case among the ancients with **Melampus**, **Tiresias**, and **Thales**. **Apollonius of Tyana** <note>A famous Greek Neopythagorean philosopher and reputed miracle-worker.</note> is recorded to have excelled in this, and it is said he was skilled in the language of birds. **Philostratus** and **Porphyry** relate a story of him: once, when Apollonius sat in a gathering of friends looking at sparrows huddling in a tree, another little sparrow flew in from elsewhere, making a great noise with its chirping and voice. When all the others followed it and flew away, he said to his companions that the sparrow had announced to the others that a donkey had fallen down in an alleyway near the city, laden with wheat, and the wheat was scattered on the ground. Moved by these words, many went to see for themselves and found it had happened exactly as Apollonius had said, much to their wonder. However, **Porphyry the Platonist**, in his third book *On Sacrifices*, says the bird was a swallow.

<margin>The voices of animals signify the passions of the soul.</margin>
For it is certain that every voice of any animal signifies some passion of its soul—be it an effect of joy, sadness, or anger—and it is not so wonderful that these voices can be understood by men who have practiced in these matters. Indeed, **Democritus** himself handed down this art, as **Pliny** says, by naming certain birds from whose mixed blood a serpent is produced; whoever eats this serpent will understand the conversations of birds. And **Hermes** <note>Referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of Hermeticism.</note> says: if anyone goes out to hunt on a certain day of the Kalends of November and cooks the first bird he catches with the heart of a fox, all who eat of this will understand the voices of birds and other animals. The **Arabs** also handed down that those who had eaten the heart or liver of dragons <note>In this period, "dragon" often referred to large serpents or pythons.</note> would be skilled in the meanings of brute animals. **Proclus the Platonist** himself believed and taught that the heart of a mole contributes to presages. There were also divinations and auspices taken from the entrails and fibers of sacrifices, the inventor of which was **Tages**, of whom **Lucan** sang:
> And let there be no faith in the fibers, but let **Tages**, 
> The founder of the art, have fashioned them.
> <note>original: "Et fibris sit nulla fides, sed conditor artis / Finxerit illa Tages,"</note>

<margin>The liver is the head of the entrails.</margin>
The Roman religion considered the liver to be the head of the entrails <term>exta</term> <note>The internal organs of a sacrificial animal, specifically those inspected by diviners.</note>. Hence the **haruspices** <note>Ancient Roman diviners who interpreted the will of the gods by inspecting entrails.</note>, searching for the future in the entrails, would first inspect the liver. They identified two "heads" within it, calling one for the citizen and the other for the enemy; by comparing these heads, they would announce victory for one side or the other. Likewise, we read in **Lucan** that the slaughter of the Pompeians and the victory of the Caesarists were signified by the entrails in these verses:
> And the horror appeared in the entrails, not to go unpunished,
> Behold, he saw a mass of fibers grow upon the head,
> A sickly and withered part of the other head hangs down,
> While another part flashes, and wickedly moves the veins with a swift pulse.
> <note>original: "Quodq; nefas nullis impune apparuit extis, / Ecce vidit capiti fibrarum increscere molem, / Alterius capitis pars ægra & marcida pendet, / Pars micat, & celeri venas mouet improba pulsu."</note>

<margin>A sign of a bad omen.</margin>
Next, having completed the viscera, they would proceed to the heart. If the victim was found to be without a heart, or if the head on the liver was missing, these were considered "pestiferous" <note>bringing destruction</note> omens and were called **piacular** <note>Requiring a sacrifice of atonement to ward off disaster.</note>. Similarly, if the victim fled from the altar, or if it gave a lowing sound when struck, or moved into a different [position] than it...

### BOOK ONE.

...had fallen from a part of the body. We read of these things: on the day that **Julius Caesar** went forth in a purple robe and sat upon a golden throne, the heart was twice found missing from the entrails <note>original: "extis"; the internal organs, especially the liver, heart, and lungs, used for divination.</note> while he was sacrificing. Similarly, when **Gaius Marius** was sacrificing at Utica, the liver was missing from the entrails. Likewise, for the Emperor **Caligula**, and for **Marcus Marcellus**; and when **Caius Claudius** and **Lucius Petellius** were Consuls and sacrificed victims, the liver suddenly wasted away; not long after, one died of disease, and the other perished by the weapons of the Ligurians, as the entrails had thus predicted. Such things are certainly thought to happen either by the power of the gods or the work of demons. For this reason, the greatest weight was always given by the ancients whenever anything unusual appeared in the entrails: just as when **Sulla** was sacrificing at Laurentum, the likeness of a crown appeared on the head of the liver. **Posthumius** the soothsayer <term>aruspex: a priest trained to interpret omens from entrails</term> interpreted this as portending victory and royal power for him, and therefore advised that Sulla alone should eat those entrails. Even the color of the entrails has its own significance, as **Lucan** <note>A Roman poet; this quote is from his epic *Pharsalia*, describing the terrifying omens before the Civil War.</note> mentions:

> The color itself terrified the seer, for the pale
> Viscera were stained with foul marks and dappled with cold gore,
> While much livid bruising varied the splattered blood.
> <note>original: "Terruit ipse color vatem, nam pallida tetris / Viscera tincta notis, gelidoq; infecta cruore, / Plurimus asperso variabat sanguine liuor."</note>

So great was the veneration for these arts in former times that the most powerful and wisest men followed them; indeed, the Senate and kings would do nothing without consulting the auspices. But all these things have been abolished today, partly through the negligence of men and partly by the authority of the Church Fathers.

### ¶ On the divination of lightning and thunderbolts, and how portents and prodigies are to be interpreted. Chapter LVI.

Furthermore, the **Etruscan Seers** and priests handed down the knowledge of the augury of lightning and thunderbolts, as well as portents, and how they and prodigies <note>In ancient Rome, a "prodigy" was an unnatural event—like a rain of stones or a talking ox—that signaled a rupture in the relationship between the gods and the state.</note> are to be interpreted. They established sixteen regions of the heavens, with their own deities assigned to each; moreover, they identified eleven types of lightning and nine gods who would hurl them, providing reasons for what they signify from each part. Truly, whenever portents, prodigies, and omens occur, it is certain that they always foretell something great.

<margin>What kind of person an interpreter of prodigies ought to be.</margin>
The interpreter of these things must be an excellent judge of similarities and, at the same time, a careful investigator of the affairs of the princes and provinces occurring at that time. For the care of the heavens is focused on princes, peoples, and provinces, such that they are prefigured and warned above others through the stars, planets, portents, and prodigies. If the same or a similar thing appeared in past ages, it will also be necessary to consider what followed from it then, and to predict either the same or similar outcomes accordingly, because the same signs belong to the same things, and likes to likes. Thus, prodigies preceded many men and kings at their birth or death: as **Cicero** relates of the boy **Midas**,
<margin>The prodigy of Midas.</margin>
in whose mouth, while he was sleeping, ants [placed] grains of wheat...
