<margin>Plato's prodigy.</margin> ...they cast, which was an omen of great riches. Thus, when bees settled on the mouth of the infant **Plato** while he slept in his cradle, the sweetness of his eloquence was foretold. <margin>Hecuba's prodigy.</margin> When **Hecuba** was about to give birth to **Paris**, she had a vision that she gave birth to a burning torch which would set fire to Troy and all of Asia. To **Phalaris**, it appeared in a vision that a statue of Mercury poured blood onto the ground, <margin>Dionysius's prodigy.</margin> flooding the entire house. To the mother of **Dionysius**, it appeared in a vision that she gave birth to a little satyr <term>satyriscum: a small satyr, a mythological creature representing wild nature and lust</term>; these prodigious dreams were followed and confirmed by the actual events. <margin>Servius Tullius's prodigy.</margin> The wife of **Tarquinius Priscus**, seeing a flame lick the head of **Servius Tullius**, predicted he would hold the kingship. In a similar way, after the fall of Troy, while **Aeneas** was debating flight with his father **Anchises**, a flame appeared licking the crown of **Ascanius's** head, causing him no injury. Since this <margin>Ascanius's prodigy.</margin> portended a kingdom for **Ascanius**, it persuaded them all to depart. Indeed, all great and notable disasters have been preceded by portents and prodigies. Thus we read in **Pliny**: during the consulship of **Marcus Attilius** and **Caius Portius**, it rained milk and blood, which foretold a powerful plague that would invade Rome the following year. Likewise, in Lucania, it rained iron bits resembling sponges the year before **Marcus Crassus** was slain among the Parthians; and all the Lucanian soldiers, of whom there were a great number in the army, were killed with him. <margin>Many portents taken from histories.</margin> Likewise, during the consulship of **Lucius Paulus** and **Caius Marcellus**, it rained wool around the fortress of Corisanum, near which **Titus Annius Milo** was killed a year later. Also, during the Cimbrian wars, the clatter of arms and the sound of trumpets were heard from the sky. And **Livy** says concerning the Macedonian war: "In the year that **Hannibal** departed, it rained blood for two days." He also reports of the Second Punic War that water mixed with blood descended from the sky like rain at the time **Hannibal** was ravaging Italy. For the Spartans, shortly before the disaster at Leuctra, weapons rattled in the temple of **Hercules**, and at the same time in Thebes, in the temple of Hercules, the doors that were closed with bars opened themselves, and weapons fixed to the walls were found on the ground. It is proper to predict similar outcomes from similar signs, just as in different times past something was divined from them. But one must also not neglect the judgments of celestial influences regarding these matters, of which we shall speak more extensively in later parts.

### ¶ On Geomancy, Hydromancy, Aeromancy, and Pyromancy: The Divinations of the Four Elements. Chapter 57.

For even the elements themselves teach us of fated events, from which those four famous kinds of divination—Geomancy, Hydromancy, Aeromancy, and Pyromancy—take their names. Concerning these, that sorceress in **Lucan** <note>Referring to the witch Erictho in Lucan's epic poem, *Pharsalia*.</note> seemed to boast when she said:

> To the truth, the earth, the air, the ether, and chaos,
> The seas, the fields, and the rocks of Rhodope shall speak. <note>original: "Ad verum tellus, aerq;, etherq;, chaosq; / Aequoraq;, & campi, Rhodopeiaq; saxa loquentur"</note>

<margin>Geomancy.</margin> First, then, is **Geomancy**, which predicts future things from earthquakes, rumblings, swellings, tremors, cracks, chasms, exhalations, and its other impressions...

<header>BOOK ONE</header>

...demonstrates; whose art **Almadel the Arab** <note>An influential medieval figure in ceremonial magic, to whom several grimoires are attributed</note> handed down. But there is also another species of **Geomancy** <term>Geomancy: divination by interpreting markings on the ground or patterns formed by tossed soil or sand</term>, which divines through points inscribed in the earth by some force or by chance, which is not part of the present study, but we shall speak of it among lots in the following sections. 

<margin>Hydromancy.</margin>
**Hydromancy** <term>Hydromancy: divination by means of water</term>, however, provides prophecies through watery impressions: their ebbs and flows, risings and depressions, storms, colors, and the like. To this are also joined visions that happen in the water—a kind of divination discovered by the Persians. **Varro** <note>Marcus Terentius Varro, an ancient Roman scholar</note> reports that a boy saw in the water an image of **Mercury**, which foretold the entire outcome of the **Mithridatic War** <note>A series of conflicts between Rome and the Kingdom of Pontus in the 1st century BCE</note> in one hundred and fifty verses. We read also that **Numa Pompilius** practiced hydromancy; for he drew out images of the gods in water, and from them learned future things. Which art **Pythagoras** also practiced a long time after Numa. 

There was also once among the Assyrians a species of hydromancy held in great value called 
<margin>Lecanomancy, a species of Hydromancy.</margin>
**Lecanomancy** <term>Lecanomancy: divination by observing objects, oil, or reflections in a basin of water</term>, named after a basin full of water. Into this basin were placed gold and silver plates and precious stones inscribed with certain images, names, and characters. To this method can also be referred the art by which, through molten lead or wax cast into water, they express the thing we desire to know by clear signs of images. There were also once prophetic springs, such as the spring of **Patras** in Achaia, and that which was called the water of **Juno** among the Epidaurians, of which more will be said in the following when we speak of oracles. 

Truly, here also can be referred the **divination by fish** <term>Aruspicina piscium: a form of omen-reading using the behavior or appearance of fish</term>, such as was once practiced among the Lycians in a place called **Dina** by the sea. In a sacred place of **Apollo**, pits were dug in the dry sand; into these, a person consulting about the future would drop roasted meats, and suddenly that place would be filled with water, and a great multitude of fish of wonderful shapes unknown to men would appear. From their forms, the prophet would predict what was to come. These things are reported more extensively by **Athenaeus** from **Polycharmus** in his histories of the Lycians. 

<margin>Aeromancy.</margin>
In a similar way, **Aeromancy** <term>Aeromancy: divination by atmospheric conditions, such as clouds, wind, and lightning</term> provides prognostications through atmospheric impressions: through the blowing of winds, through rainbows, through halos, through mists and clouds, and through imaginings in the clouds and visions in the air. 

<margin>Pyromancy.</margin>
Thus also **Pyromancy** <term>Pyromancy: divination by fire or the behavior of flames</term> is divined through fiery impressions: through comets <note>original: "stellas caudatas," literally "tailed stars"</note>, through fiery colors, and through visions and imaginings in fire. Thus the wife of **Cicero** predicted that he would be consul the following year, because when she wished to see something in the ashes after a completed sacrifice, a flame suddenly leaped out. Of this kind are the things **Pliny** says: that earthly fires are perceived as messengers of storms when they are pale and murmuring; likewise rains are foretold if "fungi" <note>original: "fungi," referring to carbon growths or "mushrooms" on lamp wicks</note> appear on lamps; if the flame flies in a wavy pattern, a wind is portended; and when lamps cast out flames or are hardly lit, it is a sign. Likewise when sparks hang together in clusters on them, or when coal sticks to pots when they are lifted, or when a contained fire shakes off soot from itself or emits a spark, or when ash grows thick on the hearth, and when a coal shines intensely. To these is added—

<margin>Capnomancy</margin>**Capnomancy** <term>Capnomancy: divination by interpreting the smoke of sacrificial fires, derived from the Greek word *kapnos* (smoke)</term>, so named from smoke, is that which scrutinizes flame and smoke: their colors, sounds, and movements—whether the smoke extends in a straight line, is carried obliquely, or rolls in a circle. One may read about these signs in these verses by **Statius** <note>Publius Papinius Statius (c. 45–96 AD), a Roman poet. These lines are from his epic, the *Thebaid*, depicting a ritual of necromancy and divination</note>:
> <note>original: "Vincatur pietas, pone eia altaria virgo..."</note>
> Let piety be overcome; come, maiden, set the altars,
> Let us seek the gods above. With a keen eye she observes
> The blood-red tips of the flames, and the fire born through
> The air, and yet the clear summits of light rising in the
> Midst; she teaches then that it is rolled in the empty likeness
> Of a serpent in a doubtful gyre, and broken by redness.

Indeed, even in the craters of **Mount Etna** and in the **Nymphaean fields** <note>A site near Apollonia (modern Albania) famous in antiquity for its naturally occurring perpetual fires</note> among the inhabitants of **Apollonia**, omens were taken from fire and flames. These were considered joyful if they consumed whatever had been cast into them, but mournful if they spat the offerings back out. We shall speak further of these matters later among the responses of the oracles.

### On the Resuscitation of the Dead, and on Long-lasting Sleep and Fasting, Chapter 58

<margin>c</margin>The **Arabian philosophers** <note>Likely referring to thinkers like Avicenna or Al-Farabi, who discussed the soul's power over the body</note> agree that some men can raise themselves above the powers of the body and above the sensory powers; having overcome these by the perfection of the heavens and the Intelligences, they receive a divine vigor within themselves. Since, therefore, the souls of all men are perpetual, and all spirits obey perfected souls, the **magi** believe that perfected men—through the power of their own souls—can restore other lower souls (which have already been somewhat separated from their dying bodies) and breathe life into them once more. 

This is not unlike how a **weasel** <note>A reference to a folk belief, often found in ancient bestiaries, that weasels could revive their dead young or companions using a specific herb</note> that has been killed is called back to life by the breath and voice of its parent; or how **lions** give life to their inanimate offspring by breathing upon them <note>A common medieval belief held that lion cubs were born dead and remained so for three days until the father lion breathed on their faces to wake them</note>. And because, as they say, all similar things applied to similar things produce similar natures, and every passive thing that receives the act of some agent is also clothed in and made natural to the nature of that agent: hence they think that certain herbs and magical concoctions contribute not a little to this resuscitation. They say such things are prepared from the ashes of the **Phoenix** and the cast-off skins of serpents. This might seem like a fable to most, and even impossible to many, were it not proven by historical credit. 

For we read that many who were submerged in water, others cast into fires and placed upon the funeral pyre, others killed in war, and others who had lost their lives in different ways, came back to life even after many days. **Pliny** <note>Pliny the Elder, in his *Natural History*, recorded several cases of "apparent death" where individuals revived just before cremation</note> testifies to this concerning **Aviola** (a man of consular rank), **Lucius Lamia**, **Caelius Tubero**, **Cofirdius**, **Gabienus**, and many others. Similarly, we read that **Aesop** the fabulist, **Tyndareus**, **Hercules**, and the **Palici** <note>Ancient Sicilian deities; legend claimed they were born twice, once from their mother and once from the earth</note> (sons of Jupiter and Thalia), returned to life after death. Many others were called back to life by magi and physicians, as has been recorded in histories concerning **Aesculapius** <note>The Greek god of medicine, said to have been killed by Zeus for bringing the dead back to life</note>. We have narrated above, from the accounts of **Juba**, **Xanthus**, and **Philostratus**, concerning **Tillo** and a certain Arab, and...

...[Abaris the Hyperborean] and **Apollonius of Tyana** <note>A famous Neopythagorean philosopher and reputed miracle-worker from the 1st century AD</note>. We also read of a certain **Glaucus** who had died, and whom they say was restored to life—beyond everyone's expectation as the physicians rushed to him—by a herb which they call "dragon-herb" <note>original: "draconem"; likely referring to *Dracunculus vulgaris* or a similar plant believed in antiquity to have life-giving properties</note>. Others say he revived after tasting a honeyed medicine, from which the proverb arose: <margin>The power of the Dragon-herb.</margin> "Glaucus rose again after drinking honey." **Apuleius** <note>A Roman novelist and Platonist, author of *The Golden Ass*</note> also, when describing the rite of such resuscitations, says of the Egyptian prophet **Zachlas**: "The prophet, having been thus appeased, places a certain small herb over the mouth of the body, and another upon its chest; then, turning toward the rising sun and silently praying for the increase of the august sun, he drew the attention of the crowd by his venerable presence to such a great miracle. Now the chest began to heave with a swelling, now the healthy pulse was felt to throb, now the body was filled with breath; the corpse rises, and the youth speaks."

If these things are to be believed as true, it must be that dying souls sometimes hide within their bodies, weighed down by violent **ecstasies** <term>Ecstasy: from the Greek *ekstasis*, meaning to stand outside oneself; here referring to a state where the soul's connection to the body's functions is suspended</term> and released from all bodily action, so that life, sense, and motion desert the whole body. Thus, the man is not yet truly dead, but lies lifeless and as if dead, even for a long period of time. And it has very often been discovered that in times of pestilence, many who were carried off in haste as dead revived in their tombs. We read that this has also frequently happened to women suffering from **suffocation of the womb** <note>original: "suffocatione matricis"; a historical medical diagnosis for a variety of conditions, often involving fainting or seizures, believed to be caused by the movement of the uterus</note>. And **Rabbi Moses** <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), the preeminent Jewish philosopher and physician</note> <margin>Wonderful examples of suffocation and ecstasy.</margin> relates from a book of **Galen** <note>The most influential physician of the Roman Empire</note>, which the **Patriarch** translated, that a suffocation happened to a man which lasted six days, during which he neither ate nor drank, and his two arteries were restored. And he said in the same book that a "repletion" <note>An excess of bodily fluids or "humors"</note> occurred to a man by which the pulse of the whole body was lost, the heart did not move, and he lay as if dead. He also says that from a fall from a high place, or a great shout, or from remaining a long time under water, a **syncope** <term>Syncope: a temporary loss of consciousness caused by a fall in blood pressure; a deep faint</term> can occur lasting forty-eight hours, and the man lies as if dead, with a greenish pallor rising on his face.

He reports in the same book of one who buried a dead man before seventy-two hours had passed after his death, and thus killed him, because he buried him alive. He gave signs there by which it may be known that these people are alive, although they lie like the dead and will certainly die unless they are aided, either by **phlebotomy** <term>Phlebotomy: the surgical opening or puncturing of a vein to withdraw blood; bloodletting</term> or other cures; and these are among those things that happen very rarely. This is the manner by which we understand how **magi** and physicians raise the dead, just as those who were once knocked lifeless by the bite of serpents were restored to life by the **Marsi** and **Psylli** peoples <note>Ancient tribes from Italy and North Africa, respectively, renowned in antiquity for their immunity to snake venom and their ability to heal bites</note>. 

However, one should judge that such ecstasies can last a long time without the man being truly dead, no differently than in **dormice**, **crocodiles**, and many **serpents**, which sleep through the whole winter and breathe so faintly in their sleep that they can hardly be revived even by fire. I have often seen a dissected dormouse remain immobile <margin>The sleep of the dormouse. Examples of long sleep.</margin> as if dead until it was cooked, and only then, in the boiling water, did its dissected limbs show signs of life. Similarly, though it is difficult to believe...

...[though the cause of this suspension] may be [unclear], we read nonetheless in the accounts of proven historians that even certain men have slept a long-lasting sleep for many continuous years, and meanwhile, until they finally woke up, they were not made any older. **Pliny** <note>Pliny the Elder, Roman naturalist and author of *Natural History*</note> himself testifies to this regarding a certain boy, whom he says slept for fifty-seven years in a cave after being exhausted by heat and travel. We also read that **Epimenides of Knossos** <note>A semi-mythical Greek seer and philosopher-poet from the 6th or 7th century BC</note> slept for fifty-seven years in a cave. From this arose the proverb "to sleep beyond Epimenides." **John of Damascus** <note>original: "M, Damascenus"; likely referring to the medieval scholar or a source attributed to the theologian</note> relates that in his own time in Germany, an exhausted peasant slept under a mound of hay through the whole autumn and the following winter continuously, until in summer, as the hay was gradually consumed by livestock, he was found and awakened; he was as if half-dead and totally out of his mind <note>original: "extra se positus," literally "placed outside himself"</note>. Ecclesiastical histories confirm this phenomenon in the story of the **Seven Sleepers**, <margin>The story of the Seven Sleepers.</margin> who they say slept for one hundred and ninety-six years <note>The "Seven Sleepers of Ephesus" were Christian youths who fled persecution and were said to have slept in a cave for centuries</note>. In Norway, beneath a towering cliff, there is a cave where, as **Paul the Deacon** and **Methodius** the martyr write, seven men lay sleeping, sunk in a deep slumber for a long time without any physical decay. They say that people who often entered to harm them were immediately struck with contractions <term>Contraction: a sudden seizing or stiffening of the limbs, interpreted here as a divine punishment</term>, and finally the local inhabitants, made cautious by this immediate punishment, ceased from harming them.

Among the philosophers, **Xenocrates**—a man of no small reputation—thought this long-lasting sleep was a kind of natural punishment, assigned from eternity for certain demerits of the soul. **John of Damascus** proves by many reasons that this is possible and entirely natural; he does not think it absurd that what is granted to certain other living creatures—to sleep for many months without food or drink, without excretion, and without wasting away or rotting—could also happen to a human. This might occur through some poisonous potion, a sleep-inducing illness, a fearful stupor <note>original: "meticuloso quodam sopore"</note>, or similar causes, lasting for many days, months, or years, depending on the intensity or relaxation of the powers and passions of the soul.

Physicians also speak of antidotes of which, if one eats even a tiny portion, he can then endure a long fast <note>original: "inedia," meaning a lack of food</note>; just as **Elijah** once, fed with a certain food by an angel, walked and fasted in the strength of that food for forty days. **Giovanni Boccaccio** <note>The 14th-century Italian author of the *Decameron*</note> relates that in his time there was a man in Venice who <margin>Wonderful examples of fasts.</margin> fasted every year for forty days without any food. And what is more wondrous, at the same time in Lower Germany there was a woman who had taken no food even into her thirtieth year. <margin>In the year 1540, a girl of 12 years in the district of Speyer lasted without food or drink for over a year and more. See Caelius Rhodiginus book 13, chapter 24.</margin> This might indeed seem incredible to us, were it not confirmed by a recent miracle of our own age in Brother **Nicholas of the Stone** <note>original: "Nicolao de Saxo"; referring to St. Nicholas of Flüe (1417–1487), the patron saint of Switzerland</note>, a Swiss by nation, who is known to have lived in the wilderness for twenty-two years without any food until he departed this life. Also wondrous is what **Theophrastus** reported: that there was a certain Philinus who used no drink or food except for milk. There are also weighty authors who describe a certain **Spartan herb**, which they say the **Scythians** use to endure twelve days without food or drink once it is tasted or held in the mouth.

### ¶ On divination which occurs through dreams. Chapter LIX.

There is also a species of divination that occurs while sleeping, which is indeed proven by the traditions of the elders and philosophers, the authorities of theologians, examples from history, and daily experience. However, I speak here of a "dream" <note>original: *somnium*</note>, not that which is a "phantom" <note>original: *phantasma*</note> or a "sleepless dream" <note>original: *insomnium*</note>: for these latter types are vain and possess nothing of divination. Instead, they arise from the remains of our waking hours or from a disturbance of the body. For as often as we are oppressed by the comforts or discomforts of the body or of fortune, then whatever state of mind fatigued the person while awake, that same state thrusts itself upon the person while sleeping—or sometimes the dreamer is deceived by an "insomnium" that presents the exact opposite. <margin>Dream.</margin> Therefore, I call a "dream" here that which occurs in the imaginative spirit <term>spiritus phantasticus; a subtle vapor in Renaissance psychology that was believed to carry sensory images to the soul</term>, when the mind and body are in a healthy state, caused by the influence of the heavens. 

The rule for interpreting such dreams is indeed found among the astrologers, in that branch of the art dedicated to "questions," yet it is often insufficient. This is because dreams of this kind happen to different people in different ways, according to the varying quality and disposition of their imaginative spirits. For this reason, one cannot apply the same common rule of dream interpretation to every individual. Instead, according to the opinion of **Synesius** <note>Synesius of Cyrene, a 4th-century philosopher-bishop who wrote a famous treatise on dreams</note>, since outcomes are consistent with the things they represent—similar things following from similar causes—one who frequently experiences the same or a similar vision should record for himself that it designates the same or a similar meaning, passion, fortune, action, or final event. 

Just as **Aristotle** says, memory is confirmed by the senses, and from memory of the same thing frequently obtained, experience is born; then, from many experiences, art and science are gradually accumulated. One must proceed by a similar reasoning regarding dreams. Hence, **Synesius** commands that everyone observe their own dreams and their subsequent outcomes—namely, which visions resulted in what events—and commit these rules (the visions and the accidents) to memory, both of the dream and of the waking state. By a diligent accumulation of such observations, a person develops their own personal art of divination and a method for interpreting their own dreams, provided nothing is allowed to slip from the memory. 

Dreams are most effective when the Moon traverses that zodiac sign which was in the "ninth house" <note>The astrological house associated with dreams, visions, and long journeys</note> of the original birth chart, or the "revolution" of that year, or in the ninth sign from the sign of progression. However, the truest and most certain divination comes neither from nature nor from human arts, but to purified minds by divine inspiration. As for what pertains to prophecies and oracles, we shall discuss those elsewhere.

<header>->**ON OCCULT PHILOSOPHY**<-</header>

<margin>A type of divination-frenzy.</margin>
This divination is what Aristotle calls "frenzy" <note>original: *furore*</note>, and he teaches in his treatise *On Divination* that it proceeds from the melancholic humor, saying: "Because of their intensity, melancholics make excellent conjectures from afar; they quickly imagine a state of being and most easily receive the impression of the celestial bodies." And in his *Problems*, he says that the Sibyls, the Bacchides, Niceratus of Syracuse, and Amon were diviners and poets because of a natural melancholic temperament. Therefore, if there is a cause for this frenzy within the human body, it is the melancholic humor—not indeed that which is called "black bile" <note>original: *atra bilis*</note>, which is such a depraved and horrible thing that its force is said by natural philosophers and physicians to induce not only the mania it brings on, but even to entice evil spirits to besiege human bodies. By "humor" here, we mean the melancholic state which is called "natural and bright bile" <note>original: *naturalis & candida bilis*</note>. For when this is ignited and burns, it stirs up a frenzy that leads us toward knowledge and divination, especially if it is assisted by some celestial influence—particularly that of Saturn. Since Saturn himself is cold and dry (as is the melancholic humor), he flows into it daily, increasing and preserving it. Furthermore, since he is the author of secret contemplation, a stranger to all public business, and the highest of the planets, he constantly recalls the soul from external duties to its innermost parts, making it ascend from lower things to the highest, bestowing knowledge and the foretelling of future events. This is what Aristotle intends in his book of *Problems* when he says: "From melancholy, some have become like divine beings predicting the future, and others have become poets." He says, moreover, that almost all men who have excelled in any science have been melancholics. <margin>Melancholics are endowed with genius.</margin> Democritus and Plato also attest to this, asserting that some melancholics excel so greatly in genius that they seem divine rather than human. Thus, many melancholics who were at first unrefined, inept, or even seemingly insane—as they say were Hesiod, Ion, Tynnichus the Chalcidian, Homer, and Lucretius—were often seized by a sudden frenzy and turned into poets, singing certain wonderful and divine things which they themselves could scarcely understand. Hence, the divine Plato says in his *Ion*: "Most prophets, after the force of their frenzy has subsided, do not sufficiently understand what they have written, even though they treated each art correctly while in that frenzy—a fact which the practitioners of those arts judge to be true upon reading them." <margin>The dominion of the melancholic humor.</margin> Furthermore, they pass down the teaching that the power of the melancholic humor is so great that by its force even celestial spirits <note>original: *daemones*; in this context, these are mediating spirits or intelligences, not necessarily "demons" in the modern sense</note> are sometimes drawn into human bodies. All of antiquity bears witness that by the presence and instinct of these spirits, men rave in divine ecstasy and speak many wonders. They believe this happens according to a triple distinction, following the soul’s three types of apprehension: namely, the imaginative, the rational, and the mental. They say, therefore, that when the soul is driven by the melancholic humor, it transcends the restraints of the body and the chains of its limbs with nothing holding it back; it transfers itself entirely into the imagination, and suddenly...

From these, it acquires the science and prudence of natural and human affairs. Thus, we see a man suddenly emerge as a philosopher, a physician, or an excellent orator. Regarding the future, they predict things that pertain to the changes of kingdoms and the restoration of ages, just as the Sibyl <note>The Sibyls were ancient prophetesses; the Romans frequently consulted the Sibylline Books in times of crisis.</note> did for the Romans. 

But when the whole soul has risen into the mind <term>mind: *mens*, the highest spiritual intellect that contemplates divine truths</term>, it is then made a receptacle for the Sublime Spirits. From them, it learns the secrets of divine things—for instance, the law of God, the orders of the angels, and those things that pertain to the knowledge of eternal reality and the salvation of souls. Regarding the future, the soul foresees things that lie within divine providence, such as future portents or miracles, a future prophet, or a change in the Law. ### ¶ On the formation of man, the external and internal senses, and the mind: on the threefold appetite of the soul, and the passions of the will. Chapter LXI.

<margin>
The external senses and which elements they correspond to.
</margin>

It is the opinion of certain theologians that God himself did not create the body of the first human directly, but composed and formed it from the elements with the assistance of celestial beings. This opinion is supported by Alcinous <note>A 2nd-century philosopher who summarized Plato’s teachings.</note> based on the dogma of Plato, who believed that the Supreme God is the creator of the entire world, the gods, and the spirits <note>original: *daemones*</note>, and that these are therefore immortal. However, he believed that the "junior gods" <note>In Plato’s *Timaeus*, these are lesser deities created by the Demiurge to handle the creation of mortal life.</note> procreated the other types of mortal living things at the command of the Supreme God; for if He had fathered these Himself, they would have been born immortal. Thus, the gods took certain portions from the earth, fire, air, and water—moving and binding them together—and fashioned one body out of them all. They subjected this body to the service of the soul, assigning specific regions within it to each of its powers. To the lower powers, they assigned lower seats: indeed, they assigned anger to the heart <note>original: *præcordia*; literally the area around the diaphragm or heart.</note> and desire to the womb. The more noble senses, however, they placed in the head, as if in the citadel of the entire body, followed by the various organs of speech. 

They divide the senses into the external and the internal. The external senses are divided into the five most well-known ones, to which five organs or subjects are attributed as foundations. These are arranged so that those placed in the higher parts of the body also possess a higher rank of purity. The eyes, being located in the highest place, are the purest, sharing a nature with fire and light. Next, the ears, holding the second rank in both place and purity, are compared to air. The nostrils hold the third place, containing a middle ground between air and water. After that is the organ of taste, which is thicker and very similar to a watery nature. In the final rank is touch, diffused through the whole body and assigned to the density of the earth. The purer senses are those that perceive from a distance without approaching the objects of the senses, such as sight and hearing. Next, smell also perceives things that are not close through the medium of the air. Taste, however, only senses things that are nearby. <margin>Touch.</margin> Touch functions in both ways, for it senses bodies that are approaching, and just as sight perceives through a medium... <note>The catchword *mes* at the bottom of the page suggests the sentence continues with "medium."</note>

...perceives the air, so also the sense of touch perceives soft and moist things through the medium of a wand or a staff. Truly, touch alone is the sense common to all animals; yet man possesses this sense most certainly, for in this 
<margin>Man excels other animals in taste and touch.</margin>
and in taste he excels all other animals, though in the other three senses he is surpassed by certain creatures—such as the dog, which sees, hears, and smells more acutely than man. Similarly, lynxes and eagles see more sharply than man and many other living beings. The internal senses, however, as Averroes <note>Ibn Rushd (1126–1198), a medieval Andalusian philosopher whose commentaries on Aristotle were foundational for Renaissance thought.</note> maintains, are divided into four parts. The first is called the "common sense" <term>common sense (sensus communis): the faculty that integrates the data from all five external senses into a single perception.</term>, because it is the first to gather and perfect all the images drawn in through the external senses. The second is the imaginative power, whose duty is—even when it perceives nothing itself—to retain the images received from the preceding senses and offer them to the third nature of sensing, which is the phantasy <note>original: *phantasia*. In this context, it refers to the faculty of "estimation" or the "cognitive power" that judges the data provided by the imagination.</note>, the power of judging and thinking. Its work is to perceive and judge, once images are received, what or of what sort that thing is to which those images belong, and to entrust those very things it has so distinguished, joined, perceived, and judged to the fourth power, which we call memory, to be preserved. For indeed, within that category of powers are the processes of reasoning, arrangements, pursuits and flights, and the incitements to action. And in the intellectual species, these include intellections, virtues, the logic of the sciences, counsel, and choice. It is this faculty, moreover, which shows us future things through dreams; hence the phantasy is sometimes called the "phantastic intellect." For it is the final trace of intelligence which, as Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 245–325 AD) who wrote extensively on the soul and the divine.</note> says, is born with all 
<margin>What the phantasy is.</margin>
the powers of the soul and fashions all figures, the likenesses of forms and operations, and transmits visions or impressions from some powers into others. These visions begin from the senses and awaken opinion; but those which come from the intellect are offered in the second place to opinion. Yet the phantasy receives images from all sources by its own nature, and through its own property, it designates them according to a specific likeness; it fashions all the actions of the soul, adapts external things to internal ones, and even prints impressions upon the body. These senses have their organs in the head; for the common sense, along with the imagination, 
<margin>The organs of the senses are in the head.</margin>
occupies the front cells of the brain—although Aristotle placed the organ of common sense in the heart—while the cognitive power occupies the highest and middle part of the head, and memory the hindmost. Furthermore, the organs of the voice and of speech are many: the muscles between the ribs of the inner chest, the thorax, the lungs, the trachea, the artery, the throat—and especially the cartilaginous part, or the recurrent nerves—and the plectrum <note>original: *plectrum linguae*. Literally "the pick of the tongue," comparing the tongue's movement to the tool used to pluck a lyre.</note> of the tongue, and all those parts and muscles which are organs of breathing. The proper organ 
<margin>The organ of speech.</margin>
of speech is the mouth, in which words and talk are molded, formed, and shaped; with the tongue and the throat <note>original: *gurgulione*, referring to the epiglottis or windpipe area.</note> taking the place of the plectrum, the palate creating the sound, and the teeth and the opening of the mouth—like strings on a lyre—matching the notes, while the nose further contributes to a good or bad resonance. # ON OCCULT PHILOSOPHY.

<margin>The dual nature of the Mind.</margin>
The mind itself is incorporeal and possesses a dual nature: one part investigates the causes, properties, and progressions of those things contained within the order of nature, finding contentment in the contemplation of truth. For this reason, they call it the contemplative intellect <note>original: *contemplatiuum intellectum*. In Renaissance philosophy, this is the faculty used for theoretical science and divine meditation.</note>. The other nature or power of the mind discerns through deliberation what things are to be sought and what are to be avoided; it is entirely engaged in consultation and action, and for this reason, they call it the active intellect. Therefore, nature established this order of powers in man: that through the external senses we might know physical bodies; through the internal senses, we might know the likenesses of bodies beyond that; and further, through the mind or intellect, we might know abstract things, which are neither bodies nor similar to them. In accordance with this threefold order of the soul's powers, three appetites <note>original: *appetitus*. Here meaning a natural "drive" or "inclination" rather than just hunger.</note> are born in the soul. The first is the natural appetite, which is a certain inclination of nature toward its own end—such as the way a stone moves downward—and this exists in all things.

<margin>The threefold appetite in the soul.</margin>
The second is the animal appetite, which follows the senses; it is divided into the irascible <term>irascible: the faculty of the soul dealing with "difficult" emotions like anger, courage, or the drive to overcome obstacles.</term> and the concupiscible <term>concupiscible: the faculty dealing with "simple" desires, such as the pursuit of pleasure or the avoidance of pain.</term>. The third is the intellectual appetite, which is called the will. This differs from the sensory appetite in that the sensory appetite desires nothing unless it is presented to the senses in some way.

<margin>Free Will. The Will of the demon.</margin>
The will, however, although it is of itself directed toward all possible things, is essentially free; therefore, it can even desire impossible things. Such was the case with the demon <note>A reference to Lucifer’s fall, common in medieval and Renaissance theology, where the "impossible" desire was for a creature to be equal to its Creator.</note> who desired to be equal to God. Thus, the will is continually altered and corrupted by pleasure and pain whenever it yields to the lower powers. From this corrupted appetite, four passions are born within it, which sometimes affect the body in a similar way. The first of these is called delight <note>original: *oblectatio*</note>, which is a

<margin>Delight.</margin>
certain softness and yielding of the mind or will, by which it most willingly consents, obeys, and submits to the sweetness offered by the senses. For this reason, they define it as the inclination of the soul toward a softening pleasure.

<margin>Outpouring.</margin>
The second is called outpouring <note>original: *effusio*</note>, which is a relaxation or dissolution of virtue; this occurs when the entire power and intention of the mind, beyond mere delight, melts and flows away due to the sweetness of a present good, spreading itself out entirely and departing from the enjoyment of God. The third is called boasting <note>original: *iactantia*</note>—namely, a fluttering elation—when the mind thinks it has

<margin>Boasting.</margin>
attained some great good, and by the possession of it, lifts itself up insolently, exulting and glorying in vain. The fourth and final passion is malevolence

<margin>Malevolence.</margin>
or malice: a certain pleasure derived from the misfortune of another without any personal gain. It is said to be "without gain" because if someone rejoices in another's misfortune for the sake of their own profit, this would be out of benevolence toward themselves rather than malevolence toward others. Just as these four passions are generated from a corrupted appetite for pleasure, the feeling of pain generates four contrary passions: namely, horror, sadness, fear, and a pain felt at the good of another without personal loss, which we call envy. That is, envy is sadness regarding another's blessings, just as

<margin>Mercy.</margin>
mercy is a certain sadness regarding another's misfortunes.

The passions of the soul are nothing other than certain motions or inclinations resulting from the apprehension of some thing, whether good or bad.

BOOK ONE.

<margin>Passions of the soul.</margin>
...whether they are fitting or unfitting. Such perceptions are of three kinds: sensual, rational, and mental. According to these three levels, there are passions in the soul. Sometimes they follow **sensory perception**, and then they regard a temporal good or evil under the logic of being convenient or inconvenient, delightful or offensive; these are called **natural or animal passions**. Sometimes they follow **rational perception**, and thus they regard good or evil under the logic of virtue and vice, praise and blame, the useful and the useless, the honorable 
<margin>Rational and intellectual passions.</margin>
and the shameful; these are called **rational or voluntary passions**. Sometimes they follow **mental perception**, and they regard good and evil under the logic of the just and the unjust, the true and the false; these are then called **intellectual passions**, or *synderesis* <note>original: *synderesis*. In medieval philosophy, this refers to the innate spark of conscience that allows a human to recognize basic moral truths.</note>. The seat of these passions of the soul is the "appetitive" power itself <note>original: *uis aĩe cõcupitiua*. The part of the soul that "wants" or "strives" for things.</note>, which is divided into the **concupiscible** <term>concupiscible: the faculty of the soul that seeks simple pleasure and avoids pain.</term> and the **irascible** <term>irascible: the faculty that deals with obstacles, such as anger or courage.</term>. Both regard good and evil, but in different ways. 
<margin>The concupiscible power.</margin>
For the **concupiscible power** sometimes regards good and evil absolutely, and thus it causes **love** (or lust) and, conversely, **hatred**. Or it regards good as being absent, and thus it causes **longing** or **desire**, and evil as absent but imminent, which causes **horror**, **flight**, and **abomination**. Or it regards good and evil as present and attained, and thus from the former arises **delight**, **joy**, and **pleasure**, while from the latter comes **sadness**, **anguish**, and **pain**. 
<margin>The irascible power.</margin>
The **irascible power**, however, regards good and evil under the logic of the difficulty in attaining or obtaining it, or in fleeing and repelling it. Sometimes this happens with confidence, and thus on one hand it causes **hope**, and on the other **daring**. Sometimes it happens with a lack of confidence, and thus arises **despair** and **dread** or **fear**. When 
<margin>Eleven passions of the soul.</margin>
this irascible power itself rises up for vengeance—and this only happens regarding a past evil, such as an inflicted injury or harm—it causes **anger**. And so we find **eleven passions** in the soul itself, which are: love, hatred, desire, horror, joy, pain, hope, despair, daring, fear, and anger.

## ¶ How the passions of the soul change the proper body by 
## changing its accidents and moving the spirit. Chapter LXIII.

When the passions of the soul follow sensory perception, the **phantasy** (or the imaginative power) holds the governing authority. For this power, by its own strength and according to the diversity of the passions, first alters and transforms the physical body in various ways through sensible change—by changing the "accidents" <note>original: *accñtia*. In Aristotelian philosophy, these are non-essential qualities like color, temperature, or moisture.</note> in the body and moving the **spirit** <note>original: *spiritum*. In this period, "spirit" referred to a subtle, vaporous substance that circulated through the nerves and arteries, acting as the bridge between the soul and the physical flesh.</note> upward or downward, outward or inward, and producing different qualities in the limbs. Thus, in **joy**, the spirits are expelled outward; in **fear**, they are pulled back; in **shame**, they move toward the brain. Likewise, in joy, the heart dilates outward gradually; in **sadness**, it constricts inward gradually; in **anger** or fear, it does the same, but suddenly. 
<margin>Signs of anger.</margin>
Furthermore, anger or the desire for revenge produces heat, redness, a bitter taste, and a flux of the bowels. 
<margin>Signs of fear.</margin>
Fear induces cold, trembling of the heart, loss of voice, as well as paleness, sadness, sweating, and a bluish-white skin tone. 
<margin>Signs of sadness.</margin>
Even **pity** (which is a type of sadness) often affects the body of the person feeling it poorly, just as the other person's body appears to be affected. Clearly...

## How the passions of the soul also work outside themselves upon another's body. Chapter LXV.

<margin>
Effects of the passions of the soul.
</margin>
The passions of the soul which follow the fantasy <term>fantasy: In this context, *phantasia* refers to the faculty of the mind that forms and retains mental images.</term>, when they are most vehement, can not only change one's own body, but can also transcend to work upon another's body, so that certain wonderful impressions are produced therefrom in the elements and external things, and they could even take away or bring on certain diseases of the soul or body. For the passions of the soul are the most powerful cause of the temperament <note>The balance of the "four humors" (blood, phlegm, black bile, and yellow bile) that determined health and personality.</note> of one's own body. Thus a soul strongly elevated and kindled by a vehement imagination sends health or sickness, not only into its own body, but also into the bodies of others. Thus Avicenna <note>The Latinized name of Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian polymath and one of the most significant physicians of the Islamic Golden Age.</note> believes that a camel might fall by the imagination of someone. Thus, for one who falls into madness after being bitten by a rabid dog, the figures of dogs appear in his urine. Thus the longing of a pregnant woman acts upon another body when she stains the fetus in the womb with the mark of the thing desired. 
<margin>

</margin>

</margin>

</margin>

### BOOK ONE.

How white peacocks are produced.

Now, through these examples, it is clear how the affects of the imagination [phantasy], when they are intensely directed, affect not only one's own body but also the bodies of others. Thus also the desire of sorcerers to do harm "fascinates" <term>fascinatio: the act of casting a spell or causing harm through a look, often called the "evil eye"</term> and harms people with fixed and most pernicious stares.

<margin>
Infection of the plague.
</margin>
<margin>
The power of the eyes.
</margin>
<margin>
The company of the wicked must be avoided.
</margin>
<margin>
Bad odors must be avoided.
</margin>
Avicenna, Aristotle, Al-Ghazali, and Galen <note>A list of the era's most respected authorities in medicine and philosophy: Avicenna and Al-Ghazali (Persian), Aristotle (Greek), and Galen (Roman).</note> agree with these points. For it is manifest that a body is very easily infected by the vapor of another diseased body, as we clearly see in cases of the plague and leprosy. Furthermore, there is such great power in the vapors of the eyes that they can fascinate and infect those nearby, just as the basilisk <note>original: "regulus"</note> and the catablepas <note>A legendary Ethiopian beast described by Pliny as having a gaze that kills instantly.</note> kill men with their sight; and certain women in Scythia, among the Illyrians and Triballians, were said to kill those they looked upon in anger. Therefore, let no one wonder that the body and soul of one person can be similarly affected by the mind of another, since the mind is far more powerful, stronger, more fervent, and more vigorous in its movement than the vapors exhaling from bodies. Nor are the means lacking through which the mind operates, and a body is no less subject to another’s mind than to another’s body. In this way, they say a person acts upon another through affect and disposition alone. Therefore, the philosophers command that the company of evil and unfortunate people should be avoided from afar, for the souls of such harmful people are full of "rays" and infect those nearby with a disastrous contagion. Conversely, they command that the company of the good and the fortunate should be sought out, because they benefit us greatly by their proximity. For just as an odor arises from asafoetida <note>A pungent resin used in medicine and cooking, often called "devil's dung."</note> or musk, so from an evil person something evil, and from a good person something good, leaps forth into those nearby and sometimes remains infused there for a long time.

<margin>
Reason is more excellent than imagination.
</margin>
Now, if the aforementioned passions have such great power in the imagination [phantasy], they certainly have a greater power in **reason**, insofar as reason itself is more excellent than imagination. Finally, they have much greater power in the **mind**; for when the mind is fixed upon some benefit with the whole intention of the soul toward the heavens <note>original: "superos" — referring to the divine powers or celestial beings above</note>, it often affects both its own body and that of another toward which it is directed with some divine gift. In this way, we read that miracles were performed by Apollonius, Pythagoras, Empedocles, Philolaus, and many prophets, and even by the saints of our own religion. These matters will be revealed more extensively below, where we shall discuss religion.

For, as Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the foundational astronomer and astrologer of antiquity.</note> says, he who chooses that which is better seems to differ in no way from him who possesses this by nature. ...through [affects], passions, imaginations, choices, deliberations, contemplations, and the like, we also make ourselves consonant with the heavens. For passions of this kind vehemently stir our spirit to their own likeness, and suddenly expose us and our affairs to the celestial powers <note>original: "superis," referring to the stars or higher spiritual beings</note> that signify such passions. Moreover, because of their dignity and proximity to these higher powers, these internal states receive celestial influence much more and more fully than any material objects do. For our soul can, through imagination or reason by a certain imitation, be so conformed to a specific star that it is suddenly filled with the gifts of that same star, as if it were the proper receptacle for its influence <term>influxus: the "flowing in" of celestial power or energy from the stars</term>. But the contemplative mind—insofar as it calls itself away from all sense, imagination, nature, and deliberation, and recalls itself to separate things (except insofar as it exposes itself to Saturn <note>In Renaissance thought, Saturn is the planet associated with deep, solitary contemplation and melancholy.</note>)—is not the subject of the present investigation.

<margin>The effect of faith.</margin>
For our mind performs many things through faith, which is a firm adhesion, a fixed intention, and a vehement application of the person acting or receiving, in whatever matter, toward that which cooperates and gives power to the work we intend to do. This is so much the case that there is formed in us, in a way, an "idol" <note>original: "idolum"; here meaning a mental image, form, or internal representation that acts as a blueprint</note> of the power to be received, and of the thing to be done in us or by us. Therefore, in any work and application of things, we ought to vehemently desire, imagine, hope, and most firmly believe, for that will be of the greatest help. And it has been verified among physicians that firm belief, indubitable hope, and love toward the physician and the medicine contribute greatly to health—sometimes even more than the medicine itself.

<margin>Belief toward the physician.</margin>
For alongside the power and effective force of the medicine, the strong soul of the physician also works, being powerful enough to change the qualities in the body of the sick person, especially when the patient, placing faith in the physician, by that very act disposes himself to receive the power of the healer and the medicine. And therefore, in magic, the operator must possess constant belief, be confident, and in no way doubt the achievement of the effect, nor hesitate in mind. For just as firm and persistent belief works wonders, even sometimes in false works, so distrust and hesitation dissipate and break the power of the operator's soul, which stands as the medium between both extremes. From this, it happens that the desired influence from the celestial powers is frustrated and lost, for it cannot be joined and united to our things and works without the stable and solid power of our own soul.

Because of this, the craftsmanship of **characters** <term>characters: mystical signs or sigils believed to hold power</term>, **images** <note>often referring to talismans or statues made under specific astrological conditions</note>, **incantations**, **speeches**, and many other marvelous experiments is proven to achieve total human obedience. But you should know that such things provide nothing (or at least very little) except to their author, or to one who is already inclined toward them as if they were already their author. This is the way in which their effectiveness is found. <margin>A general rule.</margin> And there is a general rule in these matters: that every soul which is more excellent in its desire and affection makes such things more fit and effective for that which it craves. Therefore, anyone wishing to work in **magic** <note>original: "magia"; here meaning the natural science of hidden properties</note> must know and understand the property, virtue, measure, order, and rank of their own soul within the power of the universe itself.

### ¶ How our mind can change and bind lower things to that which it desires. Chapter 68.

There is also in the minds of men a certain power of changing, attracting, hindering, and **binding** <term>binding: the magical act of "ligatio," or restricting the actions or nature of another thing</term> things and people toward that which the mind desires. All things obey the soul when it is carried into a great excess of some passion or virtue, so much so that it overcomes those things it binds. For that which is superior binds that which is inferior and turns it toward itself; and the inferior, by the same logic, is turned toward the superior, or is otherwise affected or agitated. By this reasoning, things that hold the rank of a superior star bind, attract, or hinder things that hold a lower rank, according to how they agree or disagree with one another. <margin>Why the rooster is feared by the lion; why the magnet stone draws iron.</margin> For this reason, the **rooster** is feared by the **lion**, because the presence of the **solar virtue** <note>original: "solaris virtus"; the spiritual quality or power associated with the Sun, which is traditionally stronger in the rooster.</note> is more compatible with the rooster than with the lion. So too, the **magnet** draws iron because it holds a superior rank in the order of the **Celestial Bear** <note>original: "coelestis ursæ"; the constellation Ursa Major, which was believed to govern magnetism and the north.</note>; and the **diamond** <term>adamant: a legendary stone of unbreakable hardness, often identified with the diamond</term> hinders the magnet...

<margin>The root of binding.</margin>
The root of such binding <term>ligationis: the magical act of "binding" or constraining another's will or body</term> is the vehement and unbridled passion of the soul itself, combined with the concurrence of the celestial order.

The dissolutions or hindrances of this kind of binding are achieved through a contrary passion, and one that is more excellent and stronger; for just as a greater excess of the soul binds, so also does it loosen and hinder. Finally, where you fear Venus, oppose her with Saturn; where you fear Saturn or Mars, oppose them with Venus or Jupiter; for astrologers claim these are enemies and most contrary to each other. Understand this as referring to the diverse and contrary passions caused in these lower realms; for in heaven, where nothing is lacking and where all things are ruled by love, hatred or enmity can hardly exist.

### ¶ On speech, and the virtues of words. Chapter LXIX.

<margin>Why man is [called] rational.</margin>
Having now shown that great virtue resides in the passions of the soul, it must further be known that no less virtue exists in words and the names of things, and the greatest power resides in complex speeches and orations. By these, we differ most from the beasts and are called "rational"—not because of the reason <note>Latin: "ratio"</note> which is perceived in the soul (which they call the seat of the passions, and which **Galen** <note>A famous 2nd-century Greek physician and philosopher</note> says even the brute animals have in common with us, though some more and some less), but we are called rational from the reason which is understood through the voice in words and speech. This is called **enunciative reason** <term>ratio enuntiativa: the capacity to express internal logic through external language</term>, by which part we most excel all other living creatures. For to the Greeks, **Logos** <note>original: "λoγoς"</note> signifies both reason, speech, and word. However, the "word" is twofold: namely, the internal and the spoken. The **internal word** <term>verbum internum</term> is the concept of the mind and the movement of the soul, which occurs in the thinking power without a voice; just as when we seem to speak and argue with ourselves in dreams, and even while awake and silent, we often run through an entire oration. The **spoken word** <term>verbum prolatum</term>, however, has a certain expression in the voice and the property of speech; it is brought forth with the breath of a human, the opening of the mouth, and the movement of the tongue. In this, mother nature has coupled the corporeal voice and speech to the mind and intellect, making the voice the proclaimer and interpreter of our intellectual concepts to those listening, which we must discuss here.

<margin>The medium between the speaker and the listener.</margin>
Words are, therefore, the most suitable medium between the speaker and the listener, carrying with them not only a concept but also transferring the virtue <note>in the sense of "inherent power" or "efficacy"</note> of the speaker into the listeners and observers by a certain **energy** <term>energia: an active, transformative power</term>, often with such great power that not...

### On the Power of Proper Names. Chapter LXX.

Almost all testify that the **proper names** of things are highly necessary for **magical operations**. For since the natural power of things proceeds first from the objects to the senses, then from these to the imagination, and finally from there to the mind—in which it is first conceived and then expressed through voices and words. Therefore, the **Platonists** <note>followers of the philosopher Plato</note> say that in this very voice, or word, or name (now formed into its distinct parts), the power of the thing itself lies hidden like a kind of life under the form of its meaning. It is first conceived by the mind through the "seeds of things," then brought forth through voices or words like a birth, and finally preserved in writing. 
<margin>Proper names of things are certain rays.</margin>
For this reason, **Magi** <note>wise men or practitioners of high natural magic</note> say that the proper names of things are certain **rays of the things**, always present everywhere, and preserving the power of those things. This is because the essence of the signified thing dominates and is discerned within the names, and things are recognized through them as if through proper and living images. Just as the Supreme Creator, from the influences of the heavens and the elements with the virtues of the planets, produces diverse species and particular things, so too—according to the properties of those same influences—proper names for things result. These were imposed by Him who "counts the number of the stars and calls them all by their names" <note>quoting Psalm 147:4</note>. Concerning these names, **CHRIST** says elsewhere: "your names are written in heaven" <note>quoting Luke 10:20</note>. Knowing the celestial influences and the properties of each individual thing, the **protoplast** <note>protoplastes: a term for Adam, the "first-formed" human</note> imposed names on things according to their quiddities <term>quidditates: the "whatness" or essential nature of a thing</term>, just as it is written in Genesis: for God brought all things He had created before Adam so that he might name them. And as he called the thing, so was its name. 
<margin>Names of things.</margin>
Indeed, these names contain within themselves the wondrous powers of the things they signify. Therefore, every meaningful voice signifies first through the influence of **celestial harmony**, and secondarily through **human imposition** <note>the act of humans assigning names to objects</note>, though more often it happens differently through one or the other. However, when both meanings concur in some voice or name—the one from harmony and the one imposed by humans—then that name is rendered most effective for action by a doubled virtue (namely, the natural and the voluntary). This occurs whenever it is uttered in the proper places and times, with solemnity and exact intention, upon prepared material that is naturally susceptible to it.

It is said that when a girl, who had died on her wedding day, was presented to **Apollonius** <note>Apollonius of Tyana, a first-century philosopher and reputed wonder-worker</note>, he touched the maiden and inquired carefully after her name; once he knew it, he is said to have pronounced some occult thing, by which the girl returned to life. The **Romans** also had an observation in their sacred rites: whenever they besieged a city, they would diligently seek out its proper name and the name of the deity under whose protection that city stood. Once these were known, they would summon the guardian gods of that city with a certain song <note>original: "carmine," meaning a ritual chant or incantation</note> and devote the inhabitants of the city themselves to destruction; thus, with the gods departed, they would finally conquer them, just as **Virgil** sings:

> All the gods, by whom this empire stood, 
> Have departed, leaving behind their shrines and altars.

Anyone who wishes to know the ritual song by which the deities were summoned and the enemies devoted to destruction when a city was surrounded by siege may find it in the works of **Livy** and **Macrobius**, and **Serenus Sammonicus** also recounts many of these things in his "Books of Secret Matters."

### ¶ On complex speeches, and songs, and the powers and bindings of incantations. Chapter LXXI.

<margin>Names of Magic.</margin>
Beyond the virtues of words and names, another even greater virtue is found in **complex orations** <term>orationibus complexis: structured speeches, prayers, or formal sentences</term> because of the truth contained within them. This truth possesses the greatest power for impressing, changing, binding, and establishing; so much so, that when shaken, it shines more brightly, and when attacked, it is made firmer and more consolidated. This virtue of truth is not found in simple words, but in declarations by which something is affirmed or denied—such as songs, incantations, imprecations, prayers, invocations, protestations, oaths, exorcisms, and the like. Therefore, in composing songs and orations to attract the virtue of a star or some spirit, one must diligently consider what virtues, effects, and operations each star contains. These should be inserted into the songs by praising, extolling, amplifying, and adorning those things which such a star is accustomed to bring and influence, while diminishing and rejecting those things it is accustomed to destroy and hinder. One should also plead and swear for what we desire to obtain, while accusing and detesting what we wish to be destroyed or hindered. In this way, one composes an oration for a song that is adorned, elegant, and duly distinguished into parts by certain appropriate rhythms and proportions. Furthermore, the **magi** command that one must invoke and pray using the names of that same star or spirit to which the song pertains, and by its wonders or miracles, by its courses and paths in its sphere, by its light, by the nobility of its kingdom, by the grace and clarity within it, by its strong and marvelous virtues, and by things similar to these. Just as in **Apuleius**, **Psyche** prays to **Ceres**: "I entreat you," she says, "by your fruitful right hand, I constantly pray by the joy-bringing ceremonies of the harvests, by the silent secrets of the chests, by the winged paths of your servant dragons, and the furrows of the **Sicilian** soil, and the rapacious chariot, and..."

The instrument itself of the enchanters is a certain most pure **harmonic spirit** <term>spiritus harmonicus: a refined, vital breath or essence that acts as a bridge between the physical voice and the spiritual intent</term>, warming, breathing, living, carrying with it motion, affection, and meaning, composed of its own segments, endowed with sense, and finally conceived by reason. Therefore, through the quality of this spirit and through its celestial similarity, in addition to what has been said, songs also conceive most excellent virtues from heaven through the opportunity of time. These are much more sublime and efficacious than the spirits and vapors exhaling from vegetable life—from herbs, roots, gums, spices, fumigations, and such like. 

And for this reason, magicians when enchanting are accustomed to blow upon things and inhale the words of the song, as if breathing in the virtue with the spirit itself, so that the entire virtue of the soul may be directed into the enchanted thing, which is disposed to receive the said virtue. And here it is to be noted: that just as all speech, writing, and words induce customary movements through their usual numbers, proportions, and form, so also when uttered or written out of their usual order and backwards, they move toward unusual effects.

# ON OCCULT PHILOSOPHY

A mind polluted by no draft of poison perishes when enchanted <note>original: "Excantata perit," referring to the idea that a mind can be "sung out" or destroyed by magic alone, without physical toxins</note>. Likewise, **Virgil** says in the character of **Damon** <note>In Virgil's *Eclogues* 8</note>:
> Songs can even draw the moon down from heaven.
> By songs **Circe** transformed the companions of **Ulysses**.
> The cold snake in the meadows is burst apart by singing,
> And I have seen the sown harvests moved to another place.

And **Ovid**, in his work *Without a Title* <note>original: "Sine titulo," referring to the *Amores*</note>, says:
> Harmed by a song, **Ceres** <note>The Roman goddess of grain; here used as a metonym for the crops themselves</note> withers into a barren weed,
> The waters of the spring, harmed by a song, fail.
> Acorns fall from the oaks and the grapes from enchanted vines,
> And apples drop, though none move the tree.

If these things were not true, such strict punishments would not have been established by law <note>Agrippa refers here to the **Twelve Tables**, the ancient Roman legal code, which famously forbade "enchanting" a neighbor's crops (excantassent fruges)</note> against those who had enchanted the harvests. And **Tibullus** says of a certain sorceress:
> I have seen her drawing stars down from heaven,
> She turns the course of the rapid river by a song.
> By singing she splits the ground, lures the ghosts from their tombs,
> And calls down bones from the warm pyre.
> When she pleases, she drives the clouds from the gloomy sky,
> When she pleases, she calls forth snow in the summer heat.

Concerning all these things, that famous sorceress <note>Medea</note> seems to boast much in **Ovid** when she says:
> When I wished, with the very banks marvelling, rivers returned
> To their own sources; I still the shaken waters,
> And shake the standing seas with my song; I drive away clouds,
> And I bring clouds back; I banish and summon the winds;
> I break the viper's jaws with words and song;
> I move the living rocks, the oaks torn from their earth,
> And the woods; I command the mountains to tremble,
> And the ground to bellow, and the ghosts to go out from their tombs,
> I draw you too, O Moon.

<margin>The power of songs.</margin>
Furthermore, all poets sing of it, and philosophers do not deny, that many marvelous things can be achieved by songs: such as driving away crops, forcing or obtaining lightning, curing diseases, and the like. For even **Cato** in his work on agriculture used certain incantations <note>Cato the Elder's *De Agricultura* contains various rhythmic charms for healing dislocations and sickness in oxen</note> against the

diseases of beasts, which still exist in his writings. **Josephus** <note>The Jewish-Roman historian</note> testifies that **Solomon** was also skilled in such incantations. **Celsus Africanus** also relates that according to the doctrine of the **Egyptians**, the human body—according to the number of the faces <term>facierum: the "decans" or three ten-degree divisions of each zodiac sign</term> of the signs of the zodiac—is

# BOOK ONE.

### ¶ On the power of writing, and on the making of imprecations and inscriptions. Chapter 73.

<margin>o</margin>
<margin>The power of writings.</margin>
The duty of words and speech is to announce the inner workings of the mind, to bring secrets forth from the depths of thought, and to reveal the will of the speaker. Writing, however, is the ultimate expression of the mind; it is the rhythm, collection, state, goal, containment, and repetition of speech and voice, creating a lasting "habit" <note>In this context, a "habit" refers to a stable, permanent state or quality that remains even when the speaker is silent</note> that is not achieved by the single act of a voice. Whatever exists in the mind, the voice, the word, the oration, or the speech—all of this is also present in writing. And just as nothing conceived in the mind remains unexpressed by the voice, so nothing expressed by the voice remains unwritten. Therefore, magicians command that in every work, imprecations <note>original: "imprecationes," referring here to formal verbal charges or spoken commands rather than just curses</note> and inscriptions must be made. Through these, the practitioner expresses their intent: if they are gathering an herb or a small stone, they should declare for what use they do so; if they are crafting an image, they should say and write down to what effect it is being made. Indeed, **Albertus [Magnus]** <note>A 13th-century polymath; the work cited is the *Speculum Astronomiae* (The Mirror of Astronomy)</note> does not disapprove of these imprecations and inscriptions in his *Mirror*, for without them, our works would not be led to their effect. For the "disposition" <note>The physical preparation or arrangement of an object</note> does not cause the effect, but rather the "act" of that disposition <note>The formal declaration or spiritual activation that brings the potential to life</note>. We find this same type of instruction was in use among the ancients, as **Virgil** himself testifies when he sings:

> First, I wrap these three threads of three different colors
> Around you, and three times I lead this image around
> These altars. ->And a little later:<-
> Tie three colors in three knots, Amaryllis;
> Tie them, Amaryllis, and say: "I tie the bonds of **Venus**." ->And in the same place:<-
> As this clay hardens, and as this wax melts
> In one and the same fire, so may **Daphnis** [be affected] by my love.

# ON OCCULT PHILOSOPHY.

[...as their] figure, as the masters of the Hebrews testify, the letters themselves were formed, being most full of celestial mysteries, both through their figure, form, and meanings, as well as through the numbers signified in them, and through the various harmony of their binding together. Hence the more secret **Kabbalists** <note>original: "Mecubales," a Latinization of the Hebrew "Mekubbalim," meaning those who have received the hidden tradition or Kabbalah</note> of the Hebrews promise to explain everything—how they proceeded from the first cause and are able to be led back to the same—through the forms of the figures and characters of those letters and through their signature, simplicity, composition, separation, crookedness, direction, deficiency, abundance, largeness, smallness, coronation <note>referring to the *tagin*, or decorative "crowns" placed atop certain Hebrew letters</note>, opening, closing, order, transmutation, binding, and the revolution of letters, points, and apexes, as well as the calculation of numbers signified through the letters.

<margin>The triple division of Hebrew letters. To what the Hebrew letters are likened.</margin>
Furthermore, the Hebrews divide the letters of their alphabet into three parts: namely, into twelve **simple**, seven **double**, and three **mothers**: which they say signify, as characters of things, the twelve signs [of the Zodiac], the seven planets, and the three elements: namely fire, water, and earth. For they do not consider air an element, but rather the glue and spirit of the elements. To these they also coordinate points and apexes. Therefore, just as all things were and are produced by the aspects of the planets and signs together with the elements through the craftsman-spirit <note>original: "opifice spiritu," referring to the *demiurge* or divine animating force that shapes the physical world</note> and truth, so from these letter-characters and the points signifying those produced things are formed the names of all things. These names act as certain sacraments and vehicles of the things explained, carrying their essence and powers everywhere with them. The deep meanings and sacraments of these things are inherent in those characters and their figures, numbers, position, order, and revolution. For this reason, **Origen** <note>An influential early Christian scholar (c. 184–253 AD) who argued that sacred names lose their divine power when translated out of their original tongue</note> thinks that those names, when translated into another language, retain almost none of their proper power, because they do not retain their natural significance. Only primary names that are correctly assigned possess natural activity because they signify naturally. This is not the case for names that signify by mere convention <note>original: "ad placitum," meaning by human agreement or arbitrary choice rather than inherent nature</note>, which do not have power as signifiers, but only as natural objects in themselves. If there is any first and causal language, whose words have natural significance, it is agreed that this is Hebrew. He who holds its order deeply and fundamentally, and knows how to revolve its letters proportionally, will have the norm and rule for perfectly discovering the basis of any language whatever.

<margin>The number of Hebrew letters.</margin>
Thus, there are twenty-two letters, the foundation of the world and of all creatures that exist and are named within it; and every spoken word, and every created thing, exists because of them. From their revolutions, things receive their name, being, and power. However, the investigator of these things must run through each combination of letters until the voice of God is clear, and the text of the most sacred letters offers itself openly. For from this, voices and words have efficacy in magical works, because that in which nature first exercises magic is the voice of God. But these [matters] of higher speculation...
