BOOK TWO. LXXXIII

They <note>the geometric figures mentioned on the previous page</note> do not act except through a power acquired from higher forms, born of a certain attraction—which a natural aptitude or similarity provides—insofar as they are shaped exactly to those higher forms. This is much like how an echo is caused by an opposing wall, or how a concave mirror collects solar rays, which it then reflects onto an opposing object, wood, or other combustible material, causing it to burn immediately. Or, it is like how one lute <note>original: "cithara"</note> causes a resonance in another lute, for no other reason than that a shape of the same form and likeness is placed within view; or as two strings on a lyre, stretched at equal intervals and tuned to the same pitch, will both tremble when only one is plucked.

In the same way, the figures we have discussed, and whatever characters <term>characters: magical signs or sigils</term> are used, conceive the powers of celestial figures, provided they are impressed upon things at an opportune time when those stars are dominant, or are fashioned according to the proper rites—as if one figure conspires with and requires its matching figure. And just as these things have been said regarding flat figures, they are likewise to be understood regarding **Geometric bodies**: which are the sphere, the tetrahedron, the hexahedron, the octahedron, the icosahedron, the dodecahedron, and those similar to them.

Indeed, we must not overlook which figures **Pythagoras** and his followers, **Timaeus of Locris** and **Plato**, assigned to the elements and the heavens: 

<margin>Figures of the elements and heaven.</margin>
For to **Earth**, they gave the first cube, having eight solid angles, twenty-four planes <note>referring to the edges or faces depending on the geometric convention used</note>, and six bases; it is square in the form of a die. 
<margin>The figure of Earth.</margin>

To **Fire**, they attributed the pyramid <note>the tetrahedron</note> of four triangular bases, with as many solid angles and twelve planes. 
<margin>The figure of Fire.</margin>

For **Air**, they established the octahedron, made of eight triangular bases, six solid angles, and twenty-four planes. 
<margin>The figure of Air.</margin>

To **Water**, finally, they assigned the icosahedron, with twenty bases and twelve solid angles. 
<margin>The figure of Water.</margin>

To the **Heavens**, they gave the dodecahedron, consisting of twelve pentagonal bases, twenty solid angles, and sixty planes.
<margin>The figure of Heaven.</margin>

Whoever knows the powers of these figures and bodies, and their mutual relationship and properties, will be able to perform many wonders in **natural magic** and **perspective** <note>the science of optics</note>, especially regarding mirrors. I myself have known how to construct marvelous things from them, including mirrors in which one can see whatever one wishes from a very great distance.
<margin>Wonders of mirrors.</margin>

<margin>e</margin>
<margin>The power of sound.</margin>
Furthermore, we shall not deny that there is a power in sound for receiving celestial gifts, if we agree with Pythagoras and Plato that the heavens consist of a harmonic composition, and that the heavens govern and effect all things by harmonic tones and motions. However, song can do more than instrumental sound, insofar as it proceeds—beyond harmonic concord—from the conception of the mind and the commanding passion of the imagination and the heart. Together with the broken and tempered air, it easily penetrates the aerial spirit of the listener, 
<margin>The bond of soul and body.</margin>
which is the bond between the soul and the body. By its motion, it transfers the passion and the mind of the singer into the listener, moving emotion by emotion, affecting imagination by imagination, and mind by mind. It strikes the heart and enters into the very inner chambers of the mind, gradually instilling habits and character. Moreover, it moves or stills the limbs and the humors of the body. Hence, harmony contributes so much to moving the passions that not only natural harmony, but even artificial and vocal harmony, exert a force upon minds and bodies. 
<margin>Dissonant voices of animals.</margin>
It is necessary, however, for all harmonies to proceed from compatible foundations, whether they be in strings, in pipes, or in voices, if they are to come together as one. For no one can make the roaring of lions, the lowing of oxen, the neighing of horses, the braying of an ass, or the grunting of a pig harmonize together. Nor can strings made from the guts of a wolf and a lamb be brought into any consonance, 
<margin>Harmonious voices of humans.</margin>
because their foundations are dissonant. Yet the various voices of many humans harmonize because their foundation is unique according to their species. 
<margin>Voices of birds.</margin>
Many birds also harmonize because they share a single closely related genus and a symbol from the higher powers. 
<margin>The human voice with artificial instruments.</margin>
Artificial instruments also harmonize with natural voices because there is a similarity between them, either true and expressed, or through a certain analogy. Now, every concord consists of sounds or voices. Sound is spirit; voice is sound and animated spirit; speech is spirit uttered with sound and voice signifying something.

Chalcidius <note>A 4th-century philosopher known for his commentary on Plato’s *Timaeus*.</note> says the voice is sent forth from the inner sanctuary of the breast and the lap of the heart by the striving spirit, where a boundary of nerves is placed to separate the heart from the lungs; by the pulse of both these and the other vital organs, it hits the narrowness of the throat and is shaped by the tongue and the other vocal organs. Thus, articulated sounds are emitted—the elements of speech—through which, as an interpreter, the secret movements of the mind are opened. However, Lactantius <note>An early Christian author (c. 250–325 AD) known as the "Christian Cicero."</note> says that the nature of the voice is so obscure that it cannot be fully understood how it is made, or even what it entirely is.

<margin>
In what things music is placed.
The power of the senses.
</margin>
Finally, all music is founded in voice, sound, and hearing. Sound cannot become audible without air; and although air is so necessary for hearing, yet air itself is not audible, nor can it be perceived by any sense except by accident. For the sight does not see it unless it is colored, nor the hearing unless it is sounding, nor the smell unless it is scented, nor the taste unless it is flavorful, nor the touch unless it is hot or cold or something of that kind. Therefore, although sound does not occur without air, sound is not of the nature of air, nor is air of the nature of sound. Rather, air exists as the <term>body of our sensitive life-spirit</term> <note>original: "corpus vitae spiritus nostri sensitivi"; in Renaissance thought, a "spirit" was a subtle vapor that connected the soul to the physical body.</note>. It does not belong to the nature of any sensible object, but is of a simpler and higher power. It is necessary, moreover, for the sensitive soul to vivify the air joined to itself, and in that vivified air joined to the spirit, to perceive the forms <note>original: "species"; the philosophical term for the sensible "images" or "likenesses" of objects that travel to the sense organs.</note> of objects placed in action—and this occurs in the living air. In transparent and subtle air, it perceives visible forms; in common air, audible forms; and in thicker air, the forms of the other senses.

### BOOK TWO LXXXV

<margin>Mercury’s harmony.</margin>
Furthermore, as if the <term>tetrachord</term> <note>A four-stringed scale used in ancient Greek music theory.</note> were contained by the number of the four elements, its inventor Mercury—according to the author Nicomachus <note>A mathematician and music theorist of the 2nd century AD.</note>—gave it four strings. They intended the <term>hypate</term> <note>The "highest" string in position, though lowest in pitch.</note> to represent the earth, the <term>parhypate</term> or <term>mese</term> to represent water, and the <term>nete</term>
<margin>Mercury’s lyre.</margin>
or <term>diezeugmenon</term>, or <term>hyperboleos</term> to represent fire; while the <term>paranete</term> or <term>synemmenon</term> represented the air. Later, however, Terpander of Lesbos <note>An 8th-century BC poet and musician credited with inventing the seven-stringed lyre.</note> discovered a seventh string, making them equal to the number of the planets. Moreover, those who followed the number of the elements said that the four genres of music corresponded to them as well as to the <term>four humors</term> <note>The bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—thought to control health and temperament.</note>: they believed the Dorian mode resonated with water and phlegm, the Phrygian with choler <note>Yellow bile.</note> and fire, the Lydian with blood and air, and the Mixolydian with black bile and earth. Others, looking toward the number and power of the heavens, assigned the Dorian to the Sun, the Phrygian to Mars, the Lydian to Jupiter, the Mixolydian to Saturn, the Hypophrygian to Mercury, the Hypolydian to Venus, the Hypodorian to the Moon, and the Hypermixolydian to the starry sky. Furthermore, they related the Muses and the strings to the heavens along with these modes of harmony, but not in the same order as we described regarding the nine Muses among the numbers and souls of the heavens. For they say that the Muse Thalia has no harmony, assigning her to silence and the earth. Clio, however, together with the Moon, moves the Hypodorian mode and the string called the <term>proslambanomenos</term> <note>The "added note" at the bottom of the Greek scale.</note>. Calliope and Mercury possess the Hypophrygian mode and the <term>hypate hypaton</term> string. Terpsichore with Venus governs the Hypolydian and the <term>parhypate hypaton</term>. Melpomene and the Sun are fitted to the Dorian and the <term>lichanos hypaton</term>. Erato with Mars guards the Phrygian and the <term>hypate meson</term>. Euterpe and Jupiter agree with the Lydian and the <term>parhypate meson</term>. Polymnia and Saturn keep the Mixolydian and the <term>lichanos meson</term>. Finally, the Hypermixolydian mode and the <term>mese</term> string are ascribed to Urania and the starry sky, which we read expressed in the following verses:

<margin>The space between the earth and the moon. The distance between the planets.</margin>
Some people even investigate the harmony of the heavens by calculating the distance of the spheres from one another. For that space which lies between the earth and the moon—namely, one hundred and twenty-six thousand Italian <term>stades</term> <note>An ancient unit of distance, roughly 185 meters.</note>—makes the interval of a whole tone. From the moon to <term>Mercury</term>, half of that space makes a <term>semitone</term>. An equal distance from Mercury to <term>Venus</term> makes another semitone. From there to the <term>Sun</term>, a distance three times as great (as if a tone and a half) establishes a <term>diapente</term> <note>A musical interval of a fifth.</note>. From the moon to the sun, the distance makes a <term>diatessaron</term> <note>A musical interval of a fourth.</note>, consisting of two and a half tones. From the sun to <term>Mars</term>, there is again as much distance as from the earth to the moon, making a whole tone. From there to <term>Jupiter</term> is half that, making another semitone. An equal distance from Jupiter to <term>Saturn</term> also constitutes a semitone, and from Saturn to the starry orb <note>The sphere of the fixed stars.</note>, there lies another 
<margin>The interval between the sun and the starry heaven.</margin>
space of a semitone. Therefore, the distance from the sun to the starry heaven is a <term>diatessaron</term> of two and a half tones, while from the earth to the heaven it is a perfect <term>diapason</term> <note>A musical interval of an octave.</note> of six full tones. Now, even from the proportion of the movements of the planets relative to each other and to the eighth heaven, there results a harmony most sweet of all. The proportion of the movements 
<margin>The proportion of the movements of the planets.</margin>
of <term>Saturn</term> to <term>Jupiter</term> is <term>dupla sesquialtera</term> <note>A ratio of 5:2.</note>; of Jupiter to Mars, it is sixfold; of Mars to the Sun, Venus, and Mercury (who complete their journey together), the proportion is double; of those to the moon, it is twelvefold. From Saturn to the star-bearing orb, it is one thousand two hundredfold—if it be true, as <term>Ptolemy</term> <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century astronomer.</note> says, that this heaven moves one degree every hundred years against the <term>prime mover</term> <note>The "Primum Mobile," the outermost sphere that drives the rotation of all others.</note>.
<margin>The swiftest orb of all.</margin>
Therefore, in its own proper motion, the moon’s movement is swifter and makes a sharper sound than the star-bearing orb, which, being the slowest of all, makes the deepest sound. But in the "violent" motion—which is that of the prime mover—it is the 
<margin>The motion of the moon.</margin>
swiftest and sharpest of all, while the lunar motion is the slowest and deepest. This proportion and reciprocation of movements produces a most sweet harmony. Hence, no songs, no sounds, and no musical instruments are more powerful for moving the affections of men and inducing magical impressions than those composed after the likeness of the celestial numbers, measures, and proportions.
<margin>The harmony of the elements.</margin>
The harmony of the <term>elements</term> <note>Fire, Air, Water, and Earth.</note> is also drawn from their bases and angles, which we discussed previously. For since between fire and air there is a double proportion in their bases, a <term>sesquialtera</term> <note>A 3:2 ratio.</note> in their solid angles, and again a double proportion in their planes, a harmony is born of a double <term>diapason</term> <note>Two octaves.</note> and a <term>diapente</term> <note>A fifth.</note>. Between air and water, the proportion in their bases is <term>dupla sesquialtera</term> <note>A 5:2 ratio.</note>, from which comes a <term>diapason</term>, a <term>diapente</term>, and a <term>diatessaron</term>. In their angles, the proportion is double, from which again comes a <term>diapason</term>. Between water and earth, the proportion in their bases is <term>tripla sesquialtera</term> <note>A 10:3 ratio.</note>...

...the third, from which arises the <term>diapason</term> <note>An octave (2:1 ratio).</note>, the <term>diapente</term> <note>A perfect fifth (3:2 ratio).</note>, and the <term>diatessaron</term> <note>A perfect fourth (4:3 ratio).</note>; while in the corners, it again establishes a <term>sesquialtera</term> <note>A 3:2 ratio, which produces the musical interval of a fifth.</note>, forming a diapente. Furthermore, the proportion between earth and fire in their bases is sesquialtera, making a diapente; but in their angles, it is <term>dupla</term> <note>A 2:1 ratio, which produces an octave.</note>, establishing a diapason. However, between fire and water, and between air and earth, harmony is somewhat lacking, since between these there is a complete opposition of qualities; yet they agree through an intermediate element.

### Of the proportion, measure, and harmony of the human body. Chapter XXVII.

<margin>The image of God. The minor world.</margin>
Since man is the most beautiful and perfect work and image of God, and a <term>microcosm</term> <note>original: "minor mundus"; the concept that the human being is a miniature map of the entire universe.</note>, he contains and sustains within himself all numbers, measures, weights, motions, and elements—and everything else that composes him—with a more perfect composition, a sweeter harmony, and a loftier dignity. All things in him, as if in a supreme piece of craftsmanship, achieve a certain supreme destiny beyond the common consonance they possess in other compounds.

<margin>Numbers and measures found from human joints.</margin>
Hence all the ancients used to count with their fingers and indicate numbers with their digits. They seemed to prove that all numbers, measures, proportions, and harmonies were discovered from the very joints of the human body. Thus, according to this measurement of the body, they divide and derive from the human form temples, buildings, houses, theaters, and moreover ships, machines, and every kind of craft, as well as all parts and members of buildings and crafts—such as columns, <term>epistyles</term> <note>The horizontal beams that rest on the tops of columns.</note>, bases, <term>antae</term> <note>Pilasters or pillars forming the ends of walls.</note>, <term>stylobates</term> <note>The continuous base supporting a row of columns.</note>, and all other such things. Indeed, God himself taught Noah to build the Ark according to the measure of the human body, just as He himself built the entire machine of the world symmetrical to the human body; for which reason the former is called the "great world" <note>the macrocosm</note>, and the latter the "minor world."

<margin>Microcosm. Measurement of the human body.</margin>
For this reason, some <term>microcosmologists</term> measure the human body by six feet, a foot by ten degrees, and each degree by five minutes. From this they count sixty degrees, which make three hundred minutes, which are equated to the same number of geometric cubits with which the Ark was described by Moses:

<margin>The size of the Ark of Moses <note>The text refers to the Ark of Noah, but attributes the description to Moses as the traditional author of the book of Genesis.</note>.</margin>
just as the human body is three hundred minutes in length, fifty in width, and thirty in height, so also the length of the Ark was three hundred cubits, its width fifty, and its height thirty. Thus, in both cases, the proportion of length to width is <term>sescupla</term> <note>A 6:1 ratio.</note>, to height <term>decupla</term> <note>A 10:1 ratio.</note>, and of width to height <term>superpartiens</term> <note>A ratio where one number contains another plus a fraction; here, 50 to 30, or 1 and 2/3.</note> two thirds. In the same way, the measurements of all members are proportioned and consonant, and so consistent with the parts of the world and the measures of the <term>archetype</term> <note>The original divine model or blueprint used by God to create the universe.</note> that there is no part or member in man that does not correspond to some sign, some star, or some celestial thing.
<margin>The proportion of man with celestial things.</margin>

The whole hand is as large as the whole face. The largest segment of the thumb gives the measure of the opening of the mouth and the distance from the bottom of the chin to the top of the lower lip. <margin>Equality of the hands and feet</margin>

<margin>Size of the ears</margin>
The eyebrows, when joined, equal the circles of the eyes, and the semicircles of the ears equal the mouth when closed. Thus, the circles of the eyes, the ears, and the open mouth are equal. The width of the nose is as great as the length of the eye; therefore, of that space between the two outer extremities of the eyes, the eyes occupy two parts and the nose in the middle takes up the third.

<margin>The midpoint of the body</margin>
From the crown of the head to the knees, the navel forms the midpoint. From the top of the chest to the bottom of the nostrils, the **hollow of the throat** <note>original: "nodum gulae"; the suprasternal notch</note> marks the midpoint. From the crown to the bottom of the chin, the midpoint is at the eyes. From the space between the eyes to the bottom of the chin, the bottom of the nostrils is the midpoint. From the bottom of the nostrils to the bottom of the chin, the edge of the lower lip is the midpoint; a third of that same distance gives the measure of the upper lip from the bottom of the nostrils.

<margin>The harmony of the human body with the celestial bodies</margin>
...to the end of the trunk, the ratio is double. The width of those parts compared to the width of the hip is **one and a half** <note>original: "sesquialtera"; a 3:2 ratio often associated with the musical interval of a fifth</note>. The ratio of the head to the neck is triple; the head to the knee is also triple; and the same ratio applies to the leg and the sole of the foot. The length of the forehead between the temples compared to its width is quadruple. These are the measurements commonly found by which the members of the human body—according to their length, width, height, and circumference—agree with one another and with the celestial bodies themselves. All these measures are divided through multiple, **super-particular** <note>a ratio where the larger number contains the smaller number plus one part of it, like 3:2 or 4:3</note>, or mixed proportions, from which a manifold harmony results. For a double proportion creates three **octaves** <note>original: "diapason"</note>; a quadruple proportion creates two octaves and a **fifth** <note>original: "diapente"</note>. In the same way, the elements, qualities, complexions, and humors are proportioned.

<margin>The proportion of the humors</margin>
For in a healthy and well-constituted man, these weights of the humors and complexions are assigned: eight parts of blood, four of phlegm, two of **choler** <note>yellow bile</note>, and one of **melancholy** <note>black bile</note>. Thus, a double proportion exists throughout the order; however, the ratio of the first to the third, and the second to the fourth, is quadruple; while the ratio of the first to the last is octuple.

<margin>Description of the human heart</margin>
Dioscorides <note>An ancient Greek physician and botanist</note> handed down that the human heart in the first year has a weight of two **drachms** <note>an ancient unit of weight, roughly 3.5 grams</note>; in the second year, four; and proceeding in a like course for each year, it reaches a weight of one hundred drachms in the fiftieth year.

<margin>The decrease of the heart</margin>
From that point, the decreases are calculated back toward equilibrium, so that once the circuit is finished, they return to the same starting point. He claimed that the span of life does not exceed the collapse of that organ; by this reasoning, he circumscribed the life of man to one hundred years. Pliny <note>Roman naturalist and author</note> testifies that this was also a belief held by the Egyptians. Even the movements of the human limbs correspond to the celestial movements. Every person has within themselves the movement of their heart, which, responding to the movement of the sun, is diffused through the arteries into the whole body. It indicates to us, as a most certain rule, the years, months, days, hours, and moments. Furthermore, anatomists have discovered a certain nerve near the **nape** <note>original: "micha," likely a transcription of "nucha," referring to the spinal cord or base of the brain</note> which, when pulled, moves all the limbs of a man in such a way that each is moved by its own proper motion. Aristotle believes that the members of the world are moved by God in just such a manner. There are also two veins in the neck, which enter the head at the throat where they divide; if these are gripped firmly from the outside, men immediately collapse with their senses taken away, until the grip is released. Thus, the eternal Architect of the world, when about to send the soul into the body as if into a home, first measures out a lodging worthy of it and bestows a most noble soul upon a beautiful body. Then, the soul itself, conscious of its own divinity, fashions and adorns its dwelling according to its own nature.

This was because they believed they could perceive the greatness of the soul through the outward appearance of the body. Many philosophers, both ancient and modern, considering this...

<margin>An indication of a corrupted body</margin>
Those who have searched into the secrets of causes in the majesty of nature itself have dared to assert that no physical defect occurs, and no disproportion exists in the body, which is not also followed by a vice or lack of restraint in the soul; for it is certain that each grows, unites, and operates through the office of the other.

## ¶ Chapter 28: On the composition and harmony of the human soul.

<margin>The proportion of the soul</margin>
Just as the harmony of the body consists of the proper measure and proportion of the limbs, so the harmony of the soul consists of the proper temperament and proportion of its virtues and operations, which are the **concupiscible** <note>the faculty of desire or attraction</note>, the **irascible** <note>the faculty of spirit or anger</note>, and **reason**. These are proportioned thus: for reason has an **octave** <note>original: "diapason"</note> ratio to desire, but a **fourth** <note>original: "diatessaron"</note> to anger; while the irascible power has a **fifth** <note>original: "diapente"</note> ratio to the concupiscible.

<margin>The agreement of the soul with the body</margin>
¶ Therefore, when a most well-proportioned soul is joined with a most well-proportioned body, it is certain that such a person receives the most fortunate lot in the distribution of gifts, as the soul and body agree in their natural disposition. This agreement is indeed most hidden, yet it has been somewhat outlined by the wise. But as we hasten toward the harmony of the soul, we must seek it from those mediums through which they pass to us—that is, from the celestial bodies and spheres.

<margin>To which of the planets the passions of the soul correspond</margin>
Knowing, therefore, which powers of the soul correspond to which of the planets from what has been said above, we will easily recognize their internal harmony. For the **Moon** governs the powers of growing and shrinking; the **phantastic** <note>imaginative</note> power and wit depend on **Mercury**; the concupiscible virtue on **Venus**; the vital power on the **Sun**; the impulsive power (also called the irascible) on **Mars**; the natural power on **Jupiter**; and all receptivity on **Saturn**. The **will** itself acts as the **prime mover** <note>original: "primum mobile"; the outermost moving sphere of the cosmos that drives the others</note> and the leader of all those powers at its pleasure; when joined with the higher intellect, it always tends toward the good. This intellect shows the paths to the will, just as light does for the eye; yet it does not move the will itself, but the will remains the mistress of its own operation. This is why it is called **Free Will**. And although it always tends toward the good as its proper object, it is sometimes blinded by error and driven by animal force,

<margin>The definition of Free Will and what Grace is</margin>
it chooses evil, believing it to be good. Therefore, Free Will is defined as the faculty of the intellect and the will by which good is chosen when **grace** assists, and evil when grace leaves. Thus, grace itself, which theologians also call **charity** or infused love, is in the will like a prime mover; when it is absent, the entire harmony falls into dissonance.

<margin>The agreement of the soul with the elements</margin>
Furthermore, the soul corresponds to the **earth** through the senses; to **water** through imagination; to **air** through reason; and to **heaven** through the intellect. The soul requires harmony among these according to how they are tempered in this mortal body. Thus, the wise ancients, knowing the harmonic dispositions of bodies and souls...

Why musical sound was invented; the concord of harmony is an enemy to demons.
</margin>
...rightly, according to the diversity of human **complexions** <note>the balance of humors—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—within a person</note>, they have not in vain used musical sounds and songs, both to preserve the health of the body and restore it when lost, and also to lead souls toward healthy morals, until they harmonize the person with celestial harmony and make them entirely celestial. Furthermore, nothing is more effective for driving away evil demons than musical harmony; for they, having fallen from that celestial harmony, cannot endure any true concord as it is an enemy to them, and they flee far away—just as David suppressed the evil spirit raging in Saul with his harp. Hence, by the ancient prophets and fathers who knew these harmonic secrets, songs and musical sounds were introduced into sacred offices.

### Chapter 29: On the observation of the celestials, necessary in every magical work.

<margin>Natural virtue.</margin>
Every natural virtue acts much more miraculously when it is not only composed by **physical proportion** <note>original: "proportione physica"; the correct material balance of ingredients</note>, but also informed by the timely observation of the celestials chosen for this purpose. This occurs when the celestial power is proven to be strongest for the effect we desire, and then aided by many other celestial factors, by everywhere subjecting lower things to the celestials as if they were wives to be fertilized by their own husbands. <margin>Things to be observed in any work.</margin> Therefore, in any work, the position, movement, and **aspects** <note>the specific angles planets make with one another</note> of the stars and planets in their signs and degrees must be observed, and how all these relate to the longitude and latitude of the **climate** <note>the geographic location where the work is performed</note>. For from this, the qualities of the angles are varied, which the rays of the celestial bodies describe upon the figure of the thing, according to which celestial virtues are infused. <margin>How planets are to be observed.</margin> Thus, whenever you are about to perform a work pertaining to any planet, it will be necessary for you to place it in its **dignities** <note>the 'strengths' or 'honors' a planet holds based on its position in the zodiac</note>, making it fortunate and powerful, and dominant in the day, hour, and the figure of the heavens. <margin>Power of the Moon.</margin> Nor will you only wait for a powerful **significator** <note>the specific planet representing the goal of the work</note> of the work, but you should also observe the Moon directed opportunely for this; for you shall accomplish nothing without the benefit of the Moon. <margin>How the Moon is to be observed.</margin> But if you have several patrons for the work, observe them all as powerful and looking at each other with an amicable aspect; if you cannot have such aspects, it is fitting for you at least to take them in the **angles** <note>the four most powerful points in an astrological chart: the Ascendant, Descendant, Midheaven, and Imum Coeli</note>. You will observe the Moon when she either looks at both, or is joined to one and looks at the other, or when she passes from the conjunction or aspect of one to the union or aspect of the other. <margin>Mercury must be diligently observed.</margin> I also believe that Mercury should by no means be omitted, but diligently observed in every work: for he is the messenger between both the lower and upper gods; when he joins with the good, he increases their goodness, and when with the evil, he flows in their malice. Furthermore, we call a sign or planet "unfortunate" through the aspect of Saturn or Mars, especially when in **opposition** <note>180 degrees apart</note> or **square** <note>90 degrees apart</note>; for these aspects are of enmity. However, union, **trine** <note>120 degrees apart</note>, and **sextile** <note>60 degrees apart</note> aspects are of friendship; among these, the conjunction is the strongest.

### Chapter 30: When the planets are of more powerful influence.

<margin>When the planets are more powerful.</margin>
<margin>Observation of the planets.</margin>
We shall have powerful planets when they are in their **domicile** <note>the zodiac sign a planet "rules," where it is most at home</note>, **exaltation** <note>a sign where a planet's influence is heightened</note>, triplicity, term, or face; when they are moving directly and outside of **combustion** <note>too close to the Sun</note>; when they are at their **apogee** <note>original: "auge"; the point in an orbit furthest from the Earth</note> and dominating the figure of the heaven—namely, when they are in the **angles** <note>the four most powerful houses in a chart: the 1st, 4th, 7th, and 10th</note>, especially the eastern angle [the Ascendant] or the tenth house [the Midheaven], or in the houses immediately succeeding them, or in their own **joys** <note>specific signs or houses where a planet is said to be particularly happy</note>. But caution must be taken that they are not in the "bounds" or under the dominion of Saturn or Mars <note>the two "malefic" or traditionally difficult planets</note>, nor in dark degrees, "pits," or empty degrees. You shall observe that the angles of the ascendant, the tenth, and the seventh houses are fortunate, as well as the lord of the ascendant, the place of the Sun, the place of the Moon, and the place of the **Part of Fortune** <note>a mathematical point in a chart representing prosperity and well-being</note> and its lord, and the lord of the preceding conjunction or **full moon** <note>original: "praeventionis"; the syzygy occurring just before the event</note>. But the malevolent planets should fall "unfortunate" <note>placed in weak positions</note>, unless by chance they are the **significators** <note>the specific planets representing the person or goal of the work</note> of your work, or can be useful to you by some pact; or if they have obtained leadership in your "revolution" <note>annual chart</note> or birth chart, for then they are least of all to be suppressed.

<margin>When the Moon is powerful.</margin>
We shall have a powerful Moon if she is in her own domicile, or exaltation, or triplicity, or face, and in a degree suitable for the desired work, and if she obtains a **mansion** <note>one of the 28 divisions of the lunar zodiac</note> from those twenty-eight that is competent for herself and the work. She should not be in the **burnt path** <note>original: "via combusta"; a traditionally unlucky span of the zodiac, usually late Libra to early Scorpio</note>, nor slow in her course; she should not be in the ecliptic, nor **combust** by the Sun, unless she happens to be in **unity with the Sun** <note>original: "unitate cum sole"; the "cazimi" position, where the planet is in the very heart of the Sun and becomes highly empowered</note>. She should not descend in southern latitude when she emerges from combustion, nor be opposite the Sun, nor be diminished in light, and she should not be hindered by Mars or Saturn. Regarding these matters, I do not wish to prolong the discourse further here, since these and many other necessary things are sufficiently handed down in the volumes of the Astrologers.

### Chapter 31: On the observation of the fixed stars, and their natures.

<margin>Fixed stars obtain the natures of the planets.</margin>
An altogether similar reasoning is to be held by you regarding the **fixed stars**. Know this: all fixed stars possess the signification and nature of the seven planets, but some are of the nature of one planet, and some of two. Hence, whenever any planet is joined with some fixed star of its own nature, the signification of that star becomes more powerful, and the nature of the planet is increased. But if it is a star of two natures, whichever planet with it is stronger, that planet's nature will prevail in the signification. For example, if a star is of the nature of Mars and Venus: if Mars is with it, the nature of Mars will prevail; but if Venus is with it, the nature of Venus will overcome.

<margin>From where the natures of fixed stars are discerned.</margin>
<margin>The colors of the planets.</margin>
Moreover, the natures of the fixed stars are discerned from their colors, according as they agree with certain planets and are ascribed to them. Now, the colors of the planets are: Saturn’s is livid or leaden, and also glowing; Jupiter’s is **lemon-yellow** <note>original: "citrinus"</note> bordering on paleness, and also bright; Mars' is red and fiery; the Sun's is saffron-colored, and when it rises, burning, and afterwards radiating; Venus' is white, but glowing as the Morning Star, and shining as the Evening Star; Mercury's...

And although many effects proceed from the **fixed stars**, they are nevertheless attributed to the **planets**, both because they are closer to us and more distinct and known, and because the planets themselves execute whatever the higher stars influence.

### ¶ Chapter 32: Concerning the Sun and Moon, and their magical reasons.

<margin>
The excellence of the Sun.
The dominion of the Moon.
The eyes of heaven.
</margin>
The **Sun** and **Moon** have obtained the administration of the heavens and of all bodies that are under the heavens. The **Sun** is the lord of all **elemental virtues**, and the **Moon**, by the power of the Sun, is the mistress of **generation, growth, and decay**. Hence **Albumasar** <note>a famous 9th-century Persian astrologer</note> says that life is infused into all things through the Sun and Moon, which **Orpheus** <note>the legendary Greek poet and musician</note> therefore calls the "living eyes of heaven." The Sun gives light to all things from itself, and bestows it abundantly not only in the heaven and the air, but also on the earth and in the innermost depths of the abyss.

# ON OCCULT PHILOSOPHY

<margin>Source of light</margin>
Whatever good we possess, as Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote on theurgy and the mysteries</note> says, we have from the sun—either from the sun alone, or from it through other things. Heraclitus calls the sun the fountain of celestial light, and many of the Platonists have placed the <term>World Soul</term> <note>Latin: *anima mundi*; the vital force thought to animate all nature</note> principally in the sun. They believe that by filling the entire globe of the Sun, the soul pours out its rays in every direction like a spirit through all things, distributing life, sense, and motion to the entire universe itself.

<margin>The Heart of Heaven.</margin>
For this reason, the ancient natural philosophers called the Sun the very "Heart of Heaven," and the Chaldeans <note>Ancient Mesopotamian astronomers and astrologers</note> placed it in the middle of the planets. The Egyptians also located it in the middle of the world—that is, between two groups of five. Specifically, they place five planets above the Sun, and below the Sun they place the Moon and the four elements. Among the other stars, the Sun itself is the image and statue of the highest Prince of both worlds, the terrestrial and the celestial. It is the true light and the most exact likeness of God himself.

<margin>A description of the Trinity.</margin>
Its essence signifies the Father; its splendor, the Son; and its heat, the Holy Spirit. Indeed, the scholars of the Academy <note>The Platonists</note> have nothing else by which they can more clearly demonstrate the divine essence. It corresponds to God with such great harmony that Plato calls it the "conspicuous son of God," Iamblichus calls it the "image of divine intelligence," and our own Dionysius <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian mystic</note> calls it the "clear statue of God." Like a king, the Sun sits in the throne-room <note>original: *meditullio*</note> of the other planets, excelling all in light, magnitude, and beauty, illuminating all, and distributing power to them for the arrangement of all lower things. It regulates and disposes their steps, so that from this, their movements are called diurnal or nocturnal, southern or northern, eastern or western, direct or <term>retrograde</term> <note>Appearing to move backward in the sky from the perspective of Earth</note>. 

And just as the Sun by its own light puts to flight the shadows of the night, so it also drives away whatever powers of darkness are read about in Job: *When the dawn first appears, they consider it the shadow of death.* <note>Job 24:17</note> And the Psalmist, speaking of the lion cubs seeking permission from God to devour, adds: *The sun has risen, and they are gathered together, and they shall be placed in their dens.* <note>Psalm 104:22</note> Once they are put to flight, it follows: *Man shall go out to his work.* Since the Sun holds the middle region of the world, it presides over heaven and the world just as the heart presides over the whole body in living creatures, holding command over the entire world and everything within it. 

<margin>Author of the seasons.</margin>
He is the author of the seasons, from whom come the day and the year, cold and heat, and the other qualities of the times. As Ptolemy <note>The famous Roman-era astronomer</note> says, when the Sun comes into the place of any star, it excites the power which that star has in the air; for example, it stirs heat with Mars, or cold with Saturn. It even disposes the very spirit and mind of man, which is why it is said by Homer and confirmed by Aristotle that such movements exist in the mind as the Sun, the prince and moderator of the planets, brings each day. 

<margin>The powers of the Moon over lower things.</margin>
The Moon, however, being closest to the Earth, is the receptacle of all celestial influences. Because of the swiftness of her course, she is joined each month to the Sun and the other planets and stars. Having become, as it were, the wife of all the stars, she is the most fruitful of them. Receiving the rays and influences of the Sun and the other planets and stars like a fetus, she brings them forth, as if in labor, into the lower world which is near to her. For all the stars in...

More clearly than all others, she governs these lower realms; her motion is more perceptible to us because of the familiarity and proximity she has with us. As a medium between both the superior and inferior, she communicates with all of them. 

<margin>The motion of the Moon must be observed diligently.</margin>
Therefore, her motion must be observed above all others, as she is like the parent of all conceptions, which she unfolds in various ways in these lower realms according to her varying <term>complexion</term> <note>In this context, "complexion" refers to the Moon's shifting constitutional qualities or temperament.</note>, motion, position, and her various <term>aspects</term> <note>The specific angular relationships between planets in astrology, such as conjunctions or squares.</note> to the planets and other stars. 

<margin>From where the Moon receives her powers.</margin>
And although she receives strength from all the stars, she is filled with life-giving virtue most especially by the Sun. Whenever she is joined to him, she borrows her complexion from his gaze. For in her first quarter, as the <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>Followers of Aristotle’s philosophy</note> teach, she is hot and moist; in her second, hot and dry; in her third, cold and dry; and in her fourth, cold and moist. Although she is the lowest of the stars, she explains all the "conceptions" of the superior ones. For from her begins the series of things in the celestial world which Plato calls the 

<margin>Plato’s Golden Chain</margin>
<term>Golden Chain</term> <note>A Neoplatonic concept describing the hierarchical link of causes and effects stretching from the Divine down to the material world.</note>, by which every single thing or cause is connected to another and depends on the superior, until it reaches the supreme Cause of all, from which everything hangs. It is for this reason that without the Moon as an intermediary, we could not draw down the power of the superiors at all. Thus <term>Thebit</term> <note>Thabit ibn Qurra, a 9th-century mathematician and astronomer famous for his works on talismanic magic.</note> commands that to capture the virtue of any star, one must take the stone and herb of that star when the Moon either fortunately enters the sign of that star or looks upon it with a favorable aspect.

### Concerning the 28 Mansions of the Moon and their powers. Chapter 33.

<margin>The course of the Moon.</margin>
Since the Moon traverses the entire zodiac in the space of twenty-eight days, the Indian sages and the most ancient astrologers granted twenty-eight <term>mansions</term> <note>Specific segments of the zodiac through which the moon passes daily; known as "Nakshatras" in Indian astrology or "Manazil" in Arabic tradition.</note> to the Moon. 

<margin>How many Lunar Mansions and where they are.</margin>
These are fixed in the <term>eighth sphere</term> <note>The sphere of the fixed stars, located beyond the seven planetary spheres in the medieval geocentric model.</note> and take on different properties and names from the various constellations and stars contained within them, as <term>Alpharus</term> <note>Likely referring to the astronomer Al-Farghani or Al-Farabi.</note> says. While the Moon travels through them, she acquires various powers and virtues. According to the opinion of <term>Abramus</term> <note>Abraham Ibn Ezra, a significant medieval Jewish scholar and astrologer.</note>, each of these mansions encompasses twelve degrees, fifty-one minutes, and approximately twenty-six seconds. Their names and their starting points in the zodiac of the eighth sphere are as follows:

The first is called **Alnath**, which 
<margin>Alnath, the first lunar mansion.</margin>
means "the horns of Aries." Its beginning is at the head of Aries in the eighth sphere. It is effective for journeys and discord.

The second is called **Allothaim** or **Albochan**, which is "the belly of Aries." Its beginning is at twelve degrees, fifty-one minutes, and twenty-two seconds of the same sign. 
<margin>Allothaim, the second lunar mansion.</margin>
It is beneficial for finding treasures and for the detention of captives.

The third is called **Achoamazone** or **Athoraye**, that is, "the rainy ones" or the **Pleiades**. 
<margin>Athoraye, the third lunar mansion.</margin>
Its beginning is at twenty-five degrees, forty-two minutes, and fifty-one seconds of Aries. It benefits sailors.

### On the True Observation of Celestial Motion in the Eighth Sphere, and on the Calculation of Planetary Hours. Chapter XXXIII.

<margin>Movement of the stars.</margin>
<margin>Times of the stars.</margin>
Whoever intends to work toward a celestial opportunity must observe both, or at least one of these two things: namely, the movements of the stars, or the times. By "movements," I mean when the stars are in their <term>dignities</term> or <term>debilities</term> <note>astrological positions where a planet's influence is either strengthened (dignity) or weakened (debility/dejection)</note>, whether these be essential or accidental. By "times," I mean the days and hours distributed under their lordships. Concerning all these matters, enough is taught in the books of the astrologers. But two things must be especially weighed and observed by us in this place: first, that we observe the motion of the stars, their <term>ascensions</term> <note>the rising of stars above the horizon</note>, and the <term>angles</term> <note>original: "cardines," the four pivotal points of an astrological chart: the Ascendant, Descendant, Midheaven, and Lower Midheaven</note>, as they truly exist in the <term>eighth sphere</term> <note>the sphere of the fixed stars, which in traditional cosmology sits above the spheres of the seven planets</note>. It is due to negligence in this that many err in the construction of celestial images and are cheated of their desired effect. Second, one must observe the times when determining the planetary hours. Almost all astrologers divide the entire interval from sunrise to sunset into twelve equal parts, and they call those the twelve hours 
<margin>Division of the heavens.</margin>
<margin>Diurnal hours.</margin>
<margin>Nocturnal hours.</margin>
of the day. Then, the period that follows from sunset to sunrise, divided by the same reasoning into twelve equal portions, they call the twelve hours of the night. They then distribute those individual hours to individual planets according to the order of their succession, always giving the first hour of the day to the "Lord of the Day," and then to each in order until the end of the twenty-four hours. In this distribution, the <term>Magi</term> <note>wise men or practitioners of high natural magic</note> agree with them; however, in the partition of the hours, some disagree. They argue that the interval between sunrise and sunset should not be divided into [simply] equal parts, and that these hours are not called "unequal" because the day hours are unequal to the night hours, but because the individual day and night hours are unequal to one another. Therefore, the division of unequal or planetary hours has another method of measurement observed by the Magi, which is as follows: Just as in <term>artificial hours</term> <note>standard clock hours of 60 minutes</note>—which are always equal to each other—the rising of fifteen degrees on the <term>equinoctial</term> <note>the celestial equator</note> constitutes one artificial hour, so too in planetary hours, the rising 
<margin>Artificial hours.</margin>
<margin>Planetary hours.</margin>
of fifteen degrees on the <term>ecliptic</term> <note>the path the sun appears to follow through the zodiac</note> constitutes one planetary or "unequal" hour. The measure of these must be sought and found using the tables of oblique ascensions for each specific region.

BOOK THE SECOND.

### ¶ That all man-made things, such as images and seals and the like, obtain some power from the celestial bodies. Chapter XXXV.

<margin>The power of celestial virtues</margin>
The magnitude, virtue, and power of the celestial bodies is so great that not only natural things, but even <term>artificial</term> <note>original: "artificiales"; meaning objects crafted by human skill or artifice, such as talismans</note> objects—when they are properly exposed to the heavens—suddenly undergo a change from that most powerful agent and from a wonderful life, which often bestows a miraculous celestial virtue upon them. <margin>Thomas Aquinas</margin> Saint Thomas Aquinas, the holy doctor, confirms this in his book *On Fate*, where he says that even garments, buildings, and any works of art receive a certain quality from the stars. <margin>The opinion of the Magi regarding images.</margin> Thus, the <term>Magi</term> <note>wise men or practitioners of high natural magic</note> confirm that not only through the mixing and application of natural things, but also through images, seals, rings, mirrors, and certain other instruments—provided they are crafted at the opportune time under a specific <term>constellation</term> <note>a specific alignment of stars and planets</note>—a certain celestial illumination can be captured, and some wonderful power can be received. For the rays of the celestial bodies are animated, living, and sensory; they carry with them wonderful gifts and a most vehement power. Even in a sudden moment, they imprint such miraculous forces into images, even into material that is otherwise less suited for it. <margin>The likeness of the image to the celestial.</margin> Nevertheless, they bestow more effective virtues upon images if they are crafted not from just any material, but from a specific substance whose natural virtue corresponds with the specific purpose of the work, and if the shape of the image is made similar to a celestial figure. For such an image—both because its material is naturally suited to the work and the celestial influence, and because its shape is similar to the celestial figure—is most ready to receive the actions and powers of the celestial bodies and figures. It suddenly conceives the celestial gift within itself, and then acts continuously upon others, and other things incline themselves toward it out of obedience. Hence Ptolemy says in the *Centiloquium* <note>a collection of one hundred astrological aphorisms attributed to Ptolemy</note> that inferior things obey the celestial ones, and not only the stars themselves, but also their images. <margin>Obedience of scorpions.</margin> Just as earthly scorpions obey the celestial Scorpion, they also obey the image of that scorpion which has been shaped at the opportune time under its <term>ascendant</term> <note>the sign rising on the eastern horizon</note> and its dominion.

### BOOK TWO.

...the image [represents] intellect, gentleness, joys, and beauty.

<margin>The Faces of Taurus.</margin>In the first face of Taurus <note>the first ten degrees of the sign of the Bull</note>, there ascends a naked man who is a <term>spike-bearer</term><note>original: "spiculator," which can mean a spearman or someone holding a spike; in this agricultural context, it likely refers to a laborer or guard</note> or a plowman; it is beneficial for sowing, plowing, building, populating, dividing lands, and for the arts of geometry. In the second face, there ascends a naked man holding a key in his hand; it bestows power, nobility, and dignity over peoples. In the third face, there ascends a man in whose hand is a serpent and an arrow; this is an image of necessity and utility, but also of misery and servitude.

<margin>The Faces of Gemini.</margin>In the first face of Gemini, there ascends a man in whose hand is a rod, and he acts as if serving another; it bestows wisdom and the knowledge of numbers and of arts in which there is no practical utility. In the second face, there ascends a man in whose hand is a pipe, and another who is bent over digging the earth; they signify an agility that is infamous and dishonest—such as that of <term>jugglers</term><note>original: "ioculatorum," meaning traveling entertainers or jesters</note> and <term>conjurors</term><note>original: "præstigiatorum," those who perform sleight of hand or illusions</note>—and it signifies labors and inquiries conducted with great toil. In the third face, there ascends a man seeking weapons, and a foolish man holding a bird in his right hand and a flute in his left; their significations are of forgetfulness, indignation, boldness, jokes, <term>trickeries</term><note>original: "trufarum," referring to nonsense or deceitful jests</note>, and useless words.

<margin>The Faces of Cancer.</margin>In the first face of Cancer, there ascends the form of a young maiden adorned with beautiful clothes and wearing a crown on her head; it provides sharpness of the senses, subtlety of intellect, and the love of men. In the second face, there ascends a man dressed in beautiful clothes, or a man and a woman sitting at a table and playing; it bestows riches, cheerfulness, joy, and the love of women. In the third face, there ascends a man as a hunter with a spear and horn, leading dogs to the hunt; its signification is of opposing men, pursuing fugitives, hunting, and occupying things through weapons and quarrels.

<margin>The Faces of Leo.</margin>In the first face of Leo, there ascends a man riding upon a lion; its signification is of boldness, violence, cruelty, wicked deeds, lust, and the enduring of labor. In the second face, there ascends an image with hands raised, and a man upon whose head is a crown, and the form of an angry and threatening man holding a <term>drawn sword</term><note>original: "gladium euacuatum"</note> in his right hand and a shield in his left; their significations concern secret quarrels, unknown victories gained by base men, and the occasions of lawsuits and battles. In the third face, there ascends a young man in whose hand is a whip, and a man of great sadness and an ugly face; their signification is of love and fellowship, and of one giving away his own property to avoid quarrels.

<margin>The Faces of Virgo.</margin>In the first face of Virgo, there ascends the figure of a good girl and a man throwing seeds; its signification is of gathering riches, directing one's livelihood, plowing, sowing, and populating. In the second face, there ascends a black man dressed in leather, and a man with long hair holding <term>money bags</term><note>original: "loculos," small pouches for coins</note>; their signification is toward profit and the gathering of substance, and toward greed. In the third face, there ascends a white and deaf woman, or an old man leaning on a staff; its signification is toward weakness and infirmity, the loss of limbs, the destruction of trees, and the depopulation of lands. ### OF OCCULT PHILOSOPHY.

<margin>The faces of Libra.</margin>In the face of Libra <note>The "faces" or decans are three 10-degree divisions of each zodiac sign, each associated with specific imagery and powers.</note>, there ascends the form of an angry man, in whose hand is a pipe, and the form of a man reading in a book; its operation is in justice and the assistance of the wretched and the weak against the evil and the powerful. In the second face, there ascend two men, raging and angry, and a man in ornate clothing sitting in a chair; their significance is toward indignation against the wicked, and toward the peace and security of life with an abundance of good things. In the third face, there ascends a forceful man holding a bow: and before him a naked man, as well as another man holding bread in one hand and a cup of wine in the other; the significance of these is toward abominable lust, songs, jokes, and gluttony.

<margin>The faces of Scorpio.</margin>In the first face of Scorpio, there ascends a woman of beautiful face and habit, and two men striking each other; their operation is toward grace and beauty, and toward strife, ambushes, deceptions, slanders, and betrayals. In the second face, there ascend a naked man and a naked woman, and a man sitting on the ground, and before him two dogs biting each other; their operation is toward impudence, deception, and <term>sycophancy</term><note>original: "sycophantiam"; in this period, it referred to malicious informing, slander, or deceitful accusations rather than modern flattery.</note>, and toward sowing evil and strife among men. In the third face, there ascends a man bent upon his knees, and a woman striking him with a staff; its significance is of drunkenness, fornications, wrath, violence, and strife.

<margin>The faces of Sagittarius.</margin>In the first face of Sagittarius, there ascends the form of a man armed with a breastplate, holding a naked sword in his hand; its operation is toward boldness, military service, and liberty. In the second face, there ascends a weeping woman covered in rags; her operation is toward sadness and fear for her own body. In the third face, there ascends a man similar in color to gold, or an idle man playing with a staff; his significance is in following one's own desires and persistence in them, and in agility toward evil things, strife, and horrible things.

<margin>The faces of Capricorn.</margin>In the first face of Capricorn, there ascends the form of a woman, and a black man carrying full <term>purses</term><note>original: "loculos," referring to small pouches or boxes for money.</note>; their significance is toward traveling and rejoicing, and toward gaining and losing with both weakness and utility. In the second face, there ascend two women, and a man looking at a bird flying in the air; their significance is in demanding things that cannot be done, and in inquiring into things that cannot be known. In the third face, there ascends a woman chaste in body and wise in work, and a <term>money-changer</term><note>original: "nummularius"</note> gathering money on a table; its significance is in the prudence of governing, in the desire for material substance, and in avarice.

<margin>The faces of Aquarius.</margin>In the first face of Aquarius, there ascends the form of a prudent man and the form of a woman spinning; their significance is in thought and labor for profit, in poverty and utility. In the second face, there ascends the form of a man with a long beard; its significance is the understanding of gentleness, modesty, liberty, and good morals. In the third face, there ascends a black and angry man; his significance is in detestation, insolence, and impudence.

<margin>The faces of Pisces.</margin>In the first face of Pisces, there ascends a man carrying burdens on his back, well-clothed; his significance is in journeys, the changing of place, and the anxiety of seeking substance and food. In the second face, there ascends a woman of good countenance and ornate dress; her significance is of seeking and involving oneself in great and high matters. ### SECOND BOOK.

...a beautiful girl, whose head is adorned with flowers; its significance pertains to quiet, leisure, and delight, as well as to fornication and the embraces of women. <margin>Images of the Zodiac.</margin> And so much for the images of the faces; beyond these, there are still three hundred and sixty images in the zodiac, corresponding to the number of degrees, whose forms <margin>The images of Peter of Abano.</margin> Peter of Abano described for us. <note>Pietro d'Abano (1250–1316) was a famous Italian physician and astrologer whose "Astrolabium Planum" detailed the 360 images of the degrees.</note> Outside the zodiac there are also general figures, which Hyginus and Aratus <note>Two influential classical authors on astronomy and mythology.</note> described to us, and many particular ones, according to the number of faces and degrees existing there, concerning all of which it would be too long to speak. <margin>Pegasus the horse.</margin> However, the most important of these are: Pegasus, who is effective against the diseases of horses and preserves knights in war; then there is Andromeda, who reconciles love between man and wife, and is even said to reconcile adulterers. The Deer <note>original: "Cervus"; likely referring to a specific star grouping or a variant figure in medieval catalogs.</note> heals those who are frantic and manic. Let what has been said so far suffice.

<margin>A metallic image of Mercury.</margin>

They made it on the day of Mercury at the third hour—which is the hour of Saturn—with the sign of Gemini rising (the domicile of Mercury designating prophets), and with Saturn and Mercury joined in Aquarius, the ninth region of heaven, which is also called "God." <note>The "ninth house" in astrology is traditionally associated with religion, long journeys, and the divine.</note> Furthermore, Saturn should look upon the ascendant from a trine aspect <note>A 120-degree angle, considered a very harmonious relationship between celestial bodies.</note>, and the Moon likewise, while the Sun should look upon the place of the conjunction. ## ¶ Concerning the Images of Jupiter. Chapter XXXIX.

<margin>The adornment of Jupiter’s figure.</margin>
From the operations of Jupiter, they made an image for long life during the hour of Jupiter, with Jupiter himself rising fortunately in his exaltation <note>Jupiter's "exaltation" is in Cancer, where its influence is considered most potent.</note> upon a clear and white stone. Its figure was a man crowned, dressed in saffron-colored garments, riding upon an eagle or a dragon, holding an arrow in his right hand as if about to shoot it into the head of the eagle or the dragon. They also made another image of Jupiter at the same opportune time upon a white and clear stone, especially crystal. It was a naked man, crowned, with hands raised and joined as if in prayer, sitting on a four-legged throne carried by four winged boys. They affirm that this image increases happiness, riches, and honor, bestows benevolence and prosperity, and liberates one from enemies. 
<margin>An image of Jupiter for a glorious life.</margin>
They made yet another image of Jupiter for a religious and glorious life, as well as for favorable fortune. Its figure was a man having the head of a lion or a ram, and the feet of an eagle, dressed in saffron-colored robes; he was called the "son of Jupiter."

Its form was an armed man riding upon a lion, holding a naked, upright sword in his right hand and carrying a human head in his left. 
<margin>The power of fascination.</margin>

To whoever carries it, they attribute the power of fascination <term>fascination: a historical term for a hypnotic or magical gaze that can enchant or paralyze others</term>, so that he will terrify men by his look when he is angry, and bind them in a stupor. ### ¶ Concerning the images of the Mansions of the Moon. Chapter XLVI.

<margin>
The 28 Mansions of the Moon with their images.
</margin>
They also made images for each of the Mansions of the Moon. <note>The "Mansions of the Moon" are twenty-eight divisions of the zodiac through which the Moon passes in its monthly cycle, each believed to have specific spiritual influences.</note> In the first, for the destruction of something, they made upon an iron ring the image of a black man dressed in a <term>cilice</term> <note>original: "cilicio"; a garment made of coarse haircloth, usually worn for penance</note> and girded, throwing a lance with his right hand: they would seal this in black wax and fumigate it with liquid <term>storax</term> <note>A fragrant resin often used in incense and medicine</note> and utter imprecations. In the second, against the wrath of a prince and for reconciliation with him, they would seal in white wax and mastic the image of a crowned king, and fumigate it with <term>lignum aloes</term> <note>original: "ligno aloës"; agarwood, a highly prized aromatic wood</note>. In the third, they made an image upon a silver ring, the stone of which was square, and the figure was a well-dressed woman sitting in a chair, with her right hand raised above her head; they would seal it and fumigate it with musk, camphor, and <term>aromatic ungula</term> <note>original: "vngula aromatica"; also known as onycha, a scented shell-cover used in ancient incense</note>. They asserted that this bestowed prosperity of fortune and every good thing. In the fourth, for vengeance and separation, enmity and ill-will, they sealed in red wax the image of a soldier sitting upon a horse, holding a serpent in his right hand, and they fumigated it with red myrrh and storax. In the fifth, for the favor of kings and officials and for a good reception, they sealed in silver the head of a man, and fumigated it with sandalwood. In the sixth, to create love between two people, they sealed in white wax two images embracing each other, and fumigated them with lignum aloes and <term>amber</term> <note>original: "ambra"; likely referring to ambergris, a rare substance used in high-quality perfumes</note>. In the seventh, to acquire every good thing, they sealed in silver the image of a well-dressed man extending his hands to heaven as if praying and supplicating, and they fumigated it with good odors. In the eighth, for victory in war, they sealed in tin the image of an eagle <margin>The fumigation of the images.</margin> having the face of a man, and fumigated it with sulfur. In the ninth, to inflict infirmity, they sealed in lead the image of a man lacking a penis <note>original: "virga"</note> and clothes, covering his eyes with his hands, and they fumigated it with pine resin. In the tenth, to assist in childbirth and to heal the sick, they sealed in gold the head of a lion, and fumigated it with amber. ### ¶ Concerning images whose form is not according to the likeness of any celestial figure, but according to the likeness of that which the operator's mind desires. Chapter 49.

<margin>Complex images.</margin>
There is yet another way of making images, not according to the likeness of celestial figures <note>original: "figurarum coelestium"; referring to the constellations or zodiac signs discussed previously</note>, but according to the likeness of that which the mind of the operator desires, of which these images are the effigies and traces. Thus, for love, we fashion images embracing one another; for discord, images striking each other. To bring about calamity, destruction, or hindrance to a man, a house, a city, or any other thing, we fashion images that are distorted and broken in their limbs and parts, modeled after the likeness and form of the thing we wish to destroy or impede. <margin>The inscription of images.</margin> Moreover, the Mages command that when casting or carving these images, one should inscribe upon them the name of the intended effect. This should be on the back when the effect is evil, such as "Destruction," and on the belly when the effect is good, such as "Love." Furthermore, on the forehead of the image, one should write the name of the species or the specific individual whom the image represents, or for whom—or against whom—it was fashioned. Again, on the breast, one should write the name of the zodiac sign or the "face" <note>A "face" or decan is a ten-degree subdivision of a zodiac sign</note> that is rising at the time, as well as its lord, along with the magical characters and the names of their presiding angels. <margin>The Mirror of Albertus Magnus.</margin> They command furthermore that while the image is being fashioned, the imprecation <note>A spoken prayer or ritual command</note> of the desired effect must not be kept silent. All of these instructions are likewise affirmed by Albertus Magnus <note>A 13th-century philosopher and theologian often associated with alchemy and magic in later traditions</note> in his work *The Mirror* <note>original: "Speculum"; likely referring to the *Speculum Astronomiae*</note>. <margin>The diverse positioning of images.</margin> Once these images are fashioned according to their various powers, they are used in different ways. Sometimes they are suspended or tied to the body; sometimes they are buried under the earth or beneath a river; sometimes they are hung in a chimney over smoke, or from a tree to be moved by the wind. Sometimes they are placed with the head upward, sometimes downward; sometimes they are cast into boiling water or into fire. For they say that just as the operators of the images affect the image itself, so too do they bring similar sufferings upon those to whom the image is dedicated, as dictated by the mind of the practitioner. We read that the Mage Nectanabus <note>The last native Pharaoh of Egypt, who in legend was a powerful sorcerer</note> fashioned wax images of ships with such skill that when he submerged the images in water, the ships of his enemies at sea were submerged and endangered in the same way. Truly, the constellations to be observed for these and similar images are taught to us by that branch of astrology known as "Elections" <note>The practice of choosing the most auspicious time to begin a specific task or ritual</note>.

### ¶ Concerning certain celestial observations, and the practice of certain images of the same. Chapter 50.

<margin>Fortunate images.</margin>
Now I will tell you the observations of the celestial bodies required for the practice of such images. Thus, to bring fortune to someone, we fashion an image in which these factors are made fortunate: namely, the <term>significator of life</term> <note>The planet representing the person's physical existence</note>, the givers of life, and the signs and planets. Furthermore, let us make fortunate the <term>ascendant</term> <note>The sign rising on the eastern horizon</note> and the <term>medium coeli</term> <note>The "Middle of the Sky" or Midheaven; the highest point in the chart</note>, and their lords. Likewise, we must consider the place of the Sun and the place of the Moon, the "Part of Fortune," and the lord of the conjunction or prevention <note>The New Moon or Full Moon occurring just before birth</note> that took place before the person's birth, while depressing the malevolent planets <note>Likely Saturn and Mars</note>. If, however, we wish to fashion an image to bring calamity, we shall do the opposite: where we previously placed fortunate things, we shall now place things that are ill-formed or unlucky, and we shall raise the malevolent stars to prominence. In a similar way...

Let the ascendant and its lord be fortunate <note>original: "fortuna"; meaning influenced by beneficial planets like Jupiter or Venus.</note>. Take care that the lord of the ascendant is not retrograde <note>Appearing to move backward in the sky, which symbolizes weakness or reversal.</note>, nor combust <note>Too close to the Sun, which "burns up" a planet's power.</note>, nor falling, nor in the house of opposition (that is, in the seventh house from its own home). Let it not be hindered by the "malifics" <note>Usually Mars or Saturn, which were thought to cause harm.</note>; let it be strong and in an "angle" <note>The 1st, 4th, 7th, or 10th houses, where a planet's influence is most potent.</note>. You shall make the ascendant, the lord of the second house, and the Moon fortunate. Then, make a second image for the person who has the thing you seek. Begin this under the ascendant pertaining to them: if it be a king or prince, begin under the ascendant of the tenth house from the ascendant of the first image; if a father, under the fourth; if a son, under the fifth, and so on for similar relations. Place the significator <note>The planet representing the person or object in the chart.</note> of the second image joined with the lord of the ascendant of the first image by a trine or sextile aspect, and let the former receive the latter. Place both strong and fortunate without hindrance. Make all the malifics "falling" <note>In weak positions where they cannot do harm.</note> from them. You shall make the tenth and fourth houses fortunate, if you can, or at least some part of them. When the second image is finished, join it with the first, face to face, and wrap them in a clean linen cloth. Bury them in the middle of the house of the one who seeks the thing, under a significator made fortunate with strong fortune. Let the face of the first image be toward the north, or rather toward the place where the person stays who has what is sought. Or, if it happens that the seeker travels to the person who has the sought-after thing, let them carry the images with them until they arrive. And let it be.

<margin>An image for dreams.</margin>
There is also an image for dreams which, when placed under the head of a sleeper, effectively provides true dreams about whatever matter the mind has previously pondered. The figure of it is the figure of a man sleeping in a lap. You shall make this while Leo is rising and the Sun is in Aries, holding the ninth house <note>The ninth house governs prophecy, dreams, and long journeys.</note>. Then, upon the breast of the man, you shall inscribe the name of the desired effect; upon the head, however, you shall write the name of the angel of the Intelligence of the Sun <note>original: "intelligentia solis"; in Agrippa's system, the Intelligence is a benevolent spirit governing a planet.</note>. The same image is made with Virgo rising and Mercury fortunate in Aries in the ninth house, or with Gemini rising and Mercury fortunate and holding the ninth in Aquarius; and let it be received by Saturn in a happy aspect. The name of the spirit of Mercury <note>original: "spũs Mercurii"</note> is then inscribed. This same image is also made with Libra rising and Venus in Gemini, received by Mercury in the ninth house, by inscribing the angel of Venus. Furthermore, the same image is made with Aquarius rising and Saturn in his "exaltation" <note>A sign where a planet's influence is particularly dignified; for Saturn, this is Libra.</note> (which is in Libra), happily possessing the ninth house; and you shall inscribe the name of the angel of Saturn.

<margin>Rings of dreams.</margin>
It is also made with Cancer rising and the Moon in Pisces, received by Jupiter and Venus and happily placed in the ninth house; and the name of the spirit of the Moon <note>original: "spũs lunę"</note> is inscribed. Also, rings of dreams are made of wonderful efficacy: these are the rings of the Sun and Saturn. Their constellation <note>The required planetary alignment.</note> is when the Sun or Saturn are in their exaltations while rising in the ninth house; and when the Moon is joined to Saturn in the ninth house, and in that sign which was the ninth house of one's birth <note>original: "nativitatis"</note>. The name of the spirit of the Sun or Saturn is inscribed on the rings, and it is fixed...

# Chapter 51. On characters which are constructed according to the pattern and imitation of the celestials, and how they are derived from Geomantic figures, with a table of the same.

<margin>Characters shared with the celestials.</margin>

But the true characters of the heavens are the very writing of the angels, which among the Hebrews is called the writing of the *Malachim* <note>original: "Malachim"; a celestial alphabet used by occultists, meaning "Kings" or "Angels"</note>, through which all things are described and signified in heaven for anyone who knows how to read.
