### ¶ That No Divination is Perfect Without Astrology.
### Chapter 53.

<margin>Divination linked to astrology.</margin> We have spoken in the preceding chapters about various types of divination; but it must be observed that all these require the use and rules of astrology, like a necessary key for the knowledge of all secrets. All types of divination, whatever they may be, have their roots and foundations in astrology itself, so much so that without it they seem to offer little or nothing. <margin>Praise of astrology.</margin> Yet the astrological dominion—insofar as the celestial bodies are the causes and signs of all things that exist and happen in these lower realms—provides the most certain demonstrations of whatever is hidden or future based solely on the position and motion of the celestial bodies. This is not the place to say more on this, as massive volumes have been written on this science by the ancients and are available to everyone.

<margin>Physiognomy.</margin> <note>The practice of judging character or predicting the future from physical features, especially the face.</note> Therefore, whether a physiognomist inspects the body, the face, the forehead, or the hand; or whether an interpreter examines a dream, or an omen <note>original: "auspicium"; the ancient practice of divining by the flight of birds.</note>, if the judgment is to be correct, the figure of the heavens must likewise be examined. From its indications, together with the conjectures of similarities and signs, true opinions of what is signified may be born. Even if some prodigy <note>An extraordinary or unnatural event seen as an omen.</note> should appear, a figure of the heavens must be drawn. One must also examine what preceded in the "revolutions of the years," <note>An astrological technique involving the sun's return to its original position.</note> from great conjunctions and eclipses. Furthermore, one must consider the nativities, origins, enthronements, foundations, revolutions, perfections, and directions <note>These are all technical astrological methods for calculating the lifespan or success of an entity.</note> of the leaders, nations, kingdoms, and cities where these omens appeared, and into which place of each celestial figure these signs fell. From all of these together, we may finally hunt down a reasonable and most probable meaning of these matters. They say that one must proceed by the same sequence, though with less labor, in the interpretation of dreams.

<margin>Prophecy from frenzy.</margin> Furthermore, those who, being alienated by a "frenzy," <note>original: "furore"; referring to the "divine madness" or trance states of oracles.</note> predict the future, only do so when driven by the stars or by these lower instruments. Hence, their prophecies must finally be adapted to the celestial things, just as we read in Lucan <note>A Roman poet (39–65 AD); this quote is from his epic 'Pharsalia'.</note> regarding the Tuscan seer:

> Learned in the movements of the lightning, and the warm veins
> Of the organs, and the flight of the bird wandering in the air.
<note>original: "Fulminis edoctum motus, venasque calentes / Fibrarum, & motus errantis in aere pennæ."</note>

After the city was purified, after the victim was sacrificed, and after the entrails were inspected, the final sentence was pronounced based on the dispositions of the celestial stars.

<margin>What geomancy is.</margin> Now indeed, even geomancy <note>A method of divination that interprets markings on the ground or patterns formed by tossed handfuls of soil, rocks, or sand.</note>—the most accurate of the "sortileges" <note>Divination by drawing lots.</note>—which divines through points inscribed in the earth or another surface (either by chance or by some force), first reduces those points to celestial figures. Specifically, it reduces them to those sixteen figures which we named above; from their properties and reasons, it forms a judgment in the astrological manner. And to this point belong all the various divinations of natural sortileges, whose power can come from nowhere else but from heaven and from the mind of the person performing the work.

<header>ON OCCULT PHILOSOPHY.</header>

Indeed, whatever is moved, agitated, or produced in these lower realms by any motion must necessarily imitate the influence of the motions of the higher realms. When these things are traced back to those higher realms—as if to their roots, causes, and signs—the heavens then reveal their meaning to us according to astrological rules. Because of this, dice—specifically the tetrahedron, hexahedron, octahedron, dodecahedron, and icosahedron <note>These are the five "Platonic Solids," which Agrippa suggests can be used as ritual dice for divination.</note>—when crafted and inscribed with specific numbers, signs, and stars at auspicious times under celestial influences, obtain a wonderful power of divining and predicting through their throws. This is similar to those famous Praenestine dice <note>original: "Præneſtinæ illæ teſſeræ"; referring to the famous oracle of the goddess Fortuna at Praeneste (modern Palestrina), where wooden lots or dice were used to predict the fates of the Romans.</note>, in which the fates of the Romans were said to be contained.

### ¶ On Lots, and When and From Where the Power of Divination Comes to Them. Chapter 54.

Whatever divinations and predictions of human events occur through lots <note>original: "fortem"; "sors" or "lots" refers to any method of divination using random selection, such as drawing straws or casting dice.</note> must certainly have a sublime, latent, and occult cause beyond the lot itself. This cause is certainly not "accidental," as Aristotle described fortune <note>Aristotle defined "luck" or "fortune" as a coincidental cause, but Agrippa argues that in magic, nothing is truly random.</note>. Indeed, in the chain of causes—since according to the Platonists an "accidental" cause can never be a primary and sufficient cause—we must look deeper and find a cause that knows and intends the effect itself. It is necessary to place this cause not in a corporeal nature, but in immaterial and incorporeal substances which truly administer the lot and dispense it for the disclosure of truth. These are found in human souls, or separate spirits and demons, or in celestial intelligences, or in God himself. That there can be sufficient power and virtue in the human soul to direct such lots is evident from this:

<margin>The dignity of the soul</margin>
There exists in our soul a divine power and likeness, and a grasp and power over all things. As we said in the first book, all things have a natural obedience to the soul; by necessity, they possess motion and efficacy toward that which the soul desires with a strong longing. All the powers and operations of things—both natural and artificial—obey the soul when it is carried away into an excess of its own desire <note>Agrippa refers to "excessus desiderii," a state of intense emotional or spiritual focus that allows the soul to influence physical reality.</note>. At that moment, all lots of any kind assist the appetite of such a soul and acquire for themselves marvelous powers of foretelling, both from the soul and from the celestial opportunity at that hour when the excess of desire most strongly invades it. This same principle is also the root of all astrological questions: for when the soul is elevated into an excess of some desire, it seizes for itself the most convenient and effective hour and opportunity. When a figure of the heavens <note>An astrological chart or horoscope.</note> is constructed for that moment, the astrologer can then judge and clearly know through it what the seeker wishes and desires to know. Yet, because lots are sometimes directed not by the human soul, but (as we said) by the ministry of other spirits, and because the soul of the diviner is not always disposed to that "excess of passion" we mentioned, it was the custom among the ancients before casting lots...

This is true whether that force comes from the soul of the practitioner through a great excess of their own emotion, or from a celestial influence and opportunity, or from some deity or spirit standing by and moving things from the outside. Cicero made mention of these in his orations against Verres, but those are not the subject of our current purpose. Regarding those lots which are truly divine and sacred, relating to oracles and religion, we shall discuss them in the following book. For now, I would only remind you of this: however much presage, divination, or prophecy lots are found to possess, they do not have it because they are "lots," but through the power of some more sublime operation joined to them.

### Chapter 55. On the Soul of the World and the Heavens, according to the traditions of the poets and philosophers.

Since the heavens and the celestial bodies themselves have power, influence, and a manifest operation upon these lower things, it is necessary that they be animated <note>Meaning "endowed with a soul" (anima).</note>, since an operation <margin>The Soul of the World according to the poets.</margin> can by no means proceed from a pure body. Therefore, all the most noble poets and philosophers affirm that the world itself has a soul, and the celestial bodies likewise, and that this soul is indeed intelligent. Hence, Marcus Manilius, in his *Astronomica* dedicated to Augustus, sings:

### ¶ The same is confirmed by reason. Chapter 56.

<margin>h</margin>
The world has a soul, the heavens have a soul, the stars have a soul, the elements have a soul, with which they cause a soul in these lower and mixed things. They also possess a spirit, as we said in the first book, <margin>Soul of the stars and elements.</margin> which is present to the body by means of its soul. For since the whole body of the world is a single body whose parts are the bodies of all living creatures—and just as the whole is more perfect and noble than its parts, so the body of the world is more perfect and noble than the body of any individual living thing—it would be absurd if every imperfect little body, and the tiny particles of the world, and even the most base little animals like flies and worms were worthy of life, possessed life, and had a soul, yet the complete, most perfect, total and most noble body of the world itself neither lived nor had a soul. It is no less absurd that the heavens, stars, and elements, which most generously provide life and soul to individual things, should themselves lack life and soul; and that any plant or tree should be of a more noble condition than the heaven, the stars, and the elements, which are naturally their cause. This appears most clearly in those things that sprout spontaneously, and in those which lack physical seeds. For the elements could not generate and nourish living things of this kind if they themselves were lacking life and soul. Perhaps some will say that living things of this kind are produced not from the soul of the earth or water, but from the influences of celestial souls. To these, the Platonists <note>Followers of Plato's philosophy, who believed the material world is a reflection of a higher, living spiritual reality.</note> respond that an accident <term>accident</term> <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, an "accident" is a property (like color or influence) that doesn't exist by itself, whereas a "substance" is a thing that exists independently. ### ¶ That the Soul of the World and the Celestial Souls are Rational, and Partake of the Divine Mind. Chapter 57.

That the souls we have mentioned also possess reason is evident from this: for since the universal works of the said souls conspire among themselves in a certain perpetual order, it is necessary that they be governed not by chance but by reason: by which reasons they direct and lead all their operations to certain ends. For it is necessary that the earth has the "reasons" <note>original: "rationes"; here referring to the divine patterns or governing principles of things.</note> of earthly things, and the water of watery things: similarly in the rest, by which individual things are procreated in their own time, place, and order, and often, when damaged, are restored. Therefore, philosophers do not judge the soul of the earth as the soul of some abject body, but as rational, and moreover as understanding, and being a goddess. Furthermore, it would be absurd, since we possess the reasons for our own works, that the celestial souls, and the soul of the universe itself, should not have reasons for theirs. But if (as Plato says) the world was made by the Good itself as best as it could be made, it will certainly be a partaker not only of life, sense, and reason, but also of intelligence and mind. Since the perfection of a body is the soul: and that body is more perfect which has a more perfect soul. It is therefore necessary, since celestial bodies are most perfect, that they also have most perfect souls. They are,

<margin>The soul of the world.</margin>
<margin>The machine of the world consists of three parts.</margin>
Since the soul is by its own nature free, it can easily stray and wander about, unless it be governed by the intellect and the mind—and that a perfect and most choice mind, foreseeing the way and the best end from the beginning. This perfect mind, because it is most powerfully present to the soul—such as is the soul of the world, and such as are the souls of the celestial bodies and the elements—doubtless governs the work assigned to it in the most orderly and perfect fashion. For bodies do not resist most powerful souls, and a perfect mind does not change its purpose. There is therefore a soul of the world, a single life filling all things, pouring through all things, and binding and connecting all things together, so that it renders the whole machine of the world as one. It is as if it were a single monochord <note>A monochord is a single-stringed instrument used by ancient philosophers to demonstrate the mathematical laws of harmony; here, Agrippa uses it to suggest the universe is "tuned" to a single spiritual frequency.</note>, resonating from three kinds of creatures—the intellectual, the celestial, and the corruptible <note>The "corruptible" refers to the physical world of matter that decays, as opposed to the eternal heavens or pure spirit.</note>—by a single breath only and a single life.

### ¶Of the names of the celestial souls, and of their dominion over this lower world, namely man. Chapter 58.

<margin>A</margin>
<margin>The souls of the heavens.</margin>
The names of the celestial souls are many and diverse, according to the many "yokes" of their power and virtue over these lower things. From these powers they have received various names which the ancients used in their hymns and invocations. Regarding this, it must be noted that every soul of this kind, according to Orphic theology <note>Orpheus was the legendary Greek musician whose "Orphic Hymns" were central to Renaissance magic; Agrippa views him as a primary authority on the hidden names of spirits.</note>, is said to have a twofold virtue: one situated in knowing, the other situated in giving life to and governing its own body. In this way, in the celestial spheres, Orpheus calls that first virtue "Bacchus" and the second virtue a "Muse." Hence, no one is "intoxicated" <note>Intoxication here refers to divine frenzy or spiritual enlightenment, not literal drunkenness.</note> by any Bacchus who has not first been joined to his Muse. Therefore, nine Bacchuses are designated alongside the nine Muses. Thus, in the ninth sphere, Orpheus places Bacchus Cribronius and the Muse Calliope; in the starry heaven [the firmament], he places Bacchus Picionius and the Muse Urania. In the heaven of Saturn, Bacchus Amphietus and the Muse Polyhymnia. In the heaven of Jupiter, Bacchus Sabasius and the Muse Terpsichore. In the heaven of Mars, Bacchus Bassarius and the Muse Clio. In the heaven of the Sun, Bacchus Trietericus and the Muse Melpomene. In the heaven of Venus, Bacchus Lysius and the Muse Erato. In the heaven of Mercury, Bacchus Silenus and the Muse Euterpe. In the heaven of the Moon, Bacchus Lyaeus and the Muse Thalia. Similarly, in the spheres

Furthermore, in fire they place Vulcan; in water, Neptune; and they addressed them by various names. ### ¶ Concerning the seven planets, governors of the world, and their various names serving in magical speeches. Chapter LIX.

<margin>Governors of the world and their many names. Saturn.</margin>

# OF OCCULT PHILOSOPHY

<margin>The source of virtues</margin>
Celestial souls pour their virtues into the celestial bodies, which then transmit them to this world of the senses. For the virtues of the earthly sphere proceed from no other cause than the celestial one. Hence, the **Magus** <note>a practitioner of learned magic</note>, intending to work through them, uses the artful invocation of superior beings, with mysterious words and a certain ingenious speech, drawing one thing to another through a natural force. This happens via a certain mutual correspondence <note>original: "convenientiam"</note> between them, through which things follow of their own accord, or are sometimes drawn against their will.

Hence **Aristotle** says in the sixth book of *Mystic Philosophy* <note>original: "Mysticę philosophiæ"; likely referring to the pseudo-Aristotelian "Theology of Aristotle," a Neo-Platonic text</note>: that when someone, by binding or enchanting <note>original: "fascinando"</note>, invokes the Sun or other stars, praying that they cooperate in the desired work, it is not that the Sun or other stars hear that speech, but they are moved in some way by a certain natural connection and mutual sequence. In this way, the parts of the world are mutually subordinate to one another and have a mutual consensus because of their great union. 

Just as in the human body, one limb is moved by perceiving the motion of another; and in a **lute** <note>original: "cithara"</note>, when one string is moved, another is also moved. Thus, when someone moves one part of the world, others are moved by perceiving the movement brought upon them. Therefore, the knowledge of the dependency of things following one after another is the foundation of all **miraculous operation**, which is necessarily required to exercise the power of attraction of the superior virtues. 

Human words, however, are natural things; and because the parts of the world naturally draw one another and act upon each other, the Magus, invoking through words, operates through the fitting powers of nature. He leads or draws certain things by the love of one for another, due to the sequence of one thing to another; or he repels them by the hatred of one for another, arising from the contrariety and difference of things, and the multitude of virtues. Although these virtues may be contrary or different, they still complete one part. Sometimes he even compels things by celestial virtue through a certain mastery, since he is not a stranger to heaven. 

Therefore, if a person receives the impression of any binding or enchantment, they do not receive it according to the rational soul, but the sensitive soul; and if they suffer in any part of themselves, they suffer according to the **sublunary soul** <note>the part of the soul connected to the physical, changing world below the Moon</note>. For it is not through reason, which knows and understands, that one is drawn...

<summary>This page explains the mechanism of magic as a "natural connection" between parts of the universe, comparing the world's harmony to the sympathetic vibration of lute strings. It argues that a Magus can influence the world through specific words and invocations because human speech is part of the natural order that links the earthly and celestial realms.</summary>

### BOOK SECOND. 111

...cannot [be moved], but only through the sense which conceives that impression and impulse, insofar as the **animal spirit** <note>the vital spirit that mediates between the body and soul</note> of a human is affected beyond its original or natural disposition by the influx of the heavens and the cooperation of worldly things. For example, a son moves his father to labor—even against his will—for the sake of saving him, despite the father’s exhaustion. Similarly, the appetite for dominance moves one to anger and other labors for the sake of gaining power. The needs of nature and the fear of poverty move one to desire riches. A woman's adornment and beauty act as an incentive for lust. The harmony of a skilled musician moves listeners with various passions; some follow the harmony of the art willingly, while others conform their gestures to it even against their will, because their senses are captured, even if their reason is not focused on it. Yet the common people do not marvel at or detest these forms of fascination and binding because they are familiar with them. However, they marvel at other **physical** <note>here meaning "natural magic"</note> wonders because they are ignorant of them and unused to them. Thus, they fall into error, thinking that which is from nature and according to nature is above or against it.

<margin>Movement of the superior into the inferior.</margin>
<margin>Movement of the soul.</margin>
One must know, therefore, that every superior thing moves that which is immediately below it in its own degree and order, not only in bodies but also in spirits. Thus, the **Universal Soul** <note>the *Anima Mundi* or world-soul that animates the entire universe</note> moves particular souls; the **rational soul** <note>the part of the soul capable of reasoning</note> acts upon the **sensitive soul** <note>the part of the soul responsible for sensation and movement</note>, and that acts upon the **vegetative soul** <note>the part of the soul responsible for growth and nutrition</note>. Every part of the world acts upon another, and each is fit to be moved by another; every part of this lower world is affected by the heavens according to its nature and aptitude, just as one part of an animal's body is affected by another.

<margin>Movement of the superior world.</margin>
And the superior **intellectual world** <note>the realm of pure thought and angelic intelligences</note> moves all things below itself, since it contains all the same entities from the first to the last as the inferior worlds. Therefore, the celestial bodies move the bodies of the elemental world—which are composite, subject to birth, and perceptible—from the concave <note>the inner edge of the heavens</note> to the center. This happens through superior, perpetual, and spiritual essences hanging from the **Primary Intellect**, which is the **Agent Intellect** <note>the power of the mind that makes understanding possible</note>; but also by a virtue instilled by God through His **Word**. The **Chaldeans** <note>ancient Babylonian scholars known for astrology and magic</note> and the wise men of Babylon call this Word the "Cause of Causes" <note>original: "causam causarum"</note>, because from it all beings are produced, including the Agent Intellect itself, which is second to it.

<margin>The Cause of Causes; Image of the soul.</margin>
This is because of the union of this Word with the **First Author** <note>God</note>, by whom all existing things are truly produced. Therefore, the Word is the **image** <note>original: "simulachrum"</note> of God; the Agent Intellect is the image of the Word; the Soul is the image of the Intellect; and our own word <note>human speech, prayer, or magical incantation</note> is the image of the soul, through which it acts upon natural things naturally, since nature is the work of that soul. Each of these perfects what follows it, just as a father perfects a son; and no later thing exists without the prior. For they are dependent upon one another in an ordered dependency, so that when a later thing is destroyed, it returns to the one immediately preceding it, until it reaches the heavens, then the Universal Soul, then the Agent Intellect (by which all other creatures exist), and finally it exists in the First Author.

<summary>This page explains the metaphysical hierarchy of the universe, arguing that all movement and influence—whether magical, psychological, or physical—flow from God (the First Author) through the Word and the Agent Intellect down to the material world. It asserts that magic is a natural process of this hierarchy, though it seems miraculous to the uneducated.</summary>

# ON OCCULT PHILOSOPHY.

<margin>
What he must contemplate who wishes to perform a marvelous work
</margin>
...which is the creating word, to which at last all things return. Therefore, it is necessary for our soul, when wishing to perform some marvelous work in these lower regions, to contemplate its own origin, so that it may be strengthened by it, enlightened, and receive the power of acting through every degree from the First Author <note>original: *autore primo*, referring to God as the primary cause of all things</note> himself. Therefore, care must be taken that we contemplate the souls of the stars more than their physical bodies; and the super-celestial intellectual world more than the corporeal celestial world. For that intellectual world is more noble, although this physical one is also distinguished and exists as a preliminary to it—and without this material medium, the influx <note>the downward flow of spiritual power</note> of that superior world cannot be achieved. <margin>King of the stars</margin> For example: the Sun, the king of the stars and most full of light, receives that light from the intelligible world <note>the realm of pure thought and divine ideas</note> above all other stars, because its soul is more capable of receiving that intelligible splendor. Wherefore, he who desires to attract the influx of the Sun must contemplate the Sun, not only with the observation of its exterior light, but also of its interior light. And this no one can do, unless he returns to the very soul of the Sun and becomes similar to it, comprehending its intelligible light with intellectual vision, just as he does the sensible light with the physical eye. <margin>Power</margin> For here he will be filled with its splendor and will receive into himself its light—which is a pattern <note>original: *hypotypus*, a Greek term for a model or archetype</note> impressed from the supernal sphere. Clothed in this enlightenment, truly made equal to it, and as if aided by a lifting up <note>original: *levamento*, implying a spiritual elevation or support</note>, he shall attain that supreme clarity and all its participating forms according to the wish of his intellect. And when he has drawn in the light of the highest degree, then his soul will approach its own perfection; it will be assimilated to the spirits of the Sun and will reach the virtues and enlightenments of supernatural power. He will enjoy their power, provided he has obtained faith in the First Author. First, therefore, it is necessary to implore help and assent from the First Author himself: and not only with the mouth, but with a religious gesture and a suppliant mind, praying abundantly, incessantly, and with integrity, so that He may enlighten the mind and remove the darkness growing over souls because of the body.

<margin>The greatness of man.</margin>
<margin>The effect of idleness.</margin>
<margin>A marvelous lesson of instruction.</margin>
<margin>All virtues come from God.</margin>
<margin>The effect of divine intelligence.</margin>
It is a very noble opinion of the ancient magi <note>original: *magorum*, referring to the wise men of antiquity who sought hidden knowledge</note> (Most Illustrious Prince) that there is nothing in this life for which we must labor more than this: that we do not degenerate from the nobility of the soul, by which we come closest to God and put on a divine nature. We must not let the soul grow sluggish in empty idleness, lest it dissolve into the fragility of the earthly body and the vices of the flesh, and lest we lose it as if it were cast down through the dark precipices of perverse desires. Therefore, it is fitting for us to so train the soul that it, mindful of its own dignity and nobility, always thinks of and performs works worthy of itself. But only the knowledge of divine science <term>divine science: a branch of knowledge focused on understanding God and the spiritual laws governing the universe</term> provides this for us above all. When, through the remembrance of His majesty, we are always occupied with divine studies, we contemplate divine things through every moment of every hour with a keen and watchful inquiry. By ascending through each level of created things up to the Archetype <note>the original divine pattern from which all things are derived, often used by Agrippa to mean God or the Divine Mind</note> itself, we draw from it the ineffable power of all things. Those who neglect this, trusting only in natural and worldly things, are often confused by various errors and fallacies, and are very frequently deceived by evil spirits. However, the intelligence of divine things purges the mind of errors and makes it divine; it grants infallible power to our works and drives far away the frauds and obstacles of all evil spirits. It subjects them at the same time to our command, and even compels the good angels and all the powers of the world into our service—drawing, of course, the power for our works from the Archetype itself. When we ascend to Him, it is necessary for every creature to obey us, and the entire chorus of heavenly beings follows us. For, as Homer <note>original: *Homerus*, the Greek epic poet</note> says: *None of the gods would dare to remain in their seats once Jove has moved.* And immediately then He rules, as Aristophanes <note>original: *Aristophanes*, the Greek comic playwright</note> says, through one of the gods whose right it is to carry out His commands, who then, by his office, executes our requests according to our wish. Therefore, Most Illustrious Prince, since a divine and immortal soul has been given to you, which—by the kindness of divine providence, a favorable fate, and the generosity of nature—has been so endowed that you are able to perceive, investigate, contemplate, discern, and judge the pleasant spectacles of natural things, the high dwellings of the heavens, and the most difficult sanctuaries <note>original: *adytus*, the innermost, most sacred part of a temple</note> of divine matters: being bound to you by the necessity of such great virtues, I am your debtor, and

EPISTLE

<margin>

I have learned the mysteries of divine and ceremonial magic without deception, and I intend to communicate them through true definitions of thought, without envy, and not to hide the understanding of them. Whatever the ancient priests of the **Isiac Egyptians** <note>original: *Isiaci*, followers of the goddess Isis</note>, the ancient seers of the **Babylonian Chaldeans**, and the divine wise men of the **Hebrew Kabbalists** have handed down; likewise what the **Orphics, Pythagoreans, and Platonists**—the most profound philosophers of the Greeks—as well as the **Brahmins of the Indians**, the **Gymnosophists** <term>Gymnosophists: "Naked philosophers," a term used by Greeks for Indian or Ethiopian ascetics who lived simply to focus on wisdom</term> of the Ethiopians, and the pure theologians of our own religion * have transmitted; and by what power of words, what potency of seals, what songs of blessings and imprecations, and by what virtue of observations they once performed such stupendous and admirable wonders—all these things I am making known to you in this third book of *Occult Philosophy*, bringing to light those things which have lain covered in the filth of antiquity and wrapped in the fog of oblivion as if in **Cimmerian darkness** <note>A mythological reference to a land of perpetual mist and darkness</note>.

Therefore, I now return to you this full and complete work of *Occult Philosophy* or *Magic* in these three books, which I have perfected with watchful care and with labor of both mind and body, and with the greatest effort. Though the language may be unpolished, the subject matter is clearly most difficult. For this reason, I wish to ask one thing: do not look for grace of speech or elegance of language in these books, which I wrote long ago in my youth when my speech was still raw and my oratory unformed. Now, I have only revised the sequence of the thoughts rather than the texture of the speech; for I have studied the elegance of language less, as the richness of the material took its place. I believe I have sufficiently fulfilled my duty if I have performed to the best of my ability what I promised to report concerning the secrets of Magic, thus clearing my conscience of the debt I owed to you.

But since I have no doubt that many snobbish sophists will conspire against me—those who boast that they are the grandsons of the gods and full of divinity, and who arrogantly claim judgment for themselves from the **leaves of the Sibyl** <note>referring to the Sibylline Oracles, implying they claim divine authority for their opinions</note>—they will surely attempt to judge and condemn these writings of ours with a new fire, even before they have read or properly understood any of it. This is partly because these things are like **lettuce unsuited to their lips** <note>A Latin proverb suggesting that some people lack the refined taste to appreciate certain truths</note>, and like marjoram <note>original: *amaracinum*</note> unfamiliar to their noses, but also because of the sparks of hatred once conceived against me, which they can hardly hide beneath the ashes.

Therefore (Most Illustrious Prince and wisest Prelate), I ascribe this work—already your own—to the merits of your virtues. Furthermore, I submit it to your censorship and commend it to your protection. If wicked and faithless sophists, in their thick madness of envy and slander, wish to gnaw at it, may you happily protect and defend it by the clarity of your discretion and the integrity of your judgment. Farewell, most happily.

## nelius Agrippa on Occult Philosophy, or Magic.

### ¶ On the necessity, power, and utility of religion.

### Chapter I.

<margin>
The health of the body depends on the soul.
The health of man.
Integrity of life provides a foundation.
The effect of religion.
How we can be pleasing to God.
<note>Zech. 9:17</note>
Budding wine.

IT IS TIME NOW TO TURN OURSELVES TO HIGHER THINGS, and to that portion of Magic which teaches us to be skilled in and to know the laws of religions: how we ought to obtain divine religion through truth, and how we ought to rightly cultivate the soul and mind—by which alone we can comprehend truth. For it is a common opinion among the Mages that unless the mind and soul are well, the body cannot be well. A person is truly healthy only when the soul and body are so joined and agree with each other that the firmness of the mind and soul is not inferior to the strengths of the body. Furthermore, we cannot obtain a firm and robust mind from anywhere else (as Hermes <note>original: *Hermes*, referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure associated with wisdom and magic</note> says) except from integrity of life, from piety, and finally from divine religion. For sacred religion purifies the mind and makes it divine; it also assists nature and strengthens natural virtues, just as a doctor assists the health of the body and a farmer assists the power of the earth.

Indeed, whoever abandons religion and trusts only in natural things is very often deceived by evil spirits. However, from an understanding of religion, there is born a contempt for and a remedy for vices, as well as a protection against evil spirits. Finally, nothing is more pleasing or acceptable to God than a perfectly pious and truly religious man, who excels other men as much as he himself is distant from the immortal gods. We ought, therefore, first to offer and commend ourselves as purified beings to divine piety and religion; and then, with our senses calmed and a tranquil mind, wait for that divine ambrosian nectar—nectar, I say, which the prophet Zechariah calls "the wine that makes the virgins flourish" <note>original: *vinum germinans virgines*</note>—while praising and adoring that super-celestial Bacchus <note>Here, Agrippa uses Bacchus as a metaphor for spiritual intoxication or divine ecstasy, a common trope in Renaissance Neoplatonism</note>, the supreme presiding officer of gods and priests, the author of regeneration, whom the ancient poets sang of as "twice-born," and from whom such most divine streams flow into our hearts.

DE OCCULTA PHILOSOPHIA

<margin>The silence of Pythagoras.</margin>
The knowledge of many is full of such great divine majesty (as **Mercurius** <note>original: *Mercurius*, referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary sage to whom many occult writings were attributed</note> says) that it is the mark of an irreligious mind to publish it; and the divine **Plato** commanded that those things which are sacred and secret in the mysteries should not be broadcast to the common people. **Pythagoras** also and **Porphyry** consecrated their followers with a religious silence. **Orpheus** even demanded an oath of silence from those he initiated into the ceremonies of the sacred rites, with a certain terrible authority of religion, lest the secrets of religion be betrayed to profane ears; wherefore he sings in his poem concerning the Sacred Word:

> with a deep mind, embrace these voices:

> and having entered this path, look up to Him alone of the world:

> the prophetess cries out, and depart from the entire grove.

<margin>Secrets of the Hebrews</margin>
Hence also in the celebration of the sacred rites of **Eleusinian Ceres**, only the initiated were admitted, with a herald acting as guard who shouted for the profane crowd to keep their distance; and in **Ezra** we read the same precept concerning the **Cabalistic** <term>Cabala: a tradition of Jewish mysticism based on an esoteric interpretation of the Hebrew Scriptures</term> secrets of the Hebrews, explained in these lines: *Deliver those books to the wise among the people, whose hearts you know are able to grasp and keep the secrets.* For this reason, the religious volumes of the **Egyptians** pertaining to the secrets of ceremonies were made from **hieratic** <term>hieratic: a high-quality "priestly" paper made from papyrus, reserved for sacred texts</term> paper (that is, consecrated paper); in these they wrote down unknowable letters, which they call sacred.

<margin>Hieroglyphic letters of the Egyptians.</margin>
**Macrobius**, **Marcellinus**, and others record that these are called **hieroglyphics**, so that, of course, such writings could not be understood by the profane; which **Apuleius** also testifies in these words: *The sacrifice being finished,* he says, *he brings forth from the hidden parts of the inner sanctuary certain books, marked with unknowable letters, partly suggesting condensed words of a conceived discourse through figures of animals of this kind; partly protected from the reading of the curious profane by knotted peaks, twisted like wheels and crowded together like vine-tendrils.* Therefore, by being silent and concealing what is secret in religion, we will be worthy disciples of that science. For the loyalty of silence (as **Tertullian** says) is owed to religions; those who act otherwise are close to danger. Whence **Apuleius** says, concerning the secrets of the sacred rites: *I would tell if it were permitted to tell; you would know if it were permitted to hear; but both the ears and the tongue would contract an equal penalty for such rash curiosity.* Thus we read that **Theode**— <note>The text cuts off mid-name; likely referring to Theodoret of Cyrus, a 5th-century theologian.</note>

It describes the use of hieroglyphics and specialized scripts as tools for maintaining this religious silence.</summary>

### BOOK THREE

<margin>Theodotus blinded for contempt of religion.</margin>
...when a tragic poet, because he wished to adapt some of the mysteries of Jewish scripture <note>original: *Iudaicæ scripturę mysterii*. The text refers to a legendary account where the poet Theodotus was struck blind for trying to incorporate the Torah into his plays.</note> into a play, was deprived of sight on account of his contempt for religion. **Theopompus** also, who had begun to translate several things from the divine law into the Greek language, was immediately struck with a certain disturbance of mind and spirit; when he later prayed earnestly to God to know why this had happened to him, he received an answer in a dream: it was because he was defiling divine things by making them public with seductive speech <note>original: *lenocinio*, often implying a cheapening or "pimping out" of the text through overly ornate rhetoric</note>. A certain **Numenius**, who was too curious about hidden things, also incurred the offense of the deities because he had interpreted and made public the sacred rites of the **Eleusinian goddess** <note>Demeter, whose "Eleusinian Mysteries" were the most famous secret religious rites of ancient Greece.</note>. He dreamed that the Eleusinian goddesses were standing before an open brothel in the habit of harlots; when he marveled at this, they responded angrily that they had been dragged by force from the sanctuary of their modesty by him, and were being prostituted to any passerby. By this he was warned that the ceremonies of the gods must not be made common knowledge. Therefore, it was always the study of the ancients to wrap the 
<margin>Mysteries wrapped in riddles.</margin>
mysteries <term>sacramenta</term> <note>While *sacramenta* often means "sacraments" in a church context, in this esoteric text it refers to "sacred secrets" or "mysteries."</note> of God and nature and to cover them with various riddles. This law was observed by the **Indians**, the **Brahmans**, the **Ethiopians**, the **Persians**, and the **Egyptians**. Hence **Mercurius**, **Orpheus**, and all the ancient prophets and philosophers—**Pythagoras**, **Socrates**, **Plato**, **Aristoxenus**, **Ammonius**—preserved it with inviolable faith. Hence **Plotinus** and **Origen**, and the other disciples of **Ammonius** <note>Ammonius Saccas, the mysterious teacher of both the Christian Origen and the Neoplatonist Plotinus.</note>, as **Porphyry** relates in his book on the life and discipline of Plotinus, swore an oath not to publish the master’s dogmas. Because Plotinus violated the oath made to Ammonius and published the mysteries, he was—as some report—consumed by a horrific infestation of lice <note>original: *pediculorum edulio*, a common historical trope of a "shameful death" for those who offended the divine.</note> as punishment for his transgression. Even **Christ** himself, while he still acted upon the
<margin>The secret religion of Christ.</margin>
earth, spoke by such a law and reason that only the more intimate disciples understood the mystery of the word of God, while the others perceived only parables. He commanded, moreover, that "what is holy must not be given to dogs, nor should pearls be cast before swine." Therefore the prophet says: *I have hidden your words in my heart, that I might not sin against you.* It is not fitting, therefore, to commit to public writings those secrets which are to be communicated by word of mouth alone among the few wise men. Wherefore, you will grant me pardon if I have passed over in silence many and the most important secret mysteries <term>arcana sacramenta</term> of ceremonial magic. I believe, however, that I shall have done enough if we report those things which are necessary to know, so that you do not leave the reading of this book entirely empty of those mysteries. But let these things be communicated to you under the same law by which **Dionysius** binds **Timothy** <note>Referring to the writings of Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite to his disciple Timothy, which emphasize the need to hide divine truth from the uninitiated.</note>: namely, that the secrets should not be exposed by those who perceive them to the unworthy, but, gathered among the wise, they should be guarded with the reverence they deserve. Furthermore, I want you to be warned at this beginning that, just as the deities themselves detest public and profane things and love secrets, so every magical experiment flees the public, seeks to be hidden, is strengthened by silence, but is destroyed by disclosure; nor does a complete effect follow from it. For all these things suffer loss when shared with the talkative and the incredulous.

# ON OCCULT PHILOSOPHY.

<margin>There must be a secret between the Magus and the operator.</margin>
...are instilled into these minds. Therefore, the magical operator, if he wishes to achieve results from his work, must be secretive. He must not reveal his work, nor the place, nor the time, nor his desire, nor his will to anyone, except perhaps to a teacher or a coadjutor <note>original: *coadiutori*, an assistant or partner</note>, or a companion. This companion must also be faithful, believing, silent, and dignified by nature or by training. Indeed, the very talkativeness, lack of belief, or unworthiness of a companion hinders and disturbs the effect in every operation.

### ¶ What worthiness is required for one to become a true Magus and a performer of wonders. Chapter III.

Around the beginning of the first book of this work, we spoke about what kind of person a Magus should be. Now, however, we shall recount a hidden, necessary, and secret matter for anyone who desires to work in this art, which is the beginning, the fulfillment, and the key to all magical operations: and this is the **dignification** <note>original: *dignificatio*, referring to the process of making oneself worthy, purified, or "ennobled" to handle divine power.</note> of a human being for such sublime virtue and power. For this faculty requires a wonderful worthiness in a person. Indeed, the **intellect** <note>In the Neoplatonic philosophy Agrippa follows, the "intellect" (*intellectus*) is the highest part of the soul, the spark of the divine that connects a human to God.</note> itself within us—the highest mind of the soul—is the sole operator of wonders. When it has been drowned by too much commerce with the flesh, and occupied with the soul’s sensory attachment to the body, it deserves no command over divine substances. This is why many pursue this art in vain. Therefore, we who strive for such heights must meditate on two things above all: first, by what means we may abandon carnal affects, fleeting senses, and material passions; second, by what path and in what manner we may ascend to that pure intellect, joined to the virtues of the gods. Without these, we can never successfully climb to the scrutiny of secret things or to the power of wonderful operations.

<margin>The key to magical operations.</margin>
In these things consists the whole of that "worthiness" which is provided by nature, by merit, and by a certain religious art. **Natural dignity** is the optimal disposition of the body and its organs, which does not obscure the soul with any thickness, nor disturbs it with any internal tumult or excessive humors. This arises from the position, motion, light, and influence of the celestial bodies and souls that are present at each person's birth <note>original: *genesi*, referring to one's natal astrological chart</note>. For example, there are those whose **Ninth House** <note>In astrology, the Ninth House governs religion, philosophy, and visions.</note> is made fortunate by Saturn, the Sun, and Mercury. Mars also, when in the Ninth House, commands spirits. But these matters are treated extensively in the books of the stars. He who is not naturally gifted in this way must compensate for the defect of nature through education, the best lifestyle, and the successful use of natural things, until he emerges complete in every internal and external perfection.

<margin>Two things especially in the magical art.</margin>
<margin>What a priest must avoid according to the Mosaic law.</margin>
For this reason, such great care is taken in the **Mosaic Law** <note>The laws of the Torah, specifically regarding the ritual purity of the priesthood in Leviticus.</note> concerning the priest: that he be unpolluted by the dead, by a widowed woman, or by one who is menstruating; that he be free from leprosy, from a discharge of blood, from a hernia, and that he be whole in all his limbs—not blind, not lame, not hunchbacked, nor with a deformed nose. And **Apuleius** <note>A 2nd-century Roman philosopher and author of *The Golden Ass*, who was famously accused of practicing magic.</note> says in his *Apologia* that a boy to be initiated into divination by a magical chant...

# BOOK THREE.

<margin>What kind of youth is to be initiated into the sacred rites. The goal of teaching.</margin>
...one must choose a person who is healthy, unharmed, talented, handsome, whole, skilled in mind, and eloquent in speech, so that the divine power may dwell within him as if in a goodly house. Thus, the soul of the youth, having been quickly tested, may be led back to its own divinity. Furthermore, this earned worthiness is perfected by two things: namely, **doctrine** <note>original: *doctrina*, referring to formal study and learning</note> and **work**. The goal of doctrine is to know the truth. It is necessary, therefore—as was said near the beginning of the first book—to be learned and experienced in those three faculties <note>Agrippa refers to Natural Philosophy, Mathematics, and Theology</note>. Then, once impediments have been removed, the soul itself must be moved inwardly toward contemplation and turned back into itself. For the apprehension and power of all things lie within us. However, we are prevented from enjoying these things by the passions that stand in our way from our birth <note>original: *ex generatione*, referring to the physical or "generated" world as opposed to the spiritual</note>, by false imaginations, and by immoderate desires. Once these are driven out, divine knowledge and power suddenly appear. Religious operation, moreover, is no less effective; indeed, it is often effective by itself in acquiring for us a **deifying virtue** <note>original: *deificam virtutem*, a power that makes one "god-like"</note>. For so great is the power of sacred works rightly performed and presented, that even if they are not fully understood—provided they are observed piously and with integrity, and believed with a firm faith—they are no less effective in adorning us with divine power. But that worthiness which is acquired through the art of religion is perfected by certain religious ceremonies, expiations, consecrations, and sacred rites, performed by one whose spirit has been consecrated by public religion. Such a person has the power of the laying on of hands and of initiating through a **sacramental virtue**, by which <margin>The divine character with which one is imprinted.</margin> the **character** <note>original: *character*, here used in the theological sense of a permanent spiritual "mark" or "seal" on the soul</note> of divine virtue and power is imprinted. This is called the "divine consensus," through which a human being, supported by a divine nature and made a sharer with the heavenly beings, carries within himself an indwelling power of the godhead. This rite is even counted among the ecclesiastical sacraments. If, therefore, you are now a person perfected by a sacred religious mind—one who thinks piously and most constantly regarding religion, and believes without hesitation—and if you are one to whom the authority of sacred things and nature have granted a dignity above others, whom the spirits do not despise: then you will be able, by praying, consecrating, sacrificing, and invoking, to attract spiritual and heavenly virtues. You may imprint these upon whatever things you wish and bring to life every work of magical science. But anyone who presumes to operate in magic without the authority of an office, without the merit of holiness and doctrine, and without the dignity of nature and education, will labor without fruit. He will deceive both himself and those who believe in him, and will incur the indignation of the spirits with great danger.

# OF OCCULT PHILOSOPHY

...veneration and the sanctification of worship is bestowed, and the ceremonies of divine worship are duly performed. Religion is, therefore, a certain discipline of external sacred rites and ceremonies, through which we are reminded of internal and spiritual things, as if by certain signs. This is so implanted in us by nature that we are distinguished from other living creatures more by this religious capacity than by our rationality.

<margin>Deceived by demons.</margin>
Whoever, therefore, neglects these rites and trusts only in the powers of natural things (as we said above), is very often accustomed to being deceived by evil demons. For this reason, those who are more religiously and holily educated do not plant a tree, nor plant a vineyard, nor undertake any work, however small, without divine invocation—just as the Teacher of the Gentiles <note>original: *doctor gentium*, referring to Saint Paul the Apostle</note> commands the Colossians, saying:

<margin>The Teacher of the Gentiles.</margin>
"Whatever you do, in word or deed, do all in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, giving thanks to him and to God the Father through him." To add the powers of religion to physical and mathematical virtues is so far from being a fault that not to join them is an impious crime. Hence, in the *Book of Elders*, Rabbi Henitia <note>Likely a reference to Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa or a similar figure from the Talmud; Agrippa often cites Hebraic sources to bolster the antiquity of his claims</note> says: "Whoever enjoys any of the created things while omitting a blessing is believed to have usurped it from God and the Church as if by theft and robbery." Of this, it is written by Solomon: "He who robs his father or his mother is the partner of a destroyer."

<margin>The Father is God, the Mother is the Church.</margin>
Now, the Father is God, and the Mother is the Church, just as it is written: "Is he not your Father who possessed you?" And elsewhere: "Hear, my son, your father’s instruction, and do not forsake your mother’s law." Nothing displeases God more than to be neglected or despised; nothing pleases him more than to be venerated and adored. Hence he permitted no creature of the world to be devoid of religion; all things venerate, all things pray (as Proclus <note>A 5th-century Neoplatonist philosopher who argued that all things in nature have a "sympathy" with the divine</note> says), and sing hymns to the leaders of their own order. Some do this in a natural way, others in a sensory way, others rationally, and others intellectually: and all, in their own way according to the *Song of the Three Young Men* <note>original: *Canticum trium puerorum*; a reference to the biblical "Benedicite" where all creation—frost, birds, and whales—is called to praise God</note>, bless the Lord. However, the rites and ceremonies of religion differ according to the variety of times and regions: and every religion has some good in it that is directed toward God the Creator himself.

<margin>Approval of the Christian religion.</margin>
And although God approves of only the one Christian religion, he does not utterly reject other forms of worship undertaken for his sake; and if he does not reward them with eternal prizes, he does not leave them unrewarded with temporal ones—or at least he punishes them less. But the impious and completely irreligious, he hates as enemies, striking them with lightning and exterminating them. For their impiety is greater than that of those who have followed a false and erroneous religion.

<margin>Lactantius on religion.</margin>
For no religion (as Lactantius <note>A counselor to Constantine and early Christian author</note> witnesses) is so erroneous that it does not contain some wisdom; for which reason those who have held to the highest duty of man—if not in reality, then at least in purpose—may find mercy. A human being cannot reach true religion by himself, unless he is taught by God.

<margin>What superstition is.</margin>
Therefore, every form of worship that is foreign to true religion is **superstition**; and every veneration that offers more in divine worship than true religion does is also superstition. Similarly, that which offers divine worship [to a creature], or to whom...

### BOOK THREE

...must not, or in a manner that is not proper. One must, therefore, take the greatest care lest, through some perverse practice of superstition, an injury be done to the highest and almighty God, and to the sacred divinities under Him. For this would be both wicked and most unworthy of philosophers. Superstition, therefore, although it is foreign to true religion, is not entirely or in every way rejected, since it is tolerated in many things and even observed by the prelates of religion. I speak particularly of that superstition which is a certain likeness of religion; for insofar as it imitates what is in religion—its miracles, sacraments, rites, observances, and other such things—it gains no small power from that imitation. It also derives no less force from the <term>credulity</term><note>Agrippa uses "credulity" (*credulitas*) to mean a firm, unquestioning belief or expectation of a result, which functions in the mind similarly to how religious faith functions in the soul.</note> of the practitioner. For how much a constant credulity can achieve was stated in the first book, and it is openly known among the common people. Superstition, therefore, requires credulity, just as religion requires faith. 

<margin>Religion seeks through faith.</margin>
Indeed, constant credulity is so powerful that it even works miracles in false opinions and operations. For anyone in their own religion, even if it be false, provided they most firmly believe it to be true, elevates their spirit by the very reason of that credulity until they are made similar to those spirits who are the leaders and princes of that religion. They may then perform those things which reason and nature do not discern. On the other hand, hesitation of belief and distrust weaken every work—not only in superstition, but also in true religion—and they sap the sought-after effect, even of the strongest experiments.

<margin>Superstition imitates religion.</margin>
The following examples show you how superstition imitates religion: namely, when worms and locusts are excommunicated <note>Agrippa refers to "ecclesiastical conjurations" where pests were legally and religiously summoned to court and excommunicated to protect crops—a common medieval practice.</note> so that they do not harm the crops; or when bells and images are baptized, and many more things of this kind. Because those ancient <term>magi</term><note>original: *magi*; here referring to the wise men and practitioners of high natural and celestial arts.</note>, who were the authors of this art among the ancients, were Chaldeans, Egyptians, Assyrians, Persians, and Arabs, whose religion was entirely perverse and tainted by idolatry, we must be extremely careful not to allow their errors to battle against the principles of our Catholic <note>original: *catholicae*; here meaning the universal or "true" Christian faith as understood by the author.</note> religion. To do so would be blasphemous and subject to a curse; and I would also be a blasphemer in this science if I did not warn you about them. 

Wherever, therefore, you find such things written by us, know that they are related to you from foreign authors. They are not delivered by me to you as absolute truth, but as a conjecture that is akin to truth, and as an instruction for imitation in those things which *are* true. It is necessary, therefore, that we gather truth from their errors. This is a task that requires deep intelligence, complete piety, and difficult, laborious diligence. It is the work of wisdom, which knows how to extract good from every evil and to adapt all crooked things into straightness, making use of those things which it governs. Regarding this, <term>Augustine</term><note>Saint Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), a foundational Christian theologian whom Agrippa frequently cites to justify the study of pagan knowledge.</note> gives the example of the carpenter, to whom crooked and complicated instruments are just as necessary and useful as straight ones.

### ¶ Chapter V. On the three leaders of religion, who lead us to the path of truth.

There are three leaders of religion who lead us all the way to the path of truth and who govern the whole of religion; in these three it entirely consists: namely, love, hope, and faith. For Love is the vehicle of the soul, the most excellent of all things; descending from the <term>intelligible realms</term><note>In Neoplatonic philosophy, these are the higher spiritual dimensions beyond the physical world.</note> down to the lower things, it gathers and turns our mind toward divine beauty. It also preserves us in every operation and grants results according to our wishes, supplying power to our supplications. Just as we read in Homer, Apollo heard the prayer of Chryses because he was very much his friend; and concerning Mary Magdalene, we read in the Gospels: "Many sins are forgiven her, because she loved much." Hope, truly, is suspended immovably upon those things which it desires; when it is indubitable and undisturbed, it nourishes and perfects the soul, fixing all things individually in the Good. Faith, however, is a virtue superior to all others, insofar as it does not rely on human reasoning but rests entirely upon divine revelation and shines through the whole universe. For since faith descends from the first light above and exists closer to it, it is far more noble and excellent than knowledge, or the "three types of belief" <note>original: "tres, & credulitates"</note> derived from lower things through the reflection received from the first light that reaches our intellect. Finally, through faith, a person is made one with the higher powers and enjoys the same authority. Hence <term>Proclus</term><note>A 5th-century Neoplatonist philosopher who greatly influenced medieval and Renaissance mystical thought.</note> says: "Just as the faith which is 'credulity' is below knowledge, so the faith which is 'true faith' is <term>supersubstantially</term><note>Existing in a way that exceeds the nature of physical substance or human understanding.</note> above all knowledge and intellect, joining us immediately to God."

<margin>
The root of miracles.
The effects of faith.
</margin>

For faith is the root of all miracles, through which alone—as the Platonists testify—we approach God and attain divine perfection and power. Thus we read that Daniel escaped the dangers of the lions because he believed in his God; and to the woman with the hemorrhage, **CHRIST** said: "Thy faith hath made thee whole." And from the blind men seeking light, he required faith, saying: "Do you believe that I am able to enlighten you?" Thus Pallas [Athena] in Homer consoles Achilles with these words:

> I have come to pacify your anger, if you will believe.

<margin>All things are easy for God.</margin>

Therefore, the poet <term>Linus</term><note>A legendary figure in Greek myth, often regarded as the inventor of melody and rhythm.</note> sings that all things are to be believed, because all things are easy for God; nothing is impossible for Him, and therefore nothing is unbelievable. Thus, by believing in those things which pertain to religion, we obtain their power. But where we fail in faith, we shall perform nothing worthy of admiration, but only of punishment. We read an example of this in Luke [in the Acts of the Apostles], in these words: "Then certain of the surrounding Jewish exorcists attempted to invoke the name of **JESUS** over those who had evil spirits, saying: 'I adjure you by **JESUS** whom Paul preaches.' And the wicked spirit answering said to them: '**JESUS** I know, and Paul I know; but who are you?' And the man in whom [the evil spirit resided] leaped upon them..." <note>This refers to the story of the Sons of Sceva from Acts 19, illustrating that using sacred names without true faith or authority results in disaster.</note>

<summary>Agrippa defines Love, Hope, and Faith as the three essential pillars of religious magic, arguing that true Faith transcends human intellect to grant the practitioner divine-like power. He uses both Biblical and Classical examples to show that spiritual operations succeed or fail based on the practitioner's internal state of belief.</summary>

### ¶ How the human soul, by these leaders, ascends into the divine nature and becomes a worker of miracles. Chapter VI.

<margin>Gifts of the human mind</margin>
<margin>The knowledge of a pure soul.</margin>
<margin>The power of the theological man.</margin>
<margin>The power of religion.</margin>
<margin>The force of the intellectual man.</margin>
Therefore, our mind—pure and divine, burning with the love of religion, adorned with hope, and directed by faith—when placed at the peak and summit of the human soul, draws truth to itself. It contemplates all states, reasons, causes, and sciences of both mortal and immortal things in divine truth itself, as if in a mirror of eternity, comprehending them suddenly. From this it comes to pass that we, though positioned within nature, know those things which are above nature, and understand all lower things; and not only do we understand things that are and things that were, but we also continually receive oracles regarding things that will soon happen or those that will occur in the distant future. 

Furthermore, a mind of this kind does not only claim such divine virtue for itself in the sciences, arts, and oracles, but it also takes up a miraculous power in transforming any matter by command. From this it comes to pass that we, being positioned within nature, sometimes rule over nature: we perform operations so wonderful, so sudden, and so difficult that the <term>manes</term><note>In Roman religion, the *manes* were the spirits of the dead; here, Agrippa uses the term to mean spirits or souls of the departed that can be commanded.</note> obey, the stars are disturbed, the deities <note>original: "numina"</note> are compelled, and the elements serve. Thus, men devoted to God and elevated by these theological virtues command the elements, drive away clouds, summon winds, force clouds into rain, cure diseases, and raise the dead. The poets sing of all these things being done among various nations, and historians recount them; the most brilliant philosophers, along with theologians, confirm that these very things can happen. Thus the prophets, thus the apostles, and other men of God were renowned for their great powers. 

It should be known, therefore, that just as by the influence of the First Mover <note>A term for God as the primary source of all motion and existence in the universe.</note>, something is often produced without the cooperation of intermediate causes, so also by the work of religion alone, something happens without the application of natural or celestial virtues. But no one can operate through pure and sole religion except he who has become entirely <term>intellectual</term><note>In Renaissance philosophy, the "intellectual" man is one who has transcended mere rational thought to reach a state of direct spiritual intuition or union with the Divine Mind.</note>. However, whoever operates through religion alone without the mixing of other virtues, if he perseveres long in the work, is absorbed by the divinity <note>original: "numine"</note> and cannot live long. But whoever approaches unpurified brings judgment upon himself and is delivered to an evil spirit to be devoured.

### ¶ That the knowledge of the true God is necessary for the Magician, and what the ancient Magicians and philosophers thought about God. Chapter VII.

<margin>The origin of the operations of things.</margin>
Since the being and operation of all things depend upon the highest God, the creator of all, and then also upon the other deities to whom the power of building and creating was also given—not indeed as the primary source, but by way of an instrument through the power of the first creator (for the first cause is the beginning of all things)...

<summary>Agrippa explains how a soul purified by Faith, Hope, and Love can achieve a divine state, allowing the practitioner to command nature and perform miracles like the prophets of old. He warns that this "pure religion" is dangerous for the unpurified and physically taxing for the practitioner.</summary>

### Chapter VIII. What the ancient philosophers thought about the divine trinity.

<margin>a</margin>
Augustine and Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who often critiqued Christianity but shared common ground on the nature of the "One"</note> testify that the Platonists posited three persons in God. The first they call the Father of the universe; the second they call the Son and the "First Mind" <note>original: "primam mentem"; referring to the Logos or Divine Intellect</note>, which Macrobius also refers to in this way; and the third they call the Spirit, or the "Soul of the World." 
<margin>Virgil on the Holy Spirit</margin>
Even Virgil, following the opinion of Plato, calls this the Spirit when he sings:
> A spirit within nourishes, and a mind, infused through the limbs,
> moves the whole mass,

<margin>The Son of God.</margin>
Plotinus and Philo <note>Philo of Alexandria, a Jewish philosopher who harmonized the Torah with Greek philosophy</note> teach that the Son of God is the "First Mind"—that is, the divine intellect—flowing from God the Father just as a word flows from a speaker, or as light flows from light. From this, he received the names "Word," "Speech," and "Splendor" of God the Father. For the divine mind, when it understands the Supreme Good through a single, never-interrupted act—without any mediation or change—generates a child and son within itself. This son is full intelligence, a complete image of the father, and the perfect blueprint <note>original: "exemplar"; the ideal model upon which the physical world is built</note> for the world. Our John <note>The Apostle John, referencing the beginning of his Gospel</note> and Hermes <note>original: "Mercurius"; referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary sage of the Hermetic tradition</note> call this the "Word" or "Speech"; Plato calls it the Son of God the Father; while Orpheus calls it Pallas <note>Athena</note> born from the head of Jupiter—which is to say, Wisdom.

<margin>Image of the highest father.</margin>
This is the highest image of God the parent, yet distinguished from the Begetter by a certain relation, or an internal absolute, as one begotten. This is the figure who says in the Book of Ecclesiasticus: "I came out of the mouth of the most high, the first-born before every creature." Iamblichus <note>A Syrian Neoplatonist philosopher</note> testifies that this Son is one and the same God in essence with the Father, calling God both his own father and his own son. Hermes Trismegistus also affirms the Son of God in various places in the *Asclepius*. For he says: "God, my father, brought forth for himself another craftsman-mind <note>original: "mentem aliam opificem"; often referred to as the Demiurge in Greek philosophy</note>." And elsewhere: "The Monad <note>The ultimate Unity or the One</note> begets a monad, and reflects its own heat back into itself." And in the *Pimander* <note>The *Poimandres*, a fundamental text of the Hermetic corpus</note> (where he seems to prophesy the future law of grace and the mystery of rebirth), he says: "The author of regeneration is the Son of God, a man, by the will of the one God." He also calls God most full with the fertility of both sexes. Similarly, the Indian philosophers claim the world is a living being that is part male and part female. Orpheus likewise calls the nature of the world and the "worldly Jupiter" both male and female at the same time, asserting that both sexes exist within the gods. Hence, in his Hymns, he addresses Minerva <note>Athena</note> thus: "Indeed, you were brought forth as both man and woman." And Apuleius...

<margin>Apuleius on Jupiter.</margin>

> Jupiter is both male and female, knowing no death,

### Chapter IX. What constitutes the true, most holy, and orthodox faith concerning God the Trinity.

<margin>Christian truth.</margin>
The Catholic doctors and the faithful people have decreed that it must be so believed and professed: that there is one sole true God, uncreated, immeasurable, omnipotent, eternal; Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—three persons indeed, co-eternal and co-equal with one another, yet one essence and substance, and an entirely simple nature. This is the Catholic faith, this is the orthodox religion, this is the Christian truth: that we worship one God in Trinity, and Trinity in Unity; neither confusing the persons nor dividing the substance. The Father from eternity begot the Son and gave Him His own substance, yet nevertheless retained it. The Son also, by being born, received the Father's substance; yet He did not take away the Father's own person, nor did the Father 
<margin>The birth of Christ.</margin>
transfer His person into the Son; for both are of one and the same substance, but of different persons. Also, although this Son is co-eternal with the Father, begotten from the substance of the Father before the ages, He was nevertheless born in time from the substance of the Virgin, and His name was called Jesus: perfect God, perfect man, consisting of a rational soul and human flesh; to whom nothing human was lacking, except for sin.
<margin>The faith of a Christian.</margin>
It is necessary, therefore, that we believe that our Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, is God and man: one person, two natures. God begotten before the ages without a mother, man born in time without a father, from 
<margin>The virginity of Mary.</margin>
the Virgin, who remained uncorrupted both before and after the birth. Having suffered on the cross He died, but on the cross He restored life and by death He unloosed death. He was buried and descended into the lower regions, but He led the souls of the fathers out from the lower regions; and He rose again by His own power on the third day, ascended into the heavens, and 
<margin>The Spirit, the Comforter.</margin>
sent His Spirit, the Paraclete <note>original: "paracletum." From the Greek 'parakletos', meaning 'advocate' or 'helper,' a title for the Holy Spirit.</note>, and He is to come to judge the living and the dead. At His coming all men shall rise again in their own flesh and shall give an account of their own deeds. This is the true faith, 
<margin>The Catholic faith.</margin>
which if anyone does not believe, or if anyone doubts, he is a stranger to the hope of life and eternal salvation.

We do not doubt that the things which the philosophers of the nations called "gods," and the Hebrew masters call "Numerations," we call "attributes." ->Almighty Jupiter, the very king of kings and god,<-

In this way, those most prudent theologians of the nations worshiped one God under various names and spirits, and even under various genders. As Pliny says,
<margin>Pliny’s opinion on God.</margin>

From this came that manifold variety of spirits, on account of the manifold and varied distribution of graces—yet God is one, from whom all things come. Whence Apuleius, in his book *On the World* to Faustinus, says: "Since there is one God, and the same divine power, He is indeed called by many names because of the multitude of His forms, by whose diversity He becomes multiform." And Marcus Varro says in his book *On the Worship of the Gods*: "Just as all souls are led back to the one Soul of the World or the Universe, so all gods are referred back to the one Jupiter, who is the same God worshiped under various spirits." Therefore, anyone who wishes to truly understand the hymns of Orpheus and the ancient Magi must know how to perfectly intellectualize sensible properties through the path of secret analogy. For in this way, he will find that these things differ very little from Kabbalistic secrets and orthodox traditions. For those whom Orpheus calls the "Curetes" and "untainted gods," Dionysius <note>Referring to Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian Neoplatonist.</note> calls "Powers"; the Kabbalists appropriate those to the numeration *Pahad* <note>The Hebrew term for "Fear" or "Dread," representing the Sephirah of Gevurah (Strength/Justice).</note>, which is to say "Divine Fear." Truly the *Mecubales* <note>A Latinization of the Hebrew "Mekubbalim," meaning "those who have received" or practitioners of Kabbalah.</note> of the Hebrews, who are most learned in divine matters, accepted ten principal divine names as if they were certain spirits, or limbs of God,
<margin>Sephiroth.</margin>
which flow through the ten numerations—which they call *Sephiroth*—as if through garments, or instruments, or archetypal patterns, into all things that have been created, through each higher thing down to the lowest in a certain order. For first and most closely, they flow into the nine orders of angels...

The first of these is the name **Eheie**, the name of the divine essence. Its Numeration <note>The Sephirot of the Kabbalah, which the author calls 'Numerations' or 'Numbers'.</note> is called **Cether** <note>original: "cether", Hebrew: *Keter*</note>, which is interpreted as "crown" or "diadem." It signifies the most simple essence of divinity, and designates that which "eye has not seen." It is attributed to God the Father and flows through the order of the **Seraphim**, or as the Hebrews call them, **Haioth Hacadosch** <note>original: "Haioth Hacadoſch", Hebrew: *Hayyoth Ha-Kodesh*</note>, that is, "holy living creatures." From there, through the first mover <note>The *Primum Mobile*, the outermost sphere of the universe in the medieval model.</note>, it bestows the gift of existence upon all things, filling the entire universe throughout its whole circumference and center. Its specific intelligence <note>The ruling spirit or angel of that divine level.</note> is named **Metatron**, that is, the "Prince of Faces," whose office it is to introduce others to the face of the Prince; and through him, the Lord spoke to Moses.

Wisdom.
