It is attributed to the **Holy Spirit** and flows through the order of the **Thrones**, or those the Hebrews call **Aralim** <note>original: "Aralim"</note>, that is, "great, strong, and robust angels." From there, it flows through the sphere of Saturn, ministering form to fluid matter. Its specific intelligence is **Zaphchiel**, the overseer of Noah; and another intelligence is **Iophiel**, the overseer of Shem <note>original: "Seni". This likely refers to Shem, the son of Noah, frequently associated with this intelligence in Kabbalistic texts.</note>. These are the three highest and supreme Numerations, acting as the seats of the divine persons, by whose command all things are made; but through the remaining seven, they execute these commands, which is why they are called the "Numerations of the Structure" <note>The lower seven Sephirot, which direct the manifest world.</note>.

ON OCCULT PHILOSOPHY.

### On divine names, and their power and virtue. Chapter 11.

Although God himself is most unified, he is nevertheless assigned various names. These do not represent different essences or deities, but rather certain properties flowing from him. Through these names, many benefits and diverse gifts trickle down to us and to all created things, as if through certain channels. We have described ten of these names above, which **Jerome** <note>St. Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), known for his letter to Marcella identifying ten names of God in the Hebrew Bible.</note> also enumerates in his letter to Marcella. **Dionysius** <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian mystic who listed many divine attributes in his work "On Divine Names."</note> 
<margin>How many names of God.</margin>
collects forty-five names, both of God the Father and of **Christ**. The Hebrew Kabbalists <note>original: "mecubales"</note>, using a certain text found in the Book of Exodus, derive seventy-two names of both angels and of God; they call this name of seventy-two letters the **Schemhamphoras** <note>original: "Schemhamphoras," a term for the "Explicit Name" of God derived from Exodus 14:19-21.</note>, which means "the expository." Others, going even further, find so many divine names in individual passages of scripture that their total number and what they signify are almost entirely unknown to us. From these, therefore, besides those we mentioned above, is the name of the divine essence: **I Am** <note>original: "Eheie" אהיה</note>, which **Plato**
<margin>Explanation of God's names.</margin>
translated as **Being** <note>original Greek: ὂν</note>. For this reason, some call God **The Being** <note>original Greek: τὸ ὂν</note> and others **The Eternal** <note>original Greek: ἐών</note>. There is another name, **He** <note>original: "Hu" הוא</note>, revealed to Isaiah, which points to the abyss of divinity; the Greeks translated this as **The Same** <note>original Greek: ταυτόν</note> and the Latins as **The Very Self** <note>original: "idempisum"</note>. There is also another name, **Fire** <note>original: "Esch" אש</note>, received from Moses, which sounds like fire; and there is the name of God **Please** <note>original: "Na" נא</note>, to be invoked in times of distress and trouble. There is also the name **Yah** <note>original: "Iah" יה</note>, and the name **Most High** <note>original: "Elion" עליון</note>, the name **Place** <note>original: "Macom" מקום</note>, the name **Caphu** <note>original: "Caphu" כפו</note>, the name **Iunon** <note>original: "Iunon" יונן</note>, and the name **Truth** <note>original: "Emeth" אמת</note>, which is interpreted as truth and is the seal of God. There are two other names, **Rock** <note>original: "Zur" צור</note> and **Stone** <note>original: "Aben" אבן</note>, both of which signify a solid rock, and one of them expresses the Father together with the Son. Many other names we have placed above in the scales of numbers. Many names of God and angels are also extracted from the holy scriptures through the arts of **Kabbalah**, **Calculation**, **Notaricon**, and **Gematria** <note>These are traditional Jewish methods of biblical interpretation: Gematria uses numerical values of letters; Notaricon uses the first or last letters of words to form new words; and Temurah involves letter substitution.</note>. In these arts, a single name or many sayings are gathered by pulling certain letters from them, or a single name, when dispersed into its individual letters, signifies or restores many things. Sometimes names are gathered from the heads of words, such as this name **Agla** <note>original: "Agla" אגלא</note> from this verse of Holy Scripture: **Thou art mighty forever, O Lord** <note>original: "Atah Gibor Leolam Adonai" אתה גיבר לעולם אדני</note>. Similarly, the name **Yaia** <note>original: "Iaia" יאיא</note> comes from that verse: **The Lord our God, the Lord is one** <note>original: "Yhwh Eloheinu Yhwh Echad" יהוה אלהינו יהוה אחד</note>. Similarly, the name **Iaua** <note>original: "Iaua" יאוה</note> from that verse: **Let there be light, and there was light** <note>original: "Yehi Or Vayehi Or" יהי אור ויהי אור</note>. Similarly, the name **Ararita** <note>original: "Ararita" אראריתא</note> from this verse: **One principle of his unity, the principle of his uniqueness, his transformation is one** <note>original: "Achad Rosh Achaduti Rosh Ichiduti Temurato Achad" אחד ראש אחדותי תמורתו אחד ראש</note>. There is also another name, **Hacaba** <note>original: "Hacaba" הקבה</note>, extracted from this verse: **The Holy One, Blessed be He** <note>original: "Ha-Kadosh Baruch Hu" הקדוש ברוך הוא</note>. Similarly, the name **Iesu** <note>original: "Iesu" ישו</note> is found in the heads of these two verses, namely: **Until the Messiah comes** <note>original: "Yibo Shilo" יבוא שילוהו לו</note>.

<meta>This page continues the technical explanation of how divine names are derived from the Hebrew scriptures. While the previous page introduced the general concept of God's many names (such as the ten Sephirot and the seventy-two names from Exodus), this page delves into the specific Kabbalistic methods of linguistic manipulation—acronyms, numerical values, and letter permutations—that reveal hidden aspects of the divine.</meta>

### THE THIRD BOOK OF OCCULT PHILOSOPHY

And in another place, *His name shall endure* <note>original: ינון שמו (Yinnon shemo), a reference to Psalm 72:17, traditionally interpreted as a name of the Messiah.</note>, which means his name remains. Similarly, this name **Amen** <note>original: אמן</note> is derived from this verse: *The Lord is a faithful King* <note>original: אדני מלך נאמן (Adonai Melech Ne’eman). The first letters of these three words—A, M, N—spell "Amen."</note>. Sometimes these names are extracted from the ends of words, such as the same name **Amen** from this verse: *not so the wicked* <note>original: לא כן הרשעים (Lo khen ha-reshaim), from Psalm 1:4. The final letters of these three words can be rearranged to form "Amen."</note>, but with the letters transposed. Likewise, in the final letters of this verse: *What is his name, and what is his son’s name?* <note>original: מה שמו ומה שם בנו (Mah shemo u-mah shem bno), from Proverbs 30:4.</note>, the **Tetragrammaton** <note>The "four-letter name" of God (YHWH), the most sacred name in Judaism.</note> is found. In all these instances, a single letter stands for a whole word, or a letter is extracted from a word—either from the beginning, the end, or from anywhere within.

And sometimes these names are extracted from all the letters individually, just as those seventy-two names of God are extracted from those three verses found in **Exodus** <note>Exodus 14:19-21. Each verse contains 72 letters. Kabbalists combine one letter from each to form 72 names of three letters each, known as the Schemhamphoras.</note>, beginning with these three words: *And he moved*, *And he came*, and *And he stretched out* <note>original: וַיִּסַּע וַיָּבֹא וַיֵּט (Vayis'a, Vayavo, Vayet).</note>. The first and last verses are written from right to left, but the middle one is written in reverse from left to right, as we shall show later. In this way, a word is sometimes extracted from another word, or a name from a name, through the transposition of letters—just as **Messiah** <note>original: משיח (Mashiach)</note> is derived from *He shall rejoice* <note>original: ישמח (Yismach)</note>, and **Michael** <note>original: מיכאל</note> from *My messenger* <note>original: מלאכי (Malachi)</note>. 

At other times, names are derived through alphabetical substitution, which the Kabbalists call **Ziruph** <note>original: צירף (Tziruf), meaning "permutation" or "joining." This involves swapping letters based on specific cipher patterns.</note>. For example, from the name **Tetragrammaton** <note>original: יהוה (YHWH)</note> are elicited the names **Mazpaz** <note>original: מצפץ (an Atbash cipher of YHWH)</note> and **Kuzu** <note>original: כוזו (a cipher where each letter is replaced by the one following it in the alphabet).</note>. Frequently, names are also exchanged through numerical equality—a method called **Gematria**—such as **Metatron** <note>original: מטטרון, a powerful archangel and "Prince of the Countenance."</note> for **Shaddai** <note>original: שדי (Shadai), meaning "The Almighty."</note>, for both equal three hundred and fourteen in their numerical value. By the same reasoning, the name **Iiai** <note>original: יאי</note> is equivalent to the name **El** <note>original: אל (God)</note> through numerical equality, for both equal thirty-one.

These are hidden secrets about which it is very difficult to offer a judgment or to pass on a complete science. Nor can they be understood or taught in any language other than **Hebrew**. Indeed, as **Plato** says in the *Cratylus*, divine names were possessed by "barbarians" <note>In the Greek context, "barbarians" referred to non-Greeks, specifically the ancient Hebrews or Egyptians who were thought to possess primordial wisdom.</note> who received them from God. Without these names, no one can in any way grasp the true words and the true names by which God is called. Therefore, we can say nothing else about them except what has been revealed to us from God through his kindness. 

For these names are the sacraments and vehicles of divine omnipotence. They were instituted not by men, nor even by angels, but by the most high God himself, according to a certain method, with an immovable number and shape of their characters and an eternal stability. They breathe the harmony of divinity and are consecrated by divine assistance. For this reason, those above fear them; those below tremble at them; the angels worship them; the demons are terrified by them; every creature reveres them, and every religion venerates them. 

The religious observance of these names, and their devoted invocation with fear and trembling, grants us great power and a god-like union, as well as the power to perform works and effects that are miraculous and beyond nature. Therefore, it is never right to change them for any reason. For this reason, **Origen** <note>An early Christian scholar (c. 184–253 AD) who argued that the power of names lies in their original sound and form, not their translated meaning.</note> commands that they be preserved incorrupt in their own characters. Even **Zoroaster** <note>The legendary ancient Persian prophet to whom many occult and "Chaldean" oracles were attributed.</note> forbids "barbarous" and ancient words to be changed. For as Plato says in the *Cratylus*: "All divine..."

### OF OCCULT PHILOSOPHY

...words or names were first handed down either by the gods, or by antiquity (whose beginning is not easily known), or by barbarians <note>In this context, "barbarian" refers to non-Greek and non-Latin languages, such as Egyptian, Chaldean, or Persian, which were believed to hold more ancient and primal power.</note>. Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 245–325 AD) who wrote extensively on theurgy and the power of divine names.</note> similarly teaches that these should not be translated from their own language into another; for he says that names do not preserve the same meaning <note>original: *mentem*, literally "mind" or "spirit"</note> when interpreted into another tongue.

<margin>How divine names are to be honored.</margin> Therefore, these divine names are the most fitting and effective medium for reconciling and uniting man with the gods, just as we read in **Exodus**: *In every place where there is a memory of my name, I will come to you and bless you* <note>A paraphrase of Exodus 20:24.</note>. In the book of **Numbers**, the Lord says: *Let them put my name upon the children of Israel, and I will bless them* <note>Numbers 6:27.</note>. For this reason, the divine Plato, in his works *Cratylus* and *Philebus*, commands that divine names be honored more than shrines and divine statues; for the image and power of God is more clearly expressed in the duty of the mind—especially when divinely inspired—than in the works of human hands.

Therefore, sacred words do not have their power in magic acts simply because they are words, but because of the occult power of the spirits <note>original: *numinum*</note> operating through them in the souls of those who cling to them through faith. Through these words, as if through vehicles, the hidden power of God is transmitted into those who have "ears to hear" <note>A reference to the frequent Gospel exhortation.</note> that have been purified through faith and through the purest of morals, and who, through the invocation of divine things, have become a 
<margin>The dwelling place of God.</margin> 
dwelling place of God and are capable of receiving these divine influences. Therefore, whoever rightly uses these divine words or names with that purity of mind, in that manner, and by that law by which they were handed down, will obtain and perform many marvelous things, just as we read regarding Medea in Ovid:

->And three times she spoke words that bring peaceful sleep,<-
->Which still the troubled sea and the raging rivers.<-
<note>Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, Book 7. Medea is the quintessential sorceress of Roman mythology.</note>

The ancient doctors of the Hebrews observed this more than others, for they were accustomed to performing many wonders with words. The Pythagoreans also demonstrated this, marvelously curing diseases of both the soul and the body with certain words. We also read that Orpheus <note>The legendary musician and prophet of Greek myth.</note>, while he was one of the Argonauts, averted a certain most savage 
<margin>A storm averted by words.</margin> 
storm with certain words. Philostratus <note>A Greek writer (c. 170–250 AD) who wrote the *Life of Apollonius of Tyana*.</note> relates in a similar way that Apollonius <note>Apollonius of Tyana, a Neopythagorean philosopher and miracle-worker.</note>, by speaking certain words in secret, resurrected a dead girl in Rome, and with certain other words summoned the ghost <note>original: *manes*</note> of Achilles. 

Furthermore, Pausanias <note>A Greek traveler and geographer of the 2nd century AD.</note> records that in the cities of Hierocaesarea and Hypepa, the Lydians had two temples sacred to a goddess they called "the Persian." In each of these, when a divine rite was to be performed, a great man <note>Likely a high priest or magus.</note> would place dry wood upon the altar and, singing hymns in his native language and then pronouncing certain barbarian words

from a book he held in his hand, those logs would soon be seen to burn of their own accord without any fire being applied, catching a most brilliant flame.

<margin>Abracadabra.</margin> 
is written—specifically by reducing it letter by letter in a backwards order, from the last to the first, as shown here—whoever is suffering from a

<term>semitertian fever</term> <note>original: *hemitriteo*, a fever recurring every other day, historically associated with malaria.</note> or any other fever, and wears this parchment tied and suspended from the neck, will find it avails against the ill health; the disease will pass away as it gradually declines.

But much more effective against all human illnesses and any other troubles is that which **Rabbi Hama** <note>Likely referring to the legendary author of early Kabbalistic works</note> handed down in the *Book of Speculation* <note>original: *Liber Speculationis*, referring to the Hebrew *Sefer ha-Iyyun*, a pivotal text in early mystical thought</note>: a prepared seal <note>original: *signaculum*, a physical talisman or amulet</note>, on the front side of which are four names of God, arranged in a square and interlaced so that from top to bottom four other most sacred names or divine seals emerge. # ON OCCULT PHILOSOPHY.
### THE LATTER PART. <note>original: *Pars Posterior*, referring to Book Three of the work, which focuses on Ceremonial Magic and Divine names.</note>

<image-desc>
A large circular sigil or talisman. In the center, the Hebrew word אראריתא (Ararita) is written. This is a "notarikon" or acronym for the Hebrew sentence *Achad Rosh Achdotho Rosh Ichudo Temurato Achad*, which translates to: "One is His beginning, one is His individuality, His permutation is one." Around the inner border are several Divine Names: Ehyeh (I Am), YHVH (The Tetragrammaton), Elohim (God), El (The Mighty One), and Shaddai (The Almighty).
</image-desc>

It is necessary that all these things be made in the purest gold, or on virgin parchment—as it is sincere, clean, and unspotted—even using ink formulated for this purpose from the smoke of a consecrated wax candle or incense and consecrated water. These must be made by a practitioner <note>original: *actore*, the person performing the rite</note> who is cleansed and expiated, with infallible hope and constant faith, and with the mind elevated toward the most high God, if they are to obtain and be able to manifest this divine power.

By a similar method, against the terrors and harms of evil demons and men, and against whatever dangers may be encountered—whether of journeys, or of waters, or of enemies, or of weapons—they inscribe these characters in the manner mentioned above on one side: **ויה** <note>Transliterated as *VIH*</note>; and these on the back: **צמרכד** <note>Transliterated as *Zamerkad*</note>. These are the beginnings and the ends of the first five verses of Genesis, and a symbol of the creation of the whole world. They say that by this binding <term>ligatura|A physical amulet or "binding" meant to tie a spiritual effect to a person</term>, a person will be immune from all evils, provided they hope most firmly in God, the founder of the universe.

The circle on the right (the front) contains the Hebrew letters ו י ה י ו (V-I-H-Y-V). These are the starting letters of the same verses.

<margin>The power of sacred words</margin>
Nor indeed should anyone distrust or wonder that sacred words—by which almighty God founded heaven and earth—have the greatest power when bound together. This has been proved by experience; as Rabbi Qusta ibn Luqa <note>original: *Rab Costa Ben Luca*, a 9th-century Melkite Christian physician and scholar</note> says, many non-physical things possess the greatest possible power. Experience proves this: for example, a finger from a premature birth <note>original: *digitū abortiui*</note> suspended from a woman’s neck hinders conception for as long as it hangs there. Furthermore, that there is a great and divine power in certain sacred words and divine names—which is an operative virtue producing wonderful effects—is testified to by Zoroaster, Orpheus, Iamblichus, Synesius, and Al-Kindi <note>original: *Alchindus*</note>, as well as the most illustrious of the philosophers. Even Artephius the magician and philosopher wrote a particular book on the virtues of words and characters. Origen, who is not inferior to any of the most brilliant philosophers, asserts in his work *Against Celsus* that a wondrous virtue lies hidden in certain divine words. And in the Book of 
<margin>The true name of God is known to God alone.</margin>
Judges, the Lord says: "My name is *Pele*" פלה <note>original: *Pele*, meaning 'Wonderful' or 'Miraculous' in Hebrew</note>, which is interpreted among us as "the worker of miracles" or "the one who effects wonders." However, the true name of God is known neither to men nor to angels, but to God alone; nor will it be made public (as the sacred scriptures testify) until the divine plan has been fulfilled. 
<margin>The origin of God’s names. What the Tetragrammaton is.</margin>
Nevertheless, God has other names among the angels and others among men. Yet, there is no name of God among us (as Moses the Egyptian <note>original: *Moses Ægyptius*, referring to the philosopher Maimonides</note> says) that is not taken from His works, and which we use to signify Him through our participation in those works—except for the name <term>Tetragrammaton</term> <note>The four-letter Hebrew name of God, YHWH, often considered unpronounceable or too sacred to speak.</note> itself. This is the holy name, signifying the substance of the Creator in a pure sense, in which nothing else participates with God the Creator. Therefore, it is called the "separated name," which is written but not read, nor 
<margin>The name of God which is written and not expressed.</margin>
is it expressed among us; rather, it is named and signifies according to the celestial idiom which belongs to God, and perhaps also to the angels. In a similar way, there are names for the angels—some among themselves in their own idiom, which Paul calls the "tongue of angels," of which we have very little knowledge. All their other names are derived from their offices and 
<margin>The origin of the names of angels.</margin>
works. These are not of such great efficacy, and therefore they are more effectively summoned by their true names—those heavenly names contained in the holy scriptures.

## On the influence of divine names through individual intermediaries into these lower things. Chapter XII.

<margin>Favorable angels.</margin>
Although the supreme Creator and First Cause rules and disposes of all things, He nevertheless distributes the care of executing His will to various ministers, both beneficial and malignant. In the *Apocalypse* <note>The Book of Revelation</note>, John calls these 
<margin>Harmful angels.</margin>
favorable and harmful angels. Elsewhere, the Prophet sings of them: "The angel of the Lord camps around those who fear Him, to deliver them," and in another place, he describes "visitations by evil angels." Whatever God executes through angels as His ministers, He also does through the heavens and the stars as His instruments, so that in this way all things cooperate.

...be brought into ministry so that just as any portion of the sky and every star determines a certain region or place of the earth, as well as time, species, and individual, so also it is right to adapt the angelic virtue of that portion and star to those same places, times, and species. Hence Augustine says in the *Book of Questions*: "Every visible thing in this world has an angelic power placed over it."

<margin>The office of the Angels.</margin>
Hence Origen <note>Origen (c. 184–253 AD) was an early Christian scholar who sought to harmonize Greek philosophy with scripture.</note> in his commentary on the *Book of Numbers* says: "The world itself has need of angels who preside over earthly armies, kingdoms, provinces, humans, beasts, the birth and growth of animals, shrubs, plants, and other things, bestowing that virtue which they say is in things by an occult property." <term>occult property: a hidden quality within a natural object—like the magnetic pull of a lodestone—that was believed to be a gift from the stars or divine spirits rather than physical elements.</term> Much more is there a need for angels who preside over holy works, virtues, and humans, so that they who always see the face of the highest Father might, by right guidance, be able to lead humans—and every single thing, even the smallest—to its place, as harmonious members of this world. In this world God dwells as the principal high priest, disposing all things most sweetly; he is not contained or circumscribed by the world, but contains all things within himself.

<margin>The heavenly city.</margin>
Just as John in the Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation.</note> describes that heavenly city, over whose twelve gates twelve angels preside, flowing into them, which they receive from the divine name revolved twelve times <note>original: *divino nomine... duodecies reuoluto*. This refers to the twelve permutations of the four-letter name of God (YHWH) used in Kabbalistic meditation.</note>; and in the foundations of that city are the names of the twelve apostles and the Lamb. For just as in the Law—on the stones of the breastplate <note>original: *superhumeralis*, referring to the High Priest’s ephod.</note> and the foundations of the holy city described by Ezekiel—were inscribed the names of the tribes of Israel, and the four-letter name ruled over them; so in the Gospel, the names of the apostles are inscribed on the foundation stones of the heavenly city. They stand for the tribes of Israel in the Church, and upon them flows the name of the Lamb.

<margin>The four-letter name.</margin>
This is the name JESUS, in which resides all the virtue of the four-letter name <note>original: *nomen quadriliterum*, referring to the Tetragrammaton (YHWH).</note>. Indeed, that four-lettered Father gave all things to Him. From the angels, therefore,

<margin>The number twelve.</margin>
the heavens receive that which they pour down. But the angels themselves receive it from the great name of God and JESUS, whose virtue is first in God, and then diffused into those groups of twelve and seven angels, through whom it is extended into the twelve signs of the zodiac and the seven planets, and consequently into all other ministers and instruments of God, penetrating even to the lowest things.

<margin>John 14.</margin>
Hence CHRIST says: "Whatever you ask the Father in my name, he will give you." And rising again he says:

<margin>Mark 16.</margin>
"In my name they shall cast out demons," and so forth; so that the four-letter name is no longer necessary, for its entire virtue has been transferred into the name JESUS, in which alone wonders are performed.

<margin>Acts 4.</margin>
"Nor is there any other name" (as Peter says) "under heaven given to men in which we must be saved," except that one. We should not think, however, that by naming JESUS with a polluted mouth, as if it were the name of some mere man, we can perform miracles in its virtue. Rather, it is necessary to invoke it in the Holy Spirit, with a purified mind and a fervent soul, so that we may obtain those things which were promised to us in Him—especially with prior knowledge, without which there is no hearing...

<margin>The power of the name of Jesus.</margin>
> I will hear him, because he has known my name. <note>original: "Exaudiam eum, quoniã cognouit nomen meum" (Psalm 91:14 in modern bibles, 90 in the Vulgate).</note>
From this, today no favor can be drawn from the heavenly beings unless there intervenes the authority, favor, and essence of the name **JESUS**. Hence the Hebrews and <term>Cabalists: practitioners of Jewish mysticism (Kabbalah) who believe the Hebrew alphabet and divine names hold the keys to the structure of the universe.</term>, though most skilled in divine names, can work nothing in those ancient names since the coming of **CHRIST**, as their fathers did of old. And it has now been proven by experience that no evil demon, no power of the underworld among those that vex or haunt humans, can resist this name; rather, whether they wish it or not, they must bend the knee and <margin>Power of the Cross</margin> obey when the name of **JESUS** is presented to them to be venerated with the proper pronunciation. Nor do they fear only the name, but also its seal, the cross. Not only do the knees of those on earth, in heaven, and in the underworld bend, but even inanimate things revere it, and all things tremble at its command when, from a faithful heart and a truthful mouth, the name of **JESUS** is spoken, and innocent hands trace the life-giving sign of the cross. Nor indeed did **CHRIST** say to his disciples in vain:
<margin>Mark 16.</margin>
> In my name they shall cast out demons, 
and so forth; unless a certain power were expressed in that name over demons, the sick, serpents, poisons, tongues, and the like. <margin>Where the power of the name of Jesus comes from.</margin> This power is in that name both from the power of God who established it, and from the power of Him who is expressed by this name, and from the force inherent in the word itself. Hence it is that, while every creature fears and reveres the name of Him who made it, sometimes even evil and impure men—provided they believe in such invocation of the divine—constrain demons and perform other great works.

### ¶ On the members of God, and their influence upon our own members. Chapter 13.

<margin>What the members of God are.</margin>
We read in various places of Holy Scripture of various members and ornaments of God. However, by the "members of God" are understood certain manifold and most simple powers remaining within God himself, distinguished among themselves by the sacred names of God. The garments and <margin>What the garments of God are.</margin> ornaments of God are like certain paths or relationships, or emanations—even physical ones—through which He pours Himself out. Whenever our mind touches the fringes of these garments, a divine power goes forth from some member, just as **Jesus** cried out regarding the <term>woman with the hemorrhage: referring to the biblical story of the woman who was healed simply by touching the hem of Jesus's cloak (Luke 8:43–48).</term>:
<margin>Luke 8.</margin>
> Someone touched me; for I perceived power go out from me. 
Therefore, there are in God these members similar to our own, but they are the *ideas* and archetypes of our members. If we rightly conform our members to these, then being transformed into that same image, we are made true children of God and like God, performing and operating the works of God. Much has been drawn from the scriptures regarding the members of God. For concerning His head, <margin>Song of Songs 7.</margin> it is read in the *Song of Songs*:
> Your head is like Carmel, and the hair of your head like royal purple. 
<margin>What Carmel is.</margin> Here "Carmel" signifies not that mountain on the coast of Syria, but the little worm that produces purple dye. <note>original: "vermiculum qui purpurã gignit." Agrippa is likely referring to the *kermes* insect, from which a deep red/purple dye was extracted; the Hebrew word 'Karmel' was sometimes associated with 'Karmiyl' (crimson).</note> Concerning the eyes, eyelids, and ears, it is read in the Psalms:
<margin>The eyes of the Lord.</margin>
The eyes of the Lord are upon the ju... <note>The text cuts off mid-sentence; it refers to Psalm 34:15: "The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous."</note>

<meta>This page continues Agrippa’s transition from the power of the holy name of Jesus to a mystical exploration of "Divine Anatomy." ### OF OCCULT PHILOSOPHY.

<margin>The ears of the Lord.</margin>
...the righteous, and his ears are open to their prayers. <note>original: "aures eius in præces eorum" (Psalm 34:15).</note> His eyes look upon the poor, and his eyelids examine the sons of men.

<margin>The mouth of the Lord.</margin>
Concerning the mouth also, and the taste, the throat, the lips, and the teeth, we read in the book of <term>Isaiah: a major Hebrew prophet; Agrippa uses the Latin form Esaias</term>: *You have not questioned my mouth.*

<margin>The throat of the Lord.</margin>
And in the <term>Song of Songs: a book of the Bible also known as Canticles, often interpreted by mystics as an allegory of the soul's relationship with God</term>: *Your throat is like the best wine. The wine is worthy for my beloved to drink, and food for his lips and teeth to chew.*

<margin>The nostrils of the Lord.</margin>
There are also nostrils, with which (as is frequently repeated in the Law) he smells the sacrifices as a "sweet-smelling savor." <note>original: "odorat sacrificia in odore suauitatis."</note>

<margin>The shoulders of the Lord.</margin>
There are shoulders, arms, hands, and fingers, of which we read in Isaiah: *The government is placed upon his shoulders.* To whom is the arm of the Lord revealed? And the <term>royal prophet: a common title for King David, traditionally considered the author of the Psalms</term> sings: *Your hands, O Lord, have made me and fashioned me.* And: *I will see your heavens, the work of your fingers.*

<margin>The right and left hand, heart, breast, back, hind parts, face, and other parts of the Lord.</margin>
He also has a right and a left hand; hence the Psalmist says: *The Lord said to my Lord, sit at my right hand.* We read of the left hand in the Gospels, on which side those who are to be damned shall be placed on the last day. Furthermore, we read of the heart, the breast, the back, the hind parts, and the face—as in the Book of Kings, that God found David to be a man after his own heart. We also have in the Gospel that breast upon which the sleeping disciple <note>The "beloved disciple" John, who leaned on Jesus' chest during the Last Supper.</note> conceived divine secrets; and the Psalmist describes his back in the paleness of gold. And he himself says through <term>Jeremiah: the prophet Hieremias</term>, *I will show them my back and not my face in the day of their destruction.* And he said to <term>Moses: the foundational lawgiver of Israel</term>: *You shall see my back parts.*

<margin>The feet of the Lord.</margin>
Of the feet, the Psalmist also says: *Darkness is under his feet.* And in Genesis, he is read to be walking at midday.

<margin>The garments of the Lord.</margin>
By a similar reasoning, we read of the many garments and ornaments of God, as in the Psalmist: *The Lord has reigned, he is clothed with beauty, wrapped in light as if with a garment.* And elsewhere: *You have put on praise and beauty. The deep is like his garment and covering.* And in Ezekiel, God speaks, saying: *I spread my covering over you and covered your shame.*

<margin>The rod of the Lord.</margin>
Now indeed, there is even a rod, a staff, a sword, and a shield, as in the Psalmist: *Your rod and your staff, they have comforted me.*

<margin>The shield of the Lord, the sword of the Lord.</margin>
*His truth shall surround you with a shield.* And in Deuteronomy, we read of the *sword of his glory*; and many more such things are declared to us by the sacred utterances. By these divine members and ornaments, there is no doubt that our own limbs—and those things which surround us, and all our works—are ruled, directed, guarded, governed, and judged. As the prophet says: *He set my feet upon a rock, and directed my steps.* And elsewhere: *Blessed be the Lord my God, who teaches my hands for battle, and my fingers for war.* And of the mouth, he says: *He put a new song into my mouth.* And elsewhere the Savior says: *I will give you a mouth and wisdom.* And of the hair, he says: *A hair of your head shall not perish.* And elsewhere: *The hairs of your head are all numbered.*

<margin>The likeness of God with man.</margin>
For Almighty God himself, since he willed us to be his images and like unto himself, constructed the members, joints, and figures within us—revealed in many ways—as signs according to the likeness of his own hidden virtues. <note>Agrippa is arguing for the "Microcosm" theory: that the human body is a small-scale map of the divine universe.</note>

Whence the <term>Hebrew Kabbalists: Agrippa uses "Mecubales," a Latinization of the Hebrew "Mequbbalim," meaning those who have received the tradition</term> say that if a person capable of receiving divine influence keeps any member of their body clean and purified from filth, then that part becomes a dwelling place and a proper seat of the hidden limbs and virtues of God to which the same name is ascribed. ->¶Of the gods of the nations, and the souls of celestial bodies, and<-
->by what names, and which places were formerly sacred.<-
->Chapter XIIII.<-

<margin>p</margin>
<margin>Plato on the celestial soul.</margin>
Philosophers have posited, as we have shown above, that the heavens and the stars are divine living beings, and that their souls are intelligent, participating in the divine mind. They also posited that certain separate substances—which they call <term>intelligences: pure spirits or angels that govern the motion of the planets</term> and <term>demons: here used in the Greek sense of "daimons" or guiding spirits, not necessarily evil</term>—preside over these, while others serve beneath them as rulers and ministers. Furthermore, Plato himself asserted that the celestial souls are by no means confined to their bodies as our souls are to our bodies; rather, they are wherever they wish to be, and simultaneously enjoy the vision of God. Without any labor or anxiety, they rule and move their bodies, and by moving them, they govern lower things with their presence. For this reason, people used to call such souls "gods" and established divine honors for them, dedicating prayers and sacrifices and worshipping them with various forms of cult. And these are the gods to whom all the nations have been assigned, concerning whom Moses commanded in <term>Deuteronomy: the fifth book of the Bible</term>, saying: <margin>Moses on the worship of the gods.</margin> *Lest perhaps, lifting up your eyes to heaven, you see the sun and the moon and all the stars of heaven, and being deceived, you adore and worship them, to which all the nations under the whole heaven have been assigned; but the <term>Lord Tetragrammaton: the four-letter holy name of God, YHWH</term> has taken you and brought you out of the iron furnace of Egypt, that he might have a people of inheritance for himself.* <margin>A people of inheritance.</margin> And in the seventeenth chapter of the same volume, he calls the sun, moon, and stars "gods." Moreover, the teachers of the Hebrews, commenting on the passage in Genesis where Abraham bestowed gifts upon the sons of his concubines—namely <term>Shemoth steltonia: "foreign names," likely referring to names used in planetary magic or idolatry</term>—but left Isaac as the heir of all he possessed, say that the sons of the concubines were not assigned to the Tetragrammaton and the supreme Creator in Abraham's blessing, but to foreign gods and powers. Isaac and his seed, however, were assigned to the almighty God Tetragrammaton himself, and were in no part assigned to foreign powers. This is why they are rebuked in Deuteronomy: because they served foreign gods and worshipped those whom they did not know, and to whom they had not been assigned. Even <term>Joshua: referred to here by the Latin "Iesus Naue" (Jesus son of Nun)</term>, after leading the people into the promised land, overcoming their enemies, and distributing the portions of the possessions of Israel, gave the people the choice to pick which divinity they would worship, saying:

Therefore, put away the strange gods from your midst, and incline your hearts to the Lord God of Israel." And he erected a very large stone, saying: "This stone shall be a witness to you, lest perhaps afterward you wish to deny and lie to the Lord your God."

Who the gods of the nations were.
</margin>
There were, therefore, gods to whom the other nations were assigned: the sun and the moon, the twelve signs of the zodiac, and the other celestial bodies and divine works. This was not, however, according to their nature as physical bodies, but insofar as a soul inhabits them, and the whole "host of heaven," and what <term>Jeremiah: The biblical prophet</term> calls the "Queen of Heaven." This refers to the power by which the heaven is ruled—namely, the <term>Soul of the World: A philosophical concept (Anima Mundi) suggesting the universe is a living, breathing being with a governing spirit</term>—concerning which Jeremiah says: *The children gather wood, and the fathers kindle the fire, and the women knead the dough, to make small cakes for the Queen of Heaven.* <note>original: "Filii colligunt ligna, & patres succēdunt ignem, & mulieres conspergunt adipem, vt faciāt placentulas reginæ cœli." (Jeremiah 7:18)</note>

The worship of Dulia.
The worship of Latria.
</margin>

Those who applied the latter form of worship to these beings were rejected by the Lord. We have recounted the names of these souls or gods in the preceding chapters.

<margin>
The various tutelary gods of various nations.
</margin>

Thus, individual peoples worshipped their own gods with their own ceremonies: the Boeotians worshipped Amphiaraus; the Africans, Mopsus; the Egyptians, Osiris and Isis; the Ethiopians who inhabit Meroe, Jove and Bacchus; the Arabs, Venus along with Bacchus; the Scythians, Minerva; the people of Naucratis, Serapis; the Syrians, Atargatis; the Arabs, Diaphara; the Africans, Caelestus.

# BOOK THREE

The Carthaginians and the people of Leucas worshipped Saturn. Jupiter was honored in Crete, Pyreus, Homole, Ida, Elis, and Libya, where his oracle was located; he was also worshipped in Epirus, Latium, Gnidus, and Lycia. Pisa and Macedonia worshipped Mars, as did the Thermodonians <note>A people said to live near the Thermodon river, often associated with the Amazons</note>, the Scythians, and those in Thrace. The Scythians venerated the Sun as their only god, sacrificing horses to him; the same deity was worshipped by the Heliopolitans, the Assyrians, and—under the name of Apollo—by the Rhodians, the Hyperboreans <note>A mythical people of the far north</note>, and the Milesians. Mounts Parnassus, Phaselus, Cynthus, and Soracte were sacred to him, as were the islands of Delos, Claros, and Tenedos, a place called Mallois on Lesbos, and the grove or town of Gryneium. Furthermore, the cities of Patara, Chrysa, Tarapnas, Cyrrha, Delphi, Arrephnia, Entrosi, and Tegyra were dedicated to him. He was also honored under the names of Bacchus and Dionysus in Thebes and on the island of Naxos, the city of Nisa in Arabia, and the Callichoros river in Paphlagonia. Likewise, Mounts Parnassus and Cytheros in Boeotia were sacred to him, where the <term>Bacchanalia: Wild festivals held every two years in honor of Bacchus (Dionysus)</term> were celebrated every other year. The Thamaritae people, neighbors to the Hyrcanians, also worshipped Bacchus with their own specific rites. The Assyrians were the first of all to introduce the worship of Venus, followed by the Paphians in Cyprus, the Phoenicians, and the people of Cythera; according to Aegeus, the Athenians followed these. Among the Lacedaemonians <note>Spartans</note>, Armatha was worshipped, and at Delphi, Venus Epytibia <note>original: "Venus Epytibia," meaning "Venus upon the tombs"</note>. She was also worshipped by the people of Cos, on the island of Amathus in the Aegean Sea, in the city of Memphis in Egypt, and in Gnidus, Sicily, the grove of Idalium, the city of Hypepa, on Mount Eryx in Sicily, and in Calydonia, Cyrene, and Samos. Indeed, (as Aristotle testifies), it is read that no other divinity of the ancient gods was worshipped with greater ceremonies or in more numerous locations. The Gauls especially worshipped Mercury, calling him Teutates <note>original: "Teutatem," a Celtic god often equated by Roman writers with Mercury</note>; he was also worshipped by the Arcadians, the Hormopolitae, the Egyptians, and the people of Memphis. The Tauric region of Scythia <note>Modern-day Crimea</note> worshipped the Moon under the name of Diana, and she had a most celebrated temple in Ephesus. In Mycenae, after King Thoas of the Taurians was slain, her statue was stolen by Iphigenia and Orestes; the rite of her sacred ceremonies was changed, and she was worshipped near Aricia. She was also worshipped by the Magnesian people of Thessaly, in the city of Pisa in Achaia, in Tibur, on the Aventine Hill in Rome, in the town of Perga in Pamphylia, and in the region of Agras in Attica.

ON OCCULT PHILOSOPHY.

The city of Onchestus in Boeotia, the promontory of Taenarus in Laconia, the Traezenian people, and their city were all under the protection of Neptune. Therefore, such were the gods of the nations who presided over and ruled those whom Moses himself, in his book of Deuteronomy, calls "gods of the earth" <note>original: "deos terre"</note>. All peoples are assigned to these gods; by this, Moses meant nothing other than the celestial stars and their souls.

## Chapter 15. What our Theologians think about Celestial Souls.

That the heavens and celestial bodies are animated by certain divine souls is not only the opinion of poets and philosophers, but is also the assertion of Holy Scripture and Catholic thinkers. For Ecclesiastes describes the soul of heaven <note>Agrippa likely refers to Ecclesiastes 1:6, which discusses the "circuits" of the wind/spirit</note>, and Jerome explicitly admits this in his commentary on that same book. Similarly, Origen writes in his book *On First Principles* <note>original: "de principiis"</note> that he believes celestial bodies are entirely animated, since they are said to receive commands from God—something consistent only with a rational nature. For it is written: "I have given a command to all the stars" <note>Isaiah 45:12</note>. Furthermore, Job noted that stars are not entirely free from the stain of sin, for we read: "Even the stars are not clean in his sight" <note>Job 25:5</note>, a statement which certainly cannot refer to the physical brightness of their bodies.

Moreover, Eusebius Pamphilus <note>Eusebius of Caesarea, an early Christian historian</note> in his *Theological Solutions*, and Augustine in his *Enchiridion* <note>The "Handbook" on Faith, Hope, and Love</note>, also believe that celestial bodies are animated. Among more recent authors, Albert the Great in his book *On the Four Coevals* <note>original: "de quatuor coæqueuis"</note>, Thomas Aquinas in his books *On Spiritual Creatures*, and John Duns Scotus in his second book of *Sentences* agree, as does the very learned Cardinal Nicholas of Cusa. Indeed, Peter Aureolus <note>A 14th-century Franciscan philosopher</note> proves this with vigorous argument; he does not even think it foreign to worship celestial bodies with the honor of <term>Dulia: In Catholic theology, this is the veneration or service given to saints and angels, which is distinct from "Latria," the worship reserved for God alone</term>, and to implore their support and aid. Even Thomas Aquinas himself agreed with this, unless the risk of idolatry prevented such a rite. Furthermore, Plotinus <note>A 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher</note> asserts that they know our prayers and also hear them. But if anyone wishes to oppose these views entirely and consider them sacrilegious dogmas, let him listen to Augustine in the *Enchiridion* and in the *Retractions*, and Thomas in the second book of *Against the Gentiles*, and in his *Quodlibets*, and Scotus on the *Sentences*, and William of Paris <note>William of Auvergne, Bishop of Paris</note> in his *Summary on the Universe*, who all respond with one voice: whether celestial bodies are called animate or inanimate makes no difference to the Catholic faith. Therefore, although it may seem ridiculous to many that souls are placed within the spheres and stars, and that each—like the gods of the nations—
->presides over its own regions, and cities,<-
->tribes, and peoples, and nations, and<-
->languages, yet it will not appear strange<-
->to those who truly understand.<-

BOOK THREE

### Concerning intelligences and spirits, and their three kinds, their various names, and concerning infernal and subterranean spirits.
### Chapter 16.

<margin>What an Intelligence is.</margin>
Now, consequently, we must discuss <term>intelligences</term> (spiritual beings of pure intellect), spirits, and <term>daemons</term> (intermediate spirits, not necessarily evil). An intelligence is an "intelligible substance," free from any bulk of a thick and rotting body, immortal, insensible to physical touch, present to all things, and flowing into all things. This is the shared nature of all intelligences, spirits, and daemons.

<margin>Who the spirits are here and how many kinds there are.</margin>
When I speak of "daemons" here, I do not mean those whom we call <term>devils</term>, but rather spirits named according to the literal meaning of the word, as if they were "knowers," "thinkers," and "wise ones" <note>original: "scientes, intelligentes & sapientes"; Agrippa is referencing the Greek etymology of *daimon*, meaning "to know"</note>. According to the tradition of the <term>magi</term> (wise practitioners of ancient wisdom), there are three kinds of these. The first they call <term>super-celestial</term>, which are minds entirely separated from bodies—essentially "intellectual spheres." These spirits worship the one God as their firmest and most stable unity or center. For this reason, they are even called "gods" because of their participation in divinity; they are always full of God and "drunk with divine nectar." These beings are concerned only with the one God; they do not rule over the physical bodies of the world, nor are they suited for the service of lower things. Instead, they pass the light received from God down to the lower orders and distribute specific duties to each.

<margin>Worldly spirits.</margin>
Closely following these in the second order are the <term>celestial intelligences</term>, whom they call "worldly spirits" <note>original: "dæmones mundanos"</note>. Beyond their divine worship, these are assigned to the spheres of the world, presiding over each of the heavens and stars. Because of this, they are distributed into as many orders as there are heavens in the world and stars in the heavens. Some they called "Saturnine," presiding over the heaven of Saturn and Saturn itself; others "Jovial," presiding over the heaven of Jupiter and Jupiter itself. Similarly, they name various spirits after the names and powers of other stars. Because ancient astrologers asserted there were fifty-five movements in the heavens, they devised just as many intelligences or spirits for them. They also placed spirits in the starry heaven to preside over signs, <term>triplicities</term> (groups of three zodiac signs), <term>decans</term> (ten-degree divisions), <term>quinaries</term> (five-degree divisions), degrees, and individual stars. For although the entire school of philosophers—even the <term>Peripatetics</term> (followers of Aristotle)—assigns only one intelligence to each sphere of the stars, nevertheless, since every single star and part of the heaven has its own distinct power and influence, it is necessary that it also has its own presiding intelligence to provide and direct that power.

<margin>The number and duties of the spirits.</margin>
Thus, they established twelve princes of spirits to preside over the twelve signs of the zodiac, and thirty-six to preside over as many <term>decurions</term> (decans), and seventy-two to preside over as many "quinaries" of the heaven and over the languages and nations of men. They also set four to preside over the triplicities and elements, and seven governors of the entire world according to the seven planets; they established...

...all names and <term>characters</term> <note>original: "characteres"; these are magical signs or sigils representing spiritual forces</note>, and used them in their invocations, incantations, and engravings. They would describe these upon the instruments of their operations—images, plates, mirrors, rings, papers, wax objects, and the like—so that if they were working by the Sun, they would invoke by the names of the Sun and the names of the solar <term>daemons</term> <note>Agrippa uses "daemons" in the classical sense of intermediate spirits, not necessarily demons in the modern sense</note>, and likewise for the others.

Thirdly, they place daemons as ministers to arrange those things which are in the lower regions. <term>Origen</term> <note>A prominent early Christian scholar (c. 185–253 AD) who wrote extensively on the hierarchy of angels and spirits</note> calls these "certain invisible powers" to whom the management of things upon the earth is entrusted. For often, though visible to no one, they direct our journeys and all our business; often they are even present in battles and, through secret support, they grant the desired success to friends. Indeed, they are said to be able to reconcile prosperity or inflict adversity at their whim. 

<margin>Distinction of daemons.</margin>
They distribute these in a similar way into many orders: some are fiery, others watery, others airy, and others earthly. These four species of daemons are categorized according to the four powers of the celestial souls: the mind, the reason, the imagination, and the life-giving and moving nature. From this, the fiery daemons follow the "mind" of the celestial souls, whereby they join together for the contemplation of more sublime things. 

<margin>w</margin>
The airy ones, following the "reason," favor the rational power, separating it in a certain way from the sensory and vegetative; they thus serve the active life, just as the fiery ones serve the contemplative life. The watery ones, following the imagination and the senses, serve the life of pleasure. The earthly ones, following "nature" <note>referring to the base biological and growth-oriented force</note>, favor the vegetative nature. 

Furthermore, they also distinguish this kind of daemon into Saturnine and Jovial <note>Spirits associated with the planets Saturn and Jupiter</note>, according to the names of the stars and the heavens. Furthermore, some are Eastern, others Western, others Southern, and others Northern. Finally, no part of the world is left without the specific assistance of these daemons—not because they are only there, but because they rule there most strongly; for they are everywhere, although some work and exert influence more powerfully in one place than another. Nor indeed should these things be understood as if they were subject to the influences of the stars, but rather that they correspond to the "supramundane heaven" from which all things are chiefly directed, but to which all things must conform. Hence, just as they are adapted to various stars, so these daemons are adapted to various places and times—not because they are confined by time or place, any more than they are by the bodies over which they are set as overseers, but because the order of Wisdom has so decreed. Therefore, they favor and patronize those bodies, places, times, and stars more than others. 

Thus, they called some "diurnal" (of the day), others "nocturnal" (of the night), and others "meridional" (of the midday). In a similar way, they call some forest-spirits, others mountain-spirits, others field-spirits, and others domestic. Hence come the Silvans, Fauns, Satyrs, Pans, Nymphs, Naiads, Nereids, Dryads, Pierides, Hamadryads, Potamides, Hyades, Agapae, Pales, Pareads, Dodonaeans, Feniliae, Lavernae, the Fates, Muses, Aonides, Castalides, Heliconides, Pegasides, Maeonides, Pheoiades, Camoenae, the Graces, Genii, Lemures <note>This list comprises nearly every category of Roman and Greek minor deity and nature spirit</note>, and the like, whom they call the common folk of the gods; others call them demigods or goddesses. Some of these are so close and familiar to humans...

...and are familiar ones, such that they are even affected by human passions. Plato believes that through their instruction, men often perform marvelous feats, much like how through human instruction, some animals closer to us—such as monkeys, dogs, and elephants—often perform wonders beyond their own species. Those who have written the histories of the Danes and Norwegians testify that various kinds of <term>daemons</term> <note>original: "daemones"; Agrippa uses this in the classical sense of intermediate spirits, not necessarily "demons" in the modern evil sense</note> in those regions are subject to human service. Furthermore, the opinion of the Egyptians and the Platonists (especially confirmed by <term>Proclus</term> <note>A 5th-century Neoplatonist who sought to harmonize Greek philosophy with ancient mysteries</note>) is that some of these are corporeal and mortal, having bodies that are born and perish, though they are very long-lived. Plutarch, Demetrius the Philosopher, and Aemilianus the rhetorician affirm the same; for they testify, based on many wonders of their time, that the great daemon <term>Pan</term> <note>The Greek god of the wild; Agrippa is referencing the famous legend that "Great Pan is dead," signaling the end of the old pagan world</note> and many others first wailed aloud and then even died. 

Regarding these daemons of the third kind, according to the opinion of the Platonists, they say there are as many legions as there are stars in the heaven, and that in every legion there are as many daemons as the heaven itself contains stars. But regarding the number of good daemons (as <term>Athanasius</term> <note>A 4th-century church father and Bishop of Alexandria</note> reports), there are some who believe they make up ninety-nine parts compared to the number of men, according to the parable of the hundred sheep. Others think there are only nine parts, according to the parable of the ten pieces of silver. Others judge the number of angels to be equal to the number of men, because it is written: *He set the bounds of the people according to the number of the angels of God.* 

Many have written much concerning their number. But more recent theologians, following the <term>Master of the Sentences</term> <note>Peter Lombard (c. 1100–1160), whose book was the standard textbook for medieval theology</note>, Augustine, and Gregory, easily resolve this by saying that the number of good angels transcends all human grasp. Opposed to these are countless unclean spirits, as many existing in the lower world as there are pure spirits in the higher world, as some theologians claim to have received from oracles. Below these they place the subterranean or dark genus of daemons, whom the Platonists call 
<margin>Rebel angels.</margin>
**fallen angels** <note>original: "angeli desertores"; literally "deserter angels" or those who abandoned their posts</note>, the avengers of crimes and impiety according to the decree of divine justice. They call them evil daemons and wicked spirits because they often harm and hurt of their own accord. They count many legions of these as well, distinguishing them in a similar way according to the names of the stars and elements and parts of the world, and they assign to them kings, princes, and presidents, and their specific names. 

Of these, four most harmful kings preside over the others, according to the four quarters of the world. Under these, many other princes rule over legions, as do many over private duties. From here come the **Gorgons**, the **Stheno**, and other **Furies**. From here come <term>Tisiphone</term> <note>The text reads "Cresiphone," likely a printer's error for the Fury Tisiphone</note>, **Alecto**, **Megaera**, and **Cerberus**. There is no evil that they do not dare to commit. They have an entirely violent and unhealthy character; therefore, they frequently plot and engineer vehement and sudden ambushes, and while they make their incursions..."

## ¶ On the same spirits according to the opinions of the theologians. Chapter XVII.

<margin>*The threefold distinction of angels.*</margin>
Our theologians, following <term>Dionysius</term> <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a highly influential 5th-century Christian theologian who organized the celestial beings into a formal system</note>, likewise establish threefold distinctions of angels. Each of these is divided into three orders, so that there are three distinctions and nine orders in total. These they call "hierarchies," and the orders they call "choirs," which <term>Proclus</term> <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who influenced Christian thought on how the divine world is structured</note> also distinguishes by the number nine.

<margin>*Hierarchy.*</margin>
Thus, in the superior hierarchy, they place the Seraphim, Cherubim, and Thrones. These are as if they were <term>super-celestial spirits</term> <note>original: "super coelestes daemones"; Agrippa uses "daemon" in the classical sense of an intermediate spirit, not necessarily an evil entity</note> contemplating the order of divine providence: the first in the goodness of God, the second in the essence of God as form, and the third in His wisdom. In the middle hierarchy, they place the Dominions, Virtues, and Powers, which act as <term>worldly spirits</term> <note>original: "mundanos daemones"</note> collaborating in the governance of the world. Of these, the first command what the others carry out; the second administer the heavens and sometimes work together to produce miracles; and the third restrain those things that seem capable of disturbing the divine law. In the lower hierarchy, they place the Principalities, Archangels, and Angels—whom <term>Iamblichus</term> <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher known for his work on the relationship between humanity and the divine</note> also enumerates. These descend as ministering spirits to care for lower matters. The first of these look after public affairs, princes and magistrates, provinces and kingdoms—each assigned to a specific one.

Hence it is read in <term>Daniel</term> <note>Daniel 10:13</note>: 
> "But the prince of the kingdom of the Persians resisted me for twenty-one days," 
and <term>Jesus son of Sirach</term> <note>The author of the Book of Ecclesiasticus</note> testifies that a ruling angel is set over every nation, which <term>Moses</term> also seems to indicate in the song of Deuteronomy, saying: 
> "When the Most High divided the nations, He set their bounds according to the number of the angels of God." <note>original Latin: "Cum diuideret excelsus gentes, statuit eorum terminos secundum numerum angelorum dei"</note> 
The second [Archangels] are present at sacred rites; they direct divine worship regarding individual men and offer the prayers and sacrifices of men before the gods. The third [Angels] arrange all smaller matters, and each stands as a guardian to an individual. Among them are even those who supply power to the smallest herbs and stones, and to all lower things; they have much in common with God and much with men, and they are mediating ministers.

<margin>*Athanasius's opinion on the angels.*</margin>
But <term>Athanasius</term> <note>St. Athanasius of Alexandria, a 4th-century church father</note>, besides the Thrones, Cherubim, and Seraphim who are closest to God—magnifying Him with unceasing hymns and restless praise and praying for our salvation—names seven other orders. He calls these collectively the "heavenly host" <note>original: "militiam coeli"</note>. The first of these is the **Doctrinal order**, from which came the one who spoke to Daniel, saying: 
> "I have come to teach you what shall happen to your people in the latter days." <note>Daniel 10:14</note>

<margin>*The Tutelary order.*</margin>
Next is the **Tutelary order** <note>Meaning "protective"</note>, about which it is also read in Daniel: 
> "Behold, Michael, one of the chief princes, came to help me." 
And in the same place: 
> "At that time Michael shall rise up, the great prince who stands for the children of your people." 
To this order also belonged <term>Raphael</term> <note>An archangel known for healing and guiding travelers</note>, who led the younger Tobias forth and back again. 

<margin>*The Procuratorial order.*</margin>
After this is the **Procuratorial order** <note>From "procurator," meaning one who manages or advocates on behalf of another</note>, mention of which is found in the book of Job, where it is read: "If there be an angel speaking for him, he shall pray..."

<margin>How the Hebrews number the angelic orders.</margin>

In the highest place are those they call <term>Chaioth ha-Kodesh</term> <note>original: חיות הקדש; literally "Holy Living Creatures"</note>, that is, the holy animals or the living ones, through whom God, known by the name <term>Ehieh</term> <note>original: אהיה; meaning "I Am"</note>, bestows the gift of existence. In the second place follow the <term>Ophanim</term> <note>original: אופנים; "Wheels"</note>, that is, forms or wheels, through whom God, known as <term>JHVH</term> <note>the Tetragrammaton, the four-letter name of God</note>, distinguishes chaos. In the third place are the <term>Aralim</term> <note>original: אראלים; "Great and Mighty ones"</note>, great, strong, and robust angels, through whom the pronounced name <term>Elohim</term> <note>original: אלהים</note>—or the Tetragrammaton joined with the letter *He* as <term>Hevajeh</term> <note>original: הויה</note>—administers the form of flowing matter. In the fourth place are the <term>Hasmalim</term> <note>original: חשמלים; often translated as "Amber" or "Speaking Silences"</note>, through whom <term>El</term> <note>original: אל</note>, the God of bodies, shapes their appearances. The fifth is the order of the <term>Seraphim</term> <note>original: שרפים; "Burning ones"</note>, through whom God as <term>Elohim Gibor</term> <note>original: אלהים גיבור; "God of Might"</note> draws forth the elements. The sixth is the <term>Malachim</term> <note>original: מלאכים</note>, that is, of the angels, through whom <term>Eloha</term> <note>original: אלוה</note> produces metals. The seventh is the <term>Elohim</term> <note>original: אלהים; "Gods"</note>, through whom the God of the Tetragrammaton of Hosts <note>original: יהוה צבאות; "JHVH Sabaoth"</note> nourishes the plants. The eighth is the <term>Bne Elohim</term> <note>original: בני אלהים</note>, that is, the sons of the gods, through whom God as <term>Elohim Sabaoth</term> <note>original: אלהים צבאות</note> procreates animals. The ninth and lowest is the <term>Cherubim</term> <note>original: כרובים</note>, through whom God as <term>Shadai</term> <note>original: שדי; "The Almighty"</note> cares for the human race. Below these is the <margin>Heroes.</margin> animal-like order, called <term>Ishim</term> <note>original: אישים; "Men"</note>, that is, heroes, strong and blessed men, through whom God as <term>Adonai</term> <note>original: אדני; "Lord"</note> bestows the gift of prophecy.

Origen’s opinion on demons.
</margin>
The opinion of Origen <note>An early Christian theologian known for his "Universalist" views</note> regarding demons is this: The demons who, by their own will, withdrew from God's service along with their prince the devil, may, if they begin to repent even a little, be clothed in human flesh. Thus, through this subsequent penance, they might return at last to the vision of God after the resurrection, following the same path by which they entered into the flesh. At that time, even while still in ethereal and aerial bodies, every knee shall bow to God—of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth—so that God may be "all in all." Indeed, Saint Irenaeus <note>A 2nd-century bishop and theologian</note> approves the sentiment of Justin Martyr <note>An early Christian apologist</note>, who said that Satan never dared to speak blasphemy against God until the Lord had come to earth, because he did not yet recognize his own damnation. However, many believe that there are several among the fallen demons who hope for their future salvation, a belief drawn from the history of Paul the Hermit written by Jerome, and honored by the Church in the canonical hours. They are also taught by the legend of Saint Brendan <note>A famous medieval account of a sea voyage to the "Isle of the Blessed"</note> that the prayers of demons may be heard; they even bring this argument from what is read in the Gospels: that **CHRIST** heard the prayers of the demons and granted them permission to enter into the herd of swine. This is also supported by the seventy-first Psalm according to our numbering (but the seventy-second according to the numbering of the Hebrews), where we read: "before him the Ethiopians shall fall down, and his enemies shall lick the earth." In that passage, according to the Hebrew truth, it is read: "Before him those inhabiting the wilderness shall bow their knees"—which means the aerial spirits shall adore him, as the Kabbalists <note>Jewish mystical tradition</note> assert—"and his enemies shall lick the dust." They explain this in reference to Zazele <note>likely Azazel, the wilderness demon or scapegoat</note> and his army, of whom it is read in Genesis: "You shall eat the earth all the days of your life," and elsewhere the prophet says: "Because the dust of the earth is his bread." Hence, the Kabbalists also think that some demons are to be saved, a view which Origen is known to have held as well.

### On the Bodies of Demons. Chapter 19.

Regarding the bodies of demons, there is a great disagreement between modern theologians and the philosophers. For Thomas <note>St. Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), a major Catholic philosopher and theologian.</note> asserts that all angels are incorporeal <note>original: "incorporeos"; lacking a physical body or material substance.</note>, and likewise the evil demons; <margin>The bodies of demons.</margin> however, he claims they occasionally assume bodies, which they shortly thereafter cast off. Dionysius <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, an influential Christian Neoplatonist.</note>, in *The Divine Names*, also constantly asserts that angels are incorporeal. Augustine, however, in his commentary on Genesis, reveals this: "Demons are called aerial and fiery animals <note>original: "animalia"; in the sense of living beings endowed with a soul (anima).</note>, because they thrive by the nature of aerial bodies; they are not dissolved by death, because an element prevails in them that is more suited for acting than for being acted upon." He seems to maintain that all angels had aerial bodies from the beginning of their creation, formed from the purer and higher part of the air, suited for action but not for suffering. He suggests that these bodies were preserved for the good angels after their confirmation <note>A theological term for the state of being permanently established in grace.</note>, <margin>By what punishment demons are tortured.</margin> but for the evil ones, during their fall, they were changed into a quality of thicker air, so that they might even be tortured by fire. Furthermore, Basil the Great <note>An early Church Father and Bishop of Caesarea.</note> attributes bodies not only to demons, but even to the pure angels, describing them as certain thin, aerial, and pure spirits. Gregory of Nazianzus <note>A 4th-century Archbishop and theologian.</note> also agrees with these views.

Apuleius <note>A Roman philosopher and author of "The Golden Ass."</note> does not believe that all demons have bodies; for in his book *On the Demon of Socrates*, he says: "There is another, more restricted class of demons who, being always free from bodily shackles and bonds, are reached through specific prayers." Truly, Psellus <note>Michael Psellus (c. 1017–1078), a Byzantine monk and scholar of demonology.</note>—both a Platonist and a Christian—thinks the nature of demons is not without a body. However, he does not think the angelic and demonic bodies are the same; for the former is devoid of all matter, while the demonic body is in some way material, like the bodies of shadows. It is subject to suffering, so that it may even feel pain when struck, and be burned by fire into visible ashes—an event recorded as having once happened in Tuscany. And although it is a spiritual body, it is nonetheless highly sensible and experiences touch; though it may be cut, it joins back together and heals again, just like <margin>The fear of demons.</margin> air and water. Meanwhile, however, it feels great pain; for this reason, they fear the edge of iron, and spears, and swords. This is why the Sibyl says to Aeneas in Virgil:

> And you, enter upon the path, and draw the sword from its sheath. <note>original: "Tuque invade viam, vaginaque eripere ferrum"; from the Aeneid, Book VI.</note>

Concerning this, Servius <note>A 4th-century commentator on Virgil.</note> says that Aeneas wished to have a consecrated sword. <margin>Various kinds of demonic bodies.</margin> Orpheus <note>The legendary poet to whom several mystical texts were attributed.</note> also describes the various kinds of demonic bodies. There is one body that consists only of fire, but it does not allow itself to be seen; these Orpheus calls the fiery and celestial demons. Another is tempered by a mixture of fire and air, from which they are named ethereal and aerial. If something watery is added to this, a third kind arises, which are called the watery demons, who are sometimes perceived by sight. If something earthy is added to these, though not so thick, they are called terrestrial demons; these are now more conspicuous and encountered by our senses. The bodies of the more sublime demons and angels are formed from the purest ethereal element, visible to no human by chance, unless by the divine will.

...to offer their appearance clearly; for they are woven with such splendid and thin threads that they allow all the rays of our sight to pass through because of their rarity, reflect them because of their splendor, and frustrate them with their subtlety. Of these, Chalcidius <note>A 4th-century philosopher known for his commentary on Plato's Timaeus.</note> says: "Ethereal and aerial demons, because their bodies have neither so much fire as to be transparent, nor so much earth as to resist touch by their solidity, have a structure joined from the serenity of the ether and the fluidity of the air, forming an indissoluble surface."

The remaining demons are neither so commendable nor so harmless; they are not always invisible, but sometimes conspicuous, turning into various figures. They take on the shadowy forms of bloodless phantoms, dragging the filth of a thick body. They have a great communion with *hyle* <note>original: "sylva"; the Greek term for raw matter, which ancient philosophers often associated with a chaotic or "malignant soul."</note>, and from the proximity of earth and water, they are touched by earthly pleasures and lust. Of this kind are the <term>lamiae</term> <note>monstrous female demons or hags in folklore</note>, <term>incubi</term> <note>male demons said to haunt sleepers</note>, and <term>succubi</term> <note>female demons said to haunt sleepers</note>. It is perhaps not an absurd conjecture that Melusina <note>A figure of European folklore, a water-spirit often depicted as a woman with a serpent's tail.</note> was among their number. 

<margin>There is no sex among demons.</margin> However, as Marcus <note>Likely referring to Marcus the Gnostic, a 2nd-century teacher.</note> believes, no demon should be considered male or female, as this distinction of sexes belongs to composite beings <note>things made of physical matter</note>, whereas the bodies of demons are simple. Yet, not every kind of demon can assume all shapes at will; fiery and aerial ones have an easy faculty for this, deforming themselves into whatever their imagination conceives. But subterranean and dark demons, because their phantasmic nature is confined within the narrowness of a thick and sluggish body, cannot produce the same diversity of shapes as the others. 

Water demons and those who inhabit the moist surface of the earth, due to the softness of the element, mostly resemble women—of which kind are the <term>Naiads</term> <note>water nymphs</note> and <term>Dryads</term> <note>tree or wood nymphs</note>. Those who dwell in watery and dry places, having drier bodies, show themselves as males, such as <term>Satyrs</term> or <term>Onoscelos</term> <note>original: "Onoscelos"; a Greek term for a demon with the legs of an ass</note> with donkey legs, <term>Fauns</term>, <term>Sylvans</term>, and <term>incubi</term>. 

<margin>The intercourse of demons according to Augustine.</margin> Regarding these, Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), a foundational Christian theologian.</note> records that many have learned through the mastery of experience that these have often been wicked toward women, desiring and performing intercourse with them; and that certain demons, whom the Gauls call <term>Dusii</term> <note>Gaulish forest spirits or demons associated with fertility and lust</note>, constantly attempt this lustful behavior.

->¶ On the infestation of evil demons, and the protection provided to us by<-

<margin>
The nature of evil demons.
The protection of man.
Raphael.
</margin>
It is the common opinion of theologians that all evil demons are of such a nature that they hate both God and men equally. Therefore, Divine Providence has appointed purer, neighboring demons over us, to whom we are commended as if to shepherds or rulers. They help us daily, and they ward off, restrain, and bind the evil demons so that they do not harm us as much as they would wish. This is read in the Book of Tobit <note>A book of the Catholic and Orthodox Bibles; Agrippa uses the Latin name "Thobia."</note>, where Raphael <note>The Archangel Raphael, whose name means "God Heals."</note> apprehended a demon named Asmodeus <note>A powerful demon of lust mentioned in the Book of Tobit.</note> and banished him to the desert of Upper Egypt. Of these, Hesiod <note>An ancient Greek poet (c. 700 BC).</note> says: "There are thirty thousand living upon the earth, the immortal guardians of mortal men appointed by Jove <note>Jupiter or Zeus; the high god of the Greeks and Romans.</note>, who observe justice and wretched deeds, clothed in air, going everywhere over the earth."
