...of princes, no great man would remain safe, no woman would remain uncorrupted, and no human being in this <term>valley of ignorance</term> <note>A common medieval and Renaissance metaphor for earthly life, where the full truth of God is obscured.</note> would reach the end appointed for them by God, if the good demons <note>The author uses the word "demons" in the classical sense of "daimons" or spirits, here referring to what we would call guardian angels.</note> did not stand by us for our protection, or if the evil demons were permitted to satisfy the wicked wills of men. Therefore, just as a specific guardian has been assigned to each of us from among the good demons, strengthening the spirit of man toward the good, so too is a certain enemy sent out from among the evil ones. This enemy presides over the flesh and its cravings, and while the good guardian fights for our spirit, the enemy fights for the flesh. Man, however, stands in the middle of these combatants, and being left **in the hand of his own counsel**, he grants victory to whichever side he chooses.

<margin>The malice of nations is not to be blamed on the angels.</margin>
We cannot, therefore, accuse the angels if the nations entrusted to them are not led to the knowledge of the true God and to true piety and religion, or if the angels allow them to slide into errors and perverse worship. Instead, the blame must be placed on those who, of their own accord, turned aside from the right path, clinging to spirits of error and giving the victory to the devil. For it is in the hand of man to decide whom he wishes to cling to and whom he wishes to conquer. If the demonic enemy is once defeated by a man, he is made that man’s servant; once conquered, he cannot attack another person further, just like a **wasp that has lost its stinger**.

<margin>The servitude of man.</margin>
This opinion is also supported by **Origen** <note>A prominent early Christian theologian (c. 184–253 AD).</note> in his book *On First Principles* <note>original: "Periarchon"; Origen's foundational work on Christian theology.</note>, where he concludes that the saints, by resisting and defeating evil demons, diminish their army, so that it is no longer lawful for one who has been defeated by one person to bother another thereafter.

<margin>Two spirits: a good one and an evil one.</margin>
Therefore, just as a good spirit is given to every man, so also is a bad, diabolical spirit given. Both of these seek union with our spirit and strive to draw it to themselves and mix with it, like **wine mixing with water**. The good spirit, through good works that conform to its nature, transforms us by uniting us with the angels, just as it is written of John the Baptist in the Book of Malachi:

<margin>Malachi 3</margin>
> "Behold, I send my angel before your face." <note>original: "Ecce ego mitto angelum meum ante faciem tuam." This refers to Malachi 3:1, implying that a holy man can be called an "angel."</note>

Concerning this transformation and union, it is written elsewhere: "He who adheres to God is made one spirit with him." The evil demon also strives to make us like himself and united to him through evil works, just as **CHRIST** said of Judas in the Gospel of John:

<margin>John 6</margin>
> "Did I not choose you twelve, and one of you is a devil?" <note>original: "Nonne ego vos elegi duodecim, & vnus ex vobis diabolus est?" (John 6:70).</note>

And this is what **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure associated with the Hermetic writings on philosophy and magic.</note> says: when a demon flows into a human soul, he scatters the seeds of his own notion. From this, such a soul, sprinkled with these seeds and pregnant with fury, gives birth to wonders and to whatever the duties of demons may be. For when a good demon flows into a holy soul, he raises it to the light of wisdom; but a bad demon, poured into a depraved soul, incites it to theft, murder, lust, and whatever the duties of evil demons are.

<margin>Effects of the good demon. Effects of the evil demon.</margin>
Good demons (as **Iamblichus** <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 245–325 AD) who wrote extensively on theurgy and spirits.</note> says) purify souls most perfectly; some provide us with one thing, others with another. When present, they give health to the body, virtue to the soul, and security to the mind; they wipe out what is deadly within us, foster heat, make us more effective for life, and always pour light into the mind through an intelligible harmony. However, whether there are many of these...

->CXXXIIII<-
->ON OCCULT PHILOSOPHY.<-

<margin>Psalm 90.</margin>
...of man. Whether there are many guardians for each person, or only one, is a point of contention among theologians. We believe there are many, as the prophet <note>The "prophet" refers to King David, the traditional author of the Psalms.</note> says: *He has given his angels charge over you, to protect you in all your ways* <note>original: "Angelis suis mandauit de te, vt custodiant te in omnibus viis tuis." This is from Psalm 91:11 in modern Bibles, or Psalm 90 in the Latin Vulgate.</note>. According to the testimony of Jerome <note>Saint Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), the scholar who translated the Bible into Latin.</note>, this applies not only to Christ, but to every human being. Therefore, all men are governed by the ministry of various spirits and are led to whatever level of virtue, merit, and dignity they have shown themselves worthy of. Those who prove unworthy, however, are cast down by evil <term>demons</term> <note>In this context, "demons" refers to "daimons"—intermediate spirits—rather than purely modern concepts of devils.</note> and abandoned by the good spirits, falling to the lowest depths of misery as their bad merits deserve. Furthermore, those who are assigned to more sublime angels are preferred over other men; for the angels caring for them elevate them and subject others to them by a certain hidden force. Even if neither person perceives this force, the subordinate person feels a certain "yoke of authority" from the one presiding, from which he cannot easily free himself. Instead, he fears and reveres that power which the higher angels flow into the superiors, while the higher angels induce a certain terror into the inferiors to make them feel the fear of authority.

<margin>Homer.</margin>
Homer seems to have felt this when he said that the Muses, born of Jove, sit as constant companions to kings born of Jove, and through them, these kings are made venerable and majestic. Thus we read that Mark Antony was once joined in a singular friendship with Octavian Augustus, and they often used to play games together. But because Augustus always emerged as the winner, a certain great man <note>Likely a reference to the Egyptian soothsayer mentioned in Plutarch’s "Life of Antony."</note> cautioned Mark Antony with this advice:

> "What business have you, O Antony, with this youth?
<margin>
The genius of Augustus is superior to the genius of Mark Antony.
</margin>
Flee him and avoid him: for even if you are older and more experienced in affairs, more illustrious in your lineage, and as a commander of many you have endured many wars, nevertheless your <term>genius</term> <note>The "Genius" was believed to be a personal guardian spirit or "higher self" that determined a person’s luck and character.</note> shrinks before his genius. Your fortune flatters his fortune; unless you flee far away, your glory will seem to fail and pass entirely to him."

Is a prince not a man like other men? How could other men fear and revere him unless a "divine terror" elevated him and, by striking fear into the others, pressed them down so that they might revere him as a prince? Therefore, we must strive so that—having been purified by right action and the pursuit of sublime things, and by choosing opportune times and places—we may be committed to the rank of the more sublime and powerful angels, so that they, taking care of us, may rightly prefer us over others.

<margin>The guardian spirit changes according to a change of location.</margin>
<margin>A change of name sometimes helps.</margin>
Nevertheless, although there are spirits and <term>demons</term> of every kind in every region, those who are of the same order as the governor of that specific region are more powerful than the others there. For instance, in a solar region, solar spirits flourish above all others; in a lunar region, lunar spirits do, and so on for the rest. From this, it follows that when we change our locations and provinces, various outcomes of our affairs and business offer themselves and follow us. We are more fortunate in some places than others—specifically where our <term>genius</term> <note>In the classical sense, a "genius" is a personal tutelary spirit or "higher self" that guides a person's fate.</note> has obtained greater power, or where we have acquired a more powerful spirit of that same order. Thus, "solar" people <note>People whose birth charts or temperaments are dominated by the Sun.</note>, if they migrate to a solar region or province, will be rendered far more fortunate there. This is because they will have more powerful and favorable leaders or guardians there; by their excellent protection in that place, all their affairs are often led to happy endings, even beyond expectation and the measure of their own strength. For this reason, the choice of place, region, and time—where one may exercise, live, and frequent according to the nature and instinct of one's own guardian—contributes greatly to a happy life. Even a change of name is sometimes beneficial. Since the properties of names are indicators of the things themselves—declaring the conditions of their forms as if in a mirror—it happens that when names are changed, the reality of the thing often changes as well. This is why Holy Scripture, not without cause, shows that God, when he was about to bless Abram and Jacob, changed their names, calling the former Abraham and the latter Israel.

These are undoubtedly the persuasions of the genius who is given to each person from the beginning of their birth, leading us and persuading us toward that which his star inclines us.

### ¶ That there are three guardians for every man, and from what sources each proceeds. Chapter XXII.

Every person has a triple good daemon <term>Daemon: In this context, not an evil "demon," but a tutelary spirit or guiding divine power.</term> as their own proper guardian: one is sacred, the second is of the birth-chart [geniture], and the third is of the profession. According to the doctrine of the Egyptians, the **sacred daemon** is not assigned from the stars or the planets, but from a celestial cause—from God himself, the ruler of daemons. It is assigned to the rational soul as it descends; it is universal and above nature. This spirit directs the life of the soul and always presents good thoughts to the mind, acting continually within us by illuminating us, although we do not always notice it. But when we are purified and live tranquilly, then it is perceived by us; then it speaks with us, as it were, and communicates its voice to us—though previously it was present in silence—and it continually strives to lead us to sacred perfection. 

With the help of this daemon, we are also able to avoid the malice of fate. The Platonists think that if this spirit is religiously honored by us with integrity and holiness—as we know Socrates did <note>Socrates famously claimed to have a "daimonion," a divine inner voice that warned him against making mistakes.</note>—we are wonderfully helped by it, both through dreams and signs, by turning away evils and anxiously welcoming good things. Therefore, the Pythagoreans, in harmony with this, were accustomed to pray to Jupiter that he might either lead them away from evils himself, or show them by which of the daemons that could be performed. 

However, the **daemon of the birth**, which is also called the **genius**, descends from the disposition of the world and the circuits of the stars which are involved in the generation [birth]. There are those who believe that the soul, just as it is about to descend into the body, naturally chooses for itself a guardian from the choir of daemons. They suggest that the soul does not so much choose this leader for itself, but rather is chosen by the spirit to be under its protection. This spirit is the executor of one's life, and...

### ON OCCULT PHILOSOPHY.

<margin>What the speech of angels is. The first of all speech.</margin>
of angels: but what that speech of theirs might be, or what language they use, is still a matter of doubt among many. For most people think that if they use any specific language, it is Hebrew, because this was the first of all languages, it flowed down from heaven, and it existed before the confusion of tongues arose in Babylon. In this language, the Law was given by God the Father, the Gospel was preached by Christ the Son, and so many oracles were delivered through the Holy Spirit to the prophets. And while all other languages have suffered and continually suffer various
<margin>An inviolate language.</margin>
changes and corruptions, this one alone always perseveres inviolate. Furthermore, an evident sign of this opinion is that while <term>demons</term> <note>original: "dæmones" — here referring to spiritual mediators or spirits generally, rather than strictly evil entities.</note> and individual <term>intelligences</term> <note>Celestial spirits that govern the spheres or specific nations.</note> may practice the speech of the individual nations with whom they dwell, those who know the Hebrew speech say that spirits never speak in any other idiom, but in that one alone. However, how angels speak
<margin>The speech of angels is hidden from us. Nine things necessary for speaking.</margin>
is hidden from us, just as they themselves are. For us to speak, a tongue is necessary along with other instruments, which are the throat, the palate, the lips, the teeth, the gullet, the lungs, the windpipe <note>original: "spiritualis arteria" — literally the "spirit-way," referring to the trachea.</note>, and the chest muscles, which receive the beginning of their motion from the soul. Indeed, if someone speaks to another from a distance, he needs a louder shout; so one who is close whispers in the listener's ear. And if he could be joined with the listener by a closer spirit, his speech would need no sound at all; instead, it would flow into the listener without noise, just as an image flows into the eye or a mirror. Thus the souls who have departed from the body speak, and thus do angels and demons speak; and what a human does with a sensible voice, they do by imprinting the concept of the speech upon those to whom they speak, in a better way than if it were expressed through an audible voice. Thus the Platonists say that Socrates perceived his own <term>daemon</term> by a sense, though not of this body, but by the sense of an ethereal body hidden within this one. By this same 
<margin>Avicenna.</margin>
reasoning, Avicenna <note>A famous Persian polymath and philosopher (c. 980–1037) influential in Western medieval thought.</note> believes that angels were usually seen and heard by the prophets. And that instrument—whatever that power may be—through which a spirit makes known to another spirit or to a human the things that bubble up in the mind, is called by the Apostle Paul "the tongue of angels." Yet very often they also emit a sensible 
<margin>Acts 1.</margin>
voice, as when they cried out at the ascension of the Lord: *“Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking into heaven?”* <note>original Latin: "viri Galilæi, quid statis spectãtes in cœlum" — a quote from Acts 1:11.</note> and in the Old Law they spoke with many of the fathers with a sensible voice; but this only occurred when they had taken on bodies. 
<margin>How spirits hear our prayers.</margin>
Truly, by what senses these spirits and demons hear our invocations and prayers and see our ceremonies, we are entirely ignorant. For the spiritual body of demons is, by its nature, sensible <note>Meaning "capable of perceiving through senses."</note> in a great part everywhere and on all sides, so that it touches, sees, and hears without any medium, and nothing can be an impediment to them. Yet they do not perceive in the same way we do through distinct organs; rather, just as sponges absorb water, so do they draw in all sensible things with their whole body, or in some other way unknown to us. For not all living things we see are furnished with the same sensory organs; for we know many lack ears, yet we believe sound is perceived by them, but by what means, we do not know.

### BOOK THREE

### ¶ On the names of spirits, and their various impositions, and on the spirits who preside over the stars, signs, the quarters of heaven, and the elements. Chapter XXIV.

<margin>Names of spirits.</margin>
The names of spirits, both good and evil, are manifold and diverse. However, their proper and true names—just like those of the stars—are known only to God, who alone counts the multitude of the stars and calls them all by their names. None of these can be known by us except through divine revelation, and very few have been expressed for us in the sacred scriptures. Truly, the masters of the Hebrews believe that names were imposed upon the spirits themselves by Adam, according to that which is written: "God brought all things that he had made to Adam so that he might name them, and whatever he called a thing, that is its name." Hence, the <term>Cabalists</term> <note>original: "mecubales" — from the Hebrew 'mekubbalim', those who have received the mystical tradition.</note> together with the <term>magi</term> <note>Wise men or practitioners of high natural magic.</note> think that it is within the power of man to impose names
<margin>Man cannot impose names on spirits.</margin>
upon spirits. But this applies only to a man who has already been dignified and elevated to this power by some divine gift or sacred authority. For by nature, no human voice can compose a name that is able to express the nature of divinity or the all-encompassing power of the angelic essence. Therefore, names are most often imposed upon spirits based on their works, signifying
<margin>From where names are imposed on spirits.</margin>
a certain office or effect, such as is desired from a choir of spirits. These names then, no differently than offerings and sacrifices devoted to the gods, obtain efficacy and power to draw down from the heavens and the depths a certain spiritual substance that works the desired effect.
<margin>Miraculous calling of rain.</margin>
I myself have seen and known a certain person who wrote the name and seal of a certain spirit on <term>virgin paper</term> <note>Parchment made from the skin of an unborn or newborn animal, considered ritually pure.</note> in the hour of the Moon. After he had given this to a river frog to devour and had murmured a certain charm, and the frog was released back into the water, rains and showers suddenly broke forth. I saw the same man write the name and seal of another spirit in the hour of Mars and give it to a crow; after the charm was murmured and the bird released, immediately from that quarter of the heaven where it had flown, clouds arose and lightning, quaking, and horrible thunders 
<margin>Calling of lightning and thunder. Explanation of certain angels' names.</margin>
followed. Yet those were not names of spirits in an unknown tongue, nor anything other than words signifying their offices. Of this kind are the names of these angels: Raziel, Gabriel, Michael, Raphael, and Haniel, which mean: the vision of God, the virtue of God, the strength of God, the medicine of God, and the glory of God. In a similar way, in the offices of evil demons, their names are read as: the Player, the Deceiver, the Dreamer, the Fornicator, and many more of this sort. Thus we have received from the ancient fathers of the Hebrews the names of the
<margin>Angels presiding over the planets. Seven spirits before the face of God.</margin>
angels presiding over the planets and signs. For Saturn: Zaphkiel; for Jupiter: Zadkiel; for Mars: Camael; for the Sun: Raphael; for Venus: Haniel; for Mercury: Michael; for the Moon: Gabriel. These are those seven spirits who always stand before the face of God, to whom is entrusted the disposition of the entire celestial and earthly kingdom which is beneath the sphere of the moon. For these (as the sacred [writings] say...

# ON OCCULT PHILOSOPHY.

<meta>catchword: iuxta (next to/according to)</meta>

[hol]ier theologians <note>The OCR begins with "tiores," the end of "sanctiores" (holier), continuing from the previous page.</note>) rule all things by a certain succession of hours, days, and years, just as the Astrologers teach concerning the planets over which they preside. For this reason, Hermes Trismegistus calls them the "seven governors of the world," who, through the heavens as if through instruments, distribute the gathered influences of all stars and signs into these lower realms. However, there are those who assign these spirits to the stars with slightly different names, saying that an intelligence named Orifiel presides over Saturn; Zachariel over Jupiter; Zamael over Mars; Michael over the Sun; Anael over Venus; Raphael over Mercury; and Gabriel over the Moon. Each of these governs the world for three hundred fifty-four years and four months. The rule begins with the intelligence of Saturn; afterward, the intelligences of Venus, Jupiter, Mercury, Mars, the Moon, and the Sun reign in order, and then the government returns again to the spirit of Saturn.

<margin>The treatise of Abbot Trithemius. Angels presiding over the twelve signs.</margin>
Abbot Trithemius wrote a special treatise on these matters for Emperor Maximilian; whoever examines it thoroughly <note>original: "medullitus," meaning to the very marrow or deeply.</note> can derive from it a great knowledge of future times. Truly, of the twelve signs, Malchidael presides over Aries; Asmodel over Taurus; Ambriel over Gemini; Muriel over Cancer; Verchiel over Leo; Hamaliel over Virgo; Zuriel over Libra; Barchiel over Scorpio; Aduachiel over Sagittarius; Hanael over Capricorn; Gambiel over Aquarius; and Barchiel over Pisces.

<margin>Revelation 1.</margin>
Concerning these spirits presiding over the planets and signs, John also makes mention in the Apocalypse (the Book of Revelation), saying of the former at the beginning: *And from the seven spirits, who are in the sight of the throne of God*, whom I have found to also preside over the planets. <margin>Revelation 21.</margin> In the conclusion of the volume, where he describes the structure of the heavenly city, he bears witness that at its twelve gates were twelve angels.

<margin>Angels of the mansions of the moon.</margin>
There are, furthermore, twenty-eight angels who rule in the twenty-eight mansions of the moon, whose names in order are: Geniel, Enediel, Amixiel, Azariel, Gabriel, Dirachiel, Seheliel, Amnediel, Barbiel, Ardefiel, Neciel, Abdizuel, Iazeriel, Ergediel, Ataliel, Azeruel, Adriel, Egibiel, Amutiel, Kyriel, Bethnael, Geliel, Requiel, Abrinael, Aziel, Tagriel, Alheniel, and Amnixiel.

<margin>Four angels for the four winds.</margin>
There are also four princes of angels who are set over the four winds and over the four quarters of the world, of whom Michael is set over the eastern wind; Raphael over the western; Gabriel over the north<margin>Angels of the elements.</margin>ern; and Noriel (who is called Uriel by others) over the southern. They are also assigned to the elements: Cherub to the air; Tharsis to the water; Ariel to the earth; and Seruph <note>A variation of Seraph.</note> to the fire; or, according to Philo <note>Philo of Alexandria, a Jewish philosopher.</note>, Nathaniel.

<margin>Spirits presiding over the four parts of the world.</margin>
Each of these spirits is a great prince, possessing the power of much liberty in the dominion of their planets and signs, and in their times, years, months, days, and hours, and in their elements, parts of the world, and winds. Each of them rules over many legions; and by the same reasoning, among the evil spirits, four most powerful kings preside over the others...

...according to the four parts of the world, whose names are called: Urieus, king of the east; Amaymon, king of the south; Paymon, king of the west; Egyn, king of the north; whom the doctors of the Hebrews perhaps more correctly call Samaël, Azazel, Azaël, and Mahazaël. Under these, many other princes of legions and presiding officers dominate, as well as innumerable demons of private duties.

<margin>Telchines</margin>
Furthermore, the ancient theologians of the Greeks enumerate six demons whom they call Telchines <note>original: "Telchines." In Greek mythology, these were the original inhabitants of Rhodes, often described as malignant sorcerers or spirits who could control the weather.</note>, and others call them Alastores <note>original: "Alastores," meaning avenging spirits or deities of vengeance.</note>. These are harmful to men; drawing the water of the Styx <note>The river of the underworld in Greek mythology.</note> with their hands, they scatter it upon the earth, from which calamities, plagues, and famines follow. Acteus, Megalesius, Ormenus, Lycus, Nicon, and Mimon are said to be among them. However, he who desires to know exactly the distinct names, offices, locations, and times of the angels and even the evil demons, let him seek those in the <term>Volume of Temples</term> of <term>Rabbi Simon</term> <note>Referring to the *Zohar*, specifically the sections on the celestial palaces (Heikhalot).</note>, and in his <term>Book of Lights</term>, and in the <term>Treatise on the Greatness of Stature</term> <note>original: "Magnitudine staturae," likely referring to the *Shi'ur Qomah*, a mystical text describing the dimensions of the Divine.</note>, and in <term>Rabbi Ishmael’s Treatise of Temples</term>, and he will find copious writings about these in almost all commentaries on the <term>Book of Formation</term> <note>original: "libri Formationis," the *Sefer Yetzirah*, a foundational text of Jewish mysticism.</note>.

<margin>Hebrew Kabbalists</margin>
### Chapter XXV. How the <term>Kabbalists</term> <note>original: "mecubales," a Latinization of the Hebrew word for those who receive the tradition (Kabbalah).</note> of the Hebrews derive sacred names of angels from the holy scriptures, and concerning the seventy-two angels who bear the name of God, with the tables of <term>Ziruph</term> <note>original: "Ziruph" or *Tsiruf*, a Kabbalistic method of permuting and combining letters of the Hebrew alphabet.</note>, and the commutations of letters and numbers.

There are also other sacred names of both good and evil spirits assigned to individual offices, much more powerful than those previously mentioned, which are extracted from the sacred scriptures according to the art which the Hebrew Kabbalists hand down regarding them; just as certain names of God are drawn out from specific places.

<margin>General rule concerning the divine name.</margin>
The general rule for these is that wherever something of the divine essence is expressed in the sacred letters, a divine name can be properly collected from that place; but wherever a divine name is found expressed in the sacred letters, consider the ministry that is subject to that name. Therefore, wherever scripture speaks of the ministry or work of some spirit, whether good or evil, the name of that same spirit—good or evil—can be extracted from that place, observing this unchangeable canon: that we take the names of good spirits from good things, and evil from evil things. Let us not confuse black with white, nor day with night, nor light with darkness; which shines forth from these verses as an example: *Let them be as dust before the face of the wind, and the angel of the Lord driving them away. Let their ways be dark and slippery, and the angel of the Lord pursuing them.* <note>Psalm 35:5-6.</note>

<page-num>CXXXVII</page-num>
<header>OF OCCULT PHILOSOPHY</header>

In Psalm thirty-five according to the Hebrews, which is thirty-four among us <note>The author refers to the numbering difference between the Hebrew Masoretic Text and the Latin Vulgate Bible.</note>, the names of those angels are extracted: **Midael** <note>original: "מידאל"</note> and **Mirael** <note>original: "מיראל"</note> from the order of the militants. Likewise, from the verse, *Set a wicked man over him, and let Satan stand at his right hand*—found in Psalm one hundred and nine among the Hebrews, or one hundred and eight among the Latins—from the Hebrew text <note>original: "רשע ושטן יעמד על ימינו הפקד עליו"</note> is extracted the name of the <term>cacodemon</term> <note>A "bad spirit" or malevolent entity, as opposed to an "agathodemon" or good spirit.</note> **Schihi** <note>original: "שי׳חי"</note>, which designates a "scheming demon." There is also a specific text in Exodus, contained in three verses, each of which is written with seventy-two letters. They begin: The first, *Vayissa* <note>original: "ויסע," meaning "And he moved." Exodus 14:19.</note>; the second, *Vayavo* <note>original: "ויבא," meaning "And he came." Exodus 14:20.</note>; and the third, *Vayot* <note>original: "ויט," meaning "And he stretched out." Exodus 14:21.</note>. When these are extended into a single line—namely, the first and third from left to right, but the middle one in reverse order, starting from the right and ending on the left—then each of the three letters placed one under the other constitutes one name. These are the seventy-two names which the Hebrews call the <term>Schemhamphoras</term> <note>From the Hebrew *Shem HaMephorash*, the "Explicit Name" or "Divided Name" of God.</note>. If the divine name **El** <note>original: "אל"</note> or **Yah** <note>original: "יה"</note> is added to the end of these, they produce the seventy-two trisyllabic names of the angels. Each of these angels bears the great name of God, just as it is written: *My Angel shall go before thee, observe him, for my name is in him.* <note>Exodus 23:20–21.</note> And these are the ones who preside over the seventy-two celestial quinaries <note>Five-degree segments of the zodiac, totaling 360 degrees (72 x 5 = 360).</note>, as many nations and languages, and the limbs of the human body. They cooperate with the seventy-two elders of the Synagogue, and as many disciples of Christ. Their names, according to the extraction made by the **Cabalists**, are revealed in the following table, according to the one method we have described. However, there are also many other ways of constructing the *Schemhamphoras* from those same verses, such as when all three are written under each other in the correct order from right to left, besides those which are extracted through the <term>Ziruph</term> tables <note>A Kabbalistic method of permutating and exchanging letters of the alphabet to reveal hidden meanings.</note> and tables of commutations, which we mentioned previously. And because these tables serve for all names, both divine and angelic, we shall therefore join them to this chapter.

TABLES OF NUMERICAL TRANSPOSITIONS.

### THE FIRST TABLE: UNITS
<note>This table demonstrates the "partitions" of the numbers 1 through 10. Each row shows how a single Hebrew letter's value can be reached by adding two smaller values. For example, the number 4 (Daleth) can be formed by 2+2 (Beth+Beth) or 1+3 (Aleph+Gimel).</note>

| | | | | | Aleph (1) |
| :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| | | | | A-A (1+1) | Beth (2) |
| | | | | A-B (1+2) | Gimel (3) |
| | | | B-B (2+2) | A-G (1+3) | Daleth (4) |
| | | | B-G (2+3) | A-D (1+4) | He (5) |
| | | G-G (3+3) | B-D (2+4) | A-H (1+5) | Vav (6) |
| | | G-D (3+4) | B-H (2+5) | A-V (1+6) | Zayin (7) |
| | D-D (4+4) | G-H (3+5) | B-V (2+6) | A-Z (1+7) | Cheth (8) |
| | D-H (4+5) | G-V (3+6) | B-Z (2+7) | A-Ch (1+8) | Teth (9) |
| H-H (5+5) | D-V (4+6) | G-Z (3+7) | B-Ch (2+8) | A-T (1+9) | Yod (10) |

BOOK THREE

# On finding the names of spirits and genii from the disposition of celestial bodies. Chapter XXVI.

<margin>t</margin>The ancient Magi <note>original Latin: "Magi," referring to the wise men and practitioners of high magic in antiquity</note> handed down the art of finding the name of a spirit for any desired effect, drawing it from the disposition of the heavens. For example, if you have proposed a certain celestial harmony for the purpose of making an image, a ring, or any other work to be performed under a specific constellation, and you wish to find the spirit who governs that work, follow this method. Once the figure of the heavens is erected, project the letters in their number and order starting from the degree of the ascendant <note>the point of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon</note>. Follow the succession of the signs through each individual degree until the entire circle of the heavens is filled. Then, look at the letters that fall upon the locations of the stars whose help you are using; according to the number and strength of those stars, noted down in order, these letters constitute the name of a spirit—specifically, a good one. However, if you do the same starting from the degree of the west <note>the descendant</note> and moving against the progression of the signs, the resulting spirit will be of the class of evil ones.

By this same skill, several masters of the Hebrews and Chaldeans teach how to seek out the nature and name of the genius <note>original Latin: "genii," here meaning a personal guiding spirit or "daemon" in the classical sense</note> of any man. Namely, once the degree of the ascendant of a birth is known and the other corners of the heavens are balanced, one should note which of the planets has the most dignities in those four corners. This planet, which the Arabs call the <term>Almutez: also known as the Almuten, the planet that holds the most mathematical power or "dignity" over a specific point in a horoscope</term>, is noted first among the others. Next to it, in the second place, note the one which is closest to it in the number of dignities, and so on in order for the rest of those who hold any dignity in the aforementioned corners. Once this order is held, you must find their true place and degree in the heavens. Starting from the degree of the ascendant, project the twenty-two Hebrew letters through each degree according to the order of the signs. Then, the letters that fall into the places of the aforementioned stars—noted and arranged according to the order previously found among the stars, and combined correctly according to the logic of the Hebrew language—constitute the name of the genius. To this name, according to custom, one joins some monosyllabic name of divine omnipotence, such as <term>El: a Hebrew name for God, frequently used as a suffix in angelic names like Gabriel or Michael to mean "of God"</term> or <term>Iah: a shortened form of the divine name, often used as a suffix to denote "of the Lord"</term>. 

But if the projection of letters is done from the angle of the west and against the succession of the signs, and if the letters that fall in the <term>Nadir: the point directly opposite a given position in the sky</term> of the aforementioned stars are joined in the order we have described, they will constitute the name of an evil genius. However, the Chaldeans proceed in another way: they do not take the Almuten of the corners, but the Almuten of the eleventh house, and they do everything else as was said. They seek the evil genius from the Almuten of the angle of the twelfth house—which they call the "evil demon"—projecting from the degree of the west against the progress of the signs. There are also many Arabs and some Hebrews who seek the name of the genius from the five <term>hylegiacal places: specific points in a birth chart (Sun, Moon, Ascendant, Part of Fortune, and the Pre-natal Syzygy) used to determine the "Hyleg" or giver of life</term>. By always making the projection from the beginning of Aries, and arranging and joining the letters found according to the order of the hylegs known to astrologers, they constitute the name of the good genius. They elicit the name of the evil genius from the places opposite the hylegs, with the projection made from the last degree of Pisces against the order of the signs... <note>The text ends mid-sentence here as indicated by the catchword "ordi" for "ordinem."</note>

...calculation. Others, however, do not take the locations of the *hylegi* <note>original Latin: "hylegiorum." In astrology, a hyleg is the planet that acts as the "giver of life" in a birth chart, determining longevity.</note>, but rather the locations of the *Almutez* <note>original Latin: "Almutez," or Almuten; the planet that holds the most dignity and influence over a specific degree or chart.</note> over the five *hylegi*, performing the projection from the horoscope <note>the ascendant or rising sign</note>, as was said in the previous sections. These names—distributed according to the proportionate numbers by starry calculation and compacted with joined and alternating letters—may have an unknown sound and meaning, yet one must acknowledge, out of the secret principles of philosophy, that they possess more power in magical work than meaningful names. This is because the mind, astonished by their riddles and intent with the full focus of its intellect, firmly believes some divine presence lies beneath them; thus, it reverently sounds these words and names (even if not understood) to the glory of the deity with a spiritual affection of piety, captivating itself in obedience to that deity.

### ¶ On the calculatory art of such names according to the tradition 
### of the Kabbalists. Chapter XXVII.

There is yet another technique for these kinds of names which they call "calculatory," <margin>e</margin> and it is done through the following tables <note>referring to the letter tables typically found in Agrippa's printed editions</note>. One enters with a certain sacred name—whether divine or angelic—into the descending column of letters, taking those letters which are found in the common angles under their stars and signs. Once these are arranged in order, the name of a good spirit is formed, possessing the nature of that star or sign under which you entered. If, however, you entered in the ascending column, taking the common angles above the stars and signs marked in the bottom-most line, the name of an evil spirit is formed. These are the names of the spirits from any order or ministering heaven, both good and evil, which you can multiply into nine names for the nine orders according to this method: by entering with one name, you can elicit another spirit of a higher order from it, both good and evil. 

The beginning of this calculation, however, depends on the names of God; for every voice has power in Magic insofar as it depends on and is formed from the voice of God. Therefore, we must know that every angelic name ought to proceed from some primary name of God; for this reason, angels are said to "bear the name of God," according to that which is written: *for my name is in him* <note>Exodus 23:21</note>. Thus, so that the names of good angels may be distinguished from the names of evil ones, a name of divine omnipotence is often subjoined to them—such as *El*, or *On*, or *Iah*, or *Iod*—and pronounced together with it. Since *Iah* <note>a shortened form of the Tetragrammaton, YHWH</note> is a name of beneficence, and *Iod* <note>the first letter of God's name, representing the divine spark</note> is a name of deity, these two names are attached only to the names of angels. However, the name *El* <note>meaning "God" or "Mighty One"</note>, which implies force and power, is for that reason added not only to good spirits, but sometimes even to evil ones; for not even evil spirits can exist or act without the power of God. Furthermore, it should be known that the common angles of the same star and sign must be taken, unless the entry is made with a mixed name, such as the names of genii <note>original: "geniorum," referring to personal guiding spirits</note>, and those of which we spoke in the preceding chapter...

<summary>Agrippa explains that "barbarous" names (those without known meaning) hold more magical power because they focus the practitioner's mind on the divine. He also introduces a Kabbalistic system for deriving the names of spirits by cross-referencing divine names with astrological tables and adding divine suffixes like El and Iah.</summary>

<page-num>CXLIII</page-num>
<header>BOOK THREE</header>

...which are composed from the celestial dispositions according to the harmony of various stars. For with these, whenever the table is to be entered, a common angle must be taken under the star or sign of the letter being entered. There are, furthermore, those who extend these tables so far that they believe even if the entry is made using the name of a star, or an office, or some desired effect, a spirit—both good and bad—is drawn out to serve that office or effect. By a similar reasoning, when entering with the proper name of any person, they trust that they can extract the names of genii <note>original: "geniorum"; guiding spirits or guardian angels believed to accompany a person through life</note> under that star which is seen to preside over such a person, according as they have recognized from Physiognomy <note>the practice of judging character or destiny from physical features</note>, or from the passions and inclination of the mind, or from their profession and fortune, whether that person is of the nature of Mars, or Saturn, or the Sun, or of the nature of another star.

And although primary names of this kind may have no or little power from their own meaning, nevertheless, names extracted in this manner and derived from them are of the greatest efficacy. This is just as solar rays collected in a concave mirror burn most strongly, even though the sun itself is scarcely moderately warm. <note>A common Renaissance scientific analogy: just as a lens concentrates light into a burning point, these tables concentrate "diffuse" spiritual power into a specific, potent name.</note> Moreover, the order of letters in these tables under the stars and signs is almost similar to the order of decans <note>ten-degree divisions of the zodiac</note>, novenaries <note>nine-part divisions</note>, and duodenaries <note>twelve-part divisions</note> used by astrologers. 

Alphonsus of Cyprus <note>a likely reference to a medieval or early Renaissance magical authority</note> once wrote about this calculatory art, and someone else—I know not who—also adapted it to Latin characters. But because the letters of every language (as we showed in the first book) have a celestial and divine origin in their number, order, and shape, I would easily grant that this calculation of the names of spirits can be done not only through Hebrew letters, but also through Chaldean, Arabic, Egyptian, Greek, Latin, and any others, provided the tables are rightly fashioned from them in imitation of the presiding powers. 

However, an objection is raised here by many: that it often happens in these tables that several men of different nature and fortune, due to having the same name, obtain the same genius or a genius of the same name. Therefore, it should be known that it is not considered absurd that the same spirit can be distinguished by many living beings, and the same spirit can preside over many. Furthermore, just as different men often use the same name, so also spirits of different offices and natures can be marked by one name and one and the same seal <note>original: "signaculo"; a magical signature or character</note> or character, though with a different respect. For just as the serpent at one time holds the type of Christ, and at another the devil, so the same names and the same seals are equated now to some order of evil demons, and now to some order of good angels. Finally, the ardent intention of the invoker itself, through which our intellect is joined to the "separate intelligences" <note>purely spiritual beings or angels that exist apart from matter</note>, causes us to have now that spirit, and now another, obedient to us, even if invoked under the same name.

# ON OCCULT PHILOSOPHY

There is yet another method used by the Kabbalists <note>Practitioners of Kabbalah, a school of Jewish mysticism. In the Renaissance, Christian scholars like Agrippa adapted these techniques for their own "occult philosophy."</note>, which was once held in great veneration but has today become so common that it has almost fallen into the status of the profane <note>Meaning it has become a common secret or a widely known parlor trick rather than a guarded mystery.</note>. It is as follows: Let the twenty-seven characters of the Hebrew alphabet be divided into three classes, each of which contains nine letters. 

The first class consists of: א (Aleph), ב (Beth), ג (Gimel), ד (Daleth), ה (He), ו (Vav), ז (Zayin), ח (Cheth), ט (Teth). These are the signs of the simple numbers <note>The units: 1 through 9.</note> and of intellectual things, distributed among the nine orders of angels. 

The second class holds: י (Yod), כ (Kaph), ל (Lamed), מ (Mem), נ (Nun), ס (Samekh), ע (Ayin), פ (Pe), צ (Tsadi). These are the signs of the tens <note>The "denaries": 10 through 90.</note> and of celestial things, found within the nine spheres of the heavens. 

The third class indeed holds the four remaining letters along with the five "final" forms in their proper order, namely: ק (Qoph), ר (Resh), ש (Shin), ת (Taw), ך (Kaph-final), ם (Mem-final), ן (Nun-final), ף (Pe-final), ץ (Tsadi-final). These are the signs of the hundreds <note>The "centenaries": 100 through 900.</note> and of inferior things, specifically the four simple elements <note>Earth, Air, Fire, and Water.</note> and the five types of perfect compounds <note>In the physics of the time, these "compounds" usually referred to minerals, plants, and various levels of animal life.</note>. 

These three classes they then distribute into nine chambers. The first chamber contains the three "units"—namely, the intellectual, the celestial, and the elemental <note>i.e., the letters representing 1, 10, and 100.</note>. The second chamber contains the "twos" <note>the dyads: 2, 20, and 200.</note>, the third contains the "threes" <note>the triads: 3, 30, and 300.</note>, and so on for the rest. These chambers are formed by the intersection of four parallel lines that cross each other at right angles, as is shown in the following figure.

And this method is most widely accepted among the Arabs; indeed, there is no other script that connects itself so readily and elegantly as the Arabic. However, one must understand that angelic spirits—since they are pure intellects and entirely incorporeal—are not actually compelled by seals, characters, painted figures, or any other human gestures. But because we are ignorant of their true essence and quality, we devote and consecrate characters, figures, and seals to them based on their names, their works, or otherwise according to our own dispositions. We do this not because we can compel them to us in any way, but so that we might rise toward them. 

Through such unknown characters and figures, we first direct our senses—both internal and external—toward them. Next, through a certain admiration of our reason, we are led into a religious veneration of them; and from there, we are swept up with our whole mind into ecstatic adoration. It is there, with wondrous faith, infallible hope, and life-giving love, that we invoke them in spirit and truth using their true names and characters, and thus we attain the power we have requested from them.

### Yet another method of characters, and concerning the seals of spirits which are received through revelation alone. Chapter XXXI.

<margin>e</margin>
There is another kind of character <note>In this context, a "character" refers to a magical sigil or symbolic mark</note> received by revelation alone, which cannot be discovered by any other logical reasoning. The power of these characters comes from the revealing deity itself; they are certain hidden seals of that deity, breathing the harmony of some divinity. Or, they are like certain treaties or pacts of an initiated covenant <note>A formal agreement or spiritual contract</note> between us and them. 

Of this kind is the seal shown to Constantine, which most called a cross, inscribed with Latin letters: **IN THIS CONQUER** <note>original: *IN HOC VINCE*; according to legend, Emperor Constantine saw this vision in the sky before his victory at the Milvian Bridge</note>. 

There is another revealed to Antiochus, surnamed Soter <note>Antiochus I Soter (r. 281–261 BC), a king of the Seleucid Empire</note>, in the figure of a pentagon, which proclaims health. For when this figure is resolved into letters, it spells out the word **HEALTH** <note>original Greek: *ὑγεία* (Hygeia)</note>. Through trust in the virtue and power of these signs, both kings reported a remarkable victory against their enemies. 

In the same way, Judas—who because of this event was later surnamed Maccabeus—when about to lead the Jews in battle against Antiochus Eupator, received that noble seal **MKBY** <note>original Hebrew: *מכבי* (Maccabee)</note> from an angel. By its power, they first slaughtered fourteen thousand men along with a huge number of elephants, and then later destroyed another thirty-five thousand of the enemy. For this seal is a representation of the four-letter name <note>The Tetragrammaton, the sacred four-letter name of God, YHWH</note>, and is a memorable symbol of the "Name of Seventy-Two Letters" through a numerical equality. Its full explanation is: **Who among the gods is like you, O Lord?** <note>original Hebrew: *יהוה באלים כמוך מי* (Mi Kamocha Ba’elim YHWH). The first letters of these words spell "MKBY," forming the name Maccabee</note>. Therefore, the figures of these three aforementioned seals should be formed as follows:

<note>The first seal contains a Chi-Rho symbol (the first two letters of Christ's name in Greek) with the Latin phrase "IN HOC VINCE" (In this sign, conquer). The second is a pentagram—a five-pointed star representing health and protection. The third contains Hebrew characters, specifically the word "Maccabee" (מ כ ב י), which was used as a protective name derived from the phrase "Who is like unto Thee among the gods, O Lord?"</note>

Furthermore, Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonic philosopher (c. 234–305 AD) who wrote extensively on magic and spirituality</note> speaks of these seals and characters in his book *On Oracles*, saying that the gods themselves indicated what things they take pleasure in, by what things they may be summoned, and what should be offered to them. They also showed what the figures of their own <term>simulacra</term> <note>A "simulacrum" is a physical image or statue believed to house a portion of a deity's essence</note> should look like, as well as the characters and the forms of Hecate; he notes that he learned these things from the oracle of Proserpina. And he says, <insert>as for the image,</insert> moreover, that Hecate prescribed how statues of her were to be fashioned: that they should be surrounded with wormwood, and that <insert>and how to prepare</insert> domestic mice should be painted, which were the most beautiful ornaments to her and most pleasing to her mind. <insert>And sacred rites for her</insert> required taking as many mice as she had forms; then blood, myrrh, storax, and certain other things were to be burned as incense. If these things were done, she would appear in a dream and give answers to the person performing the work. But we will provide the oracle of Hecate itself, for thus it says:

<margin>The Oracle of Hecate.</margin>
> Pay heed, I shall teach you what sort of image to make for me:
> Take a branch grown in a wild place, and place wormwood
> Around it; then carve it and paint mice,
> Such as are accustomed to dwell in houses; let these
> Be the most beautiful ornaments and most pleasing to our mind.
> Then grind together myrrh, incense, storax, and their blood;
> Sing sacred words over the mouse, and offer as many
> Mice as you see I have forms; then take laurel,
> And from its trunk fashion a sheath, and then
> Pour out pious prayers to the image, and pay the
> Required vows; if you do these things, you shall see me in sleep.

Such were the secret mysteries of the pagan gods and <term>daemons</term> <note>In this context, "daemons" refers to intermediary spirits, not necessarily "demons" in the modern sense</note> in ancient times, by which they persuaded men that they could be compelled, restrained, and bound. For this reason, Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who specialized in "theurgy," or divine magic</note> and Porphyry teach that it is necessary for one invoking sacred spirits to honor each one with its own proper respect, and to distribute to each what is fitting—consisting of thanks, offerings, gifts, sacrifices, words, and characters suitable to their condition and as similar to them as possible. Otherwise, one will by no means achieve the presence of the deities or spirits, nor the desired effect; indeed, those who are summoned will attempt to do harm, especially to those who behave negligently in such matters.

# ON OCCULT PHILOSOPHY.

## ¶ How good spirits are attracted to us, and how evil spirits are overcome by us. Chapter XXXII.

<margin>
How it is necessary to call upon spirits.
</margin>

<margin>
Book 11 of *The Golden Ass*.
</margin>

<margin>
Coptic matters. Coptos, a city of Egypt: where the divinities... <unclear>gather</unclear>, and every hour change their form, which is called Coptic. See Philis. Beroaldus. <note>Beroaldus was a 15th-century commentator on Apuleius; Coptos was an ancient Egyptian city associated with Isis.</note>
</margin>

The effective presence of religion achieves the results of spirits; for no work of any wonderful efficacy can be performed in religion unless some good spirit is present as the director and fulfiller of the work. As for good spirits: even if they are attracted to us in various ways, they can be bound by no chains—or at least only with great difficulty—but rather they are to be called upon by certain sacred adjurations. We read of this in Apuleius <note>Apuleius (c. 124–170 AD) was a Roman philosopher and author of *The Golden Ass*, a novel central to Renaissance magic</note>, calling "by the stars of heaven, by the powers of the underworld, by the natural elements, by the silences of the night, by the concepts attained, by the rising of the Nile, by the secrets of Memphis, and the <term>sistra</term> <note>A sacred rattle used in ancient Egyptian religious ceremonies, particularly those for the goddess Isis</note> of Pharia." And elsewhere in Porphyry:

> You who have emerged from the linen, who sit in the place, who sail in the ship, who change your shape every hour, and are transformed in every sign of the zodiac. <note>original: "Tu qui è lino emerſiſti..." This refers to Egyptian priests or deities associated with linen garments and the celestial journey.</note>

Through these and similar symbolic prayers and hymns, which are signs of divine virtues, spirits would sometimes accommodate themselves to human needs—not because they were compelled by any necessity, but freely and by a certain custom, being more easily reached when overcome by the prayers of those invoking them. Hence Hecate says in Porphyry’s *Book of Responses*:

->I have come here, entreated by your words.<-

->And in the same book she says elsewhere:<-

> Overcome by the prayers of men, the celestial powers
> Are forced to seek the earth, and reveal future events.

<margin>
The reason for the assistance of spirits.
</margin>

<margin>
Hence Jean Brodeau writes such things of the discoveries of the Magi: Angels sent by the Lord... the pious... with a flaming sword... <unclear>punishments</unclear>... and impose just duties upon them; thereafter he restrains them so they do not harm. If by chance he draws them by grace... he promises much by his virtue; for many spirits... will perform what one desires in his commands. Likewise regarding the penalty... This from the <term>bibio</term> <note>A bibio is a type of small insect, used here perhaps in a metaphorical or obscure alchemical sense</note> of Saturn.
</margin>

Moreover, the fellowship of divinity with the human mind ensures that the good spirits themselves willingly assist us. They communicate their power and virtue to us daily, helping us through illuminations, inspirations, oracles, prophecies, dreams, miracles, wonders, divinations, and omens. They act upon our souls as images fellow to themselves, shaping them by their own influences and making them most similar to themselves—to such an extent that our souls often perform wonders almost as great as those usually performed by the celestial spirits. Evil spirits, however, are overcome by us with the help of good ones, especially when the practitioner is strong in holiness toward God and chants sacred words and a "terrible speech"—that is, by conjuring through divine power, through the venerable names and signs of supernatural virtues, through miracles, through sacraments, through sacred mysteries, and the like. Malignant spirits fear these conjurations or exorcisms insofar as they are performed in the name of religion and divine virtue. Thus, even profane men often bind or cast out evil spirits through such sacred conjurations, for the spirits cannot endure them. Hence Cyprian <note>Saint Cyprian (c. 210–258 AD), an early Christian bishop</note> says in his book, *That Idols Are Not Gods*: "Demons, when adjured by the true God, immediately yield to us and confess, and are forced to depart from possessed bodies; they either leap out instantly or vanish gradually, according as the faith of the sufferer assists, or the grace of the one swearing inspires..."

# BOOK THREE

And Athanasius <note>St. Athanasius of Alexandria (c. 296–373 AD), a prominent Church Father</note> in his book *On Various Questions* says that there exists no word more terrible or more effective at destroying the power of demons than the beginning of the sixty-seventh Psalm: "Let God arise, and let his enemies be scattered" <note>original: "Exurgat deus, & dissipétur inimici eius." In modern Bibles, this is Psalm 68:1.</note>; for as soon as this word is spoken, the devil immediately vanishes, wailing and disappearing. Origen <note>An early Christian scholar (c. 184–253 AD) whose works were central to early theology, though later controversial</note>, in his work *Against Celsus*, says that the naming of the name of Jesus has often been seen to cast out countless demons from the souls and bodies of men, and to have exercised a very great power over those from whom the demons had been driven.

Often, even with threats and insults alone, we can restrain or repel evil demons—especially the lesser ones, such as <term>lamias</term> <note>In folklore, female spirits or monsters who were often said to haunt children or travelers</note>, <term>incubi</term> <note>Demons traditionally thought to visit people in their sleep</note>, and their like. We read of this in the works of Lucan <note>A Roman poet (39–65 AD), author of the epic *Pharsalia*</note> concerning that malevolent witch, who said:

> Now I shall call you by your true name,
> And leave the Stygian dogs in the light above;
> I shall follow you through the pyres; as a guardian at funerals
> I shall drive you from the tombs; I shall hunt you from every urn.
> And you, Hecate, who are accustomed to appear to the gods
> With a different, borrowed face—I shall show you in your pale, wasted form,
> And I shall forbid you from changing your hellish countenance.

And we read in the works of Philostratus <note>Flavius Philostratus (c. 170–247 AD), author of *The Life of Apollonius of Tyana*</note> that when Apollonius and his companions were traveling at night by the light of a clear moon, a phantom of a *lamia* encountered them. It turned itself now into one shape, now into another, and sometimes suddenly vanished from their sight. Apollonius, recognizing immediately what it was, rebuked it with heavy and insulting words and urged his companions to do the same; for he knew this was the best remedy against such invasions. When his companions obeyed his words, the shrieking phantom fled quickly like a ghost. For this kind of demon is so fearful that it is moved, trembles, and is driven away even by a feigned terror or by false and impossible threats. Concerning this, Chaeremon the sacred scribe says that these are the primary means by which demons are compelled.

Furthermore, as was said above, there is a certain kind of demon that is not so harmful, but is very close to humanity, so much so that they are even affected by human passions. Many of these enjoy the conversation of men and gladly live with them; some fall desperately in love with women, others with boys; others take pleasure in the company of various animals, whether domestic or wild. Some inhabit the woods and groves, others live around springs and meadows. Thus the **Fauns** and **Lemures** <note>spirits of the dead or restless ghosts</note> haunt the fields; the **Naiads**, the springs; the **Potamides**, the rivers; the **Nymphs**, the pools and waters; the **Oreades**, the mountains; the **Humedes**, the meadows; and the **Dryads** and **Hamadryads**, the forests. These same forests are also inhabited by **Satyrs** and **Sylvans**, who take pleasure in trees and grassy turf, just as the **Naptae** and **Agaptae** delight in flowers; the **Dodonae**, in acorns; and the **Paleae** and **Feniliae**, in fodder and the countryside. Therefore, whoever wishes to invoke these may easily do so in the places where they dwell, by alluring them with fragrant fu- <note>The text cuts off mid-word, likely "fumigations" or "fumes."</note>

The same man also discovered a similar thing among the Ephesians in the form of an old beggar, who was the cause of a plague; who, having been crushed by stones at his command, appeared as a Molossian dog <note>a large, ancient breed of guard dog</note>, and soon the plague ceased. This should be known: whoever works intellectually with evil demons will bind them through the command of good ones; but whoever works only in a worldly manner will work a judgment upon himself for Gehenna <note>a place of spiritual punishment or hell</note>.

### ¶ Concerning the bonds of spirits, and their adjurations and banishments. Chapter XXXIII.

The bonds by which spirits are bound, entreated, or banished are threefold. Some of them are taken from the elemental world: for instance, when we adjure a spirit through lower and natural things related or adverse to it, insofar as we wish to invoke or banish it—such as by flowers, herbs, animals, snow, ice, the underworld, fire, and the like—just as these are also often included in divine praises, blessings, and consecrations, as is evident in the *Song of the Three Children* <note>A biblical hymn from the Book of Daniel</note> and in that Psalm, *Praise the Lord from the heavens* <note>original: "Laudate dominū de cœlis," Psalm 148</note>, and in the consecrations and blessing of the Paschal candle. For this bond works upon the spirits' power of perception by reason of love or hatred, insofar as those spirits preside over or favor some natural thing (or even something beyond nature), and abhor another; just as things of this kind are mutually bound among themselves...

From this comes that saying of Proclus <note>A Greek Neoplatonist philosopher (412–485 AD) who wrote extensively on magic and theology</note>: "Just as the lion fears the rooster, especially a white one, so a spirit appearing in the form of a lion suddenly vanished when a rooster was presented." The second bond is taken from the celestial world, when for instance we adjure by the heaven, by the stars, by their motions, rays, light, grace, brightness, nobility, strength, influence, wonders, and such like: and this bond operates on spirits by way of a certain admonition and example. <margin>The third bond:</margin>
The third bond is from the intellectual and divine world itself, which is perfected by religion; as for example when we adjure by the <term>sacraments</term> <note>sacred rites of the church</note>, by miracles, by the divine names, by the sacred seals, and the other mysteries of religion: wherefore this bond is the highest and strongest of all, acting upon spirits

<margin>How much power superstition has:</margin>
Superstition also has great power in these matters, through the transfer of some sacramental rite to that which we intend to bind or hinder—such as, for example, the rites of excommunication, burial, or funeral services—for the purpose of exterminating diseases, or serpents, mice, or little worms, which we read has been done in many places, and is still customary to be done.

### On the animatical order and heroes, Chapter XXXIV.

After the choirs of blessed spirits, the next is the <term>animatical order</term> <note>the order pertaining to "souls" (animae) that have attained a higher state</note> which Hebrew theologians call <term>Issim</term> <note>original: "Issim," often translated as "men" or "strong ones" in angelic hierarchies</note>, that is, strong and robust men. We read many such accounts regarding Hercules, Atlas, Aesculapius, and other heroes of the nations among the ancient poets, historians, and philosophers. ### ¶ On mortal and earthly gods. Chapter XXXV.

<margin>Mortal gods.</margin>
<margin>Moses to Pharaoh.</margin>
<margin>The God of Abraham.</margin>
<margin>The gods of the earth.</margin>
<margin>Princes of god.</margin>
<margin>Janus.</margin>
<margin>Ovid.</margin>
**A**fter these, the next are the mortal gods, whom we likewise call heroes, and earthly gods, or companions of the celestial gods; namely, the kings, princes, and pontiffs by whom this world is ruled, and by whose laws it is arranged. We look up to, worship, and venerate them as gods for this reason: because God himself allowed his own name to be shared with them. He confirmed this to them by their own title, calling them "gods," just as he said to Moses: *I have made you a god to Pharaoh* <note>Exodus 7:1</note>. Elsewhere he commanded concerning them, saying: *You shall not revile the gods* <note>Exodus 22:28</note>. And again: *If the theft is hidden, the master of the house shall be brought to the gods* <note>original: "ad deos"; often translated as "to the judges" in Exodus 22:8</note>. The Psalmist also says: *The princes of the peoples are gathered together with the God of Abraham, for the mighty gods of the earth are greatly exalted* <note>Psalm 47:9</note>. And elsewhere: *God stands in the council of the gods; in the midst, however, he judges the gods* <note>Psalm 82:1</note>. And a little later: *I said, you are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High* <note>Psalm 82:6</note>. Indeed, he even commanded that they be worshiped and venerated, decreeing tithes and first-fruits for them, granting them the right of the sword, forbidding that they be cursed, and commanding that obedience be rendered to them even if they are ill-tempered. For this reason, all antiquity called its princes "gods" and worshiped them as divine powers, just as Janus testifies in Ovid, in the first book of the *Fasti*, saying:

> ->Then I was reigning, when the earth was capable of gods,<-
> ->And divine beings were mingled in human places.<-

And the divine Plato, in the third book of the *Republic*, established that princes, both living and dead, should be celebrated with divine honors. This institution has been received among all nations and from the very beginning: namely, to deify princes with divine honors and to consecrate them with eternal memory. Hence...

They also called the heavens, the stars, the days, and the months by their names. Hence, January is named after Janus, July after Julius [Caesar], and August after Augustus. In this same way, the day of Mercury <note>Wednesday</note> is named after Mercury Trismegistus, and the day of Jove <note>Thursday</note> is named after Jove. We read that this custom was observed not only by the Egyptians, Greeks, and Romans, but even by the most distant barbarians, such as the Goths, Danes, and Teutons.

Hence, as witnessed by Saxo Grammaticus <note>A 12th-century Danish historian and author of the *Gesta Danorum*</note>, the day those [Romans] call "Mercury’s day," these [Norsemen] call "Odin’s day" [Wednesday]. What those call "Jove’s day," these call "Thor’s day" [Thursday], named after Odin and Thor, who were once kings of the Goths and Danes. Nor is it without reason that the Goths are so named, since in their own language they call the supreme god "Goth" <note>Agrippa is suggesting a folk etymology connecting the tribe of the Goths to the word "God"</note>. From this, the Teutons are also so named because they called the god they worshipped, Mars, "Teutan," by which name the Gauls also referred to Mercury.

Therefore, kings and high priests—provided they are just—are associates of the gods and are endowed with similar power. Hence, they cure diseases by touch or word alone, and sometimes they even command the seasons and the heavens, just as Virgil sang of Augustus:

Moses also divided the Red Sea, and Joshua the Jordan, and they led the people across with dry feet. Alexander the Macedonian did something similar when leading his army across [the sea]. Sometimes they are even empowered by a prophetic spirit, as we read of Caiaphas in the Holy Scripture, who prophesied because he was the high priest of that year. Since it is so—that the Lord of the earth willed for kings and high priests to be called "gods" through the sharing of name and power—it certainly befits us to deserve well of them, to prefer their judgments to our own, and clearly to obey, supplicate, and adore them, and to honor them with every kind of veneration, and to revere the supreme God himself within them.

<margin>God’s omnipotence.</margin>
Since God is himself omnipotent, by His will alone—not by any necessity of nature—He created the world not from pre-existing matter, but from nothing <note>original: "ex nihilo"</note>. And since He is the highest goodness, He embraced His Word <note>original: "verbum"</note>—which is the primary Idea of all things—with His perfect will and essential love. He fabricated this external world according to the model of the internal, namely the "ideal" world <note>The world of archetypes or perfect concepts in the mind of God</note>. He 
<margin>The image of God, the world, the measure, and man.</margin>
put forth nothing from the essence of the Idea, yet He created from nothing that which He held from eternity through that Idea. God also created man in His own image. For just as the world is the image of God, so man is the image of the world. From this, 
<margin>The lesser world.</margin>
some believe it was said that man was not simply created as the "image of God," but *unto* the image <note>original: "ad imaginem"</note>, as if he were the image of an image. Therefore, he is called the **Microcosm** <term>Microcosm: From the Greek 'mikros' (small) and 'kosmos' (world), meaning 'the lesser world'</term>, which is to say, the "minor world." The world is a rational and immortal living being <note>original: "animal"</note>. 
<margin>Death is a hollow name.</margin>
Man is likewise a rational living being, but mortal—that is, dissolvable. For (as **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure to whom many esoteric writings are attributed</note> says), since the world itself is immortal, it is impossible for any part of it to perish; therefore, "to die" is a hollow name. And just as a vacuum is nowhere to be found, so too is death. We say that man [dies] when the soul and body are separated, not because any part of them perishes or is turned into nothing. Nevertheless, the true image of God is His Word: wisdom, life, light, and truth, existing through itself. 
<margin>Similarity of the human soul.</margin>
Of this image, the human soul is a reflection. It is because of this that we are said to be made "in the image of God," and not in the image of the world or other creatures. For just as God can neither be touched, nor perceived by the ears, nor seen by the eyes, so the soul of man can neither be seen, heard, nor touched. And just as God Himself is infinite and can be compelled by no one, so too the human soul is free, and can neither be forced nor measured. Furthermore, as God carries this entire world and whatever is in it by His mind alone, so the human soul encompasses the world in its thought. And what is unique to it alone along with God: as God moves and governs the whole world by His will alone, so the human soul acts upon and rules its own body by its will alone. 
<margin>The honor of man.</margin>
Therefore, it was necessary that the soul of man, thus "sealed" by the Word of God, should also clothe the corporeal man according to the most perfect model of the world. 
<margin>What is contained within man.</margin>
Man, therefore, is called "another world" and "another image of God," because he holds within himself everything that is contained in the greater world <note>the macrocosm</note>, so that nothing is left out that cannot be found truly and realistically within man himself. And all these things within him perform the same functions as they do in the greater world. There are in him the elements, through the truest properties of their nature. There is in him an ethereal body <note>original: "ethernum corpusculum"</note>, the vehicle of the soul, corresponding in proportion to the heavens. There are in him the vegetative life of plants, the senses of animals, a celestial spirit, angelic reason, and a divine mind—and the true union of all these flowing together into one is a divine possession. 
<margin>Man is every creature.</margin>
Hence, in the sacred scriptures, man is called "every creature." And not only is man made into "another world" by encompassing all its parts within himself, but he even conceives and contains God Himself. Hence **Xystus** the Pythagorean <note>Sextus, a philosopher whose "Sentences" were popular in the Renaissance</note>...

### ->ON OCCULT PHILOSOPHY<-

<margin>Man is the temple of God.</margin>
**Pythagoras** <note>original: "Pythagoricus"</note> says that the mind of man is the temple of God, which **Paul** expressed much more clearly when he said: "You are the temple of God." The Holy Scripture testifies to this same truth in many places. Man is therefore the most expressive likeness of God, because man contains within himself everything that is in God. But God contains all things through a certain excellence, by His own power and in simplicity, as the cause and principle of all things; yet He gave to man the power to contain all things in a similar way, but in act and composition, as a kind of nexus, bond, and knot of all things <note>This refers to the "Great Chain of Being" where man sits in the middle, connecting the spiritual and material worlds</note>. Therefore, man alone enjoys this honor: that he shares a correspondence <note>original: "symbolum"</note> with all things, a cooperation with all things, and a communion with all things. 

<margin>The symbols of man.</margin>
He corresponds with matter in his own physical substance; with the elements in his fourfold body; with plants in his vegetative power; with animals in his sensory power; with the heavens in his ethereal spirit and the influence <term>influence: the celestial "flowing in" of power from stars to the earthly realm</term> of the higher parts upon the lower; with angels in intellect and wisdom; and with God in the containment of all things. 

<margin>Man’s communion with God.</margin>
He communes with God and the divine Intelligences through faith and wisdom; with the heavens and celestial beings through reason and discourse; and with all lower things through the senses and dominion. He acts with all things and has power over all things—even over God Himself—by understanding and loving Him. And just as God knows all things, so too can man know all knowable things, since he possesses as his proper object "being" in general, or (as others say) Truth itself. Nor is there anything found in man—no disposition—in which some spark of divinity does not shine; nor is there anything in God that is not also represented in man.

<margin>Knowledge of oneself.</margin>
Whoever, therefore, shall know himself, shall know all things in himself. He shall know, first of all, God, in whose image he was made; he shall know the world, whose likeness he bears; he shall know all creatures, with whom he shares a correspondence. He will know what nourishment <note>original: "fomenti," implying support or vital fuel</note> he can obtain from stones, plants, animals, elements, the heavens, spirits, and angels, and from every single thing. He will understand how he may adapt each thing to another in its proper place, time, order, measure, proportion, and harmony, and how to draw them to himself and lead them down, just as a magnet draws iron. 

And **Geber** <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan, the legendary 8th-century polymath and "father of alchemy"</note>, in his *Summa of Alchemy*, teaches that no one can reach the perfection of that art who does not know its principles within himself. The more one knows himself, the greater the power of attraction he acquires, and the greater and more wonderful works he performs. He shall ascend to such perfection that he is made a son of God. 

<margin>The perfection and dignity of man: The Son of God.</margin>
He is transformed into that same image which is God and is united with Him—a gift granted neither to angels, nor to the world, nor to any other creature, but only to man: namely, the ability to become a son of God and be united to God. When man is united to God, all things within man are also united: first the mind, then the spirit and the animal powers, the vegetative power, and the elements, even down to matter itself. This draws the body—of which the mind is the form—along with it, leading it into a better lot and a celestial nature, until it is glorified in...
