### ->BOOK THREE<-

mortality; and this which we have already said is the peculiar gift of man, from which this dignity of the divine image is his own, and not shared with any other creature. <margin>The three powers of man.</margin> There are other theologians who assign the three powers of man—memory, intellect, and will—as the image of the Divine Trinity. And there are those who, going further, place this image not only in those three powers (which they call **primary acts**), but also in **secondary acts**. Thus, just as memory represents the Father, intellect the Son, and will the Holy Spirit; so too the word produced by our intellect, the love flowing from the will, and the intellect itself (having its object present and producing) denote the same Son, Spirit, and Father. More secret theologians <note>referring to practitioners of mystical or esoteric theology</note> teach that, moreover, each of our individual members represents something in God, whose image they bear. We also represent God in our passions, though only by a certain analogy; for we read in the Sacred Scriptures of God’s anger, fury, repentance, satisfaction, love, hatred, play <note>original: "ludum"</note>, delight, pleasures, indignation, and similar things. We have spoken of the divine members previously in a way that may be relevant here.

<margin>Hermes Trismegistus acknowledged the mystery of the Trinity</margin> **Hermes Trismegistus** <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure regarded by Renaissance scholars as a contemporary of Moses and a primary source of ancient wisdom</note>, having also confessed the Divine Trinity, describes it as Intellect, Life, and Radiance—which elsewhere he calls Word, Mind, and Spirit. He says that man, made in the image of God, represents this same trinity. For in man there is an understanding mind, a life-giving word, and a spirit that diffuses itself everywhere like a divine radiance, filling, moving, and connecting all things. However, this is not to be understood as the **natural spirit** (which is the medium by which the soul is united with the flesh and body, through which the body lives and acts, and through which one limb acts upon another, as we discussed in the first book). Instead, we are dealing here with the **rational spirit**, which is nonetheless "corporeal" in a certain way; yet it does not have a thick, tangible, and visible body, but a most subtle body that easily unites with the mind—specifically, that higher and divine part that is within us. Nor should anyone wonder if we say the rational soul is that spirit and something corporeal, or that it possesses some flavor of corporality while it is in the body and uses it as an instrument—provided you understand what the **Platonists** mean by that ethereal "small-body" <note>original: "corpusculum"</note> of the soul, which is its **vehicle** <note>In Neoplatonism, the "vehicle of the soul" (okhema) is a subtle body that mediates between the immaterial soul and the physical body</note>.

<margin>The Platonists posit three things in man.</margin> **Plotinus** and all the Platonists after Trismegistus similarly posit three things in man, which they call the supreme, the lowest, and the middle. The **supreme** is that divine thing which they call the Mind, or the "higher portion," or the illuminated intellect. **Moses** in Genesis calls it the "breath of life" <note>original: "spiraculum vitarum"</note>, breathed into us by God or His spirit. The **lowest** is the sensitive soul, which they also call the "image" <note>original: "idolum"</note>. The Apostle **Paul** calls it the "animal man."

<meta>This page continues from the previous discussion on the spiritual "Word" and the generation of miracles. -># ON OCCULT PHILOSOPHY.<-

...a certain divine substance, indivisible, and present in its entirety to every part of the body, produced by an incorporeal author in such a way that it depends solely upon the power of the agent, and not upon the womb of matter. The soul is a **substantial number** <term>substantial number: a Pythagorean and Platonic concept where "number" refers not to a count, but to a formal, harmonizing principle that gives reality to a being</term>, uniform, self-turning, and rational, surpassing all material and bodily things by a vast interval. Its allotment is not according to matter, nor does it proceed from lower and coarser things, but from an efficient cause. For it is not a "quantity" number, but is removed from all bodily laws; hence it is neither divided nor multiplied by parts. Therefore, the soul is a certain divine substance, emanating from divine fountains, carrying a number with it—not indeed that divine number by which the Creator disposed all things, but a **rational number** <note>original: "rationalẽ numerũ"</note>, through which, having a proportion with all things, it is able to understand all things. 

Such a human soul, according to the opinion of the Platonists, proceeding immediately from God, is joined to this coarser body through appropriate intermediaries. Hence, first in its very descent, it is wrapped in a celestial and airy little body, which they call the **ethereal vehicle of the soul** <note>original: "æthereum animæ vehiculum," also known as the "astral body" or *okhema* in Neoplatonism; it serves as a bridge between the immaterial soul and the physical flesh</note>, and others call the chariot of the soul. By this medium, at the command of God—who is the center of the world—it is first infused into the middle point of the heart, which is the center of the human body. From there, it is diffused through all the parts and members of its body, when it joins its "chariot" to the natural heat, and through that heat to the **spirit** <term>spirit: here meaning the "vital spirit" or *pneuma*, a subtle vapor generated in the heart that carries the soul's commands to the nerves</term> generated from the heart. Through this spirit, it immerses itself in the humors <note>The four bodily fluids: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile</note>, and through those it clings to the limbs. It becomes equally close to all of these, even though it is poured from one into another, just as the heat of a fire clings closely to air and water, even though it is carried through the air to reach the water. Thus it is clear how the immortal soul, by means of an immortal little body (namely, the ethereal vehicle), is enclosed in a coarser and mortal body. 

When, however, through disease or some evil, these intermediaries are loosened or fail, then the soul itself recollects itself through each intermediary and flows back into the heart, which was the soul’s first receptacle. But when the spirit of the heart fails and the heat is extinguished, the soul leaves the heart and the man dies. The soul then flies away with this ethereal vehicle, and once it has departed, guardian **geniuses** <note>Guiding spirits or "daemons" assigned to a person at birth</note> and demons follow it and lead it to the judge. Once the sentence is passed, God leads the good souls peacefully to glory, while a violent demon drags the evil ones to punishment.

### ¶ What divine gifts man receives from above from the individual orders of the heavens and intelligences. Cap. XXXVIII.

<margin>
What man receives from the planets:
Saturn.
Jupiter.
Mars.
</margin>
Through the seven planets, as if through instruments from the highest source of all goods, all virtues are diffused into men: through **Saturn**, sublime contemplation, profound understanding, gravity of judgment, firm speculation, stability, and immovable purpose. Through **Jupiter**, unshakable prudence, temperance, benignity, piety, modesty, justice, faith, grace, religion, equity, clemency, and royalty. Through **Mars**, undaunted truth, constant strength and fortitude, the ardor of high spirit, and the power of action and practice.

<margin>Vain is the labor of men.</margin>
Therefore, they all labor in vain who, trusting only in the natural course and the strength and favor of lower things, believe they can reach the divine; and those who, fixing their foot in the heavens, strive to seize from celestial favor those things which ought to be received from God alone. For these lower things—I mean animals, herbs, stones, and metals—have their power supplied by the heaven; the heaven truly by the intelligences; and these by the Creator, in whom all things pre-exist with the greatest power. Just as in man himself—the **microcosm** <term>microcosm: literally "the lesser world," the idea that a human being is a miniature map of the entire universe</term>—there is no limb that does not correspond to some element, some planet, some intelligence, and some measure and numbering in the **archetype** <term>archetype: the original divine blueprint or "Master Idea" in the mind of God</term>, as we have shown above.

### ¶ Chapter XXXIX. How celestial influences, though they are good by nature, are corrupted in these lower things and become the causes of evil.

<margin>Chrysippus</margin>
<margin>Who is the cause of evils.</margin>
Since all virtue and power is from above—from God, from the intelligences, and from the stars, who can neither err nor do evil—it is necessary that all evils, and whatever discordant and dissonant thing is found in these lower realms, proceed not from the malice of the influence, but from the bad disposition of the recipient, just as Chrysippus <note>A Stoic philosopher (c. 279–206 BC) known for his works on logic and ethics</note> rightly sang:

> How falsely mortals accuse the gods, and foolishly complain:
> For we ourselves are the cause of our own evils,
> And each man is harmed by his own folly.
> <note>original: "Quàm falſo accuſant ſuperos, ſtulteq; queruntur / Mortales: etenim noſtrorum cauſa malorum / Ipſi nos ſumus, & ſua quenq; vecordia lædit."</note>

Hence Jupiter, remembering the fate of Aegisthus <note>The lover of Clytemnestra who murdered Agamemnon; he was eventually killed by Agamemnon's son, Orestes</note> who was killed by Orestes, says in the council of the gods in Homer:
<margin>Homer.</margin>

> O what a deed! The mortal race first blames the gods,
> And thinks us the cause and fountain of the evils
> Which come: but they themselves, through their own wicked deeds,
> Seek out troubles for themselves by their own will, even against fate.
> <note>original: "O facinus, mortale genus nos numina primum / Incuſat, cauſamq; putat fontemq; malorum / Quæ veniunt: ſua ſed peſſunt ob facta nefanda, / Cum præter fatum ſibi ſponte incommoda quęrant."</note>

¶ Therefore, when the perversity of the subject receives the influence perversely, or when its weakness cannot tolerate the power of the higher things, then from the influence of the celestials—received thus into matter full of discords—there results something dissonant, deformed, and evil. Nevertheless, the celestial powers always remain good. While they exist in themselves and flow from the Giver of Lights <note>A reference to James 1:17, "Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, and cometh down from the Father of lights."</note> through the holy intelligences and the heavens until they reach the Moon, their influence is good, as if in the first degree. But afterward, when it is received in a baser subject, the influence itself becomes base: for then, because of the diverse nature of the recipient, it is received in diverse ways; and since the qualities within that same subject are in conflict with one another, the influence also varies, and as the subject suffers...

### BOOK THREE. CLVI

...it suffers: from which at last, out of all things contained within the subject, something results that is quite different from what the higher powers pour in. Thus, a harmful quality in these lower things is far removed from the celestial influence itself. And therefore, just as the misfortune of a bleary-eyed person <note>original: *lippientis* — referring to someone with inflamed or watery eyes who finds light painful</note> should not be blamed on the light, nor a fire on the element of fire, nor wounds on the iron, nor chains and prisons on the judge—but rather on those who are poorly disposed and who act wickedly—so also the blame for the flow of evils must not be cast upon the celestial influences.

<margin>In the well-disposed, all things work together for good.</margin>
Therefore, in those of us who are well-disposed, the influences of the higher powers all work together for good; but in those poorly disposed, and in whom that divine spark within us has receded because of our sins, all things turn toward evil.

<margin>The cause of evils.</margin>
The cause of all our evils is therefore sin, which is the disordering and **distemper** <term>distemper: a lack of balance or harmony among the bodily fluids or spiritual states</term> of our soul. When the soul is thus poorly governed, or prostrate and declining from what the celestial influences require, all things rebel and are thrown out of balance to our destruction. Then, in the human body—which is otherwise most temperate and composed of the most harmonious symmetry—there arises a disorder of the elements.

<margin>Effects of a distempered element.</margin>
Evil **humors** <term>humors: the four vital fluids (blood, phlegm, black bile, yellow bile) believed to control health and temperament</term> rise up, and even the good humors become disordered and separated from one another, and they vex and torment the body in a cycle. Then a most violent dissonance is felt, whether from excess, or from lack, or from some internal accident, or from excessive food, whence surplus humors are produced. For the same reason, illnesses arise, and even the **animal spirits** <term>animal spirits: subtle vapors believed to carry instructions from the brain to the muscles; the "drivers" of the nervous system</term>, having lost their restraint, clash in battle. Then the celestial influences, which are otherwise good in themselves, are rendered harmful to them, just as the light of the Sun is to poorly-functioning eyes.

<margin>What superior things flow into the wicked.</margin>
Then **Saturn** pours in anxiety, weariness, melancholy, delusions, sadness, stubbornness, rigidity, blasphemy, despair, lies, the phantoms of spirits <note>original: *laruas lemurū*</note>, the terrors of the graves, the dread of funeral pyres, and the provocations of demons.

<margin>Effects of adverse planets.</margin>
**Jupiter** then pours in greed and wicked opportunities for wealth, and tyranny. **Mars** pours in impetuous rage, profane arrogance, the rashness of audacity, and fierce stubbornness. The **Sun**, however, pours in imperious pride and unquenchable ambition. **Venus** pours in the deceptions of concupiscence, lewd loves, and shameful lusts. **Mercury** pours in frauds, deceits, lies, the machinations of evil-doers, and a readiness for sinning. The **Moon** pours in the unstable progress of all things, and whatever is contrary to human nature. And in this way, man himself, because of his own lack of likeness to the celestial things, receives harm where he ought to have gathered a benefit. Because of this same dissonance with the celestial things (as Proclus <note>Proclus (412–485 AD) was a Greek Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote extensively on how divine power descends through the levels of reality.</note> says), men are then subjected to evil demons, who exert themselves like the **officers of God** <margin>Officers of God</margin> <term>lictores: in ancient Rome, lictors were officials who carried the fasces (rods and axes) to execute the commands and punishments of magistrates</term> in tormenting them. Then there come upon them visitations by evil angels until they are purged again by the necessary cleansings, and man is returned to his celestial nature. Therefore, the **best Magus** <term>magus: a wise practitioner of natural and divine philosophy</term> can prevent many evils that would otherwise proceed from the arrangement of the stars, by sensing their nature beforehand, and by anticipating, guarding against, and fortifying the self.

### ¶ Chapter XL. That a divine character is impressed upon every human being, by the power of which one can attain to the working of wonders.

<margin>
The nature of the elephant.
The nature of the tiger.
Why fierce beasts fear fragile man.
The obedience of elephants.
The excellence of man.
The seal of God.
The sword of God.
Why man is loved above others.
Adam’s power before sin.
The loss of the sinner.
</margin>

It has been proven through significant experience that a certain power of dominating and binding is implanted in man by nature. As Pliny <note>Gaius Plinius Secundus (AD 23–79), a Roman author who wrote the *Natural History*.</note> testifies, it is said that an elephant will kindly and peacefully show the way to a traveler wandering lost in the wilderness. The same elephant, it is said, if it notices a man's footprints before seeing the man himself, will tremble with fear of an ambush, stop still, look around, and be struck with terror. In the same way, the tiger, more ferocious than all other wild beasts, is said to immediately move its cubs upon seeing a man. We read many similar things in various authors who have written great volumes about animals. Yet, from where do these animals recognize that man is to be feared, when they have never seen him? And if they have often seen and known him, why do they fear him, being so much greater than him in size, strength, and speed? All the historians of animals inquire into and hint at what this human nature might be that strikes such fear into wild beasts, but they have left it to others to teach and prove.

Concerning this, therefore, Apollonius of Tyana <note>A Greek Neopythagorean philosopher and reputed miracle-worker from the 1st century AD.</note> (as we read in Philostratus), upon seeing a boy leading a massive elephant, was asked by Damis why such a vast animal showed such obedience to a small child. He responded that it was due to a certain "active tremor" <note>original: *tremore quodam actiuo* — a spiritual vibration or aura of authority</note> instilled into man by the Creator. Sensing this, all lower creatures and animals fear and revere man himself, who is like a terrifying **character** <term>character: in this context, a mystical mark, brand, or seal of identity and power</term> and a seal of God impressed upon him. By this mark, all things subjected to him recognize their superior, whether it be a servant or an animal. For otherwise, neither would a boy rule over herds and elephants, nor a king terrify a people, nor a judge frighten the guilty.

This character, therefore, is impressed upon humans by the divine Idea, which the Kabbalists <note>Followers of Kabbalah, a school of Jewish mysticism.</note> of the Hebrews call *Pahad* <note>original Hebrew: פחד — meaning "Dread" or "Fear." It is the fifth Sephirah (divine attribute) in the Tree of Life.</note>, and also the "left hand" and the "sword of God." Nor indeed does man only possess a sign by which he may be feared, but also one by which he may be loved, the Idea of which in the divine numerations <note>original: *numerationibus* — referring to the Sephiroth, the ten attributes or emanations in Kabbalah.</note> is called *Hesed* <note>original Hebrew: חסד — meaning "Mercy" or "Loving-kindness." It is the fourth Sephirah.</note>, which signifies clemency, and the "right hand" and "scepter of God."

From these divine numerations, through the Intelligences and the stars, signs and characters are impressed upon each of us according to our capacity and purity. These signs the first-formed man <note>referring to Adam</note> undoubtedly possessed in all integrity and fullness when, attracted by peaceful gentleness or subjected by terror, all living creatures came to him as if to their lord, so that he might give them names. However, after the sin of transgression, he fell from that dignity, along with all his descendants. Nevertheless, that character is not entirely extinguished within us; but the more someone is weighed down by sin, the further they are removed from these divine characters and the less they receive of them. Thus, where he ought to receive kindness and reverence, he instead finds himself...

<margin>Cain’s fear.</margin>
...falls into servitude and fear, both of animals and of men and demons. Sensing this, Cain was afraid, saying to God: *Everyone who finds me will kill me* <note>Genesis 4:14.</note>. Indeed, he feared beasts and demons, not so much men, who were very few at that time. In ancient times, however, many men who lived in innocence and led the best of lives still enjoyed that obedience and power, just as Samson, David, and Daniel had power over lions; Elisha over bears; Paul over the viper; and many anchorites <note>term for early Christian hermits who lived in the desert.</note> lived in the deserts, in the dens and caves of wild beasts, without fear and without receiving any harm. For just as that <margin>The power of the just.</margin> divine character <note>original: "character," referring to the spiritual "mark" or seal of God's image in man.</note> is darkened by sin, so when sin is purged and expiated, it shines forth again more and more.

### ¶ What happens to man after death: various opinions. Chapter XLI.

<margin>Death is common to all men.</margin>
It is established as a law for all men to die once, and death is fatal to all. But one kind of death is natural, another is violent, another is voluntarily undertaken, and another is imposed by human laws for a crime, or inflicted by God because of a sin, so that they seem to have paid a penalty for their faults rather than simply paying a debt to nature—a penalty which (as the masters of the Hebrews <note>the Rabbis.</note> say) God remits to no one. Hence, the assembly of Hezekiah <note>referring to the "Men of Hezekiah," a group of scholars mentioned in Jewish tradition and the Bible.</note> handed down that after the destruction of the sanctuary <margin>Many kinds of deaths.</margin> <note>The Temple in Jerusalem.</note>, even though no order of judicial execution remained, nonetheless no one guilty of death escaped without retaliation through the fourfold types of punishments by which they used to be condemned. For he who had deserved death by stoning was, by God’s dispensation, either thrown from a height, or trampled by beasts, or overwhelmed by a ruin or some other cause. He who had deserved fire was consumed either by a conflagration, or by a poisonous bite, or by the strike of a serpent, or by toxin. He who would have perished by the sword was slaughtered either by the violence of the state, or by a popular riot, or by a faction, or by the treachery of bandits. He who was to be hanged by a noose was either suffocated in a whirlpool of water or extinguished by some other strangling plague. And by this same reasoning of doctrine, the great Origen <note>An early Christian theologian (c. 184–253 AD).</note> judged that the Gospel of Christ should be explained: *He who strikes with the sword, perishes by the sword* <note>Matthew 26:52.</note>. Furthermore, the pagan philosophers declare that such an order of retaliation is **Adrastia** <margin>Adrastia.</margin> <note>The Greek goddess of inescapable destiny and retribution.</note>, namely, the inevitable power of divine laws, by which it is repaid to everyone in future circuits according to the reason and merits of their prior life. Thus, he who ruled unjustly in a prior life might fall back into a state of servitude in another life; he who polluted his hands with blood would be forced to undergo <margin>The penalty of retaliation.</margin> retaliation <note>term: "talio" or Lex Talionis, the law of "an eye for an eye."</note>. He who lived a beastly life might be cast down, having rolled back into a brutal body. Plotinus writes about these things in his book *On One’s Own Proper Demon* <margin>Plotinus.</margin> <note>Plotinus (c. 204–270 AD) was the founder of Neoplatonism; the work cited is Ennead III, 4.</note>, saying: "Those men who preserved their human character are born again as men. But those who used only their senses return as brute animals, in such a way that those who were guided by sense accompanied by anger are born as <note>The word "fera" (wild beasts) appears with a horizontal strike-through line in the original printing</note> wild beasts; while those who were guided by sense through lust..."

...and they turn into deceitful and gluttonous animals for their pleasure. Truly, if they lived not so much by their senses but by a degeneration of the senses, they sprout again as plants; for in these, the vital force alone flourished most greatly, and their whole care was directed toward being transformed into plants. Truly, those who lived excessively charmed by musical melodies, but were not otherwise depraved, are reborn as musical animals. And those who ruled without reason become eagles, unless they were infected by some other wickedness. But he who has achieved civic virtue returns as a man. Even Solomon himself in the Proverbs calls man now a lion, a tiger, a bear, or a boar; now a hare, a greyhound, or a rabbit; now he names him an ant, a hedgehog, a serpent, or a spider; now an eagle, a lizard, a rooster, or another bird, and many things of this kind.

<margin>The Hebrew Kabbalists on the soul.</margin>
<margin>Souls return three times into this life.</margin>
<margin>The science of the ancients regarding the dead.</margin>
Truly, the Hebrew Kabbalists <note>Jewish mystics who interpret the hidden meanings of the Torah.</note> do not admit that souls are cast down into brute beasts; however, they do not deny that those who have utterly shaken off reason are left to brutal affection and imagination in the next life. They also assert that souls revolve back to this world three times, and no more, because they believe this number is abundantly sufficient for the purging of sins, according to that passage in Job: *He delivered his soul from going into destruction, but living he should see the light. Behold, God works all these things three times for each, that he may call back their souls from corruption, and enlighten them with the light of the living.* <note>Job 33:28–30. Agrippa interprets "three times" as three cycles of reincarnation.</note> But now at last, let us see what the ancients thought concerning the dead. When a man dies, the body returns to the earth from which it was taken, and the mind returns to the heavens from which it descended, just as Ecclesiastes says: *The dust returns to its earth from which it was, and the spirit returns to God, who gave it,* <note>Ecclesiastes 12:7.</note> which Lucretius expressed in these verses:

> Likewise, that which was from the earth before returns
> To the earth; and that which was sent from the ethereal regions,
> The shining temples of heaven receive it once again. <note>original: Lucretius, *De Rerum Natura* 2.999–1001.</note>

<margin>Ovid.</margin>
->But Ovid says it better in these verses,<-
> Man has four parts: the shades, the flesh, the spirit, and the ghost:
> Four places receive these four things:
> The earth covers the flesh, the ghost flits around the tomb,
> The Underworld holds the shades, the spirit seeks the stars.

<margin>The rite for expiating a corpse.</margin>
Therefore, the forsaken flesh and the body deprived of life is called a corpse (*cadaver*). According to the Hebrew theologians, this is left in the power of the demon Zazel <note>often identified with the scapegoat or a desert demon in Jewish tradition</note>, of whom it is said in Scripture: *You shall eat earth all the days of your life,* and elsewhere: *The dust of the earth is his bread.* Since man was created from the dust of the earth, that demon is called the lord of flesh and blood so long as the body has not been expiated and sanctified by the proper funeral rites. For this reason, and not without cause, the ancient fathers ordained the expiations of the corpse: that which is greatly impure is sprinkled with holy water, perfumed with incense, exorcised with holy prayers, illuminated with lights, and so long as it remains upon the earth, is finally buried in a sacred place.

<summary>Agrippa discusses the different destinations of the soul based on its earthly conduct, citing the Kabbalistic belief in triple reincarnation and the classical division of the human being into four parts: flesh, ghost, shade, and spirit.</summary>

### THIRD BOOK. CLVIII

<margin>The opinions of the Pagans regarding burial. The Human Mind. The Good Soul.</margin>
Hence in Homer, Elpenor says: "I ask you, Ulysses, be mindful of me, and do not depart from there leaving me unburied, lest being unsepulcherous I become an object of the gods' wrath." <note>Homer, *Odyssey*, Book 11. Elpenor was a companion of Odysseus who died and remained unburied, pleading for a proper funeral so his spirit could find rest.</note> Truly, the human Mind <term>Mens: The highest, divine part of the human intellect, which Agrippa views as distinct from the lower soul.</term>—whose nature is sacred and of a divine race—because it is always free from fault, also escapes all punishment. But the Soul, if it has acted well, rejoices with the Mind; departing with its ethereal vehicle, it transcends freely to the choirs of heroes or seeks the celestial heights. There, blessed with perpetual happiness in all its senses and powers, it enjoys a perfect knowledge of all things, and furthermore, shares in the divine vision and the possession of the kingdom of heaven. Participating in divine power, it bestows benefits and various gifts upon these lower realms, like an immortal god.

<margin>The evil Soul.</margin>
If the Soul has acted badly, the Mind judges it and leaves it to the whim of a demon. Then the mournful soul, without the Mind, wanders among the inhabitants of the underworld as an "idol" <note>original: *idolum*</note>—which they call an image—just as Dido laments in Virgil:
> And now a great image of me will go beneath the earth. <note>original: "Et nunc magna mei, sub terras ibit imago." Virgil, *Aeneid*, Book 4.</note>

Therefore, this soul, then deprived of its intelligible essence and left to the command of a raging fantasy, is subjected to the torment of corporeal qualities. It recognizes itself, by the just judgment of God and because of its own fault, to be perpetually deprived of the divine vision for which it was created. This divine vision, as Scripture testifies, is the presence of all good things; however, the deprivation of that vision is the presence of all evils, which is the most bitter punishment of all, and which the Sacred Scriptures call the "outpouring of the wrath of God."

<margin>The most bitter punishment of all.</margin>
Thus, this image of the soul sometimes enters an aerial body—a shadow—enveloped in which it now consults friends and now harasses enemies, just as Dido threatens Aeneas in Virgil, saying:
> I will be present as a shadow in all places; you wicked man, you shall pay the penalty. <note>original: "Omnibus Vmbra locis adero, dabis improbe pœnas." Virgil, *Aeneid*, Book 4.</note>

<margin>The souls of those killed.</margin>
For since disturbances and the memory of the senses remain in the soul when it is separated from the body, the Platonists say that the souls—especially of those who were murdered—haunt their enemies. This is effected not so much by human indignation, but also by the divine Nemesis <note>The Greek goddess of retribution or divine vengeance.</note> and the providence and permission of a demon. Thus the spirit of Naboth (as the masters of the Hebrews interpret) because he departed at the end of his life with a desire for vengeance, was made (to fulfill that vengeance) a lying spirit. By God's permission, he went forth as a lying spirit in the mouths of all the prophets, until he caused Ahab to go up to Ramoth-Gilead. <note>Refers to 1 Kings 22, where a spirit volunteers to deceive King Ahab to lead him to his death in battle as punishment for the murder of Naboth.</note> And Virgil himself, along with the Pythagoreans and Platonists—whom our Augustine also follows—confesses that the separated souls of those who lived in this life retain their memory and will, which have not yet been extinguished, where he sings:
<margin>The reminiscence of souls.</margin>
> What joy they had in chariots
> and arms while alive, what care for feeding
> sleek horses, the same follows them when they are laid in the earth. <note>Virgil, *Aeneid*, Book 6. Agrippa uses this to argue that earthly passions persist after death.</note>

And Algazel <note>Al-Ghazali (c. 1058–1111), a major Persian theologian and philosopher.</note> in his book *On Divine Science*, as well as other Arab and Muhammadan philosophers, feel that the operations of the soul joined to the body...

<header># ON OCCULT PHILOSOPHY</header>

...common [habits], imprint upon the soul a character of use and practice. Once this character is strongly imprinted, the separated soul will use it for similar operations and <margin>The operation of the soul after death.</margin> passions that were not erased during life. Thus, although the body and its organs may decay, the soul's operation will not cease for that reason; instead, the affections and similar dispositions will remain.

The ancients called these souls by the common name "Manes" <note>In Roman mythology, the *Manes* were the souls of deceased loved ones, sometimes viewed as benevolent deities of the underworld.</note>. Among these, those who were innocent in this life, or purified by moral virtues—just as *Virgil* sings:
> Those who suffered wounds fighting for their fatherland,
> And those who were chaste priests while life remained,
> And pious bards who spoke things worthy of Apollo,
> Or those who improved life through discovered arts,
> And those who made others remember them by their merit—

<margin>The Fortunate Fields.</margin> Although they may have departed this life outside of grace and the righteousness of faith, most theologians believe that they are carried away, incapable of suffering, into certain "fortunate fields" <note>The *Elysian Fields* or *Campi Fortunati*, the classical Greek and Roman conception of paradise for the virtuous.</note>. And as *Virgil* says:
> They came to the joyful places and the pleasant greenery
> Of the fortunate groves and the blessed seats,

<margin>No one is saved without the faith of Christ.</margin> where they enjoy certain wondrous pleasures and delight in both sensory and intellectual revealed knowledge. Perhaps they are even instructed in faith and righteousness, no less than those spirits to whom *Christ* once preached the *Gospel* in prison <note>A reference to the "Harrowing of Hell," based on 1 Peter 3:19, where Christ is said to have preached to the souls of the departed between his crucifixion and resurrection.</note>. For as it is certain that no one can be saved without the faith of *Christ*, it is likewise probable that this faith is still preached to many Pagans and Saracens <note>A medieval term for Muslims.</note> after this life in those <margin><insert>These things are incredible and clearly contrary to my view.</insert></margin> receptacles of souls for their salvation. There, they are held as if in a common custody until the time comes when the Great Judge shall make an examination of merits. <margin>The opinion of the Doctors [of the Church] regarding salvation after death.</margin> This is an opinion from which even *Lactantius*, *Irenaeus*, *Clement*, *Tertullian*, *Augustine*, *Ambrose*, and many other *Christian* writers do not shrink.

<margin>The fear and punishment of impure souls.</margin> Truly, those souls who depart impure, incontinent, and unjust through sins are not so much driven by unhappy dreams, but wander through horrible phantasms and worse places. They rely on no free knowledge, except that which is abstractly granted or manifested to them. Then, because of a continuous craving for flesh and blood—arising from the "rust" of bodily filth—they are even subjected to the sense of pain and fear swords and blades. *Homer* undoubtedly seems to have perceived this when, in the eleventh book of the *Odyssey*, he introduces the deceased mother of *Ulysses* <note>Odysseus</note> standing by him as he offered a sacrifice. However, he neither recognized her nor spoke to her as long as he himself, with drawn sword, kept the shades away from the sacrificial blood. But after the mother, at the urging of the prophet *Tiresias*, had tasted of that sacrifice and drank the dark, cloudy blood, she immediately recognized her son and spoke to him weeping. Yet the soul of the prophet *Tiresias*—despite the prohibition of the drawn sword—even before tasting the blood, both recognized *Ulysses* and spoke to him, and pointed out that his mother's shade was standing there. Therefore, those souls...

# BOOK THREE

<margin>The expiation of souls according to pagan belief.</margin>
The vices of crimes contracted in the body, which they did not expiate in this life, carry their habits with them; these souls are forced to wash away those stains in the underworld and pay the penalties for their commissions, as the poet <note>The author is quoting the Roman poet Virgil from Book 6 of the *Aeneid*.</note> explained in these verses:

> Even when life’s last light has left them, 
> nonetheless, not every ill, nor all the plagues 
> of the body, wholly depart from the wretched ones; 
> it is unavoidable that many things, long hardened 
> by various means, should become deeply ingrained. 
> Therefore, they are exercised with punishments, 
> and they pay the penalties for ancient evils.
> <note>original: "Quin & supremo cum lumine vita reliquit, / Non tamen omne malum miseros, nec funditus omnes / Corporeæ excedunt pestes, penitusq; necesse est / Multa diu concreta modis inolescere mores / Ergo exercentur pœnis, veterumq; malorum / Supplicia expendunt."</note>

<margin>The affections of souls after death.</margin>
<margin>The disturbances of demons.</margin>
<margin>Lemures and Lares.</margin>
<margin>The disturbances of souls.</margin>
For such as the character and habits of men are in this life, so for the most part do the affections of the soul follow after death; the soul still flutters with a remembering mind over the things it once did in life. These things then occur to it more intensely and sharply, because the various duties of life—nourishing, growing, reproducing—as well as the various occupations and comforts of the senses and human business, and the obstacles of the heavy body, have all ceased. At that time, those appearances <note>original: "species"</note> occur to the imaginative reason <note>original: "phantasticæ rationi"</note> with more turbulence and great fury, depending on how much the intellectual spark lies more or less asleep, or is entirely extinguished, within such a soul. To these souls, evil demons then also introduce either the falsest or most terrifying images. 

As a result, in the <term>concupiscible power</term> <note>The faculty of the soul responsible for desire and longing.</note>, the soul is tortured by the lust for an imaginary good and for those things which it once affected in life, being deprived of the ability to obtain them. Although it sometimes seems to itself to almost reach its delights, it is driven away from them by demons to sharper punishments—just as, among the poets, **Tantalus** is kept from the feast, **Sardanapalus** from the embrace, **Midas** from the gold, and **Sisyphus** from power. These souls they called **lemures** <note>Restless or malevolent ghosts of the dead in Roman religion.</note>; but if any of them, caring for domestic affairs, inhabits the house in peace, it is called a **lar familiaris** <note>A household deity or tutelary spirit believed to protect the family.</note>. 

Furthermore, they are most bitterly tortured in the <term>irascible power</term> <note>The faculty of the soul associated with anger, courage, and the rejection of perceived evils.</note> by the hatred of an imaginary evil, whose disturbances, most false suspicions, and most horrible phantasms then fall upon them. Sad images turn within them: now the sky seems to fall upon their heads, now they are consumed by the force of flames, now they are merged under a vast whirlpool of water, now they are swallowed by the openings of the earth. At times, they seem to be transformed into various beasts, or to be torn or devoured by deformed monsters; now they are driven here and there through forests, through seas, through fires, through the air, and through the most foul places of the underworld. Now they perceive themselves being seized and tortured by demons. We believe that all these things happen to them after death no differently than they happen in this life to those who are delirious with <term>phrenesis</term> <note>Acute inflammation of the brain or delirium.</note> or <term>mania</term>, or those suffering from <term>melancholy humor</term> <note>In the theory of the four humors, an excess of black bile was thought to cause deep depression or delusions.</note>, or those who are tortured in sleep, terrified by horrible visions, as if these things were truly happening to them. Though these things are not truly present with them, but are only appearances apprehended in the imagination, so after death these horrible images of sins terrify those souls as if they were dreaming, and the conscience of their crime drives them.

There is also in Norway a certain mountain, the most fearsome of all, surrounded by the sea, which the common people call **Mount Hekla** <note>original: "Hechelbergium." While Hekla is in Iceland, early modern writers often grouped these northern Atlantic territories together under "Norway" or "Scandia."</note>. It bears the appearance of hell itself, for from it are heard such lamentable voices of wailing and crying out that these horrid-sounding noises spread for nearly a mile around. Furthermore, giant vultures and pitch-black ravens fly around it with terrifying cries, preventing any approach by frightening those who draw near. Beyond this, two springs gush forth from there: one is intolerable for its unmanageable cold, and the other for its most intense heat, both far exceeding the usual nature of the elements.

There is also in that same region, toward the southern side, a promontory called **Nadhegryn**, where the demons of the place are clearly seen by everyone in "aerial bodies" <note>This refers to the belief that spirits could condense the air into a visible, though non-solid, physical form.</note>.

Similar wonders exist in various regions and provinces, but I myself am unwilling to recount here what I have seen with my own eyes and touched with my own hands, lest I happen to be accused of lying by the skeptical because of the astounding nature of these things.

Nor do I think I should pass over here what many of our own writers have felt regarding the "receptacles" of souls, which do not differ greatly from what we have already said.

# OF OCCULT PHILOSOPHY. BOOK THREE.

<margin>Paradise.</margin>
Those who pleased his will were translated to paradise, to be preserved for the kingdom; however, for those who were not able to fully fulfill the law of justice, but held some remains of malice in their flesh, their bodies are indeed dissolved. Their souls, however, are preserved in happy and joyful regions, so that in the resurrection of the dead, when they have received their bodies—now purified by that very dissolution—they may obtain their eternal inheritance in exchange for the good they had done.

<margin>Irenaeus.</margin>
Irenaeus himself also, at the conclusion of the book he wrote *Against the Heresies of the Valentinians* <note>Saint Irenaeus of Lyons (2nd century AD) was a prominent theologian whose work "Against Heresies" is a foundational text in early Christian dogma.</note>, says: "Since the Lord went into the midst of the shadow of death where the souls of the dead were, and afterwards rose again in the body, and was taken up after the resurrection, it is manifest

<margin>Christ descended to the lower world and rose again.</margin>
that the souls of his disciples as well (for whose sake the Lord performed these things) shall go into an invisible place defined for them by God. There they shall dwell until the resurrection, awaiting the resurrection; afterwards, receiving their bodies and rising perfectly—that is, corporally—just

<margin>The resurrection of souls and bodies.</margin>
as the Lord rose again, they shall so come into the presence of God. For no disciple is above his master; but every master shall be perfect" <note>Refers to Luke 6:40, emphasizing that the believer's path follows Christ's own path through death to resurrection.</note>.

<margin>The time of the resurrection.</margin>
Therefore, since our Master did not immediately fly away and depart, but waited for the time of his resurrection defined by the Father (which was also manifested through Jonah <note>The "Sign of Jonah"—spending three days in the belly of the whale—was interpreted by Christ as a prophecy of his three days in the tomb.</note>), and rose after three days and was taken up; so we also must wait for the time of our resurrection defined by God,

<margin>Lactantius on the resurrection.</margin>
foretold by the prophets, and thus rise and be taken up, as many of us as the Lord shall deem worthy of this honor. To these is also added Lactantius Firmianus <note>Lactantius (c. 250 – c. 325) was an early Christian author and advisor to Constantine I.</note> in that book of *Divine Institutes* titled *On the Divine Reward*, saying: "Let no one think that souls are judged immediately after death. For all are detained in one common custody until the time arrives when the Great Judge makes an examination of merits."

<margin>The reward of the upright.</margin>
Then, those whose justice has been approved shall receive the reward of immortality; but those whose sins and crimes are uncovered shall not rise, but

<margin>The punishment of the wicked.</margin>
shall be hidden away with the ungodly in the same darkness, destined for certain punishments.

<margin>Augustine on the time between death and resurrection.</margin>
Augustine and Ambrose are of the same opinion. The former says in his *Enchiridion* <note>Augustine’s "Handbook" on faith, hope, and love.</note>: "The time which is interposed between a man's death and the final resurrection holds the souls in hidden receptacles, according as each is worthy of rest or of misery, based on what it earned in the flesh while it lived."

<margin>Ambrose on the dwelling place of souls.</margin>
And Ambrose, in his book *On the Good of Death*, says: "The Scripture of Esdras <note>Referring to the apocryphal book 2 Esdras (or 4 Ezra), which was highly influential in medieval and Renaissance thought regarding the afterlife.</note> called the dwelling places of souls 'storehouses' <note>original: "promptuaria"</note>. Meeting the human complaint (because the just who have gone before seem to be cheated of their due reward for a great length of time until the day of judgment), he marvelously says that the day of judgment is like a crown."

<margin>The expectation of the crown.</margin>
For the day of the crown is expected by all, so that within that day both the defeated may blush and the victors may obtain the palm of victory. Therefore, while the fullness of time is expected, souls await their due reward; for some, punishment remains; for others, glory. And in the same chapter...

# BOOK THREE.

<margin>
The Underworld.
The uncertainty of the future judgment.
On the judgment of souls.
Trajan freed by Gregory.
Various opinions of theologians concerning the damned.
Augustine’s noble opinion on intercessory prayers.
The rich man and the beggar.
</margin>

[Ambrose] calls the underworld <term>Infernus<note>original: "infernum". Derived from the Latin for "lower," this term refers generally to the place of the dead, whether a place of punishment or a neutral "invisible" realm.</note></term> a "place that is not seen," which souls seek once they are freed from their bodies. And in the second book of his work *On Cain and Abel*, he says: "The soul is released from the body, and after the end of this life, it is still held in suspense regarding the uncertainty of the future judgment." This is supported by that Gospel passage concerning the final judgment, where Christ says in Matthew: <note>Matthew 7:22-23</note> "Many will say to me on that day, ‘Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, and in your name cast out demons, and in your name perform many miracles?’ And then I will declare to them, ‘I never knew you.’" From this discourse, it seems evident that they remained uncertain of their sentence until that day; because of their confidence in the miracles they performed in the name of Jesus while they still lived, they were meanwhile held in suspense by a certain hope of salvation.

Because the final judgment of souls is delayed until the last day, many theologians believe that intercessory <term>suffrages<note>original: "suffragia". These are spiritual aids, such as prayers, alms, or the Mass, offered by the living to assist the souls of the dead.</note></term> can be of help not only to those destined for justification, but even to the damned before the appointed day of judgment. Thus, it is said that the Emperor Trajan was freed from the underworld by Saint Gregory and justified unto salvation <note>A famous medieval legend claimed that Pope Gregory the Great was so moved by the justice of the pagan Emperor Trajan that he prayed for his soul, resulting in Trajan being briefly revived to be baptized or otherwise saved.</note>; although some think he was not freed from the guilt of his punishment, but rather that the execution of justice was merely postponed until the day of judgment. However, Thomas Aquinas says it seems more probable that Trajan was restored to life by the prayers of Saint Gregory and obtained the power of grace, through which he was freed from the penalty and the bond of his sins.

There are also theologians who believe that through the offerings of these suffrages, the punishment is neither removed nor the fine taken away, but rather that certain comforts and <term>soothings<note>original: "fomenta". Literally "poultices" or "warm soaks," used here metaphorically for spiritual relief.</note></term> for their pains are provided. They compare this to a sweating porter who, by the splashing of water, feels himself relieved of the pressure of his load, or is helped to bear it more easily, even though nothing has been taken away from the weight itself. Nevertheless, the common opinion of theologians denies that prayers or funeral rites offer any help at all to the accused in the <term>cave of Dis<note>original: "Ditis antro". Dis was the Roman god of the underworld; Agrippa uses this classical name for Hell.</note></term>. 

Yet, since all these matters are of an incomprehensible obscurity, many have sharpened their wits upon them in vain. Therefore, agreeing with the opinion of Augustine, as he says in the tenth book of *On Genesis*, let us say: "It is better to doubt concerning hidden things than to litigate concerning uncertain ones." I do not doubt that the rich man is to be understood as being in the heat of his punishments and the poor man in the refreshment of his joys; but how that flame of hell is to be understood, or that <term>bosom of Abraham<note>original: "sinus Abrahae". A term for the place of comfort where the righteous dead awaited the Resurrection.</note></term>, or the tongue of the rich man, the finger of the poor man, the thirst of the torment, or the drop of refreshment—these things are scarcely found by those who seek them meekly, and are never found by those who contend over them with strife. But leaving these things aside now and hurrying on to further matters, we shall discuss the restorations of souls.

-># ON OCCULT PHILOSOPHY<-

...those who left their bodies by a violent death still wander around their corpses in that turbid and humid spirit <note>Renaissance magic held that the "spirit" was a vaporous substance connecting the soul and body; a "humid" spirit was one weighed down by earthly attachments or sudden trauma, preventing the soul from ascending.</note>. They are drawn as if to something familiar that lures them. Recognizing those means through which they were formerly joined to their bodies, they can be easily evoked and attracted through similar vapors, liquids, and odors. This is achieved by employing certain artificial lights, songs, sounds, and similar things that stir the imaginative and spiritual harmony of the soul. 

<margin>
On the evocation of souls.
</margin>

Furthermore, sacred invocations and religious rites must not be neglected, out of respect for the rational portion of the soul, which is superior by nature. Thus we read that the Witch of Endor <note>original: "Pythonissa". A reference to the medium in 1 Samuel 28 who summoned the spirit of the prophet Samuel for King Saul.</note> evoked Samuel; and thus the Thessalian prophetess in the works of Lucan <note>Lucan was a Roman poet; his epic *Pharsalia* features the gruesome witch Erichtho.</note> raised a corpse. Hence we read among the poets and narrators of such things that the souls of the dead are not evoked without blood and a corpse. However, they say that shades are easily attracted by fumigations, adding eggs, milk, honey, oil, wine, water, and flour, which provide a suitable medium for the souls to take on [temporary] bodies—just as Circe teaches Ulysses <note>Odysseus</note> in Homer with lengthy instructions. 

It is believed, however, that these things can only happen in places where such souls are known to linger most frequently. This may be due to some kinship—such as the abandoned corpse attracting them—or due to some affection impressed upon them during life that draws the soul to certain places. It may also be due to the "Tartarean" <note>infernal or hellish</note> nature of a place that is suitable for purifying or punishing souls. Experience shows that such places are recognized by the occurrence of visions, nocturnal incursions, and similar apparitions. Some are well known enough on their own, such as cemeteries and those places where the execution of criminal judgments usually takes place, or where public slaughters have occurred in recent years, or where the corpses of the slain—not yet expiated nor properly buried—have been interred in recent years. For the expiation and exorcism of a place, as well as the sacred rite of burial duly applied to bodies, often prohibits the souls themselves from approaching and repels them further away to the places of judgment.

<margin>
Necromancy: what it is and from where it comes.
</margin>

This is where necromancy <term>Necromancy<note>From the Greek 'nekros' (dead) and 'manteia' (divination). Agrippa explains it here as a practice specifically tied to physical remains.</note></term> gets its name, because it operates upon the corpses of the dead and seeks responses through the *manes* <note>The spirits of the deceased ancestors.</note>, the shades of the dead, and subterranean demons. It lures them into the corpses of the dead through certain Stygian songs, infernal invocations, funeral sacrifices, and wicked immolations. We read of such things in Lucan concerning that sorceress Erichtho, who evoked a dead man to predict the entire outcome of the Pharsalian war to Sextus Pompeius. There were also in Phigalia, a city of Arcadia, certain Priests of Magic <note>original: "Magi sacerdotes"</note> most skilled in sacred rites, who were evokers of souls that had finished their lives. Sacred Scripture also testifies that a certain "Pythoness" woman evoked the soul of Samuel. Indeed, even the souls of the saints love their bodies, and are accustomed to hear prayers more readily and promptly where the pledges of their relics are preserved. 

<margin>
Two species of necromancy.
</margin>

There are, however, two species of necromancy. One is **Necyomancy** <note>original: "necyomantia". Specifically the reanimation of a physical corpse.</note>, which raises a corpse and cannot be done without blood. The other is **Sciomancy** <note>original: "scyomantia". From the Greek 'skia' (shadow); divination by calling up only the spirit or shadow of the dead.</note>, in which the evocation of the shade alone is sufficient.

<summary>Agrippa describes the mechanics of necromancy, explaining how souls (especially those of the violently killed) linger near their bodies and can be summoned using specific sensory catalysts, rituals, and locations. He distinguishes between 'necyomancy,' which involves the physical corpse and blood, and 'sciomancy,' which summons only the spirit's shadow.</summary>

### BOOK THREE. ###

Finally, they perform all their experiments through the corpses, bones, and limbs of those who have been slaughtered, and through those things that belong to them. They believe a demonic power, friendly to such things, is present within them. For this reason, they easily entice the "outpourings" of wicked demons <note>original: "defluxus"; these are spiritual influences or emanations believed to flow from the demonic realm into the material world</note> due to a very familiar similarity and property between them. Relying on the works of these demons—who are quite powerful in human and earthly matters—the necromancers <term>necromantici: practitioners of "death-magic" who communicate with or manipulate the dead</term> kindle illicit loves, and send dreams, diseases, and hatreds, along with similar passions. To these ends, they can even gather the strengths of those souls which, still wrapped in a moist and clouded spirit <note>Renaissance occultists believed that a "heavy" or "damp" spirit—the vaporous medium between soul and body—kept the soul tethered to the physical world, preventing it from ascending</note>, wander around their own remains and commit the same deeds as wicked demons. 

Since these practitioners have learned through experience that the depraved and impure souls of those violently torn from their bodies, or of men not yet purified or lacking burial, linger about their corpses and are easily drawn back to what is familiar, these evildoers abuse them to perform their wicked deeds. They lure the unhappy souls by placing the body nearby or taking a part of it, then compel them with Stygian <note>relating to the River Styx in the Underworld</note> invocations, appealing to them by the shapeless corpses scattered across broad fields, the wandering shades of those lacking burial, the spirits <note>original: "manes"</note> sent back from Acheron <note>the "River of Woe" in the Underworld</note>, and the guests of the infernal regions whom an immature death dragged down into Tartarus <note>the deepest abyss of the Underworld</note>, as well as by the horrendous desires of the damned and the proud demons who avenge crimes.

<margin>
One who wishes to know what is necessary to truly restore a soul to a body.
</margin>

However, he who would truly restore souls to their bodies must be one who knows the proper nature of the soul: where it proceeds from, with how many and which degrees of perfection it is filled, what intelligence it is fortified by, through what means it is diffused into the body, and by what harmony it was joined to that body. He must know what affinity it has with God, with the intelligences <note>angelic or celestial beings</note>, with the heavens, elements, and all other things of which it holds the image and likeness. Finally, he must know by what influences the body is joined together. For the art of "resuscitation" (raising the dead) requires all these things, and it belongs not to men, but to God alone—communicated to those whom He wills, such as Elisha <note>original: "Helizeo"</note>, who made the dead son of the Shunammite woman live again. So too is Alcestis said to have been revived by Hercules and to have lived a long time thereafter; and Apollonius of Tyana <note>a famous Greek philosopher and miracle-worker from the 1st century AD</note> restored a dead girl to life.

<margin>
A girl restored to life by Apollonius.
</margin>

And here it should be noted that it occasionally happens to men that the "life-giving spirit" is withdrawn, so that they appear dead and without sensation, even though the intellectual nature remains united to the body and maintains the same form. The body remains the same, even if the power of giving life does not actively extend into it but remains withdrawn in union with the intellectual nature. Nevertheless, it does not cease to exist. Although that man might truly be called "dead"—insofar as death is the absence of a life-giving force—the body would not be truly separated [from the soul] and could be awakened and revived once more. Many such miracles appear in these cases, many of which were seen in previous centuries among the Gentiles and the Jews. Among their number is the story Plato recounts in the tenth book of the *Republic*: namely, that a certain Er the Pamphylian <note>original: "Phęreū quēdā Pāphiliū." This refers to the "Myth of Er," a soldier who died in battle but returned to life on his funeral pyre to describe the afterlife.</note> lay for ten days among those who had fallen in battle...

<margin>
Er the Pamphylian lived after 12 days.
</margin>

### Chapter XLIII. On the Power of the Human Soul in Mind, Reason, and the Idol.

<margin>The components of the human soul.</margin>
<margin>a</margin>
The human soul consists of mind, reason, and the idol <note>original: "idolo"; in this Neoplatonic context, the "idol" or "eidolon" refers to the lowest part of the soul—the "image" or "phantom"—that connects the higher soul to the physical body and governs imagination</note>: the mind illuminates the reason, reason flows into the idol; all together, it is one soul. Unless the reason is illuminated by the mind, it is not immune from error.

<margin>The light of the mind is from God.</margin>
However, the mind does not provide light to the reason unless God—the first light, naturally—is shining. For the first light in God surpasses all understanding; therefore, that light cannot be called "intelligible" <note>meaning, it is beyond the grasp of simple intellect</note>. But when that light is infused into the mind, it becomes intellectual and can be understood. Then, when it is infused through the mind into the reason, it becomes rational and can be not only understood but also thought upon. Furthermore, when it is infused through the reason into the soul’s idol, it is made not only thinkable but also imaginable—yet not yet corporeal. But when it migrates from there into the soul's ethereal vehicle <term>ethereum animæ vehiculum: the "spirit-body" or astral vehicle that Neoplatonists believed carried the soul between the material and divine realms</term>, it first becomes corporeal, though not yet clearly perceptible to the senses, until it passes into an elemental body—whether simple and airy or composite—in which it becomes a clearly visible light.

<margin>The power of the mind.</margin>
Considering this progression of light, the Chaldean philosophers <note>The "Chaldeans" were often cited by Renaissance authors as ancient masters of wisdom, magic, and astrology</note> tell of a certain astounding power of our mind: specifically, that it is possible for the mind itself—with its whole focus fixed upon God—to be filled with the divine spirit. Thus filled with light, it pours out rays through each medium, down to this thick, dark, heavy, mortal body. It surrounds even the body with abundant light, making it like the stars and equally shimmering. Then, through the abundance and lightness of its rays, it lifts the body on high, just as tow <note>coarse flax or hemp fibers used for lighting fires</note> is lifted by a flame of fire. Sometimes it transfers the heavy body to distant parts like a spirit—just as we read of Philip in the Acts of the Apostles, when, after baptizing the Eunuch in India, he was immediately found in Azotus; and similar things are said of Habakkuk in the book of Daniel. Thus others, passing through closed doors, escaped guards and chains, as we read of Peter the Apostle and Peter the Exorcist. Let him who has seen those famous melancholics <note>In the Renaissance, "melancholy" was associated both with depression and with a temperament prone to genius and mystical visions</note> wonder at this less; they walk in their sleep, travel through trackless places, climb inaccessible heights, and perform the deeds of those who are awake—deeds they could by no means do while conscious. There is no other reason for this in nature than a strong and out-stretched imagination. This power is in every human being and is present in the human soul from the root of its creation, but it varies in different men in strength and weakness; it is increased or diminished according to exercise and use, through which it is drawn out from potential into act. He who rightly knows this can ascend in his knowledge as far as imagi... <note>the catchword "ima=" indicates the next page begins with "imaginationis," or imagination</note>

<margin>
Acts of the Apostles.
The stories of Habakkuk, Daniel, and Peter.
The works of melancholics in dreams.
</margin>

CLXIIII
# BOOK THREE #

<margin>The ethereal sense of nature and of the vehicle.</margin>
...so that its generative power <note>original: "gignatiua virtus"</note> might transcend and be joined with the universal power—which Al-Kindi <note>An influential 9th-century Arab philosopher known for his work on "stellar rays"</note>, Roger Bacon, and William of Paris <note>William of Auvergne, a 13th-century theologian</note> call the "sense of nature," which Virgil calls the "ethereal sense," and Plato calls the "sense of the vehicle" <term>sense of the vehicle: the "ochema," a subtle, luminous body that Neoplatonists believed carried the soul</term>—and its thought might be made most strong when that ethereal and celestial power is poured over it. By the splendor of this power, the soul is strengthened until it grasps the forms, notions, and knowledge of true things, so that what it has conceived in its mind comes to pass just as it thought. Thus, it acquires such great power that it can immerse, join, and instill itself into the minds of men, making them certain of its thoughts, its will, and its desires, even across great and remote distances, as if they perceived those things with their own senses from a present object. It can also perform many things in a short time, as if they were done outside of time. These gifts are not granted to everyone, but only to those whose imaginative and cognitive power is strongest and has reached the peak of contemplation. Such a person is fit to perceive and announce all things through the splendor of the universal power—that is, the intelligence and spiritual perception that is above him. This is the necessary power which must be followed, and which everyone who pursues virtue must obey.

<margin>The power of imagination.</margin>
If, therefore, the power of imagination is so great that it can instill itself into whomever it wishes, hindered or prohibited by no interval of place or time—and if, wherever it dreams and imagines, it sometimes drags a heavy body along with it—then there is no doubt that the power of the Mind is even greater when it has attained its own nature. When it is not weighed down by the allurements of the senses and remains incorrupt and true to itself, it possesses even more potency. But now, as an archetype <note>original: "exemplar"</note>, the souls of the celestial stars abound with such copious light that a vast abundance of light overflows from them into their bodies. 

<margin>Moses' face.</margin>
Thus, the face of **Moses** shone so brightly that the children of Israel could not look upon him because of the splendor of his countenance. So also we read that **Socrates** was transfigured, as if he surpassed the light-bearing wheels of the sun with his own radiance. So too was **Zoroaster** transfigured and lifted up bodily. Thus **Enoch** and **Elijah** ascended to the heavens in a certain fiery chariot; thus **Paul** was snatched up into the third heaven. In this same way, we can say that our own bodies, which will then be called "glorified" after the judgment of the world, will likewise be snatched up and shine like the sun and moon. That this can indeed happen, and has happened, is admitted and shown by Avicebron the Moor <note>Solomon ibn Gabirol, an 11th-century Jewish philosopher</note>, the Arab Avicenna, Hippocrates of Cos, and the entire school of the Chaldeans.

<margin>The splendor of Alexander the Great.</margin>
Furthermore, it is recorded in the monuments of history that **Alexander the Great**, when surrounded by great danger in India, became so inflamed in spirit that he appeared to the barbarians to pour forth light. The father of **Theodoric** <note>The Ostrogothic king</note> is also said to have emitted sparks from his entire body. A certain wise man reported the same of himself, so that sparkling flames leaped out here and there, even with a sound. 

<margin>Tiberius's horse.</margin>
Nor is this force of the spirit found only in men, but it is also sometimes discovered in brute animals, as in the horse of **Tiberius**, which is said to have vomited flames from its mouth.

# ON OCCULT PHILOSOPHY #

...seemed to have grasped <note>The text continues a thought from the previous page regarding the soul's perception</note>. But the **Mind** is above fate, within providence: for this reason, it is affected neither by the influxes of celestial bodies, nor by the qualities of natural things: therefore, religion alone heals it. The **Idol** <note>original: "Idolum." In Neoplatonic philosophy, this refers to the "image" or the lower, animating shadow of the soul that governs the physical body</note> of the soul, however, is within fate; it is above nature (which is in some way the measure of the body and soul) and below fate, but above the body. For this reason, it is changed by the influxes of celestial bodies and is affected by the qualities of natural and corporeal things.

<margin>What the idol of the soul is.</margin>
By the **idol of the soul**, I mean that vivifying and governing power of the body, the origin of the senses, through which the soul itself unfolds its powers of perceiving within this body: it perceives corporeal things through the body, moves the body through space, rules it in its place, and nourishes the body within the body.

<margin>Two virtues in the idol.</margin>
In this idol, two most powerful virtues dominate: one is called the **phantasy** <note>The power of imagination</note>, or the imaginative or cogitative virtue, concerning whose power much has already been said, and also where we discussed the passions of the soul; the other is the virtue called the **sense of nature**, about which we also spoke when we made mention of divination by entrails <note>original: "aruspicina," the ancient Roman practice of searching for omens in the organs of sacrificed animals</note>. Thus, man by the nature of his body is under fate; the soul of man, through the idol, moves nature within fate; but through the mind, he is above fate, in the order of providence. Reason, however, is free and under its own law. Therefore, the soul through reason ascends into the mind, where it is sometimes filled with divine light; or it descends into the idol, where it is affected by the influences of celestial bodies and the qualities of natural things, and is distracted by the passions and encounters of sensible things. Sometimes the soul folds itself entirely back into reason, either investigating other things by arguing, or contemplating itself. For it is possible 

<margin>The Intellect.</margin>
that the rational part of the soul—which the **Peripatetics** <note>Followers of Aristotle’s philosophy</note> call the *possible intellect*—may reach the point where it discourses and operates freely without turning toward mental images <note>original: "phantasmata"</note>. Finally, so great is the command of reason itself that whenever anything runs into either the mind, the idol, the nature, or the body, it cannot pass into the soul unless the reason intends itself toward it. In this way, in the external senses, the soul perceives itself neither seeing, nor hearing, nor feeling, nor suffering anything, until the thinking reason first grasps it. It grasps it, however, when it calls upon it, and not when it is gaping at something else—as we clearly see in those who do not notice people passing them while they are thinking more intently on something else. Know, therefore, that neither celestial influxes, nor natural affections, nor sensations, nor the passions of the body or mind, nor anything sensible can act upon or penetrate into the soul, except through the judgment of reason itself. Thus, by its own act, and not by any outward violence, can the mind be either affected or disturbed, which even countless martyrs have proven by their very deeds.

<margin>The constancy of Anaxarchus.</margin>
Thus **Anaxarchus of Abdera** <note>A Greek philosopher of the 4th century BCE</note>, the philosopher: by the command of Nicocreon, the tyrant of the Cypriots, he was cast into a hollow stone, and while he was being beaten with iron hammers, disregarding the punishment of his body, he is said to have cried out: "Pound, pound the vessel <note>original: "vasculum," referring to his body as a mere container for his soul</note> of Anaxarchus, for you do not terrify Anaxarchus himself." And when the tyrant ordered his tongue to be cut out, he bit it off with his own teeth and spat it into the tyrant's face.

<insert>111</insert> <margin>The rational mind.</margin> Being, insofar as it is from God, or from the intelligible world <note>The realm of pure, divine intellect</note>, is therefore immortal and eternal. However, the celestial **reason**, by the benefit of its origin from heaven, is long-lived; but the **idol** <note>original: "idolum." The "image" or lower animating spirit that governs the physical body</note>, because it depends on the bosom of matter and sublunary <note>Everything beneath the moon, i.e., the earthly realm of change and decay</note> nature, is subject to death and corruption. <margin>The Soul.</margin> The **soul**, therefore, is immortal through its **mind**; through its **reason** in its ethereal vehicle <note>A Neoplatonic concept of a "star-body" or spirit-shell that carries the soul between incarnations</note> it is long-lived, yet capable of being dissolved unless it is restored in the circuit of a new body. It is not, therefore, immortal unless it is united to the immortal mind. Likewise, the **idol** of the soul—or the sensible and animal soul itself—because it was drawn forth from the bosom of corporeal matter, perishes along with the body when it is dissolved; or, its shadow does not survive for long in the vapors of its dissolved body, participating in nothing of immortality unless it too is united to a more sublime power. The soul which is thus united to the mind is called the "standing and not falling" soul. <margin>Not all men attain the mind.</margin> But not all men have attained the **mind**, because (as **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure associated with the *Hermetica*</note> says) God the Father wished to propose it as a contest and a prize for souls. Those who neglect this, being devoid of mind and enslaved to corporeal senses, are made like irrational animals and obtain the same destruction as them, just as **Ecclesiastes** says:

> There is one destruction for man and beast, and the condition of both is equal: as a man dies, so they also die. All breathe similarly, and man has nothing more than the beast. <note>original: "Vnus interitus est hominis & iumentorum..." quoting Ecclesiastes 3:19</note>

From this, many theologians believe that no immortality remains for such souls after this body is cast off, except the hope of the resurrection, when all men are to be restored. **Augustine** reports that such was the heresy of the Arabs, who said that souls perish together with the body and will rise again with it at the judgment. However, whoever is supported by divine grace and has attained the **mind**, these become immortal according to the comparison of their works, as Hermes says, having embraced all things by their intelligence—those on earth, in the sea, and in the heavens; and if there is anything besides those above the heaven, they look upon the **Good** itself. 

But for those who happen to live a "middle life"—though they have not attained divine intelligence, but only its rational image—their souls, when they have departed from the body, are relegated to certain secret receptacles. There, affected by sensible powers and engaged in a certain kind of activity, they either rejoice excessively or grieve heavily based on their habits of opinion, anger, and desire. Saint Augustine was also of this opinion in the book he wrote, *On the Spirit and the Soul* <note>original: "De spiritu & anima." A work traditionally attributed to Augustine in the Middle Ages, though now considered to be by a later medieval author</note>. The sages of the **Indians**, **Persians**, **Egyptians**, and **Chaldeans** handed down that this soul survives its body for a long time, but does not immediately become immortal unless through **transcorporation** <note>original: "transcorporationem," referring to the migration of the soul or reincarnation into new bodies</note>. <margin>Our theologians on the soul</margin> But our theologians philosophize far differently about these things; for they say that although the origin and birth of all souls are common, they are nevertheless distinguished among themselves by the Maker in various grades—not only by accidental differences, but by certain intrinsic grades rooted in their very essence, by which each soul differs from another through that which is unique to itself. **John Duns Scotus** <note>original: "Ionnes Scotus," the influential medieval Scholastic philosopher</note> holds this opinion, <margin>Parisian theologians.</margin> and the **Parisian theologians** thus feel...

Such is divine justice in the distribution of gifts, so that they correspond to the virtue of each recipient; to these people, rewards are also rendered according to their works, so that as the proportion of gifts is to gifts, and merits to merits, the same is the proportion of rewards to rewards.
<margin>The fourfold operation of the noble soul.</margin>
Finally, it must be known that every noble soul has a fourfold operation: first, a **divine** one through the image of the divine property; second, an **intellectual** one through the formality of participation with the Intelligences <note>Angelic or celestial beings of pure thought</note>; third, a **rational** one through the perfection of its own essentiality; and fourth, an **animal** or **natural** one through its communion with the body and these lower things. <margin>The soul standing and not falling.</margin>
