Therefore, the form of all magical power comes from the human soul that is standing and not falling.

## On Prophecy and Frenzy. Chapter 45.

<margin>What prophecy is.</margin>
Prophecy <note>original: "vaticinium"</note> is that by which priests or others, being moved, both perceive the causes of things and foresee the future; specifically, when oracles descend into them from the gods or from spirits <note>original: "demonibus"</note>, and breaths are passed down by them. The Platonists call these descents "illapses" <note>Sudden infusions or flows</note> of higher souls into our own souls; and **Mercurius** <note>Hermes Trismegistus</note> calls them the "senses of spirits" and the "minds of spirits."
<margin>Foreknowledge of the future belongs to the gods alone.</margin>
The ancients called such spirits "Eurideans" and "Pythons," <note>Spirits associated with oracular sites like Delphi</note> and antiquity firmly believed that they were accustomed to entering the bodies of men and using their voices and tongues for predictions of the future. **Plutarch** also mentions these in his *Dialogue on the Causes of the Decline of Oracles*. Truly, **Cicero** [notes that] the Stoics...

### On the first kind of frenzy, from the Muses. Chapter XLVI.

<margin>Frenzy.</margin> Frenzy <note>Latin: "furor," meaning a state of divine madness or inspired agitation.</note> is an illumination of the soul proceeding from gods or from demons, whence comes this poem by **Ovid**: <note>Agrippa refers to "Naso," the poet's family name.</note>
> There is a god within us, and we have dealings with heaven;
> That spirit comes from ethereal seats. <note>From Ovid’s *Fasti*.</note>

<margin>Four kinds of divine frenzy.</margin>
<margin>Frenzy from the Muses.</margin>
<margin>The effects of Vervain.</margin>
<margin>The heart of a mole for divination.</margin>
**Plato** defines this through alienation and connection: for it draws the soul away from those things by which the bodily senses are stirred, and being alienated from the animal nature of man, it clings to the divine power. From this power, the soul receives things that it cannot investigate by its own strength. For when the mind is free and loosened, with the reins of the body relaxed—or as if it has escaped more freely from a guarded prison—it transcends the bonds of the limbs. With nothing holding it back, driven by its own impulses and stirred by a divine spirit, it comprehends all things and foresees the future. Now, there are four kinds of divine frenzy, proceeding from different deities: namely, from the **Muses**, from **Dionysus**, from **Apollo**, and from **Venus**. 

Therefore, the first frenzy, proceeding from the Muses, stirs and tempers the soul, and makes it divine, drawing higher things to lower things through natural objects. Now, the Muses are the souls of the celestial spheres, according to which individual steps are found by which the attraction of higher things to lower occurs. The lowest of these, reflecting the sphere of the **Moon**, holds those things which are from the vegetable kingdom, such as plants, the fruits of trees, roots, and those from harder materials such as stones and metals, as well as their ritual bindings and suspensions. Thus it is said that the *selenite* stone <note>A stone associated with the moon, often identified with gypsum.</note> and the *hyena* stone <note>Latin: "lapis hyenę," a mythical stone supposedly found in the eye of a hyena.</note> provide divination; similarly, **vervain** and the herb **theangelis** <note>Agrippa writes "the angelida," a plant mentioned by Pliny the Elder as being used for prophecy.</note> provide prophecy, just as was said of these things above. 

The second step, reflecting **Mercury**, holds those things which are from the animal kingdom, and those composed of a mixture of various natural things with one another, such as drinks and foods. In this way, the heart of a **mole**—if someone eats it while it is still fresh and pulsating—is said to contribute to divination and the successful outcome of things to be done. And **Rabbi Moses of Coucy** <note>A 13th-century French rabbi known as the "Smag."</note> relates in his commentaries on Leviticus about an animal called the <term>Yidua</term> <note>original Hebrew: ידוע (Yiddo'ni). In medieval folklore, this was often described as a "vegetable lamb" or a human-shaped creature joined to the earth by a stem.</note>, of human form, from the middle of whose navel a cord grows, like gourds in...

the man stands and is afflicted; as far as the length of that cord extends, it devours and consumes everything surrounding it. Deceiving the sight, it cannot be captured unless the cord is cut by the strike of an arrow. Once cut, the creature expires. When its bones are later placed in the mouth according to a certain rule, whoever does so is immediately seized by frenzy and delivers oracles concerning any matters that have been tested. <note>This likely refers to the "Scythian Lamb" or "Barometz," a legendary plant-animal hybrid that was said to be tethered to the earth by a stem-like umbilical cord.</note> 

The **third degree** corresponds to the sphere of **Venus**: <note>Venus was traditionally associated with the senses, beauty, and physical attraction.</note> this level governs the finest powders, vapors, and scents, as well as the ointments and fumigations made from them, which were discussed previously. 

The **fourth degree** pertains to the sphere of the **Sun**: this level governs voices, words, songs, and harmonic sounds. Through their sweet consonance, it drives turbulent discord from the soul and uplifts the mind. For this reason, **Hermes**, **Pythagoras**, and **Plato** command that a dissonant soul be composed and elevated through song and harmony. Thus **Timotheus** <note>Timothy of Miletus, a famous Greek musician and poet.</note> is said to have incited King **Alexander** to a frenzy by means of sounds. Likewise, a priest of **Calama** (according to the testimony of **Aurelius Augustine**) <note>St. Augustine mentions this in *The City of God*, Book XIV, Chapter 24, describing a priest who could enter a trance at will through music.</note> used to call himself away from his body into rapture and ecstasy at his own will by means of certain mournful harmonies. These matters have also been discussed above. 

The **fifth degree** belongs to **Mars**: this level governs powerful imaginations, the passions of the mind, concepts, and movements, all of which have been explained above. 

The **sixth degree** corresponds to **Jupiter**: this level governs the discourses of reason, deliberations, consultations, and moral purifications; some of these have been mentioned previously, and some will be discussed later. It also has under its domain "wonders" and "venerations," through the awe of which the imagination and reason are sometimes so restrained that they suddenly cease all their own actions. <note>This refers to a state of "holy dread" or profound wonder that silences the internal monologue of the ego.</note> From this, the mind itself, being free and exposed to a single divine power—whether a god or a spirit—conceives celestial and divine influxes. 

<margin>The method of the Sibyls.</margin> These are specifically the matters about which the mind had previously deliberated. Thus we read that the **Sibyls** <note>The Sibyls were female prophets in the ancient world, often associated with specific holy sites.</note> and the priestesses of the **Pythia** were accustomed to receive oracles in the caves of **Jupiter** and **Apollo**. 

<margin>Contemplation</margin>
The **seventh degree** reflects **Saturn**: this level governs the more secret intelligences and the tranquil contemplations of the mind. By "contemplation," I mean here the free insight of the mind, suspended in wonder at the spectacles of wisdom. For that process of thinking which occurs through riddles or images is actually "speculation" or a kind of discourse belonging to **Jupiter**, not true "contemplation." <note>Agrippa draws a sharp distinction here: Jupiter represents the active, reasoning mind (speculation), while Saturn represents the silent, direct perception of truth (contemplation).</note> 

The **eighth degree** reflects the **Stellated Heaven** <note>The sphere of the fixed stars, beyond the individual planets.</note>: this level observes the position, motion, rays, and light of the celestial bodies. It also governs images, rings, and similar items manufactured according to the celestial patterns, of which we spoke above. 

The **ninth degree** corresponds to the **First Mobile** <note>The *Primum Mobile*, the outermost sphere in the Ptolemaic system that moves all the inner spheres.</note>—that is, the ninth sphere or the universe itself: this level governs more "formal" things, such as numbers, figures, characters, and the hidden influences of the celestial intelligences. It also observes other mysteries which, because they carry the likeness of celestial powers and invoked spirits, easily entice them and compel them to approach as if driven by a necessity of conformity. Moreover, it holds them so they do not easily depart, as we read in **Porphyry’s** <note>Porphyry of Tyre, a 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote extensively on theurgical practices and oracles.</note> writings on the oracles.

The second kind of divine frenzy <term>furor; the state of being inspired or possessed by a divine power</term> proceeds according to **Dionysius** <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a highly influential Christian mystic and theologian.</note>. This occurs through external and internal purifications, exorcisms, sacraments, solemnities, rites, sacred places, and observances. It directs the soul into the mind—its highest part—and makes it a worthy and uncontaminated temple of the gods in which divine spirits may dwell. The soul, possessing these spirits as companions for life, is filled by them with happiness, wisdom, and oracles. This happens not through signs, marks, or conjectures, but by a certain stirring of the soul and a loose, free movement. In this way, **Bacchus** prophesied to the Boeotians, **Epimenides** <note>OCR reads "Epimenipes"; a famous Greek seer and philosopher.</note> to the people of Cos, and the **Erythraean Sibyl** to the Trojans. Sometimes this frenzy happens through a clear vision, and sometimes through an express voice. In this manner, **Socrates** was guided by his **daemon** <term>a tutelary or guiding spirit, not necessarily an evil entity</term>, whose warnings he diligently obeyed, whose voice he frequently heard with his ears, and to whom the form of the daemon often appeared. For prophetic spirits are accustomed to show themselves as visible companions to well-purified souls. There are many examples of this in the Holy Scriptures, such as with **Abraham** and his handmaid **Hagar**, in **Jacob**, **Gideon**, **Elijah**, **Tobias**, **Daniel**, and many others.

Thus **Adam** had a familiar acquaintance with the angel **Raziel**; **Shem**, the son of Noah, with **Jophiel**; **Abraham** with **Zahiel**; **Isaac** and **Jacob** with **Peliel**; **Joseph**, **Joshua**, and **Daniel** with **Gabriel**; **Moses** with **Metatron**; **Elijah** with **Maltiel**; the younger **Tobias** with **Raphael**; **David** with **Cerniel**; **Manoah** <note>OCR reads "Manne."</note> with **Phadael**; **Kenaz** <note>OCR reads "Cenez."</note> with **Ceruel**; **Ezekiel** with **Hasmael**; **Ezra** with **Uriel**; and **Solomon** with **Michael**. 

Sometimes these spirits, by their own power, enter and seize both the soul and the physical body—whether of an animal or a human—and using that soul as a foundation, <margin>Balaam's ass.</margin> they produce voices through the bodily instruments. This is manifest in the story of **Balaam's ass**, and in **Saul**, upon whom the spirit of the Lord leapt and he prophesied. Concerning these things, **Apollo** says the following in the oracles found in **Porphyry** <note>Porphyry of Tyre, a Neoplatonic philosopher.</note>:

> The light of Phoebus, tamed by songs, flowed down from on high; carried silently through the clear air, breathing with a sonorous inspiration and gliding into hearts, it entered the innocent mind capable of receiving the holy divinity, and brought forth a voice from a mortal throat. <note>original: "Carminibus domitus Phœbeus fulgur..."</note>

<summary>Agrippa describes the second type of divine frenzy, which involves the purification of the soul to become a temple for divine spirits or angels. He provides a list of biblical figures and the specific angels who acted as their guides or "familiars."</summary>

# ON OCCULT PHILOSOPHY

### ¶ Concerning the third kind of frenzy, from Apollo.
### Chapter XLVIII.

<margin>The Ephod. Eleazar.</margin>
The third frenzy indeed proceeds from Apollo, that is, from the mind of the world. This frenzy—through certain sacred mysteries, vows, sacrifices, adorations, invocations, and certain sacred crafts or secret preparations <note>original: "arcanis quibusdam confectionibus"</note> into which the gods have infused the power of their spirit—causes the soul to rise above the mind by joining it with names and spirits. This is as we read concerning the **Ephod** <note>A garment worn by the High Priest of Israel, used in divination to determine God's will.</note>, which, once applied, immediately caused men to prophesy. Thus we also read in the *Book of Senators*, in the chapters of **Eleazar**, that **Rabbi Ishmael** <note>A famous Jewish sage and mystic to whom many early Kabbalistic texts were attributed.</note> prepared certain little cakes inscribed with certain divine and angelic names and so consecrated them; whoever ate them with faith, hope, and charity soon shone with the prophetic spirit of wisdom. We read in the same place that **Rabbi Johanam**, the son of Jochahidis, similarly illuminated a certain unrefined farmer named **Eleazar** who was completely devoid of all learning; surrounded by a sudden radiance, he unexpectedly preached such deep mysteries of the law in the assembly of the wise that he was a source of wonder to all standing by. And it is recorded in memory concerning a certain Egyptian, **Heraiscus**, that he was endowed with a certain divine nature such that by the mere sight of statues which possessed some divinity within them, he was immediately stirred by a divine frenzy.

<margin>Saul the prophet.</margin>
We read also in the sacred scriptures that when **Saul** was among the prophets, the spirit of the Lord rushed upon him and he prophesied; but when he departed from the band of prophets, he ceased to prophesy. Something similar happened to those guards whom Saul sent to capture **David**; when they saw the band of prophets and **Samuel** standing over them, the spirit of the Lord came upon them too, and they also prophesied. So great is the abundance of divine light in prophets seized by divine frenzy that it often seizes those near them and compels them to rave with a similar spirit. It is therefore not incredible that someone can suddenly become wise from being ignorant, and again become ignorant from being wise.

<margin>A wondrous art.</margin>
For there is a certain art (but known to very few) for thus informing, adorning, and illuminating the faithful and pure soul of a man, so that it may be raised from the darkness of ignorance suddenly to the lights of wisdom and learning. Conversely, there is a capacity to strip the impure and the unbelieving of that same gift of wisdom and learning through certain hidden secrets, and restore them to their former ignorance. The human soul can also (as **Apuleius** <note>A Roman writer and Platonist who was famously accused of practicing magic.</note> testifies), especially when simple and pure, be lulled and drawn out by the distraction and charm of certain sacred things to the point of forgetting the present; thus, with the memory of the body removed, it is brought back into its own divine nature. Thus enlightened by divine light and inspired by divine frenzy, it may then foretell future things and receive the power for certain marvelous effects. Hence **Iamblichus** <note>A Syrian Neoplatonist philosopher who emphasized the use of ritual or 'theurgy' to communicate with the divine.</note> says: "When the seers are inspired by the power of a god, they fear nothing, they dread nothing: for through..."

<summary>This page describes the third type of divine frenzy, attributed to Apollo, which allows the soul to transcend the intellect and gain prophetic wisdom through sacred rituals, objects like the Ephod, or even proximity to other prophets. Agrippa argues that this "wondrous art" can suddenly illuminate the ignorant or strip the unworthy of their knowledge.</summary>

In both cases, driven by this divine spirit, she would pour forth her prophecies. Then, a great fire flying out from the cave would surround the prophetess on all sides, and filling her with its divine power, it would move her; or, while clinging to the sacred seat, through which she was inspired by the god, she would immediately break forth into prophecy. 

But also the prophetic seer among the **Branchidae** <note>The priests of the oracle of Apollo at Didyma, near Miletus.</note>, who sits upon an axle, either carries a wand in her hand granted to her by some deity, or sometimes washes her feet and waist in the waters, or breathes in the vapor of the fire from the waters. By all these means, she is filled with divine splendor and, being full, she reveals the oracles she has produced. We also read that in the region of Thrace there was an inner shrine sacred to **Liber** <note>The Roman name for Bacchus or Dionysus, the god of wine and ecstasy.</note>, from which prophecies and oracles were typically given; the attendants of this temple performed their duties after drinking a great deal of wine. 

Among the people of **Claros**, where there was a temple of Clarian Apollo, those permitted to speak divine truths performed their tasks after first drinking water. There was also a prophetic spring at **Patras** in **Achaia** established before the temple of **Ceres** <note>The Roman goddess of agriculture (Greek: Demeter).</note>; those consulting it about the recovery of the sick would lower a mirror tied to a thin cord until it touched the surface of the spring's water. After performing certain prayers and burning incense, the outcome of the matter would reveal itself in the mirror. 

There was also, not far from **Epidaurus** in the city of Laconia, a deep pool called the "Water of Juno." After throwing small wheat cakes into it, responses were given: they were favorable if the water calmly retained what had been thrown in, but unfavorable if it rejected them as if in scorn. It is recorded that the craters of **Mount Etna** acted in a similar way: coins or sacrificial victims thrown into them would show the same omen of a happy or sad outcome by the retention or rejection of the offerings. **Dio** <note>Cassius Dio, a Roman historian of the 2nd and 3rd centuries AD.</note> tells similar stories in his Roman history about a place he calls the **Nympheum** <note>A monument or sanctuary dedicated to nymphs.</note>; there, by throwing incense into the flames in this manner, oracles were obtained regarding everything one wished to know, except for matters concerning death and marriage. 

It is also a marvel what **Aristotle** recorded about the spring of the **Palici** <note>Ancient Sicilian twin deities of the underworld and geysers.</note> in Sicily; those about to take an oath would come to it, and whatever they wished to affirm, they would write on tablets and seal them before throwing them into the spring. If the statements were true, the tablets were seen to float on the water; but if they were false and sworn with evil intent, they sank immediately to the bottom. Then, a fire would suddenly leap out and seize the person guilty of perjury, burning them to ashes. There was also an oak tree in the city of **Dodona** <note>The oldest Hellenic oracle, where the rustling of oak leaves was interpreted as the voice of Zeus.</note> which, whenever someone entered to receive a response, would immediately move and produce a sound...

### Chapter XLIX. On the fourth kind of frenzy, from Venus.

The fourth frenzy, proceeding from **Venus** <note>In this context, Venus represents the Neoplatonic concept of divine beauty and the "Celestial Venus" who draws the soul toward God, rather than mere physical desire.</note>, turns and transforms the mind into God through burning love, and makes it entirely like God, as if it were God’s own image. Regarding this, **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure to whom the Hermetic writings are attributed.</note> says: *O Asclepius, man is a great miracle, a living being to be honored and adored; for he passes into the nature of God as if he himself were God. He knows the race of demons, since he recognizes that he has the same origin as them; he despises the part of human nature within himself, having put his trust in the divinity of his other part.* Therefore, the soul, having now been turned and made like God, is so formed by God that, above all intellect, it knows all things by a certain essential contact with the divinity. 
<margin>Why Love is blind</margin>
For this reason, **Orpheus** <note>The legendary musician and prophet; here Agrippa refers to the "Orphic" tradition of theology.</note> describes Love as being without eyes, because he is above the intellect. And now the soul, having been so turned toward God by love and raised above the intellectual sphere—beyond the fact that it has attained the spirit of soothsaying and prophecy by its complete virtue—sometimes performs even more wonderful and greater things than the very nature of the world itself performs. This kind of work is called a **miracle**. For just as the heavens, by their own image and by their light and heat, perform those things which the power of fire does not achieve by its natural quality (which is most well-known in **alchemical** <note>original: "alchymicis"; referring to the practice of alchemy, where celestial influences were believed to aid in the transformation of matter.</note> matters through experience itself), so also God, through His own image and light, perfects those things which the world cannot do by its own innate power. But the **image of God is man**—at least the man who, now made like God by the frenzy of Venus, lives by the mind alone and "receives Jove with his whole heart." <note>original: "capit toto pectore Iouem"; a poetic way of saying the soul is filled with the presence of the highest deity.</note> Then the human soul, according to the 
<margin>The human soul.</margin>
teachers of the Hebrews and the **Cabalists** <note>Followers of Kabbalah, a school of Jewish mysticism; Agrippa heavily integrated these ideas into his philosophy.</note>, is defined as being the light of God, created after the image of the **Word** <note>original: "verbi"; the Logos or divine reason.</note>, the cause of causes and the first exemplar, shaped by the substance of God and by His seal, the character of which is the eternal Word. Looking upon this, Hermes Trismegistus says that such a man is either superior to the dwellers in heaven, or at least possesses an equal fate.

### Chapter L. On rapture and ecstasy: and the prophecies that happen to those seized by the falling sickness and fainting, and those that occur to the dying.

<margin>What rapture is</margin>
**Rapture** is a withdrawal, an alienation, and an illumination of the soul proceeding from God, through which God draws back the soul—which had fallen from the upper world to the lower—from the lower regions back to the upper. The cause of this in us is the continuous contemplation of sublime things, which, insofar as it joins the mind to incorporeal wisdom by the deepest intention of the soul, so far does it call the soul away from sensible things and the body by its more vehement agitations, and (as in...

...as **Plato** says, sometimes the soul even escapes the body itself and seems, in a way, to be dissolved, just as **Aurelius Augustine** <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD); this refers to a story in *The City of God* regarding a priest named Restitutus.</note> relates concerning the priest of **Calama** (whom we mentioned above). "He lay there," Augustine says, "exactly like a corpse, without breath; and when he was burned and cut, he felt nothing." So great, therefore, is the command of the soul when it has followed its own nature and is not weighed down by the allurements of the senses. By its own virtue, it suddenly ascends—not only while remaining in the body, but sometimes, freed from its shackles, it flies outside the body toward that super-celestial cohabitation. There, now most proximal and most similar to God, it becomes a receptacle for divine effects, filled with divine light and oracles. Regarding this, **Zoroaster** <note>The legendary ancient Persian prophet, often cited in Renaissance magic as a source of "Chaldean" wisdom.</note> says: *You must ascend to the light itself, and to the rays of the Father, from whence the soul was sent to you, clothed in much Mind.* And **Trismegistus** says: *It will behoove you to ascend above the heavens, and to be far distant from the choirs of demons.* And **Pythagoras** says: *If you, leaving the body behind, pass into the free ether, you shall be an immortal god.* Thus we read that **Hermes**, **Socrates**, **Xenocrates**, **Plato**, **Plotinus**, **Heraclitus**, **Pythagoras**, and **Zoroaster** were accustomed to be called away by rapture, and in this way, they learned the wisdom of many things. We also read in **Herodotus** that there was a philosopher of wonderful <margin>The soul of Artheus.</margin> knowledge in **Proconnesus** named **Artheus** <note>Likely referring to Aristeas of Proconnesus, a semi-legendary Greek poet and miracle-worker.</note>, and his soul would sometimes leave his body; after seeing long distances and paths, it would return to the body more learned. **Pliny** relates the same thing: <margin>The soul of Harmonis.</margin> that the soul of **Harmonis of Clazomenae** <note>Commonly known as Hermotimus of Clazomenae, a philosopher whose soul was said to wander the world while he slept.</note> was accustomed to do this; having left the body, it used to wander and report many true things from afar. And there are even <margin>The wonders of the Norwegians and Lapps.</margin> to this day many among the **Norwegians** and **Lapps** <note>original: "pilappios," referring to the Sámi people of northern Scandinavia, frequently associated with shamanism and astral travel in early modern literature.</note> who withdraw themselves entirely from the body for three days, and having returned, report many things from distant places. Meanwhile, it is necessary to guard them so that no living animal happens to step over them; otherwise, they say the soul cannot return to its body. It must be known, therefore, (according to <margin>The soul freed from the body encompasses all space and time.</margin> the doctrine of the **Egyptians**) that since the soul is a certain spiritual light, when it is freed from the body, it encompasses all space and all time—not unlike a light enclosed in a lantern, which, once opened, is diffused everywhere and does not fail, for it is everywhere and always. And **Cicero**, in his book *On Divination*, says: *The mind of man never divines unless it is so free that it has absolutely nothing, or very little, to do with the body.* Therefore, when it has reached that state which is the highest degree of contemplative perfection, it is then snatched away from all created forms and understands not through acquired appearances, but through an inspection of the **Ideas** <note>In the Platonic sense, "Ideas" are the perfect, eternal blueprints of all things in the divine mind.</note>, and it knows all things in the light of the Ideas. Plato says very few men become participants in this light in this life, but all the gods do. **Syncope** <note>Fainting or loss of consciousness.</note> and the **falling sickness** <note>original: "morbiq̄ comitiales," a historical term for epilepsy.</note> also imitate rapture in a certain way, and in these states, prophecies very often occur just as they do in rapture. We read that **Hercules** and many **Arabs** excelled in this kind of prophesying. There are also certain prophecies that stand midway between natural divinations and supernatural oracles—namely, those which are pronounced from an excess of passion, such as from excessive love, or sadness, or amidst frequent sighs, or in the agony of death, as in **Statius** concerning the mother of **Achilles**:

->Neither did he fear the idle [terrors] of his parents<-
->Nor did he tremble at the oars beneath the glassy whirlpool<-

For there is in our souls a certain clear power, capable of all things, but it is obscured and hindered by the gloom of the body and our mortality. However, once the soul has achieved immortality after death and is released from the body, it possesses full and perfect knowledge. For this reason, it often happens that those close to death, or those weakened by old age, experience an unusual light, because the soul is then less hindered by the senses and understands more sharply. Now, as if the chains were slightly relaxed and the soul were no longer entirely subject to the body—being close, as it were, to the place where it is about to migrate—it easily perceives revelations that offer themselves, mingling with its final struggles. 

On this matter, **Ambrose** <note>St. Ambrose (c. 339–397 AD), the Bishop of Milan. This quote comes from his work *On the Belief in the Resurrection*.</note> says in his book *On the Belief in the Resurrection*: "Our soul longs to escape this bodily prison <note>original: "ergastulum," a term for a Roman workhouse or private prison for slaves</note>, and being free with a movement like the air, it knows not where it goes or where it comes from. We know, however, that it survives the body, and having moved beyond the barriers of its own senses, it discerns with a free gaze those things which it did not see while situated in the body. We can estimate this by the example of those who sleep; their souls, while the body is buried in rest, raise themselves to higher things and report to the body visions of absent or even celestial things."

### Chapter LI. Concerning Prophetic Dreams.

<margin>An oracle in a dream.</margin>
I speak now of all that proceeds from the <term>phantastic spirit</term> <note>The "spiritus phantasticus" was believed to be a subtle, vaporous substance that acted as a bridge between the physical senses and the higher mind.</note> and the intellect when they are joined together—either through the illumination of the <term>Agent Intellect</term> <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, the part of the mind that actively creates universal concepts out of sensory data.</note> upon our soul, or through the pure revelation of some divine power, occurring when the mind is purged and tranquil. From this, our soul receives true oracles and provides us with prophecies in abundance. For in dreams, we seem to ask questions, to learn, to read, and to find things out. Many doubts, many counsels, and many things unknown or unexpected—never before attempted by our minds—are revealed to us in dreams. There appear images of unknown places and the likenesses of men, both living and dead; future events that have not yet occurred are foretold, and things that have happened elsewhere, of which no news has yet arrived, are revealed. These dreams require no other art of interpretation, unlike those we spoke of in the first book, which belong to <term>divination</term> rather than <term>prescience</term> <note>Agrippa distinguishes between "divination" (interpreting symbols/omens) and "prescience" (direct, clear foreknowledge).</note>. 

It happens that those who see these things often do not understand them; for (as **Abdala the Arab** <note>Likely referring to a medieval Arabic philosopher or dream interpreter known to Renaissance scholars.</note> says), <margin>From where it happens that one sees dreams and understands them.</margin> just as seeing dreams comes from the strength of the imagination, so understanding them comes from the strength of the intellect. Therefore, he whose intellect is drowsy, being too deeply submerged in the business of the flesh—or whose phantastic spirit is so dull and unpolished that it cannot receive the forms and flowing images of the higher intellect, or cannot retain them once received—such a person is clearly useless for the prophecy of dreams. 

It is necessary, therefore, for one who wishes to receive true dreams to keep the phantastic spirit pure, unshaken, and undisturbed, and to compose it in such a way that it is made worthy for the mind and intellect to preside over it and make things known to it. Such a spirit is most fit for prophecies; it is (as **Synesius** <note>Synesius of Cyrene (c. 373–414 AD), a Neoplatonist philosopher and bishop who wrote a famous treatise on dreams.</note> says) the clearest mirror for all the "idols" <note>Images or subtle forms emitted by objects.</note> flowing from things everywhere. When we are healthy in body, not disturbed in mind, and not weighed down by food or drink...

<summary>This page explains that the soul possesses inherent universal knowledge which is usually clouded by the body, but manifests during sleep or near death. It introduces prophetic dreams as the result of a purified imagination (phantastic spirit) receiving truths from the higher intellect or divine revelation.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of how the soul, when less hindered by the physical body—specifically during sleep—can perceive divine truths and prophetic visions. It emphasizes the need for a pure lifestyle to achieve this clarity.</meta>

# BOOK THREE. CLXX

[not] weighed down [by food], nor grieving in poverty, and with no vices of lust or anger clamoring against us, we go to bed chastely and sleep; then our soul, pure and divine, released from every harmful thought and now free through sleep, relies on this divine spirit as an instrument. It receives into itself the radiating and shining rays and images from divine minds. As if in a certain **deific mirror** <note>original: "deifico speculo," a mirror that reflects the divine</note>, the soul gazes upon these things far more certainly, clearly, and effectively than through any common investigation of the intellect or wandering of reason. The divine powers, taking advantage of the opportunity of nightly solitude, invite the soul to their assembly. Nor, even then, will the propitious divinity be lacking to the waking person to moderate their actions. Whoever, therefore, keeps their spirit pure through tranquil and religious meditation, as well as through a diet that is temperate and moderated according to nature, uses a spirit that is perfectly prepared. In this way, he becomes <margin>likewise</margin> **divine and knowing**. 

On the other hand, whoever languishes with a "fantastic spirit" <note>Referring here to a mind filled with disordered or hallucinatory "phantasms"</note> does not receive clear and distinct visions. Rather, just as a bleary eye judges confusedly and indistinctly because of its weakness, so also when we are filled with excess food and wine, our spirit is oppressed by harmful vapors. In such a state, it is deceived and grows dull—just as murky water is affected differently under the same form. For this reason, the seer **Amphiaraus** <note>A legendary hero and prophet in Greek mythology</note> (as we read in **Philostratus**) <margin>Philostratus, Book 2, Chapter 14</margin> ordered those wishing to receive oracles to abstain from food for an entire day, and from wine for three days. This was because the soul could not prophesy rightly unless it were liberated from wine and food. For the gods are accustomed to grant oracles to sober and religious souls who are vacant for divine worship. Whence **Orpheus** exclaims:

> O messenger of things to come, greatest of seers,
> You approach souls soothed by the quiet of sleep.
> Calling to them, you rouse the mind,
> And whisper the intentions of the blessed gods into them through dreams.
> Silently pronouncing future things to silent souls.

<margin>The abstinence of seers</margin> I say it is to these souls, whose minds make the most upright use of divine worship, [that these things are revealed].

ON OCCULT PHILOSOPHY.

...they were accustomed to lie down for the sake of dreaming; the same was done in the temple of **Aesculapius** <note>The Greek god of medicine and healing, known as Asclepius; his temples were centers for "incubation," a practice where patients slept in the sanctuary to receive healing dreams</note>, from whom they believed true dreams were sent. Similarly, the Calabrians, wishing to consult **Podalyrius** <note>A legendary healer and son of Asclepius</note>, the son of Aesculapius, would fall asleep near his tomb upon lambskins; 
<margin>The time for dreams is night.</margin>
for in this way, he would advise them in their dreams about whatever matter they desired to know. However, the most favorable time for dreams is the night, when the senses are free from wandering objects and the errors of the day, as well as from vain distractions. When no fear strikes the soul and thoughts do not waver, the mind is most peaceful and remains persistently attached to the divinity.
<margin>Four kinds of true dreams.</margin>
Furthermore (as **Rabbi Yohanan** <note>A prominent Jewish sage of the 3rd century, often cited in the Talmud</note> says in the book *Sanhedrin* <note>original: "libro senat," referring to the Talmudic tractate Sanhedrin</note>), there are four kinds of true dreams: First, the morning dream, which occurs between sleep and wakefulness; second, that which one sees concerning another; third, one whose interpretation is shown to the dreamer himself through a nightly vision; and fourth, that which is repeated to the same dreamer, according to what **Joseph** said to **Pharaoh**: "As for the dream having been seen by you a second time regarding the same matter, it is a sign of its certainty." The firmest dream, however, is that concerning things which one has revolved within oneself and agitated in the mind when going to sleep, just as it is written: "O King, you began to think upon your bed what should come to pass hereafter." It is necessary, moreover, for an 
<margin>Interpreter of dreams.</margin>
interpreter of others' dreams to possess the knowledge by which he can distinguish and discern the similarities of all things, and to know the customs of all nations according to the laws they have received from God and from the angels. Beyond this, it should be known that there is hardly any, or perhaps no dream, that is without some degree of vanity—just as no grain of wheat exists 
<margin>Vain things mixed with dreams.</margin>
without chaff. This is proven by the dream of the patriarch Joseph itself, which 
<margin>Joseph's dream.</margin>
his father **Jacob** interpreted, saying: "What does this dream that you have seen mean? Shall I and your mother and your brothers indeed come to bow down to the earth before you?" This was not fulfilled regarding his mother, who had died shortly thereafter. These things are also found in the aforementioned book by Rabbi Yohanan; to which **Rabbi Levi** adds, saying that every prophetic dream can be delayed in its fulfillment for up to twenty-two years. Thus, Joseph dreamed in the seventeenth year of his age, and it was later brought into action in the thirty-ninth year of his age. Therefore, one wishing now 
<margin>Requirements for receiving divine dreams.</margin>
to receive divine dreams should be well-disposed in body, with a brain free from vapors and a soul free from perturbations. On that day, let him abstain from dinner, and let him not drink anything that could intoxicate him. Let him have a clean and bright bedroom, even one that is exorcised and consecrated. There, having performed a fumigation <note>The burning of incense or herbs to purify the air</note> at the appropriate time, with his fingers bound by **dream-rings** <term>somniorum annulis</term> <note>Magical rings inscribed with names or symbols intended to facilitate prophetic dreams</note>, and having placed a celestial image and a sacred paper beneath his head, let him seek his bed after invoking the deity with sacred prayers, with his thought intent upon the matter he desires to know. For in this way, he shall see most true and indubitable dreams, with a true illumination of the intellect. Whoever, therefore, knows how to combine those things which we have said scattered throughout these books concerning this matter, shall easily obtain the gift of oracles and dreams.

## ¶ How he who wishes to receive oracles should dispose himself. Chapter LIII.

<margin>1</margin>
Whoever desires to approach the highest state of the soul and sets out to seek oracles must be disposed in a chaste and holy manner. He must approach pure and clean, so that his soul is not defiled by the infection of any filth, nor bears the scars of sins impressed upon his breast. It is necessary to thoroughly segregate and purge the mind—as far as the necessity of nature permits—from every disease, dullness, malice, and similar passions, and from every irrational condition which follows the soul like rust follows iron. This is done by rightly composing and ordering those things that pertain to the tranquility of the mind; for in this way, he will receive truer and more effective responses.

<margin>
The conjunction of religion and wisdom. Wisdom according to Solomon and Lucretius.

->**THIRD BOOK.**<-

<margin>All virtue</margin>
He says: I can do all things in Him who strengthens me, namely God <note>original: "Omnia possum in eo, qui me confortat deus," referencing Philippians 4:13</note>: for He is our virtue, without whom (as He Himself testifies) we can do nothing. This is even admitted by **Aristotle** in his *Meteorology* and *Ethics*, where he states that there is no virtue, whether natural or moral, except through God. Furthermore, in his secret writings, he asserts that a good and healthy <term>intellect</term><note>In this context, "intellect" refers to the highest faculty of the soul, capable of perceiving divine truths</note> can penetrate the secrets of nature, provided that the influence of divine virtue is present; otherwise, it is impossible. We receive this influence only when we release ourselves from the heavy impediments of carnal and earthly occupations and from all external agitation. For a bleary and unclean eye cannot look upon things that are excessively bright; nor can anyone grasp divine things who is ignorant of the <margin>One must arrive at purity of mind step by step.</margin> purification of the soul. However, it is necessary to reach this purity of mind gradually and as if by certain steps. Not everyone newly initiated into these mysteries immediately comprehends all bright things; instead, the mind must be accustomed little by little until the intellect stands out within us and, applying itself to the divine light, becomes mixed with it. Thus, when the human soul has been rightly purged and <margin>The effects of the soul's purgation.</margin> expiated, and then released from all variety, it shines forth with free motion, ascends upward, grasps divine things, and even instructs itself when it happens to be instructed from elsewhere. At that point, it requires neither recollection nor demonstration because of its natural skill, for through its <term>mind</term><note>The "mens" or "mind" was considered the "charioteer" or guiding head of the soul in Platonic thought</note>—which is the head and charioteer of the soul—it imitates the angels by its own nature. It attains what it desires not by succession or time, but in a <margin>David, Solomon, and others, including the apostles, were suddenly taught.</margin> sudden moment. For **David** did not learn letters, yet from a shepherd, he became a prophet and most learned in divine matters. **Solomon**, in a single night's dream, was filled with the wisdom of all things above and below. Likewise were **Isaiah**, **Ezekiel**, **Daniel**, and the rest of the prophets and apostles instructed. For the soul (which is the common opinion of the **Pythagoreans** and **Platonists**) can, through the <term>purgatory path</term><note>A spiritual process of cleansing the soul of material attachments to reach a state of enlightenment</note> without any other study or investigation, acquire a perfect knowledge of all things knowable through a simple and easy gathering of divine influences upon the intelligible things it already possesses. It can also arrive at this state through external expiation, so that it understands all things indivisibly through its own <margin>How the mind is to be expiated.</margin> substantial form. The mind is purged and expiated through cleanliness, abstinence, penitence, and almsgiving. Furthermore, certain sacred institutions contribute to the same end, as will be shown below; for the soul must be cared for through the study of religions—which are generally hidden—so that, being restored to health, confirmed in truth, and fortified by divine protections, it does not fear the shocks that may arise.

For this reason, the **Pythagorean** philosophers, captivated by the greed for oracles, would wash in rivers after celebrating divine praises...

<margin>The habits and bearing of the Brahmans.</margin> Similarly, the **Brahmans** <note>The priestly caste of India, highly regarded by Renaissance occultists as ancient keepers of wisdom.</note>, the wise men of the Indians, were accustomed to wash in the fountain called Dirce <note>Agrippa likely references a tradition—possibly from Philostratus—associating these sages with specific ritual sites, though Dirce is classically located in Boeotia, Greece.</note>, having first stripped off their clothes and anointed their heads with amber drops and scents suitable for that purpose; then, after they were sufficiently clean according to the rite, they would go out around noon, dressed in white linen, with a white miter, wearing rings on their fingers and carrying staves in their hands.

For it was the custom of the nations, when they were about to perform sacrifices to the celestial gods, to purify the body with washing; however, when one was to make a sacrifice to the infernal gods <note>The gods of the Underworld.</note>, a mere sprinkling was sufficient. And also where he narrates the burial of **Misenus**, he sings:

> The same man thrice circled his companions with pure water, 
> sprinkling them with light dew and a branch of a fertile olive tree.

For when cleanliness is achieved, man becomes celestial and spiritual, and it disposes him toward the vision and union with God, provided that he serves God with a clean body and a pure mind, and embraces cleanliness in all things: in the internal organs, in the skin, in clothes, in utensils, in dwellings, in gifts, offerings, victims, and sacrifices. ### On abstinence and fasting, and chastity, solitude, and tranquility of the mind and ascent. Chapter 55.

Abstinence also everywhere protects and defends its followers against vices and <margin>a</margin> evil demons, and renders the soul like an untainted temple of God, joining the mind with God. Nothing is better for the health and balance of one's constitution than to accumulate as little surplus as possible and not to exceed the measure of necessary food. Indeed, one should not take in more nourishment than nature can handle, but rather only that which makes nature stronger. As some say of **CHRIST**, he took food with such a limit that it did not generate the "superfluous waste of the fourth digestion" <note>In ancient medicine, the "fourth digestion" was the final process where nutrients were assimilated into the tissues; Agrippa implies Christ's body was so refined it left no waste.</note>. Many others have also enjoyed health and physical agility through a scarcity of food, such as <margin>The Fast of Moses and Elijah.</margin> **Moses** and **Elijah**, who extended their fasting for forty days. Because of this, the face of the former shone with light, and the latter was carried away, leading his body as easily as a spirit at his slightest whim. 

For the Magi and philosophers assert that our spirit <term>spiritus: a subtle, vaporous substance that mediates between the immaterial soul and the physical body</term> is not nourished in the same way as the earthly body, which receives its food through certain organs after the cooking of food or drink. Instead, they claim it draws its nourishment from all sides through the whole body in the manner of a sponge—specifically from the thinnest vapors that penetrate the body everywhere. Therefore, those who desire to have this spirit pure and powerful use drier foods and thin out this thick body through fasting, making it easily permeable so that the spirit is neither made heavy nor suffocated by the body's weight. Then, through washings, rubbings, exercise, and clean clothing, they keep the body itself pure, and they strengthen the spirit with ritual cleansings and incense <note>original: "suffitibus" — fumigations or incense</note>, leading it toward a pure and thin sincerity. 

We ought, therefore, to be pure and abstinent in taking food, just as the **Pythagorean** philosophers, who, by keeping a sacred and sober table, lived their lives <margin>The effects of temperance.</margin> in total temperance. For temperance of life and constitution—which brings us no "uproar of the humors" <note>The four bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) believed to govern health and personality; an excess of one was thought to cause illness or mental disturbance.</note> that might provoke the imagination toward any false image—ensures that our soul, whether dreaming or sometimes even while awake, is always subject to heavenly influences. Furthermore, the Pythagoreans promise that if anyone wisely moderates every movement of both their mind and body through abstinence, they will enjoy perpetual health of both and even a long life. 

So it was with the <margin>The college of the Brahmans.</margin> **Brahmans** <note>The priestly caste of India, admired by Renaissance scholars for their asceticism and wisdom.</note>, who admitted no one into their college unless they abstained from wine, meat, and vices, saying that no one can understand God except the one who emulates Him through divine conduct. Phraotes <note>A king of India described in the writings of Philostratus.</note> also taught this to the lower Indians. Moreover, <margin>From what one must especially abstain.</margin> it is necessary for us to abstain from everything that infects the mind and spirit, from cravings and envy, which (as **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary sage and purported author of the Hermetic corpus.</note> says) are the servants of injustice used for building up evil.

...driving the mind and hand toward crimes; likewise from leisure and luxury, for the soul, suffocated by sluggishness and lust, cannot foresee anything celestial.
<margin>Hierophants: Athenian priests.</margin>
For this reason, the priests of the Athenians, who are called Hierophants in Greek (as Jerome reports), in order to act more chastely in sacred rites and to devote themselves to divine matters, <margin>Chastity of the mind.</margin> were accustomed to castrate themselves by drinking hemlock <note>Ancient writers like Jerome believed hemlock could physically suppress sexual desire, though it is a lethal poison.</note>. Furthermore, a chastity of the mind devoted to God makes our soul (as Orpheus teaches Musaeus in the hymn to the God of all) a perpetual and ever-ready temple of God. Moreover, we must abstain from all multitude and variety of senses, affects, imaginations, opinions, and such passions which wound the soul and pervert the judgment of reason, as we see clearly in those captured by love, the envious, and the ambitious. Because of these passions, Cicero (in his *Tusculan Disputations*) names them as distresses of the soul and pestilential diseases. Horace, indeed, calls them furies or insanities when he sings:

->A thousand madnesses for girls, a thousand for boys.<-

It seems he also feels the same in this: that all men are fools in some respect; hence it is read in Ecclesiasticus: <margin>Ecclesiastes 1: The number of fools.</margin> The number of fools is infinite. For this reason, the Stoics deny that <margin>Passions do not fall upon the wise.</margin> passions fall upon the wise man—passions, I say, which follow sensory perception—for they grant rational and mental passions to the wise man. Boethius also seems to feel this way where he sings that certain passions must be cast aside in the search for truth, in these verses:

| | |
|---|---|
| If you also wish | Drive away fear, |
| To see the truth | Let not grief be present, |
| With clear light, | And put hope to flight; |
| To keep to the path | The mind is cloudy, |
| On the straight track: | And bound with bridles |
| Drive away joys, | Where these things reign. |

It is necessary, therefore, for us to strip and turn the soul entirely away from all multitude and such passions, so that we may attain the simplest truth. Indeed, many of the philosophers are read to have attained this through long periods of solitude. For the soul, freed through solitude from every care of human business, being vacant for the sacred spirits and celestial beings, feels daily those same things which the celestial gifts intend to effect. Thus Moses, the <margin>The contemplation of Moses.</margin> legislator of the Hebrews and the greatest of prophets, and learned in all the wisdom of the Chaldeans and Egyptians, when he wished to withdraw himself from the senses, retired into the vast solitudes of Ethiopia. There, with all human business set aside, he turned his soul and mind to the contemplation of divine things alone; in which he so pleased almighty God that he earned the merit of seeing and gazing upon Him face to face, having also received that stupendous power of miracles which the sacred scriptures witness concerning him. So Zoroaster, the father and prince of the Magi, is said to have attained the knowledge of all natural and divine things by twenty years of solitude, where concerning every kind of divining and...

<header>BOOK THREE.</header>

...wrote and performed many things regarding the art of prophecy <note>original: "vaticinandi arte"</note>. The writings of Orpheus to Musaeus declare that he performed similar works in the deserts of Thrace. Thus we read 
<margin>The learning of Epimenides.</margin>
that Epimenides of Crete was educated in a certain very long sleep; for they say he slept for fifty years. By this, they understand that he remained hidden <note>The author interprets the legendary 50-year sleep of the philosopher Epimenides as a metaphor for a long period of meditative seclusion or "hiding" from the world.</note>. Pythagoras is also said to have remained hidden in a similar way for nearly ten years, and Heraclitus and Democritus delighted in solitude for the same reason. For the more we leave behind the animal and human life, the more we live as angels and God; joined to them and restored to a better lot, we are able to do all things, being masters over everything. 
<margin>What things a human must especially flee.</margin>
How our soul is to be separated from animal life and from every multitude, and how it is to be raised up until it ascends to the One itself—the Good, the True, and the Beautiful—is taught by Proclus <note>Proclus (c. 412–485 AD) was a Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote influential commentaries on Plato.</note> in his commentaries on the *Alcibiades*. He shows how sensible things <note>Objects perceived by the physical senses.</note> are first to be fled so that we may transfer ourselves to an incorporeal essence. There, one must overcome the order of souls—though it is multiplied through many reasons, various habits and proportions, many bonds, and a multiform variety of powers—and strive toward the intellect and the intelligible kingdoms, contemplating by how great a distance these are better than souls. Furthermore, it is permitted to leave behind even that intellectual multitude, though it is united and indivisible, and to arrive at the super-intellectual and essential Unity, which is absolute and free from all multitude: the very fountain of the Good and the True. By a similar reasoning, we must flee every multifaceted knowledge that distracts and deceives us, so that we may attain the simplest truth. Therefore, we must leave behind the multitude of affects, senses, imaginations, and opinions, which are so diverse in themselves that some are contrary to others in any given thing. We must instead ascend to the sciences, in which, although there is a varied multitude, there is nonetheless no contrariety. For all sciences are connected to one another, and one serves and ministers to the other in turn, right up to the one science presupposed by all <note>Likely referring to Metaphysics or "First Philosophy."</note> and which presupposes no other, to which all others must be referred. Yet even that is not the highest peak of knowledge; rather, above it is the pure intellect. Thus, having laid aside all composition, division, and multiform discourse, we ascend to the intellectual life and simple intuition, gazing upon the intelligible essence with indivisible and simple perceptions. In this way, we may attain the very highest existence of the soul—through which we are "one," and under which our internal multitude is united—and so we may reach that first One, from which union resides in all things, through that "One" which is, as it were, the flower of our essence <note>original: "essentiæ nostræ florem"; a Neoplatonic concept referring to the highest, most divine spark within the human soul.</note>. This we finally achieve only when, fleeing every multitude, we rise up into our own unity, are made one, and act in a uniform manner.

<margin>What penance is.</margin>
<margin>A pure sword.</margin>
[It] opposes celestial delights and purges dull joy from the soul, and bestows a certain peculiar power leading back to the higher things. Therefore, penance is not only the mortification <note>In this context, "mortification" refers to the practice of subduing physical desires to strengthen spiritual discipline.</note> of vices, but also a spiritual martyrdom of the soul, which is pierced on every side by the sword of the spirit; but the sword of the spirit is the word of God. Whence 
<margin>Oral confession.</margin>
Jeremiah the prophet says, and also Paul writing to the Ephesians: "Cursed is he who keeps back his sword from blood" <note>original: "Maledictus qui prohibet gladium suum à sanguine" (Jeremiah 48:10). Agrippa interprets this "blood" as the purging of the old self.</note>; and the Psalmist sings: "A sword is in their lips." Therefore, the thoughts and affections of the mind, and all the evils that come out of our heart and mouth, must be explained to the priest in confession, so that he may judge them according to the word of God, and—by the power granted to him by God—cleanse and purge them through enjoined penance, and direct them toward the good. Nor
<margin>Ovid.</margin>
indeed is any sacrament found in religion more powerful for abolishing sins than penance; hence the gods themselves (as Ovid testifies in his letters from *Pontus*)

->They often lighten the punishments, and restore lost sight,<-
->When they see that one has truly repented of the sin.<-

<margin>Praise of almsgiving.</margin>
And there is yet another sacrament of expiation, namely almsgiving <note>The practice of giving money or food to the poor.</note> itself, about which I remember reading little or nothing among the philosophers; but the highest Truth <note>Agrippa refers to Christ as the "highest Truth."</note> taught it to us, saying: "Give alms, and all things are clean to you." And in the book of *Ecclesiasticus* it is read: "As water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving extinguishes sin." And Daniel taught the king of Babylon to redeem his sins with alms, and the angel Raphael 
<margin>The almsgiving of Tobias.</margin>
testifies to Tobias: "For almsgiving delivers from death, and it is that which purges sins and makes one find eternal life." Hence Christ commanded us to pray to the Father, "forgive as we forgive," and "give as we give." Of this he said elsewhere: "You shall receive a hundredfold, and shall possess eternal life." He, when judging the living and the dead, will above all others reproach the damned for neglected alms and works of mercy, saying: "I was hungry and thirsty and you gave me nothing to eat or drink." And yet in another place, speaking of the poor, he said: "What you did for one of these, you did for me." Homer also seems to have felt this, where he introduces a young man speaking to the suitor Antinous in these words: "Antinous, you did not do well to strike the wretched beggar; he will destroy you if there is indeed a god in heaven, for even the gods, taking the form of foreign guests, go everywhere through cities, beholding the injuries and lawlessness of men."

<margin>Purification by sulfur.</margin>
<margin>Sea water.</margin>
<margin>Cinquefoil.</margin>
<margin>The purity of the Olive.</margin>
<margin>Valerian.</margin>
<margin>Wonders of the Baaras root.</margin>
<margin>Fire in Sicily.</margin>
Proclus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote extensively on theurgy and ritual.</note> also writes that priests were accustomed to using sulfur and asphalt in their purifications, or washing with sea water; for sulfur purifies because of the sharpness of its odor, and sea water because of its "fiery" quality <note>In ancient physics, salt and sea water were thought to contain a portion of the element of fire.</note>. In a similar way, the herb cinquefoil <note>original: "pentaphylon," meaning "five-leaved."</note> purifies, which is why ancient priests used it in rituals because of its inherent purity. Likewise with olive branches: for the olive is said to be of such great purity that it is said if a prostitute plants it, the tree will either remain forever barren or wither away entirely. In the same manner, frankincense, myrrh, vervain, and Valerian (which is also called the "shining herb" and in Arabic is called *Fu*) contribute to expiation. So too do the "blessed herb" <note>likely Herb Bennet or Avens</note> and the clove-scented herb. Similarly, the smoke from the gall of a black dog is said to be most powerful in these matters, both for driving out evil demons and for dispelling witchcraft wherever it may be. Likewise, the feathers of a hoopoe, when burned as incense, drive away phantasms.

Yet there is something wonderful and hardly believable, were it not told by Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus, the 1st-century Romano-Jewish historian.</note>, a serious and significant author, in his *History of Jerusalem*, concerning the Baaras root. It is named after a place near Machaerus, a town in Judea. He says it is the color of flame and emits a glow at night, but it is very difficult to catch, as it eludes the hand of the one trying to take it and shrinks from the eye; it does not stay still until it is sprinkled with the urine of a menstruating woman. Even then, it cannot be pulled up without danger, for instant death follows the one who extracts it, unless they are protected by an amulet made from that same root. Those who lack this amulet dig around the earth, performing sacrifices, and then tie the root with a cord to a dog, and quickly move away. At last, the dog, struggling to follow, pulls the root out, and as if paying the price for its master, the dog dies immediately. Afterward, the root can be handled by anyone without danger. Its power in purifications is most excellent, and it has been found to instantly free those who are vexed by unclean spirits.

Theologians believe that these kinds of materials act upon spiritual substances—by putting them to flight, or drawing them near, or soothing them, or inciting them—in the same way that the fire in Sicily acts upon souls. According to William of Paris <note>William of Auvergne (c. 1180–1249), Bishop of Paris and author of *De Universo*.</note>, this fire does not harm bodies, but it intolerably torments the souls of those who approach it. However, we have treated these matters in part above.

### ¶ On Adorations and Vows. Chapter LVIII.

Adorations and vows, sacrifices and offerings, are indeed the steps in sacred rites for seeking God. They are the things which principally provoke the divine will and kindle a sacred and indissoluble union between souls and the gods. For from the prayers which we utter with true and sacred words, and with a focused sense and mind, we acquire great power; for when we apply these to some divine power, they move that power to direct its speech and response toward us through a "divine ray." By this ray (as Dionysius <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, an influential mystical theologian.</note> says), God speaks with men, but so secretly that only a few perceive it. # ON OCCULT PHILOSOPHY

<margin>Adoration.</margin>
That king and prophet David said most frequently: "When," he says, "shall I hear what the Lord God speaks in me?" <note>original: "Quādo audiam quid in me loquatur dominus deus." A reference to Psalm 85:8.</note> Therefore, Adoration, continued for a very long time and practiced very frequently, perfects the intellect. By kindling divine love, it makes the soul larger and more capable of receiving divine lights, bringing in hope, faith, and sacred character. It purges the soul of every contrary and adverse thing, and even repels many evils which would otherwise occur naturally.

<margin>The effects of prayer.</margin>
Hence Ovid sings:
> An angry god is swayed by a pleading voice,
> I have often seen Jove, when he wished to hurl his
> Lightning bolts, hold back his hand when incense was given. <note>original: "Flectitur iratus voce rogante deus..." from Ovid's *The Art of Beauty* (De Medicamine Faciei Femineae).</note>

<margin>How man returns to God.</margin>
Man returns to God through prayers; arriving there (as Plato says in the *Phaedrus*), he stops his horses and enters the banquet hall, where he feeds on ambrosia and drinks nectar. <note>Plato uses the metaphor of the soul as a chariot with two horses; when it reaches the height of heaven, it participates in the feast of the gods.</note> Therefore, those who desire to possess any virtue must pray and supplicate frequently to Him who contains all virtue within Himself.

<margin>The best kind of prayer.</margin>
However, the better and best prayer is not that which is brought forth by the mouth, but that which is offered to God in holy silence and with an untainted mind. It calls out with the "voice of the mind" and venerates the presiding gods <note>original: "p̄sules deos," referring to the higher spiritual entities or planetary governors in the Neoplatonic hierarchy.</note> with the words of the intellectual world.

<margin>What is a vow.</margin>
A Vow, moreover, is an ardent affection of a chaste soul dedicated to God, which, by vowing, earnestly desires that which appears to be good. This affection (as Iamblichus and Proclus <note>Two influential Neoplatonist philosophers who argued that ritual and prayer could bridge the gap between humans and the divine.</note> testify) joins souls to God in such a way that sometimes the operation of God and the soul becomes one: namely, God as the craftsman, and the soul as the divine instrument. All antiquity testifies that through vows, miracles are sometimes performed, diseases are cured, storms are turned away, and similar things occur. Hence we read that the most excellent and wisest men among all nations—the **Brahmans** of the Indians, the **Magi** of the Persians, the **Gymnosophists** <note>literally "naked philosophers," a term used by Greeks for Indian ascetics.</note> of the Egyptians, and the theologians of the Greeks and Chaldeans—who established the festivals of the gods and the hidden mysteries, devoted themselves chiefly to divine vows and prayers and achieved many wonderful things.

<margin>Two things required for the perfection of a vow.</margin>
For the perfection of a vow and adoration (for a vow is not without adoration, nor is adoration entirely perfect without a vow), two things are primarily required: first, the knowledge of that which is to be adored and to whom the vow is to be made; and by what reason, in what order, and by what means the worship is to be performed. For there are many co-operators and instruments of God: namely, the heavens, the stars, the administering spirits, the celestial souls, and the heroes, whom one must first implore as gatekeepers, interpreters, administrators, and mediators.

<margin>Christ is the one Mediator.</margin>
He who proceeds toward the archetypal <note>The "Archetype" refers to the original, supreme model of the Divine from which all other things are copied.</note> God—who alone is the ultimate end of adoration—must do so through these; the other powers are like entrances to God Himself. Know therefore that

<margin>Supplication must be made to God alone.</margin>
adorations and vows must be made primarily with a pure and pious mind to the one supreme God, the Father, King, and Lord of all gods. When, however, these proceed to the inferior gods, it should only be done with the intention of their administration being sub-delegated by the supreme Father. Thus, when adorations and vows are directed to the lower divine powers, Zoroaster and Orpheus <note>Legendary founders of the Persian and Greek mystery traditions, respectively.</note> thought it permissible to use incense, characters, and such things; but when one turns to the supreme...

They elevate the majesty of Jove <note>Agrippa frequently uses the name "Jove" or "Jupiter" to refer to the Supreme Deity in a classical sense.</note>, asserting that those material things ought least to be done; which even Hermes and Plato forbid. Whence Hermes says to Tat: "It is like sacrilege when you pray to God to wish to burn incense and offerings; for these things are foreign (as Porphyry says) to all true piety." <note>original: "Hoc... sacrilegio simile est cum deũ ores, uelle thus & filia accẽdere." Secondly, however, a certain assimilation of our life to the divine life is required—proceeding from purity, chastity, and holiness—along with a lawful desire for that which we hope for. For by this we most highly capture the divine benevolence and are subjected to the divine bounty. For unless we are worthy to be heard because our minds are purged, and unless the things we ask for are worthy to be done, it is manifest that God is not present to our prayers at all. Whence the divine Plato says that God is turned toward injustice by no prayers or gifts. Let us, therefore, ask nothing of God that would be unbecoming for us to want; for we see many frustrated in their prayers and vows for this reason alone: neither are they themselves religiously disposed, nor are their desires and petitions made concerning those things which are pleasing to God. Nor do they know how to discern in what order he should be adored, or through which mediators God Himself is to be approached. Ignorance of these things very often reduces our orations and prayers to nothing, and causes our vows to be denied to our supplications.

## Concerning sacrifices and offerings, their kinds and manners. Chapter LIX.

<margin>
What sacrifice is.
The effect of an offering.
To whom one must sacrifice.
Kinds of sacrifices.
</margin>
A sacrifice is an offering which is made sacred by the act of offering, and it consecrates or sanctifies the one who offers it, unless irreverence or some other sin stands in the way. Therefore, these sacrifices and offerings provide us with great confidence, make us of the "household of God," and repel many evils hanging over us. Indeed, the doctors of the Hebrews confirm this above all others, saying: because we slaughter our animals and consume our possessions in sacrifice, imminent evils are deflected from us to such things. Furthermore, just as a mortal priest in this lower world sacrifices the souls of irrational animals to God through the destruction of the body from the soul, so <term>Michael the Archangel</term> <note>In Kabbalistic tradition, Michael is the High Priest of the Heavenly Jerusalem who offers the souls of the righteous.</note>, the priest of the higher world, sacrifices the souls of men. This occurs through the separation of the soul from the body, not of the body from the soul—except by accident, as happens in <term>divine frenzy</term>, rapture, ecstasy, sleep, and similar vacations of the soul, which the Hebrews call the <term>Death of the Kiss</term>. <note>original: "morte osculi." A mystical term (*Neshika*) referring to the soul leaving the body out of intense love for the Divine.</note> Sacrifices and offerings are to be made first and principally to the most high God. However, when they are directed to secondary powers, understand this to be done in the same manner as was said regarding prayer and vows; whatever was said there, we shall also understand here by similarity. There are indeed many classes and many types of sacrifices: for a certain kind is called a <term>holocaust</term> <note>original: "holocaustũ," a "whole-burnt" offering.</note> when the victim is consumed by fire; another is called <term>immolation</term> because of the shedding of blood. Furthermore, some are called "salutary" sacrifices, which are made for the obtaining of health or salvation; some are "peaceful," for the obtaining of peace; some are "praises"...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Book Three, Chapter 59, regarding the nature of sacrifice. <header>BOOK THREE. 177</header>

<margin>The true priest of God.</margin>
...[no one] can be [a priest], unless he offers himself as a victim, building his own soul like a certain statue, and establishing his mind and intellect as a temple in which he can receive divine light. External sacrifices, however (as **Heraclitus** <note>Heraclitus (c. 535 – c. 475 BC) was a pre-Socratic Greek philosopher who often spoke in riddles about the nature of the soul and the universe.</note> says), are certain remedies for souls, instituted by the highest physician. For an evil demon possesses a man (as **Proclus** <note>Proclus (412–485 AD) was a Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote extensively on how rituals and "theurgy" could help the soul ascend.</note> says) until he is purified through sacrifices.

<margin>Sacrifices are necessary to appease God. The true pontiff. The sacrifice of Christ. 666 kinds of sacrifices among the Egyptians. Stars hear prayers and grant celestial gifts.</margin>
Therefore, sacrifices are sought out to appease God and the celestial powers, and to purify man, who himself bears the image of both God and the world. But our Lord **Jesus Christ**, the true pontiff and high priest, concluded all sacrifice in bread and wine alone, as if in the primary substance of human food—requiring no animals or other things, nor the shedding of blood in immolation to cleanse us—for we have already been perfectly cleansed in his blood. There were also among the **Egyptians** six hundred and sixty-six kinds of sacrifices; they established divine honors and sacred sacrifices for individual stars and planets, because these were divine living beings participating in an intellectual soul and a divine mind. Hence, they say that the stars themselves, when humbly entreated, hear our prayers and grant celestial gifts, not so much by a natural law as by their own free will. And this is what **Iamblichus** <note>Iamblichus (c. 245 – c. 325 AD) was a Syrian Neoplatonist who emphasized the importance of ritual to reach the divine.</note> says: that celestial bodies and the deities of the world have certain divine and superior powers within themselves, and others that are natural and inferior. **Orpheus** calls these "keys" for opening and closing; through the natural powers they bind us to the influences of fate, but through the divine powers they release us from fate. Hence, if some misfortune looms over someone from **Saturn** or **Mars**, the Magi command them not to flee immediately to **Jupiter** or **Venus**, but rather to take refuge with that same Saturn or Mars.

<margin>In Metamorphoses, book 6.</margin>
In this way, that **Psyche** of **Apuleius** <note>A reference to the story of "Cupid and Psyche" from the 2nd-century Roman novel "The Golden Ass" by Lucius Apuleius.</note>, who was pursued by Venus because of their similar beauty, was forced to earn favor not from **Ceres** or **Juno**, but from Venus herself.

<margin>To which stars the ancients sacrificed.</margin>
They sacrificed, moreover, to individual stars with things pertaining to them: to the **Sun**, with solar things and his own animals, such as the laurel, the rooster, the swan, or the bull; to **Venus**, through her animals, like the dove or the turtledove, and through her plants, like verbena <note>original: "verbenam." Used here to mean sacred greenery or sacrificial herbs.</note>, just as **Virgil** sings:

> Bring water and encircle these altars with a soft ribbon,
> And burn fatty verbenas and masculine incense. <note>original: "Effer aquam & molli cinge hæc altaria vitta, / Verbenasqʒ adole pingues, & mascula thura." From Virgil's Eclogue 8. "Masculine incense" refers to high-quality frankincense shaped like beads.</note>

Furthermore, any Magi who had completed some preparation—whether natural or artificial—pertaining to a certain star, would later religiously consecrate and offer it to that same star. They did this not just to gain natural power from its timely influence, but also to receive that preparation back strengthened and confirmed by the divine through the religious offering itself. For the offering of any thing, when it is rightly offered to God in some way, is—no differently than a sacrifice—sanctified by the offering itself and made a part of Him. Moreover, white victims were slaughtered to the celestial and ethereal gods, but black ones to the terrestrial and infernal ones; to the terrestrial ones upon altars, but to the infernal ones in pits. To the aerial and aquatic gods, they offered birds; but white ones were slaughtered to the former, and black ones to the latter alone.

<margin>Which victims were usually slaughtered to which gods.</margin>
Finally, to all gods and demons except the terrestrial and the infernal, they [vowed]...

> Indeed, three-fold victims must be slain for the celestial gods,
