<margin>
A middle path between God and man.
</margin>
Porphyry <note>Porphyry of Tyre (c. 234 – c. 305 AD), a Neoplatonist philosopher and student of Plotinus.</note> relates these things in his books of *Responses*, and others agree with him. For he says these sacrifices are a certain natural "middle path" between gods and men; asserting this, **Aristotle** says that the act of sacrificing to God is inherent in man by nature. Therefore, they say these are intermediaries that savor of the nature of both sides and represent the divine by analogy. They possess certain most fitting symbols—shared both with the deity to whom they are offered and with those who are being purified—but these symbols are so hidden <note>or "occult"</note> that the human wit can scarcely grasp what God and the spirits require in particular for our expiation. By these rituals, the celestial powers are pleased, and they restrain themselves from the execution of the punishment which our sins deserve. And these are what **Orpheus** calls the keys that open the gates of the elements and the heavens, so that through them man may penetrate to the super-celestial realms, and the intelligences of the heavens and the spirits <note>demones</note> of the elements may descend to him. However, perfect and truly religious men do not need these things; they are for those alone who, as **Trismegistus** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure to whom the Hermetic writings are attributed.</note> says, have "fallen into harmony" and become servants of the heavens and of created things. Because they are subject to the heavens, they believe they must be strengthened by the favor of celestial virtue, until, flying higher, they are absolved from that planetary presidency and emerge more sublime than the heavens themselves.
<margin>
The keys of the heavens according to Orpheus.
</margin>

...praying and sacrificing to God. "I, your servant, offer and sacrifice these things to you; <margin>Words of the one sacrificing.</margin> I confess you as the author of holiness, and I invoke you to sanctify this offering, so that you may pour into it the power of your high and honored spirit, that through it we may obtain what we seek. Moreover, just as this present offering of mine becomes yours, so that henceforth it lives and dies to you, so also let me become yours, who through this offering and communion—and by the fact that I come to offer and sacrifice to you—confess myself to be of your family and your worshippers." Furthermore, during the immolations, one would say: "Just as this animal is in <margin>Words of those immolating.</margin> my power to kill if I wish, or to save, so it is in your power to take away through your anger, or to grant through your benevolence, that which we desire." Finally, where a sacrifice was made for the expiation or the avoidance of some evil, one would say: "Just as this animal dies in my hand, <margin>Words of expiation.</margin> so let every vice and all uncleanness die in me, or let such-and-such an evil or inconvenience die and be annihilated. Likewise, just as the blood of this animal is poured out from its body, so let every vice and uncleanness flow away from me." During a burnt offering <term>holocaust: an offering where the entire victim is consumed by fire</term>, one would say: "Just as this offering is consumed by this present fire <margin>Words for burnt offerings.</margin> so that nothing remains of it, so let every evil, or such-and-such an inconvenience which we then wish to repel and avoid, be consumed in me." It was also the custom during the prayer to touch the altar itself with the hands, <margin>The altar was touched by the sacrificers.</margin> on behalf of all those for whom the sacrifice was being made; and whoever touched it desired to be a participant, because prayer alone cannot be favorable unless the one who prays also touches the altar with his hands. Whence, in Virgil:

> The Almighty heard him praying with such words and holding the altars <note>original: "Talibus orantem dictis arasque tenentem / Audiit omnipotens" — Aeneid, 4.219-220</note>,

> I touch the altars and the fires between them, and I call the deities to witness <note>original: "Tango aras medios ignes & numina testor" — Aeneid, 12.201</note>.

### ¶ How these things are to be offered both to God and to the lower deities. Chapter 61.

Every adoration, offering, or sacrifice, prayer, and invocation is distinguished by this difference: namely, whether it is directed to God alone or to lower deities, such as angels, stars, and heroes. In these matters, you must observe these rules: that whenever a prayer is to be offered to God alone <margin>What kind of prayer is for God.</margin> to obtain some effect, this should be done with the commemoration of some miracle, sacrament, or promise of the body, drawn from the holy scriptures. For example, if a prayer is made for the destruction of enemies, let it be commemorated how God destroyed the giants in the flood of waters, and the attempt at Babel in the confusion of tongues, Sodom and Gomorrah in the rain of fire, the army of Pharaoh in the Red Sea, and such things; adding to these whatever curses can be gathered from the Psalms and elsewhere in the holy scriptures. By the same logic of counsel, when about to pray against the dangers of waters, let us commemorate the salvation of Noah in the flood, the passage of the children of Israel through the middle of the Red Sea, and Christ walking with dry feet upon the waters, and the same [saving his disciples] from dangers...

Because if prayer is necessary for seeking oracles or dreams, whether from God or from angels and heroes <note>original: "heroas"; in this context, "heroes" refers to elevated or semi-divine spirits in the Neoplatonic tradition</note>, there are already countless places in the Old Testament where it is read that God spoke with men, along with very many verses promising omens and revelations, as well as various prophetic dreams: those of Jacob, Joseph, Pharaoh, Daniel, and Nebuchadnezzar. Then there are all the revelations found in the New Testament and throughout the whole religion: those of John, Paul, and the Holy Magi; then those of Helena, Constantine, and Charles <note>likely Charlemagne</note>; and also those of more recent prophets: <margin><insert>From the list of these: John Savonarola <note>Girolamo Savonarola (1452–1498), a Dominican friar and reformer in Florence known for his prophetic claims</note> and others</insert></margin> Methodius, Cyril, Joachim, Merlin, Bridget, Mechthild, and Hildegard <note>Hildegard of Bingen (1098–1179), the famous German mystic and polymath</note>, whose divine spirits, when piously invoked, often make us participants in divine revelations. Furthermore, we also invoke the sacred names of God, but especially those that are signifies of the desired thing, or are in some way adapted to them: for example, for the destruction of enemies, we invoke the names of God’s wrath, God’s vengeance, God’s fear, God’s justice, and God’s strength. To avoid some danger, however, we invoke the names of mercy, defense, salvation, goodness, and the like. Furthermore, we ask for the execution of our desired longing from some angel, or a star, or one of the heroes to whom that office is assigned, to whom a similar invocation is directed. This invocation itself must be fashioned with the proper number, weight, and measure, according to the rules handed down where we treated the composition of incantations.

<margin>The difference between incantations and prayers.</margin>
For there is no difference, except that they are "incantations" insofar as they affect our mind and dispose its passions to be in conformity with certain divine powers; they are "prayers," however, insofar as they are offered to some divine power for worship and veneration. From this same root, the method of consecrating can also be taken, which we shall now speak of consequently.

## ¶ On consecrations and their rationale. Chapter LXII.

<margin>C</margin>
<margin>The efficacy of consecrations is accomplished by two things.</margin>
Consecration is the sublimation <term>sublimatio: the process of elevating or refining a material object to a spiritual state</term> of experiments <term>experimentorum: in magical texts, an "experiment" refers to a specific ritual procedure or spell</term>, through which a spiritual soul, drawn by proportion and conformity, is infused into the material of our works—prepared rightly and lawfully according to the tradition of the magical art—and vivifies our work through the spirit of the intellect. The efficacy of consecrations is accomplished chiefly by two things: namely, by the virtue of the person consecrating, and by the virtue of the prayer and the rite by which the consecration is administered. In the person, holiness of life and the power of sanctifying are required. Nature and merit provide the first; the second is acquired through imitation and dignification, which we have spoken of elsewhere. Next, it is necessary that the one consecrating recognizes this virtue and power within themselves with firm and indubitable faith.

<margin>Prayer and its power.</margin>
Our intention now is to speak of what is required in the prayer. Prayer itself is a certain power of sanctifying implanted in it from the divine, as if it were ordained by God for this very purpose—many of which we read in the sacred utterances of the Bible—or if it is instituted for this through the ordination of the Church by the power of the Holy Spirit. Many of this kind exist everywhere. Or, this holiness is present in the prayer itself, not by the virtue of institution, but by commemoration—

It also defines consecration as the spiritual "vivification" of a ritual object, which depends on the practitioner's personal holiness and the inherent power of the prayers used.</summary>

### THIRD BOOK ###

<center>z iii</center>

...of sacred things, such as sacred writings, stories of miracles and deeds, the effects of grace, and the promises of sacraments and sacramentals: which were seen to belong to the thing to be consecrated, either strictly or loosely, or through some likeness. We shall now give some examples of this, through which the way to this entire line of reasoning will easily open.

<margin>Consecration of water</margin>
Thus, in the consecration of water, a commemoration is made of how God placed the firmament in the midst of the waters; how he established a sacred fount in the earthly paradise, from which the entire world is irrigated by four sacred rivers <note>referring to the Pishon, Gihon, Tigris, and Euphrates</note>; how he made the waters an instrument of his justice in the destruction of the giants through the general deluge over all the earth; and in the destruction of Pharaoh’s army in the Red Sea; and how he led his people with dry feet through the middle of the Red Sea and through the middle of the Jordan; and how he miraculously brought water out of the rock of the desert, and brought a fount of living water out of the molar tooth of the jawbone of an ass at the prayers of Samson <note>Judges 15:19; in the Latin Vulgate, God makes water spring from the jawbone Samson used as a weapon</note>; how he placed the waters as an instrument of his mercy and a washing of salvation for the remission of sins; and how Christ, baptized in the Jordan, cleansed and sanctified the waters, and the like. This is done by invoking divine names adapted to these things—for instance, when God himself is called the living fount, living water, or living river.

<margin>Consecration of fire</margin>
By a similar logic, in the consecration of fire, a commemoration is made of how God created fire as an instrument of his justice for the punishment, vengeance, and purging of sins, and how, when he is about to judge the world, he will command its conflagration to go before him. He is the one who appeared to Moses in the bush of burning fire, who preceded the children of Israel in a pillar of fire, who established the unquenchable fire to be preserved in the tabernacle of the covenant, and miraculously rekindled the same when it was extinguished, and kept it unextinguished while hidden under the waters <note>a reference to 2 Maccabees 1, where the sacred fire was hidden in a well during the Babylonian exile and later recovered</note>, and similar things. Then divine names also present themselves, such as because God is a "consuming fire" or a "refining fire," and terms proper to these, such as the splendor of God, the light of God, the lamp of God, and such like.

<margin>Consecration of oil</margin>
Thus in the consecration of oil, sacred things pertaining to this are commemorated, as in the book of Exodus concerning the oil of anointing and incense, and sacred names conformed to these—such as the name "Christ," which means "Anointed" <note>original: "Christus quod vnctum sonat"; the Greek 'Christos' translates the Hebrew 'Messiah,' both meaning 'Anointed'</note>, and whatever like this is found in the mysteries. This includes the passage in the Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation 11:4</note> concerning the two olive trees dripping holy oil into the burning lamps before the face of God.

<margin>Consecration of places</margin>
So in the consecration of places, a commemoration is made of Mount Sinai, the tabernacle of the covenant, the "holy of holies" of Solomon’s temple, and the sanctification of the hill of Golgotha through the mystery of the passion of CHRIST, and the field which was bought with the price of the blood of CHRIST <note>The "Field of Blood" or Aceldama, purchased with the thirty pieces of silver returned by Judas</note>. Likewise, mention is made of Mount Tabor, where the transfiguration and the ascent to the heavens took place, with sacred names applied such as: place of God, throne of God, chair of God, tabernacle of God, altar of God, seat of God, dwelling-place of God, and such like. In a similar way you shall proceed in the blessings of other things, by searching out from the sacred scriptures, divine names, and the sanctity of religion those things which are seen to agree in some way with the object. For example: if the paper is vellum...

¶ Which things are called sacred, which consecrated: and how these relate to us and the gods, and concerning sacred times, Chapter LXIII.

<margin>What things are sacred</margin>
Now, those things are called sacred which are sanctified by the gods themselves or by their attendant spirits <note>original: "daemonibus"</note>, as if (so to speak) dedicated to us by the gods themselves. In this way we call spirits sacred, because God dwells in them, whose name they are often said to bear. Hence we read in Exodus: "I will send my angel who shall go before you; observe him, and do not think he is to be despised, because my name is in him" <note>Exodus 23:20-21</note>. Thus also mysteries are called sacred.
<margin>Mystery</margin>
For a "mystery" <term>mysterium: a hidden ritual or truth</term> is something that is sanctified and has a hidden power and grace bestowed by the gods or spirits, or dispensed by the most high God himself—such as the sacred names and characters mentioned above. So the Cross itself is sacred and mysterious, sanctified by the passion of **JESUS CHRIST**. Hence also certain prayers and petitions are called sacred and mystical, which were not instituted by human devotion but by divine revelation, just as we read in the Gospels that Christ instituted the Lord’s Prayer. In a similar way, certain compositions are called sacred, into which God has placed a singular ray of his power, just as we read in Exodus regarding the incense and the oil of anointing, and as among us the sacred font, the sacred chrism, the oil of catechumens <note>oil used in the ritual preceding baptism</note>, and such. There is also another kind of sacred things which we call sacred because they have been dedicated and hallowed to God by men, such as vows and sacrifices, of which we spoke above. Hence Virgil...

> And the scent, accepted by the gods, ascended into the air:
> The sacred rites claimed their portion, the rest was given to the tables. <note>original: "Festa dies aderat..." from Ovid's Metamorphoses, Book 12</note>

<margin>Sacred statues. Sacred pictures.</margin>
In a similar way, they call "sacred" those likenesses, shrines, idols, statues, images, and paintings made in the likeness of the gods, or dedicated to the gods themselves, just as Orpheus sings in the hymn to Lycian Venus:
> For our leaders, looking after the divine things of the fatherland,
> Established a sacred colossus near the small town.
And Virgil:
> You, father, take the sacred objects and the ancestral household gods in your hand... <note>original: "penates," the protective spirits of the Roman household</note>

<margin>Why the images of gods are honored. Interpretation of the statue of Jupiter.</margin>
From this, the divine Plato, in the eleventh book of the *Laws*, commanded that the sacred statues and images of the gods should be honored, not for their own sake, but because they represent God to us. In this same way, the ancients venerated that image of Jupiter, interpreting it thus: because it bears the likeness of a man, it signifies that he is the Mind <term>Mens: the highest aspect of the soul or a cosmic intellect</term> which produces all things by seminal reason. <term>Seminal reason: the creative principles or "seeds" of all things inherent in the divine mind</term> He is depicted sitting so that his stable and unchangeable power might be expressed. He has his upper parts naked and open, because he is visible to the intelligences <note>higher spiritual beings</note> and superior beings; his lower parts, however, are covered, because he is hidden from the lower creatures. <margin>The scepter in Jupiter's left hand.</margin> He holds a scepter in his left hand, because in these parts of the body the most spiritual home of life <note>the heart</note> is found. For the creator is the intellect, the king and life-giving spirit of the world. In his right hand, he holds out both an eagle and a Victory. <margin>The eagle in Jupiter's right hand.</margin> The former, because he is the lord of the other gods, just as the eagle is of the other birds; the latter, because all things are subject to him.

In a similar way, we also venerate the figure of a lamb, because it represents <margin>The Lamb for Christ.</margin> CHRIST; and the figure of a dove, because it denotes the Holy Spirit; and the figures of a lion, an ox, an eagle, and a man, signifying the evangelists, and other similar figures which we find <margin>The dove for the Holy Spirit. Figures of the Evangelists.</margin> expressed in the revelations of the prophets and in various places in the sacred scriptures. Indeed, these figures themselves contribute to similar revelations and dreams, and for that reason they are called "sacred pictures."

There are also sacred rites and sacred observations which are performed for the veneration of the gods of religion, such as: devout gestures, genuflections <note>kneeling</note>, the uncovering of the head, washings, the sprinkling of holy water, fumigations <note>burning incense</note>, <margin>The "Sacred" and what is contained under this name.</margin> external purifications, likewise processions of supplications, and the external decoration for divine praises—such as the resonance of music, the lighting of wax candles and lamps, the ringing of signals and bells, and the decoration of temples, altars, and images. In all of these, the highest and most beautiful worship and grace are required; wherefore, whatever things are most beautiful, lovely, and precious—gold, silver, and stones—are employed for these purposes.

<summary>Agrippa defines "sacred" objects as physical representations of the divine, using the iconography of Jupiter and Christian symbols like the Lamb and Dove to show how images mediate between the human mind and spiritual truths. He also lists the physical components of religious worship, such as incense, music, and precious metals, which serve to honor the divine through beauty.</summary>

This is because their power and influence does not descend so much from the elements or celestial bodies, but from the intelligible and super-celestial world. ON OCCULT PHILOSOPHY

### Concerning certain religious observations, ceremonies, and rites of fumigations, unctions, and the like. Chapter 64.

<margin>How we should approach God.</margin>
Therefore, whoever you are who desires to work in this art <note>original: "facultate"; referring to the practice of occult philosophy or magic</note>, you must first of all, with pious prayers, entreat the one God the Father, so that you also may be "one," worthy of His mercy. You must be clean both inwardly and outwardly, and in a clean place; for it is written in Leviticus: *Every man who shall approach those things which are consecrated, in whom there is uncleanness, shall perish before the Lord.* <note>Referencing Leviticus 22:3, emphasizing the danger of approaching the sacred while ritually impure.</note> For this reason, wash

<margin>Purity of clothing.</margin>
yourself often, and on appointed days according to the mysteries of numbers, put on clean clothes and abstain from all uncleanness, pollution, and lust. For the

<margin>Those who are not heard by God.</margin>
gods do not wish to hear a man (as **Porphyry** <note>A 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote extensively on the soul and ritual.</note> says) who has not abstained for many days from the works of Venus <note>original: "operatione Venerea"; a common euphemism for sexual intercourse.</note>. Do not join with a woman who is polluted or menstruating, nor with one who suffers from a flow of blood; do not touch anything unclean, nor a carcass. Hence **Porphyry** says: *He who has touched a dead body is not permitted to approach the oracles.* Perhaps this is because the soul, corrupted by a certain affinity for the stench of death, is rendered unfit for receiving divine influences. You shall wash yourself,

<margin>An odor acceptable to God.</margin>
anoint yourself, and use fumigations, and offer sacrifices; for God receives as a most sweet savor those things which are done for Him by a man who is purified and prepared. At the same time, his prayer and offering ascend with that fumigation, just as the **Psalmist** sings: *Let my prayer, O Lord, be directed toward you like incense in your sight.* <note>Psalm 141:2.</note> Furthermore, the soul of man—which is the offspring and image of God—delights in these fumigations and fragrances, drawing them in through those nostrils through which the soul itself entered into this corporeal man. It is through these (as **Job** testifies) that at times the most lively spirits are sent out, which cannot be held back in the heart of a man who is parched by bile or labor. For this reason, the sense of smell is considered by many to be the most vigorous and spiritual of all the senses.

<margin>The effects of fumigations.</margin>
Fumigations, moreover, along with sacrifice and unction <note>Anointing with oil.</note>, penetrate all things and open the gates of the elements and the heavens, so that through them a man may be able to see and know the secrets of the Creator—celestial things, things above the heavens, and things that descend from the heavens. These include angels and spirits of caves and the depths, and phantoms of desert places, so that they may come, appear, show themselves, and obey. They make all spirits peaceful and attract them just as a **Magnet** <note>original: "Magnes"</note> attracts iron; they join them with the elements and cause spirits to take on bodies. Indeed, the spiritual body grows thick and becomes more robust by these means, for it lives on vapors, fumigations, and the scents of libations. Whatever you

<margin>The intention of the practitioner.</margin>
work at, do it with full affection and the desire of your heart, so that the mercy of heaven and the celestial citizens may favor you. To better pursue their favor, the adaptation of the place, time, profession, custom, food,

<margin>A fortunate place contributes to favor.</margin>
clothing, exercise, and even the name, contribute in a wonderful way. For in these things, not only is the force of nature changed, but it is even overcome; a fortunate place contributes much to favor. It was not for nothing that God spoke to **Abraham**, telling him to come to the land He would show him; and **Abraham** proceeded, journeying toward the south. Similarly, **Isaac** came to Gerar, where he sowed and reaped a hundredfold, and became very wealthy. But what place is appropriate for each person is determined by each person’s birth...

Thus, they established that **Epidamnus** should be called **Dyrrachium**, lest those sailing there should go "to their loss" <note>original: "in damnum"; playing on the sound of the city's original name.</note>. Times can provide fortune.

For the Astrologers have taught, and the Magi have observed, that certain times can provide a specific fortune for our affairs. Finally, all the wisest ancients agree on this: it is of the greatest importance at what moment of time, and under what celestial disposition, anything receives its existence in this world—not only natural things, but also artificial ones. For they taught that this moment of initiation has such great power that the entire course of fortune depends upon it and can be predicted from it. By the same logic, they firmly believed, and asserted by the testimony of experience, that the beginning of a thing can be traced backward from its successful outcomes; just as **Sulla** the Astrologer predicted a most certain death approaching for **Caligula** when he consulted him about his nature. **Metheon** the astrologer, when the Athenians were considering an expedition against the Syracusans, foresaw the future calamity of the war; and when the same people were about to sail to Sicily, **Meson** the astrologer predicted a storm. **Anaxagoras**, through this knowledge of times, forewarned on which days a stone would fall from the sun, just as it later happened at the river **Aegos** in Thrace <note>Referring to the meteorite at Aegospotami in 467 BCE, famously predicted by Anaxagoras.</note>. Tarnucius Firmianus"; a Roman mathematician and astrologer, friend of Cicero.</note> discovered both the conception and birth of **Romulus** from his deeds and fortune. He likewise discovered the birthday of the city of Rome from the recorded successes of its fortune. So too, **Maternus** <note>Julius Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century astrologer and author of the "Matheseos Libri VIII."</note> reports that the beginning or "nativity" of the world was found from the events of things.

That times have the greatest power over natural things can be shown by many examples. For there are trees that turn their leaves after the solstice, such as the poplar, the elm, the olive, the lime, and the white willow. And shellfish, crabs, and oysters increase as the moon waxes and grow thin as it wanes. The seas, by their ebb and flow, observe the movements and times of the moon. And does not the **Euripus** in **Euboea** <note>A narrow channel of water in Greece famous for its complex, shifting currents.</note> flow down and back seven times with wonderful speed? Likewise, for three days in each month—namely the seventh, eighth, and ninth day of the moon—it stands motionless. And among the **Troglodytes** <note>A legendary group of people said to live in caves; often used by ancient geographers to describe tribes in Africa or near the Red Sea.</note> there is a lake that three times a day becomes bitter and salt—

The persistent prayer of a righteous person also avails much. For Elijah <note>original: "Helias"</note> (as James says) was a man like us, subject to suffering, and he prayed a prayer that it might not rain upon the earth, and it did not rain for three years and six months; and he prayed again, and the heaven gave rain, and the earth gave its fruit. But beware in your prayers, lest you desire something vain, or that which is against the divine will: for God wills all good things, nor shall you take the name of your God in vain, because he who takes His name for a vain thing shall not go unpunished. Practice abstinence and give alms, for as the angel said to Tobias: *Prayer is good with fasting and alms.* And in the book of Judith we read: *Know that the Lord will hear your prayers, if you continue steadfast in fastings and prayers in the sight of the Lord.*

### Conclusion of the Whole Work - Chapter LXV ###

<margin>h</margin>
These are the things which we have gathered into this book as an introduction to magic from the tradition of the ancients and from various compilations. We have written in a brief style, yet one sufficient for those who are meant to understand. Some of these things are written in order, and some without order; some are handed down through fragments, and some are even hidden and left to the investigation of the intelligent. Those who look more sharply into what is written and search thoroughly may obtain at once the complete teachings of the magical art and infallible experiments. For we have handed down this art in such a way that it will not be hidden from the prudent and intelligent; however, it will not admit the wicked and incredulous to the secrets of those mysteries, but will leave them destitute, driven into a stupor under the shadow of ignorance and despair. You, therefore, sons of doctrine and wisdom, search in this book by gathering our dispersed intention, which we have set forth in various places.

The author explains that the secrets of magic are intentionally scattered throughout the text to ensure they are only discovered by the wise and diligent.</summary>

<meta>This page concludes Book Three of "De Occulta Philosophia," transitioning from the discussion of spiritual and ceremonial magic to the author's personal correspondence. It reinforces the theme that magical knowledge is intentionally veiled to protect it from the unworthy.</meta>

DE OCCVLTA PHILOSOPHIA
e

And what was hidden by us in one place, we have made manifest in another, so that it might be revealed to you who are wise; for we have written for you alone, whose minds are incorrupt, established in the right order of living, whose chaste and modest minds and unblemished faith fear and revere God, whose hands are separated from every crime and wickedness, and whose habits are modest, sober, and temperate. For you alone will find the doctrine preserved for you, and the secrets hidden by many riddles, which are not drawn out except by hidden intelligence. Once you have attained this, the whole knowledge of the <term>unconquerable science of magic</term><note>original: "inexpugnabilis magicæ disciplinę scientia"; suggesting a system of knowledge so well-founded that it cannot be defeated by critics</note> will instill itself into you, and those powers will appear to you, such as <term>Hermes</term><note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure regarded as the founder of Hermeticism and alchemy</note>, <term>Zoroaster</term>, <term>Apollonius</term><note>Apollonius of Tyana, a 1st-century philosopher and reputed miracle-worker</note>, and other operators of miracles once achieved.

But you, malevolent detractors, children of depraved ignorance and foolish wickedness, flee from these writings of ours, for they are hostile to you and set upon a precipice, so that you may wander and fall into misery. If anyone, therefore, because of their own disbelief and the sluggishness of their intellect, does not obtain their desire, let them not impute the fault of their ignorance to me, nor say that I have erred, or written false things on purpose, or lied; but let them accuse themselves, who do not understand our writings. For they are obscure and covered with various mysteries, in which it will easily happen that many may wander and lose their way. Let no one, therefore, be angry with me if we have hidden the truth of this science, entangled in riddles and dispersed in various places. For we have not hidden it from the wise, but from the depraved and the wicked, and we have delivered it in such a language that it must necessarily remain hidden from the foolish, yet easily admit the wise to its understanding.

### TO THE VENERABLE FATHER, MASTER OF SACRED THEO-
### logy, Aurelius of Aquapendente, Augu-
### stinian, Henry Cornelius Agrippa sends greetings.

From the letter which you gave to me on the second of this month, I have perceived the candor of your mind toward me, Reverend Father, and I have known you to be a man of <term>comprehensive learning</term><note>original: "cyclice doctum"; literally "cyclically taught," referring to someone who has mastered the entire circle of the liberal arts or an encyclopedia of knowledge</note>, and a curious explorer of those things which still lie hidden in darkness. I rejoiced immediately, and I congratulate myself on having found the friendship of such a man, with whom I might one day cultivate both my spirit and my intellect: and I now receive you (witnessed by this handwriting) among my closest friends. But look here! Who are your leaders whom you follow, you who dare to enter the <term>untraceable house of Daedalus</term><note>A reference to the Labyrinth of Crete, built by the inventor Daedalus to hold the Minotaur; it symbolizes the complexity and danger of occult studies</note> and the house of the dreadful Minos, to pass through the sentries, and to commit yourself to the <term>Fates</term><note>original: "Parcis"; the three goddesses who spin, measure, and cut the thread of human life</note>? Who are your teachers, you who deal with immense things, daring to attempt to make the <term>wandering stable</term><note>An alchemical and philosophical metaphor for "fixing the volatile"—making a changing or gaseous substance solid and permanent</note>, the treacherous constant, and the most fleeting of all gods more steadfast even than <term>Adrastia</term><note>Another name for the goddess Nemesis, representing inescapable destiny or divine retribution</note> herself? Beware lest you be deceived by those who have themselves been deceived.

### BOOK THREE.

For here, no amount of reading books will be able to direct you, since they sound like nothing but pure riddles. Oh, how many writings people read concerning the <term>invincible power of the magic art</term><note>original: "inexpugnabili magicæ artis potentia"</note>, the prodigious images of the astrologers, the monstrous transformations of the <term>alchemists</term><note>Those who sought to transform base metals into gold and discover universal cures</note>, and of that blessed stone, by which—like <term>Midas</term><note>The mythical king whose touch turned everything to gold</note>—brass is touched and everything is soon changed into gold or silver! All of these things are found to be empty, fictional, and false as often as they are practiced according to the literal word. And yet, these things are handed down and written by great and most serious philosophers and holy men. Who would dare to say their traditions are false? Indeed, it would be impious to believe that they went to the trouble of writing lies. Therefore, there is another sense <margin>Lu. f. 2.</margin> than what is handed down in the letters, one veiled in various mysteries, but so far explained openly by none of the masters. I do not know if anyone could attain it through the reading of books alone without a skilled and faithful master, unless he were illuminated by a divine power, which is granted to very few. Therefore, many who pursue these most secret mysteries of nature run in vain, applying their minds only to the bare sequence of the reading. For, with an ill-fated talent, having fallen away from true understanding into false imaginations, and ensnared by the deceits of external spirits (whom they were meant to rule), they have become dangerous servants. Ignorant of themselves, they go backward, following the tracks of their own flocks, seeking outside themselves what they possess within. And this is what I want you to know now: that within ourselves is the operator of all wonderful effects. Whatever the portentous mathematicians, the prodigious magi, the envious alchemists (who persecute nature), or the <term>necromancers</term><note>Those who practice magic involving the dead, here described as worse than demons</note> (worse than demons) dare to promise—the spirit itself knows how to discern and accomplish it. And it does so without any crime, without offending God, and without injury to religion. In us, I say, is that operator of miracles:

> The Spirit that thrives in us performs those deeds;
> It dwells in us—not in the underworlds, nor even in the <gloss>highest</gloss> stars of heaven.

Truly, we would need to confer with you most extensively about these things, but in person. For these matters are not committed to letters, nor written with a pen; they are poured from spirit to spirit with a few sacred words. This shall happen if ever I am able to come to you. As for the books you request: some of them were with me at times, but they are no longer. As for the books titled *On Occult Philosophy* from my youth which are circulating among you, the first two of these are lacking in many things, and the third is entirely mutilated, containing nothing but a certain summary made by my scribes. But, the Lord favoring me, I will one day give the whole work, complete and revised, to the light—though the key to the work shall be reserved for only my closest friends, of whom you should not doubt you are one. Fare most happily. From <term>Lyons</term><note>original: "Lugduno"; a major printing and intellectual center in France</note>, September 24th, in the year 1527.

# ON OCCULT PHILOSOPHY.

...could be most pleasing and sink most deeply into the soul: that I am indeed such a person, since I write this out of the abundance of my heart, and I am one who never abandons those who commit themselves to my friendship, no matter what storm may blow. Therefore, so that you may achieve your desires, which are no less than my own, I shall come to you very soon. There, when opportunity is given to hear and return words face to face, I know our friendship will be indissoluble and last forever. 

<margin>What is required for philosophy</margin> Now indeed, as pertains to the <term>Philosophy</term><note>Here meaning the "Occult Philosophy" or high magic that Agrippa has been teaching throughout the three books</note> you requested, I want you to know that it is to know the Creator himself—God—of all things, and to pass into Him with the whole image of one’s likeness (as if by an essential contact or bond), by which you yourself may be transformed and made a god, just as the Lord says concerning <margin>Moses established by God as Lord of Pharaoh</margin> Moses, saying: "Behold, I have made you a god to Pharaoh." <note>original: "Ecce ego constitui te deum pharaonis" — Exodus 7:1</note> 

<margin>The keys of philosophy.</margin> This is that true and supreme most occult philosophy of miraculous works: its key is understanding. For the more deeply we understand higher things, the more sublime the virtues we put on, and the greater the works we perform, both more easily and effectively. But our understanding, enclosed in corruptible flesh, unless it overcomes the way of the flesh and obtains its own proper nature, will not be able to be united with those divine virtues (for they do not join together except with those like themselves). It is entirely ineffective at foreseeing those most hidden secrets of God and nature; and, <margin>From Virgil</margin> "this is the task, this is the labor, to escape to the upper airs." <note>original: "hoc opus, hic labor est, superas evadere ad auras" — A famous line from Virgil’s Aeneid (6.129), describing the difficulty of returning from the underworld</note> 

For how shall he who has lost himself in ash and mortal dust find God himself? How shall he, immersed in flesh and blood, grasp spiritual things? Shall a man see the Lord and live? What fruit shall a grain of wheat bring forth unless it first dies? <margin>The words of Christ.</margin> For it is necessary to die—to die, I say, to the world and the flesh, and to all the senses, and to the whole <term>animal man</term><note>The "soul-led" man who lives according to natural instincts rather than spiritual revelation</note>—whoever wishes to enter into these inner shrines of secrets. Not that the body should be separated from the soul, but that the soul should leave the body. 

<margin>How one must die</margin> Concerning this death, Paul writes to the Colossians: "You are dead, and your life is hidden with Christ." <note>Colossians 3:3</note> And elsewhere more clearly he says of himself: "I know a man, whether in the body or out of the body I know not, God knows, caught up even to the third heaven," and so forth. <note>2 Corinthians 12:2</note> In this death—precious in the sight of the Lord—one must die. This happens to very few, and perhaps not always. 

<margin>Virgil.</margin> "For the few whom impartial Jupiter has loved, or whom burning virtue has carried up to the heavens, born of the gods, were able." <note>Another reference to Aeneid 6.129-131</note> First, those who are born not of flesh and blood, but of God; next, those who, by the benefit of nature and the gift of their celestial birth-chart, have been made worthy of it. The rest strive by merits and by art, concerning which a living voice will inform you more certainly. 

But I want you to be warned of this: do not be deceived regarding me, as if I—having experienced divine things—were preaching these things to you, or wished to claim such a thing for myself, or hoped it could be granted to me. I, who have been until now a soldier consecrated with human blood, almost always a courtier, bound by the bond of the flesh to a most dear wife, and exposed to all the blasts of unstable fortune, driven crosswise entirely by the flesh, the world, and domestic cares, have not attained such sublime gifts of the immortal gods. But I wish to be accepted like a <term>guidepost</term><note>original: "indicem" — literally an index or pointer</note>, which, always remaining before the gates itself, shows others the path that must be traveled. Otherwise, regarding my love for you, you are not at all mistaken...

### HENRY CORNELIUS AGRIPPA to a
### certain friend of his in the King’s Court. Greetings.

<margin>A proverb of folly</margin>
The ancients used to mark notable folly with a well-known proverb: "To carry owls to Athens" <note>original: "Noctuas Athenas inferre" — a Greek proverb meaning to do something redundant or useless, like bringing coal to Newcastle, since Athens was already famous for its owls.</note>. But it is no less foolish—indeed, it is of the greatest impiety—to add demons to hell. You know what "hell" I mean: I mean that school of crimes, the [royal] Court, which I have elsewhere indignantly depicted in its true colors. But never before has such a just and unworthy occasion for writing been given as now, if only my preoccupations allowed me to treat the matter with the dignity it deserves. Nevertheless, I cannot restrain my pen from laying out the argument of the matter to you. 

Hear now, therefore, a thing both foolish and impious: a certain man of demons has been summoned from Germany at no small expense—that is, a <term>cacomagus</term><note>A "bad magician" or sorcerer, from the Greek words "kakos" (evil) and "magos" (magician). Agrippa uses this to distinguish this man from the "true" or "natural" magician he defends in his books.</note>, in whom the power of demons dwells. Just as Jannes and Mambres <note>The traditional names for the Egyptian sorcerers who opposed Moses in Exodus 7-8.</note> resisted Moses, so might this man resist the Emperor. For they have been persuaded by the father of lies [the Devil] that this man has foreknowledge of all future events, is privy to all secret counsels, and is an interpreter of deliberate thoughts. They believe he is endowed with such power that he can bring back the royal children <note>A reference to the sons of King Francis I of France, who were held as hostages in Spain at this time.</note> through the air, just as it is read that Habakkuk <note>In the biblical book of "Bel and the Dragon," the prophet Habakkuk is miraculously carried by an angel to feed Daniel in the lions' den.</note> was transported with his pottage to the lions' den. They believe he can, like Elisha when besieged in Dothan, show mountains full of horses and chariots of fire, and a vast army. Furthermore, they believe he can reveal and transfer the treasures of the earth, compel marriages as he wishes, or break apart loves. He claims he will cure all desperate diseases with a Stygian drug <note>A medicine associated with the River Styx, implying it is of a hellish or demonic origin.</note>—namely, deep-rooted wasting, established dropsy, and hideous elephantiasis—and that which:

> Medicine knows not how to loosen the knotty gout,
> And many other things besides, which obscure fame hides:

You see where their faith is placed and where their hope resides—they who attempt to subject the elements, heaven, the fates, nature, providence, God, and all things to the command of a single magician. They seek the safety of the kingdom from the demons, who are the enemies of public safety, saying in their heart with Ahaziah: "Is there no God in Israel, that we go to consult Beelzebub, the god of Ekron?" <note>original: "Non est deus in Israel, eamus ad consulendum Belsebub deum Acharon" — 2 Kings 1:3.</note> And just as Saul spoke to the Pythoness <note>The Witch of Endor.</note>, saying: "The Philistines fight against me, and the Lord has departed from me, and refused to hear me: therefore I have called you." Has God been so despaired of by these people that they have decided the help of demons must be sought? Is this not, according to the word of Jude and Peter, to deny God and our Lord JESUS CHRIST the savior, who redeemed us, and to bring upon themselves swift destruction? Do they not treasure up for themselves the wrath of the Lord’s indignation, who sends upon them his visitations through evil angels? Have they not been surrendered to a reprobate mind, they who seek the truth of a secret counsel from the devil, the father of lies, and ask for victory from another...

->### LETTER.<-

...of which [a man of demons] he was warned by the Lord of Hosts. And yet, this so wicked a craftsman of idolatry and sacrilege is granted boldness by the authority of that "Orthodox Mother" <note>likely referring to Louise of Savoy, the Queen Mother of France</note> who favors him so intensely, and by the "Most Christian Sons" <note>a traditional title for the Kings of France</note> who accommodate him. Moreover, gifts are bestowed upon him from sacred funds, while the very pillars of the Church—the bishops and cardinals—turn a blind eye and even facilitate such a nefarious work. The wicked nobles applaud this minister of impiety, just as ravens might congratulate the works of a wolf. 

What greater sin did Pharaoh, Balak, Saul, Ahab with his Jezebel, Ahaziah, Nebuchadnezzar, Belshazzar, Sennacherib, and the other worshipers of Baal commit? Pharaoh called his mages against Moses, and they, being defeated at the third plague, confessed "the finger of God"; yet the king, remaining obstinate through ten plagues, perished in the Red Sea. Balak the Moabite called Balaam the diviner to curse Israel, but God Himself turned the curse into a blessing, while Balak himself was cursed. What did the responses of Samuel or the Witch <note>original: "Pythonis" — refers to the medium or "Witch of Endor" whom Saul consulted in 1 Samuel 28</note> profit Saul? Was he not pierced through on Mount Gilboa? Ahab and Jezebel, joined in their wicked marriage, put their trust in the prophets of Baal; and according to the word of God, a lying spirit went out into the mouths of all the prophets who promised success to Ahab as he was about to go up to Ramoth-Gilead. Thus Ahab fell, and Jezebel was cast down, and the dogs devoured them. Asa, King of Judah, was rebuked by the prophet of the Lord because in his illness he did not seek the Lord, but put his trust in the art of physicians.

<margin>Great sinners and worshipers of Satan</margin>
Will they not be held to have a greater sin, who, abandoning God the Savior and the healthy forces of nature, seek salvation from Satan? Ahaziah once did so, and for that reason he heard from the prophet of the Lord: "From the bed which you have climbed, you shall not descend, but you shall surely die." Let the series of other unfaithful kings be examined, as well as the histories of the gentiles: Zoroaster, Deiotarus, Croesus, Pompey, Pyrrhus, Crassus, Nero, Julian—what did they gain from their mages and diviners who lied to them of happy outcomes?

<margin>Magical trifles.</margin>
Have they not all been reduced to nothing, and perished miserably in their sins? Thus those impious trifles <note>original: "nugæ" — refers to worthless or deceptive magical practices</note> are always accustomed to bring destruction to their devotees; and truly, those who trust in them the most are rendered the most unhappy of all. I do not deny that there are **natural sciences**, there are **metaphysical arts**, and there are **hidden talents**, through which—without offense to God and without injury to faith or religion—kingdoms can be defended, plans explored, enemies conquered, captives rescued, riches increased, the goodwill of men won over, illnesses repelled, health preserved, life prolonged, and the strength of youth restored. There are, moreover, the intercessions of sacred religion: public supplications and the private prayers of the good, by which we can not only turn away the wrath of God but also obtain Him as a benefactor. But if, besides these, there is a certain art of foreknowledge and of wonderful works which the ancients call **Calomagia** <term>Calomagia</term><note>From the Greek "kalos" (good) and "magia" (magic); Agrippa uses this to mean "Good Magic" or "White Magic," which he distinguishes from sorcery.</note> or **Theurgy** <term>Theurgia</term><note>A form of "high magic" aimed at communing with divine spirits or the One, rather than conjuring demons.</note>, this is certainly unknown to those triflers and slaves of demons. For indeed—

->## E P I S T O L A.<-

<margin>Predictions of the future.</margin> To search out things to come, or other hidden and imminent matters, and to bring forth truthful declarations of things divinely portended to men, as well as to perform works of power that exceed the common custom of nature—these belong only to those of profound and perfect learning, and of the most upright life and faith, not to men of the most frivolous and unlearned character. <margin>The dominion of the innocent.</margin> Moreover, for those men who are innocent and learned in the law of the Lord, every creature serves them according to the desire of their faith, and they are heard in whatever they might ask. <margin>A raven fed Elijah.</margin> Thus, a raven fed Elijah, and at his prayers the earth withheld its fruit, the heavens denied rain, and vomited forth its fires upon the impious. <margin>Bears served Elisha.</margin> Thus, bears served Elisha, angels fought for him, and rivers were crossed with dry feet. For Daniel, the lions laid aside their ferocity and ignored their hunger to flatter him; and the fire kindled in the furnace did not burn the boys <note>A reference to Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego in the Book of Daniel</note>. Works of this kind belong not to <term>Cacomagi</term> <note>original: "Cacomagorum"; literally "evil magicians"</note>, nor to <term>Goetic</term> sorcerers <note>original: "Goeticorum"; practitioners of "low" or demonic magic</note>, nor to men of demons, but to faithful and divine men; for it is not demons, but the spirits of God who minister to them. <margin>Virtues of the good.</margin> There are, I confess, even to this day (and perhaps many) men grave in wisdom, distinguished in science, and prevailing in virtues and powers: upright in life and character, unconquered in prudence, and even disposed in age and strength so that they might greatly benefit the commonwealth by their counsel and labor. <margin>The learning of courtiers.</margin> But your courtiers despise these men, as being far different from their own purpose; for these courtiers, malice stands in the place of wisdom, fraud and deceit in the place of counsel, craft and cunning in the place of science, and deception and treachery in the place of prudence. Superstition occupies the place of religion, and God is blasphemed in afflictions; and that faith which (as the Apostle says) is made perfect in weakness <note>referring to 2 Corinthians 12:9</note>, is despised; instead, they resort to the invocation of evil demons. Every good man among them is mocked, bold hypocrisy is promoted, truth is treated as a crime, and praise and rewards are reserved for folly and wickedness. <margin>The reward of the bold and hypocrites.</margin> O foolish and impious ones, who wish to stabilize a kingdom with those arts by which once-mighty empires fell and were utterly overturned! Of whom it was truly said through Jeremiah:
> Our crown has fallen; woe to us, for we have sinned. <note>Lamentations 5:16. In the original Latin, the letters that can be read as Roman numerals—M, C, V, I—were often used as a "chronogram" to encode a date.</note>
Which verse might fit you not so much by truth as by an ingenious, perhaps even devised, chance. For that little verse, if you collect the numeral letters—M, C, V, I—expresses the year 1523, in which, according to your own calculation, your king was captured at Pavia. <margin>The capture of the King of the Gauls.</margin> Did you not see these things and marvel at them, which you judged impossible before they had happened? And yet you are still proud and hardened in your misfortunes. You despise the prophets, and God’s threats are like fables to you. Behold, it is near, and you shall yet see and feel the Great Works <note>original: "magnalia"</note> of God in the world; and having collapsed into your fates, you shall tremble, because misery shall come upon you suddenly, and you shall not know where to flee. Stand now with your enchanters and with the multitude of your sorcerers, if perhaps they may profit you, or if you might become stronger. Will that summoned German <term>cacomagus</term> <note>evil magician</note> save you, and make the prophets liars, and prevail against the wrath of the Lord, and deliver you from evil? Not so, the impious, not so! Unless the Lord builds and guards the cities and the kingdom...

<header>ON MAGIC IN GENERAL. 187</header>

# HENRY CORNELIUS AGRIPPA’S Censure, or Retraction concerning Magic, from his declamation on the Vanity of the Sciences, and the Excellence of the Word of God.

## ON MAGIC IN GENERAL.

<margin>Magic and astrology joined.</margin>
This place also requires that we speak of Magic, for it is so joined and related to astrology that he who professes magic without astrology accomplishes nothing, but wanders entirely from the path. Some think magic took its name and origin from the Maguseans <note>The Maguseans or Magusaeans were a group of Persian Zoroastrians living in the diaspora</note>. The common opinion is that the name is Persian, which Porphyry and Apuleius support, and it signifies in their language the same as a priest, a wise man, or a philosopher. Magic, therefore, having encompassed all of philosophy—Physics and Mathematics—joins to them the powers of religions. Hence it also contains within itself Goetia <note>Low magic or sorcery, often associated with the conjuring of spirits</note> and Theurgy <note>High magic or "divine work," aimed at uniting the practitioner with the divine</note>. For this reason, many divide magic into two parts: namely, natural and ceremonial.
<margin>Origin of Magic</margin>

## ON NATURAL MAGIC.

They consider natural magic to be nothing other than the highest power of the natural sciences, which they therefore call the highest peak of natural philosophy, and its most absolute consummation. It is the active portion of natural philosophy which, by the assistance of natural virtues and through their mutual and opportune application, produces works that are beyond all grasp of wonder. The Ethiopians and Indians especially used this magic, where the power of herbs, stones, and other things pertaining to it was available. They wish Jerome to have remembered this in his letter to Paulinus, where he says Apollonius of Tyana <note>A 1st-century philosopher and reputed miracle-worker often compared to Jesus</note> was a magus, or a philosopher, like the Pythagoreans. Of this kind also were the Magi who, visiting the newborn Christ with gifts, adored him, whom the interpreters of the Gospels explain as Chaldean philosophers: such as were Hiarchas among the Brahmins, Thespion among the Gymnosophists <note>Literally "naked philosophers," ancient Indian ascetics known for their wisdom</note>, Buddha among the Babylonians, Numa Pompilius among the Romans, Zamolxides among the Thracians, Abaris among the Hyperboreans, Hermes among the Egyptians, and Zoroaster the son of Oromasius among the Persians. For the Indians, Ethiopians, Chaldeans, and Persians especially excelled in this magic: for which reason (as Plato narrates in the *Alcibiades*) the sons of the Persian kings are imbued with it, so that they might learn to administer and distribute their own republic according to the image of the world's republic. And Cicero, in his books on *Divination*, says that no one attains the throne among the Persians who has not first learned magic. Natural magic, therefore, is that which, having contemplated the powers of all natural and celestial things, and having searched out their sympathy <note>The occult theory that all parts of the universe are interconnected and can influence one another through "natural attractions"</note> with curious investigation, brings forth into the open the recondite and latent powers in nature: thus coupling lower things to the gifts of higher things, as if they were certain enticements, through their mutual application to each other, so that from there often stupendous
<margin>Magi adoring Christ.</margin>
<margin>Magi as Chaldean philosophers.</margin>
<margin>What natural magic is.</margin>

<sig>iii</sig>

He traces the art's prestige through Persian, Indian, and Greco-Roman traditions, identifying it as the practical application of nature's hidden "sympathies."</summary>

<header>ON MATHEMATICAL MAGIC</header>

...wonders arise, not so much by art as by nature, to which this art offers itself as a servant in these operations. For magicians, as the most accurate explorers of nature, by bringing together those things prepared by nature and applying active powers to passive subjects <note>The principle of "applying actives to passives" (activa passivis) was the standard Renaissance definition of natural magic—marrying the "masculine" celestial influences to "feminine" earthly materials</note>, very often produce effects before the time ordained by nature. The common people think these are miracles, though they are actually natural works, achieved only through the acceleration of time. This is seen, for example, if someone were to produce roses and ripe grapes in the month of March, or make sown beans or parsley grow into a perfect plant within a few hours. Even greater things than these are possible: such as clouds, rains, thunder, various kinds of animals, and many transformations of things. 
<margin>
Roger Bacon.
</margin>
Roger Bacon <note>Roger Bacon (c. 1214–1292) was an English philosopher and friar known for his emphasis on empiricism and legends of his mechanical inventions</note> boasts that he performed many such things through pure and natural magic.
<margin>
Ancient philosophers who wrote on magic.
</margin>
Zoroaster, Hermes, Evanthes the King of the Arabs, Zacharias the Babylonian, Joseph the Hebrew, Bocus, Aaron, Zenotenus, Kiranides, Amadal, Thetel, Al-Kindi, Abel, Ptolemy, Geber, Zahel, Nazabarub, Rebith, Berith, Solomon, Astaphon, Hipparchus, Alcmaeon, Apollonius, Triphon, and many others wrote about its works. Some of their works still exist in their entirety, and many fragments survive, which have occasionally come into my hands.
<margin>
More recent authors who wrote on magic.
</margin>
Among more recent authors, however, few have written on natural magic, and even they have written little: such as Albertus, Arnold of Villanova, Ramon Llull, Bacon, and Peter of Abano. There is also the author of the book dedicated to Alfonso, published under the name *Picatrix* <note>The *Picatrix* is a famous 11th-century Arabic grimoire of astrological magic, translated into Spanish and Latin in the 13th century</note>, who nevertheless mixes a great deal of superstition with natural magic, as indeed others have done.

## ON MATHEMATICAL MAGIC:

There are, furthermore, other most sagacious emulators of nature and most daring investigators who—without natural virtues, but using only the mathematical disciplines and calling down the influences of the heavens—promise that they can produce works similar to nature. These include bodies that walk or speak, though they do not possess animal souls.
<margin>
The dove of Archytas.
</margin>
Such was the wooden dove of Archytas <note>Archytas of Taras (4th century BC) was a Greek mathematician said to have built a steam-powered flying wooden pigeon</note>, which flew.
<margin>
The statue of Mercury, and the bronze head of Albertus Magnus.
</margin>
There were also the statues of Mercury that spoke, and the bronze head fashioned by Albertus Magnus <note>Legend claimed Albertus Magnus built a mechanical "brass head" that could answer questions, which his pupil Thomas Aquinas supposedly destroyed for being "demonic"</note>, which they say spoke. Boethius excelled in these things—a man of the greatest genius and multifaceted erudition. Cassiodorus, writing to him about such things, says:
> "It is your purpose to know difficult things and to demonstrate miracles. By the genius of your art, metals bellow; 
<margin>
A bronze snake hissing.
</margin>
Diomedes trumpets loudly in brass; a bronze snake hisses; artificial birds are created, and those which cannot have a voice of their own are proven to emit the sweetness of song. We report small things of him for whom it is permitted to imitate the heavens." I think it was said of these artificial devices what we read in Plato in the eleventh book of the *Laws*:
> "Art was given to mortals so that they might generate certain later things, not indeed sharing in truth or divinity, but so they might produce certain likenesses akin to themselves."
And thus have magicians, the most daring of men, progressed to the point of performing all things—aided greatly by that ancient and powerful 
<margin>
The promiser of sciences.
</margin>
serpent, the promiser of sciences <note>original: "serpente scientiarum, pollicitatore"—a reference to the Serpent in Eden promising the knowledge of good and evil</note>, so that they might attempt to emulate God and nature as if they were fictions.

## ON POISONOUS MAGIC.

<margin>
Pharmacy or poisoning.
Understanding the voices of birds.
</margin>
There is, moreover, a species of natural magic which they call poisonous <note>original: *venefica*</note> or pharmacy <note>The Greek word *pharmakeia* implies both healing medicine and harmful poison/sorcery</note>, which operates through potions, philtres, and various poisonous medicaments. We read that Democritus prepared such a mixture to ensure the birth of good, happy, and fortunate children, and another mixture by which we might rightly understand the voices of birds, just as Philostratus and Porphyry <note>Neoplatonist philosophers who wrote biographies of famous miracle-workers</note> relate regarding Apollonius of Tyana. Virgil also, speaking of certain herbs from Pontus, said:

> By these have I often seen a man become a wolf and hide in the woods,
> Often seen souls emerge from the depths of the tombs,
> And seen sown harvests moved from one field to another.

<margin>
Sacrifices of the Arcadians:
Sacrifice of human victims.
Men turned into beasts of burden.
</margin>
And Pliny relates that a certain Demarchus of Parrhasia, at a sacrifice which the Arcadians were making to Lycaean Jupiter with human victims, tasted the entrails of a sacrificed boy and was turned into a wolf. Because of this transformation of men into wolves, Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Hippo, who discussed these pagan "miracles" in *The City of God*</note> thinks the names "Lycaean Pan" and "Lycaean Jupiter" were established <note>The name "Lycaean" derives from *lykos*, the Greek word for wolf</note>. The same Augustine relates that while he was in Italy, certain sorceresses—much like Circe <note>The enchantress from Homer’s *Odyssey* who turned men into swine</note>—gave travelers a poisonous substance in cheese that turned them into beasts of burden; and when they had carried whatever loads were required, they were restored to men. This is said to have happened to the father of a certain man named Prestantius. But lest anyone think these are entirely the delusions of madmen and impossible, let them remember how

<margin>
Nebuchadnezzar turned into an ox.
</margin>
Holy Scripture relates that King Nebuchadnezzar was changed into an ox and lived on hay for seven years, until at last, by the mercy of God, he returned to humanity. After his death, his son Evil-Merodach gave his body to be eaten by vultures, so that he might never rise again from the dead—he who had already returned from being a beast to a man. Exodus relates many similar things regarding the magicians of Pharaoh. Truly, the author of the Book of Wisdom speaks of these people, whether they be called magicians or poisoners, when he says: "You detested them, O God, because they performed horrible works for you through their medicines." I want you to know, furthermore, that these magicians do not only investigate natural things, but also those things that accompany nature or even seem to strip it away—such as motions, numbers, shapes, sounds, voices, harmonies, lights, the passions of the mind, and words. Thus the Psylli and Marsi <note>Ancient tribes famous for their power over snakes</note> used to call forth serpents, while others, by suppressing them, put them to flight. Thus Orpheus calmed the storm of the

<margin>
Orpheus calmed the storm.
</margin>
Argonauts with a hymn; and Homer relates that the blood of Ulysses was restrained with words. In the Law of the Twelve Tables <note>The earliest code of Roman law</note>, a penalty was established for those who "enchanted away" harvests. Thus there is no doubt that magicians, through words and emotions alone and other similar means, often produce a wonderful

<margin>
The power of words.
</margin>
effect, not only upon themselves but even upon external objects. They believe that all these things pour an inherent power into other things, drawing them toward themselves or repelling them, or affecting them in any other way, just as a magnet draws iron and amber draws chaff <note>original: *paleas*</note>, or as a diamond and another magnet bind each other. Thus, through this gradual and chained sympathy of things, Iamblichus, Proclus, and Synesius <note>Later Neoplatonists who merged philosophy with "theurgy" or divine magic</note> confirm that, in the opinion of the magicians, not only natural and celestial gifts but even intellectual and divine ones can be received from above.

<meta>This page continues Henry Cornelius Agrippa’s categorization of magic. # ON GOETIA AND NECROMANCY.

As Proclus <note>Proclus (412–485 AD) was a Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote extensively on the "hieratic art" or theurgy.</note> admits in his book *On Sacrifice and Magic*, magicians were accustomed to summoning even divine powers through a certain "consensus" or harmony <note>original: *consensum*</note> of these kinds of things. Indeed, some of them have fallen into such great madness that they believe a constructed image—built from various constellations of stars at specific intervals of time and with a strictly observed ratio of proportions—will receive a spirit of life and intellect by the will of the heavens. They believe this image will then answer those who consult it and reveal the hidden secrets of the truth. From this, it is clear that natural magic sometimes leans toward *goëtia* <note>Low magic or sorcery, often associated with the conjuration of spirits.</note> and *theurgy* <note>High magic or "god-working," aimed at purifying the soul and communicating with divine beings.</note>, and is very often ensnared by the tricks and errors of evil demons.

### ON GOETIA AND NECROMANCY.

<margin>What Goetia is.</margin>
The parts of ceremonial magic, however, are *goëtia* and *theurgy*. Goetia is unfortunate because of its dealings with unclean spirits; it is composed of the rites of wicked curiosity, illicit songs, and charms. It has been banished and cursed by the decrees of all laws. To this category belong those whom we today call <margin>Necromancers.</margin> necromancers and witches <note>original: *maleficos*</note>.

> A race hated by the gods, skilled at staining the heavens,
> Whom an evil nature brought forth; who can subvert 
> The stars of the world and the laws of fixed things.
> For now they know how to make the poles stand still and turn rivers,
> They drive the ether beneath the earth and tear up mountains.

<margin>Those who rouse boys.</margin>
These are the people, therefore, who call upon the souls of the dead, and those whom the ancients called "epodoi" <note>Greek for incantators or enchanters.</note>, who enchant boys and draw them out into the speech of an oracle. There are also those who carry around "assistant spirits" <note>original: *dæmones paredros*</note>, such as we read about regarding Socrates, and those who—it is said—feed spirits in glass, through which they falsely claim to prophesy. All these proceed in two ways. For some strive to call forth and compel evil demons by the power of certain divine names used in adjuration; since every creature fears and reveres the name of Him who made it, it is no wonder if the practitioners of goëtia—and even infidels, pagans, Jews, Saracens, and men of any profane assembly or sect—bind demons by the invocation of the divine name.

<margin>Idolatry.</margin>
Others, however, are most wicked, committing a crime that should be detested and punished with every fire. By submitting themselves to demons, they sacrifice to them and worship them, becoming guilty of idolatry and the vilest degradation. Even if the former group is not subject to these specific crimes, they nonetheless expose themselves to manifest dangers. For even when compelled, demons remain watchful, always seeking to deceive us when we wander. Indeed, from this sinister gathering <note>original: *anagyri*</note> of goetic practitioners have flowed all those "books of darkness" which the jurist Ulpian <note>Domitius Ulpianus (c. 170–223 AD), a famous Roman jurist who sought to suppress magic.</note> calls "prohibited reading," decreeing that they should be destroyed. Zabulus <note>A name often used for the Devil or a legendary sorcerer.</note>, a man devoted to illicit arts, is said to have first devised such things, followed by a certain Barnabas of Cyprus. Even today, books are circulated under forged titles, bearing the names of Adam, Abel, Enoch, Abraham, Solomon, as well as Paul, Honorius, Cyprian, Albert, Thomas, Jerome, and of York ca...

### ON GOETIA AND NECROMANCY.

...of the same: whose trifles have been foolishly followed by King Alfonso of Castile <note>Alfonso X (1221–1284), known as "The Wise," who commissioned the translation of many Arabic magical and astronomical texts.</note>, Robert the Englishman <note>Robert of Chester, a 12th-century translator of Arabic mathematical and alchemical works.</note>, Bacon <note>Roger Bacon (c. 1214–1292), the Franciscan friar often falsely accused of being a magician.</note>, and Abano <note>Peter of Abano (1250–1316), a philosopher and physician whose works on magic, like the *Heptameron*, were widely circulated.</note>, and many other men of deplorable talent. Furthermore, they have made not only men, but even saints, patriarchs, and the angels of God, the authors of such execrable doctrines; they even display books handed down by the angels Raziel and Raphael to Adam and Tobit. Yet to one looking more closely, these books openly betray themselves—by the canon of their own precepts, their habitual rituals, the kind of words and characters used, their order of construction, and their tasteless phrasing—as containing nothing but mere trifles and impostures. They were forged in later times by most ruinous masters of betrayal, men ignorant of all ancient magic, who mixed and grafted certain profane observations onto the ceremonies of our religion. They used many unknown names and signs to terrify the unrefined and simple, and to strike wonder into the senseless and those who do not know good literature.

Nor, however, is it evident from this that these arts are mere fables; for unless they were real, and many wonderful and harmful things were done through them, divine and human laws would not have so strictly decreed that they must be exterminated from the earth. The reason why these goeticists <note>Practitioners of "low" or demonic magic.</note> use only evil demons is because good angels appear with difficulty, since they wait for God's command and do not associate except with men pure of heart and holy of life. Evil spirits, however, show themselves easily to invocation, falsely favoring the practitioner and lying about their own divinity; they are always at hand so that they may deceive by their cunning, and so that they may be venerated and adored. And because women are more greedy for secrets, less cautious, and prone to superstition, and are more easily deceived, the demons show themselves more readily to them and perform great wonders, of the sort poets sing about regarding Circe, Medea, and others. To this, Cicero, Pliny, Seneca, Augustine, and many others testify—both philosophers and Catholic doctors and historians—as do even the Sacred Scriptures themselves. 

For in the Books of Kings, we read that a woman with a familiar spirit <note>original: *pythonissam*</note> who was at Endor summoned the soul of the prophet Samuel, although many interpret that it was not the soul of the prophet, but a malignant spirit who took on his likeness. Yet the masters of the Hebrews say—which even Augustine in his work *To Simplician* does not deny could have happened—that it was the true spirit of Samuel, which can be easily summoned before a year has passed since its departure from the body, as the goeticists teach. Indeed, even magicians and necromancers maintain that this can be done by certain natural powers and bonds, just as we treat in our books on *Occult Philosophy*. And therefore the ancient fathers, skilled in spiritual matters, not without reason ordained that <margin>Burial of bodies.</margin> the bodies of the dead should be buried in a sacred place, and comforted with lights, sprinkled with holy water, fumigated with frankincense and incense, and expiated with prayers as long as they remained above the earth. 

For as the masters of the Hebrews say, our whole body, and the carnal animal, and whatever in us rests upon the ill-disposed matter of the flesh, is left as food for the serpent, or as they call him, <margin>To Azazel.</margin> Azazel <note>In Leviticus 16, Azazel is associated with the scapegoat in the wilderness; here, Agrippa identifies him as a demonic prince of the physical world.</note>, who is the lord of flesh and blood and the prince of this world. In Leviticus, he is called the prince of the deserts <note>original: *princeps difertoꝝ*</note>, to whom it was said in Genesis: "You shall eat the dust all the days of your life." And in Isaiah: "Dust shall be your bread," that is, the body...
