<header>ON THEURGY.</header>

<margin>The resurrection of the dead.</margin>
<margin>The devil's dispute with Michael.</margin>
...our [body], created from the dust of the earth, so long as it has not been sanctified and transformed for the better, so that it is no longer the serpent's but God’s effect—that is, from a carnal to a spiritual state, according to the word of Paul who says: "It is sown a natural body, and it shall rise a spiritual body." <note>original: "Seminatur quod animale est, & resurget quod spirituale est." From 1 Corinthians 15:44.</note> And elsewhere: "Indeed all shall rise, but not all shall be changed," <note>original: "Omnes quidem resurgent, sed non omnes immutabuntur." A reference to the Vulgate version of 1 Corinthians 15:51.</note> because many are destined to remain forever as the food of the serpent. Therefore, we lay aside this foul and horrid matter of the flesh—this food of the serpent—at death, so that it may one day be resumed having been transformed into a better and spiritual lot, which shall occur at the resurrection of the dead. And this has already happened in those who have tasted the first fruits of the resurrection; indeed, many have attained this very thing by the power of the deifying spirit in this life, such as Enoch, Elijah, and Moses, whose bodies, transformed into a spiritual nature, did not see corruption; nor, like other corpses, were they left to the power of the serpent. And this is that dispute of the devil with Michael over the body of Moses, which Jude mentions in his epistle. <note>Jude 1:9 mentions the archangel Michael contending with the devil over Moses' body.</note> But enough has been said regarding <term>Goetia</term> <note>Low magic or sorcery involving the invocation of malevolent spirits.</note> and <term>Necromancy</term>.

## ON THEURGY.

<margin>Cleanliness of soul and body.</margin>
Many people believe that <term>Theurgy</term> <note>Literally "God-working"; a form of high ritual magic intended to invoke divine or angelic presence.</note> is not at all unlawful, as if it were governed by good angels and the divine power. Yet, most often, it is bound by the deceits of evil demons under the names of God and angels. For we conciliate and attract the celestial—and through them, the divine—powers to ourselves, not only by natural forces, but also by certain rites and ceremonies. The ancient Magi discussed these matters in many published volumes. Furthermore, the greatest part of all ceremonies consists in observing cleanliness: first of the soul, then also of the body, and of those things which are around the body, such as the skin, the clothes, the dwellings, the vessels, the utensils, offerings, victims, and sacrifices. The cleanliness of these things disposes us toward the custom and contemplation of divine things and is most highly demanded in sacred acts, according to the words of Isaiah: "Wash yourselves and be clean, and take away the evil of your thoughts." <note>Isaiah 1:16.</note> Truly, because impurity frequently infects the air and the person, it disturbs that most pure influx of celestial and divine things and puts the clean spirits of God to flight. However, sometimes the unclean spirits and deceptive powers, so that they may be worshipped and adored as gods, also demand this cleanliness. Therefore, the greatest caution is needed here, as we have discussed at length in our books on <italic>Occult Philosophy</italic>. <note>Agrippa refers to his own major work, *De Occulta Philosophia libri tres*.</note> Indeed, Porphyry, <note>A 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher.</note> after disputing many things concerning this theurgy or "magic of divine things," finally concludes that while the soul of a man can indeed be rendered fit for the reception of spirits and angels and for seeing the gods by theurgic consecrations, he entirely denies that a return to God can be provided by this art. Of this school, therefore, are the <term>Art Almadel</term>, the <term>Notary Art</term>, the <term>Pauline Art</term>, the <term>Art of Revelations</term>, <note>These are titles of famous medieval grimoires or "magical arts" that claimed to provide divine knowledge or angelic conversation through complex rituals.</note> and many other such superstitions, which are all the more ruinous the more "divine" they appear to the unskillful.

<summary>Agrippa concludes his discussion on the physical transformation of the body at the resurrection before turning to a critique of Theurgy, arguing that while it claims to be holy, it is often a deceptive form of ritual magic.</summary>
<keywords>Theurgy, Resurrection, Moses, Michael the Archangel, Porphyry, Art Almadel, Notary Art, Pauline Art, spiritual body, ritual purity</keywords>

<header>ON THE KABBALAH.</header>

## ON THE KABBALAH.

<margin>What Kabbalah is.</margin>
Indeed, there occur to me here the words of Pliny, who said: "There is also another faction of magic, depending even now on the Jews Moses and Latopeia." <note>original: "est & alia inquit magices factio, a Mose etiamnū & Latopeia Iudeis pendens." See Pliny the Elder, Natural History, Book 30, Chapter 2. "Latopeia" is likely a corruption of Jochebed, the mother of Moses, or Iotape.</note> These words remind me of the Kabbalah of the Jews, which is a constant opinion among the Hebrews to have been given by God himself to Moses on Mount Sinai. Since then, it was passed down through successions of degrees without written monuments, by the living voice alone until the times of Ezra. In the same way, the Pythagorean dogmas were once passed down by Archippus and Lysis, who held schools at Thebes in Greece; in those schools, the disciples held the precepts of the teachers in their memory, using their wits and memory in place of books. Thus, certain Jews, scorning letters, placed this knowledge in memory, observation, and vocal tradition; 
<margin>Whence Kabbalah is named.</margin>
hence it is called "Kabbalah" by the Hebrews, as if it were a reception of one from another by hearing alone. It is an art (as they say) of great antiquity, but its name was not known among Christians until recent times.

They hand down two types of this science. One is called *Bereshit* <note>original: "Brefith." From the Hebrew for "In the beginning," the first word of Genesis.</note>, which they also call cosmology, namely that which explains the forces of natural and celestial created things and expounds the secrets of the Law and the Bible through philosophical reasons. In this respect, it differs in no way from natural magic, in which we believe King Solomon excelled. For one reads in the sacred histories of the Hebrews that he used to discourse from the cedar of Lebanon even unto the hyssop; likewise concerning beasts, birds, reptiles, and fish—all of which can display certain magical 
<margin>Moses the Egyptian</margin>
powers of nature. Moses the Egyptian <note>original: "Moyses ægyptius." This refers to the famous medieval Jewish philosopher Maimonides (Moses ben Maimon).</note> among the later writers was the first to follow this in his expositions on the Pentateuch, as did several Talmudists. The other science they call *Merkavah* <note>original: "Mercaua." From the Hebrew for "Chariot," referring to Ezekiel’s vision of the divine throne-chariot.</note>, which deals with the more sublime contemplations of divine and angelic virtues, and of sacred names and seals. It is a kind of symbolic theology, in which letters, numbers, figures, things, and names, and the points of elements, as well as lines, dots, and accents, are all significant of the most profound things and great secrets. This they again divide into two parts: into Arithmancy <note>original: "Arithmātiam." Here used to describe the "notary art" or Notarikon, where letters are treated as numbers or shorthand.</note>, namely that which deals with the "notary" art, treating of angelic virtues, names, seals, and even the conditions of demons and souls; and into Theomancy, which scrutinizes the mysteries of the divine majesty, emanations, sacred names, and pentacles. They say that whoever knows this is empowered with admirable virtues, so that when he wishes, he may foreknow all future things, command all of nature, have authority over demons and angels, and perform miracles. 

<margin>The wonders of Moses.</margin>
By this art, they believe Moses performed so many signs: turning his staff into a serpent and the waters into blood; sending frogs, flies, lice, locusts, grubs, fire with hail, blisters, and pestilence upon the Egyptians; slaying every firstborn from man to beast; and while leading his own people out, opening the sea, bringing forth a spring from a rock and quails from heaven; sweetening bitter waters; sending before his people lightning and clouds by day and a pillar of fire by night; calling down the voice of the living God to the people from the heavens; and destroying the arrogant with fire, and the murmurers...

<summary>Agrippa defines the Kabbalah as an ancient Jewish oral tradition and divides it into two branches: Bereshit (natural cosmology) and Merkavah (symbolic, supernatural theology), the latter of which he identifies as the source of Moses’ miracles.</summary>

<keywords>Kabbalah, Moses, Pliny the Elder, Bereshit, Merkavah, Arithmancy, Theomancy, Jewish mysticism, Maimonides, Solomon, miracles of Exodus</keywords>

--- Page 408 ---
<meta>This page continues the author's critical examination of the Kabbalah. Having defined its origins on the previous page, he now lists the miraculous powers attributed to it before offering a sharp critique of its validity compared to Christian faith.</meta>

[Moses] struck the rebellious with leprosy; he afflicted those who deserved it with sudden slaughter; others were swallowed by the opening of the earth; he fed the people with celestial food; he appeased serpents and cured the venomous; he kept a numerous crowd from infirmity, preserved their garments from wearing away, and made them victorious over their enemies. Finally, they claim that by this art of miracles Joshua commanded the sun to stand still, Elijah called down fire from heaven upon his adversaries and restored a dead boy to life, Daniel closed the mouths of lions, and the three boys sang songs in the furnace of the burning blaze. Furthermore, the perfidious Jews maintain that even Christ often performed such admirable things by this same art. They claim Solomon also was thoroughly skilled in it, and from it he handed down the art against demons, their bonds, and the methods of conjurations, as well as incantations against diseases, as Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus, a 1st-century Romano-Jewish historian who wrote extensively about Jewish history and traditions.</note> is witness.

But while I do not doubt that God revealed many mysteries to Moses and the other prophets—mysteries contained beneath the "rind" <note>original: "sub cortice." A common Renaissance metaphor for the outer, literal meaning of scripture hiding a deeper spiritual truth.</note> of the words of the Law and not to be shared with the profane common people—nevertheless, this art of Kabbalah which the Hebrews boast of, and which I have investigated with much labor at some point, I recognize as nothing but a mere rhapsody of superstition and a certain theurgical magic <note>original: "theurgicā quādā magiam." Theurgy is a form of high magic intended to invoke the presence of divine spirits or gods.</note>. For if (as the Jews boast) it proceeded from God for the perfection of life, the salvation of men, the worship of God, and the truth of understanding, surely that Spirit of Truth—who came to teach us all truth after the Synagogue was rejected—would not have hidden it from his Church until these final times. Indeed, the Church knows all things that are of God, whose blessing, baptism, and other sacraments of salvation have been revealed and perfected in every language. For the power of every language is equal and the same, provided that piety is equal and the same; nor is there any other name in heaven or on earth in which we must be saved, and in which we may work virtue, except the one name 
<margin>The power of the Name of Jesus.</margin>
of Jesus, in which all things are recapitulated and contained. Hence the Jews, though most skilled in the divine names, can do little or nothing after Christ, just like their ancient fathers. 

However, as for what we experience and see regarding the "revolutions" <note>Refers to *Temurah* or *Gematria*, the Kabbalistic practice of rearranging or calculating the numerical value of letters to find hidden meanings.</note> of this art (as they call it)—whereby wondrous sentences of great mysteries are often extorted from the sacred letters—all of this is nothing other than a certain game of allegories. Idle men, occupied with individual letters, points, and numbers—which this language and style of writing easily permit—invent and reinvent these things according to their own whim. Even if these things sometimes sound like great mysteries, they can prove or demonstrate nothing, since, according to the words of Gregory, they may be dismissed with the same ease with which they are asserted. 

The monk Rabanus <note>Rabanus Maurus (c. 780–856), a Benedictine abbot famous for his "In honorem sanctae crucis," a collection of complex shaped poems and acrostics.</note> constructed many things with a similar artifice, but using Latin characters and verses, inserting various images, so that whatever verses are read through any line of the surface or the images, they announce some sacred mystery representing the histories depicted there.
<margin>The *Centos* of Valeria Proba.</margin>
No one is ignorant that such things can even be extorted from profane literature, as anyone knows who has read the *Centos* of Valeria Proba <note>A 4th-century poet who repurposed lines from Virgil’s pagan epics to tell the story of the Old and New Testaments. A "cento" is a poem made entirely of patches from other works.</note> composed from the poems of Virgil concerning Christ. All such things are merely the speculations of idle men. As for what pertains to the operation of miracles, I think none of you is so stiff-necked as to believe any man has [the power...]

<summary>The author lists the biblical miracles the Jews attribute to the Kabbalah but dismisses the practice as a superstitious "game of allegories" that can be replicated in any language, arguing that the only true source of power is the name of Jesus.</summary>
<keywords>Kabbalah, Moses, Solomon, miracles, name of Jesus, Rabanus Maurus, Valeria Proba, allegory, theurgy, superstition</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the author’s critique of the Kabbalah, moving from its alleged origins to a sharp condemnation of its methods. It transitions from discussing Kabbalah as a form of "theurgic magic" to its role in fueling early Christian heresies, eventually returning to the broader topic of "prestiges" or illusions.</meta>

...art or science. Therefore, this Jewish Kabbalah is nothing other than 
<margin>The Jewish Kabbalah: a most pernicious superstition.</margin>
a most pernicious superstition, by which they collect, divide, and transfer words, names, and letters scattered throughout the scriptures according to their own whim. By making one thing out of another, they dismember the truth, constructing speeches, inductions, and parables here and there from their own fictions. They wish to adapt the eloquence of God to these fictions—defaming the scriptures and claiming their own figments consist of them. They slander the law of God, and through impudently extorted calculations of words, syllables, letters, and numbers, they attempt to introduce violent and blasphemous proofs for their own perfidy. Furthermore, puffed up by these trifles, they boast that they find and know the ineffable mysteries of God and secrets that are above scripture; through these, they do not blush to lie with great audacity, claiming they can prophesy and perform virtues and miracles. But it happens to them as it did to Aesop’s dog, <note>original: "cani Aesopico." Referring to the famous fable where a dog drops a real piece of meat to snap at its larger-looking reflection in the water.</note> who, leaving the bread behind and gaping at its shadow, lost its food. So this perfidious and stiff-necked race of men, always occupied in the shadows of scripture and making an assault upon those vanities with their artificial but superstitious Kabbalah, loses the bread of eternal life and, feeding on empty names, loses the word of truth. From this Jewish ferment of Kabbalistic superstition, I believe, arose the Ophites, Gnostics, and Valentinian heretics, <note>Early Christian sects from the 2nd century often characterized by "Gnosis" (secret knowledge) and complex systems of divine emanations.</note> who themselves, along with their disciples, devised a certain Greek Kabbalah. They perverted all the mysteries of the Christian faith and, with heretical depravity, dragged them toward Greek letters and numbers. From these, they constructed a "body" which they call "of truth," teaching that without these mysteries of letters and numbers, the truth cannot be found in the Gospel writings. They argued this because the scriptures are diverse and sometimes repugnant to themselves, and are written full of parables so that "seeing they might not see, hearing they might not hear, and understanding they might not understand," <note>A reference to Mark 4:12 or Isaiah 6:9-10.</note> but were instead set forth for the blind and wandering according to the capacity of their blindness and error. They believed the sincere truth lying hidden beneath those parables was entrusted only to the "perfect," not through writings, but through the successive pronunciation of a living voice <note>original: "viuæ vocis." This refers to an oral tradition passed down directly from teacher to student.</note>. This, they claimed, is that alphabetical and arithmetical theology which **CHRIST** manifested in secret to the Apostles, and which Paul says he speaks "only among the perfect." <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 2:6.</note> Since these are the highest mysteries, they were neither written down nor should be written, but were to be preserved in silence among the wise, guarding them with themselves in secret. However, among them, no one is "wise" unless he knows how to manufacture the greatest monsters of heresy.

### ON DELUSIONS.

But let us return to magic, a small part of which is also the artifice of "prestiges"—that is, of illusions—which occur according to appearance only. By these, magi produce phantasms, and they play at many miracles through the frauds of traveling entertainers <note>original: "circulatoriis fraudibus." Likely referring to street performers, jugglers, or "circulators" who used sleight of hand.</note> and send dreams, which [does not...]

as much by goetic <note>original: "goëticis." Referring to black magic or the invocation of low-ranking spirits, as opposed to "theurgy" or high divine magic.</note> incantations and imprecations, and the deceptions of demons, as also by certain fumes of vapors, lights, love potions, eye-salves, binding-amulets, and charms worn around the neck; furthermore by rings, images, mirrors, and similar pharmaceuticals and instruments of the magic art, it is perpetrated by natural and celestial power. Many things are also done by a ready subtlety and industry of the hands, the sort of which we see done daily by actors and jugglers, whom we therefore call **chirosophos, that is**, skilled with the hands. <margin>Books of illusions.</margin> There exist books on this craft of illusions by Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure to whom many hermetic and alchemical texts were attributed.</note> and certain others: we also read that a certain Pasetes, a most well-stocked illusionist, was accustomed to show his guests a most abundant feast, and then, whenever he pleased, it vanished again, leaving all the guests mocked by hunger and thirst. We read that Numa Pompilius <note>The legendary second king of Rome, known for establishing religious rites.</note> also used illusions of this kind. But even the most learned Pythagoras <note>The famous Greek philosopher and mathematician.</note> sometimes practiced that ridiculous trick: whatever he wished, he would write in blood on a mirror, and when this was turned toward the full orb of the moon's light, he would show the person standing behind him the things carved on the disk of the moon. This also pertains to whatever is sung of the transformations of men by poets, believed by historians, and asserted by some Christian theologians, and moreover by the sacred scriptures. Thus men appear as donkeys or horses, or other animals, with their eyes fascinated <note>In this context, "fascinated" means "bewitched" or "under a spell" rather than "interested."</note> or the medium disturbed, and this by natural art. Sometimes these things are also done by good and evil spirits, or at the prayers of the good by God himself, as we read in the sacred scriptures about the prophet Elisha, besieged by the army of the King of Syria at Dothan; but these things cannot deceive eyes that are pure and opened by God: thus that woman, who was judged by the common people to be a beast of burden, appeared to Hilarion <note>Saint Hilarion (291–371 AD), an early Christian anchorite who lived in the Egyptian desert.</note> not as a beast but as she was, a woman. Therefore, those things which happen in this way according to appearance are called illusions; but those which happen by the art of those changing or transferring things, as with Nebuchadnezzar, or harvests moved to other fields, we spoke of these above. Indeed, regarding this art of illusions, Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote extensively on theurgy and the occult.</note> says thus: "What the deluded or fascinated imagine has no truth of action or essence beyond the imagination." For the end of such a craft is not to simply create, but to extend images to the point of appearance, of which soon no trace remains. Now, therefore, from what has been said, it is clear that magic is nothing other than a complex of idolatry, astrology, and superstitious medicine. And now also from the magi, a great crowd of heretics has arisen in the church, who, just as Jannes and Jambres <note>Names given by tradition to the Egyptian sorcerers who opposed Moses in the Book of Exodus.</note> resisted Moses, so they resisted apostolic truth. Their leader was <margin>Simon the Samaritan.</margin> Simon the Samaritan <note>Commonly known as Simon Magus.</note>, who was granted a statue at Rome under Claudius Caesar on account of this art, with this inscription: *To Simon, the holy god.* <note>original: "Simoni sancto deo." Historical scholars note that Simon Magus likely claimed divinity, though some suggest he was confused with the Sabine deity Semo Sancus.</note> Clement, Eusebius, and Irenaeus narrate his blasphemies copiously. From this Simon, as if from a nursery of all heresies, through many successions came the monstrous Ophites, the filthy Gnostics, the impious Valentinians, Cerdonians, Marcionists, Montanists, and many other heretics...
